scenes.title: Born in the purification
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Purification'
scenes.text: The deity who rules Takamagahara, who came into being when Izanagi-no-Mikoto washed his left eye.

scenes.title: The Heavenly Rock Cave
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Heavenly Rock Cave'
scenes.text: Angered by the violence of her younger brother Susanoo-no-Mikoto, she hid in the rock cave and the world went dark. Through the rites of the deities she showed herself again.

amaterasu.note_full: The enshrined deity of Ise Jingū (Inner Shrine).

toyouke.name: Toyouke-no-Ōmikami
toyouke.note: Deity of food, enshrined at the Outer Shrine
toyouke.kojiki_where: Part 1, the sections known as 'Birth of the Gods' and 'Descent of the Heavenly Grandson'
toyouke.nihonshoki_name: (Not found in the books obtained; to be confirmed)

scenes.title: The deity enshrined at the Outer Shrine
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Descent of the Heavenly Grandson'
scenes.text: In the section on the Descent of the Heavenly Grandson, she is named, after the deities who enshrine the mirror, as 'the deity who dwells at Watarai of the Outer Shrine'. She is a deity born as the child of the deity who governs food.

toyouke.note_full: The origins of the Outer Shrine rest largely on traditions of the Jingū outside the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (to be confirmed). In the Nihon Shoki, she was not found in the books checked (Books 1–3); the check of all books is not yet complete.

ookuninushi.name: Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami
ookuninushi.note: Central figure of the Kojiki's 'building the land' tale
ookuninushi.kojiki_where: Part 1, the sections known as 'Genealogy of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami', 'White Hare of Inaba', 'Ne-no-Katasu-kuni', 'Building the Land' and 'Transfer of the Land'

scenes.title: Building the Land and the Transfer of the Land
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the sections known as 'Building the Land' and 'Transfer of the Land'
scenes.text: Overcoming the persecution of his elder brothers and the trials of Susanoo-no-Mikoto, he became lord of the land and carried forward the building of the land with Sukunabikona-no-Kami. Later, in response to the demand of the envoys from Takamagahara, and after the responses of his children Kotoshironushi-no-Kami and Takeminakata-no-Kami, he transferred the land and withdrew, asking to dwell in a grand shrine like the palace of the child of the heavenly deities. The building of this shrine is regarded as the origin tale of Izumo Taisha.

ookuninushi.note_full: The Kojiki gives his father as Ame-no-Fuyukinu-no-Kami and his mother as Sashikuni-wakahime, and records him as a sixth-generation descendant of Susanoo-no-Mikoto (only the parents are shown in the chart). The Nihon Shoki sets different accounts side by side: in the main text he is the child of Susanoo-no-Mikoto and Kushi-inada-hime, and in a variant account a sixth-generation descendant.

munakata3.name: The Three Munakata Goddesses
aliases: Tagori-hime, Tagitsu-hime and Ichikishima-hime (spellings of the Nihon Shoki main text)
munakata3.kojiki_name: Takiri-bime-no-Mikoto (also called Okitsushima-hime-no-Mikoto), Ichikishima-hime-no-Mikoto (also called Sayori-bime-no-Mikoto), Takitsu-hime-no-Mikoto (Tagitsu-hime-no-Mikoto in another passage)
munakata3.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'The Pledge (Ukei) at Ame-no-Yasu-no-Kawa'
munakata3.nihonshoki_name: Tagori-hime, Tagitsu-hime and Ichikishima-hime (main text); Okitsushima-hime (also called Ichikishima-hime), Tagitsu-hime and Tagiri-hime (variant account)
munakata3.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 6 (the pledge)

scenes.title: Three goddesses born from the pledge
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'The Pledge (Ukei) at Ame-no-Yasu-no-Kawa'
scenes.text: Amaterasu-Ōmikami broke Susanoo-no-Mikoto's ten-span sword into three pieces, rinsed them in Ame-no-Manai, chewed them to bits and blew them out; from the mist, three goddesses were born.

scenes.title: The three great deities (Mimae-no-Ōkami) enshrined at Munakata
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'The Pledge (Ukei) at Ame-no-Yasu-no-Kawa'
scenes.text: The three deities dwell at Okitsu-miya, Nakatsu-miya and Hetsu-miya, and are regarded as the three great deities worshipped by the Munakata no Kimi and others. The Kojiki writes Takiri-bime-no-Mikoto at Okitsu-miya, Ichikishima-hime-no-Mikoto at Nakatsu-miya and Tagitsu-hime-no-Mikoto at Hetsu-miya.

scenes.title: The three goddesses are children of Susanoo-no-Mikoto
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 6 (the pledge), main text
scenes.text: Amaterasu-Ōmikami produced the three goddesses from Susanoo-no-Mikoto's sword and gave them to him, saying 'Since this sword is Susanoo's, the three goddesses are your children.' It records that they are the deities worshipped by the Tsukushi no Munakata no Kimi and others.

scenes.title: Descend to Usa Island (variant account)
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 6, variant account (the third)
scenes.text: A variant account says that the three goddesses, who were born of the sun deity, descended to Usa Island in the Central Land of Reed Plains and now dwell in the midst of the sea road to the north, where they are called 'Michinushi-no-muchi'. An account that offers a clue for thinking about the connection with Hime-ōkami of Usa Jingū.

scenes.title: Takiri-bime, who becomes the wife of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'The Genealogy of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami'
scenes.text: Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami took Takiri-bime-no-Mikoto, the deity of Okitsu-miya at Munakata, as his wife and had a child with her. An account of the marriage of one of the three deities.

scenes.title: Offering a craftswoman to Munakata-no-Ōkami in the reign of Emperor Ōjin
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 10, the 41st year of Emperor Ōjin
scenes.text: It records that Achi no Omi and others, who had reached Tsukushi from Wu, offered Ehime to Munakata-no-Ōkami because the deity wished for craftswomen. An example of the Munakata deity appearing in an account of Emperor Ōjin's time.

virtues: Protection at sea, protection of the state and the safety of the imperial family (the official site of Itsukushima Jinja records that they have been worshipped as deities of these)
munakata3.note_full: In both the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki the names of the three goddesses are not fixed, and in the Nihon Shoki the names and their order differ between the main text and the variant accounts. The Kojiki gives Okitsu-miya = Takiri, Nakatsu-miya = Ichikishima, and Hetsu-miya = Tagitsu (Takitsu). The present Munakata Taisha gives Okitsu-miya = Tagori-hime, Nakatsu-miya = Tagitsu-hime, and Hetsu-miya = Ichikishima-hime, so the assignments of Nakatsu and Hetsu look reversed from the Kojiki. As for their parentage, the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki main text treat them as children of Susanoo-no-Mikoto (the owner of the sword), but the official site of Munakata Taisha explains them as 'the three goddesses of Amaterasu-Ōmikami', and a variant account of the Nihon Shoki also has a passage saying that they were born of the sun deity. According to the official sites, the Hime-ōkami of Usa Jingū and the deities of Itsukushima Jinja have the same names as these three goddesses.

ketsumiko.name: Ketsumiko-no-Ōkami
ketsumiko.note: Chief deity of Kumano Hongū Taisha
ketsumiko.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
ketsumiko.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
ketsumiko.note_full: Chief deity of Kumano Hongū Taisha. The official site identifies this deity with Susanoo-no-Mikoto (the official site's own statement). The name 'Ketsumiko' does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki, and the identification is not an account of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. The official site also records that the deity was called Funadama Daimyōjin as the one who handed down the art of shipbuilding.

susanoo.name: Susanoo-no-Mikoto
susanoo.kojiki_where: Part 1, the sections known as 'Purification', 'Heavenly Rock Cave' and 'Yamata-no-Orochi'
susanoo.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part)

scenes.title: One of the Three Noble Children
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Purification'
scenes.text: A deity who came into being in the purification of Izanagi-no-Mikoto, after Amaterasu-Ōmikami and Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto. He is regarded as an ancestor of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami (Ōkuninushi is recorded as a sixth-generation descendant of Susanoo-no-Mikoto).

susanoo.note_full: A 'linking' deity. The generations between him and Ōkuninushi-no-Kami are omitted in the chart.

hayatamano.name: Hayatama-no-O-no-Kami
hayatamano.note: Deity of the Second Hall, Kumano Hongū Taisha
hayatamano.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
hayatamano.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 5 (a variant account; the scene in the Land of Yomi; the number of the variant account is to be confirmed)

scenes.title: Comes into being from the spittle of Izanagi-no-Mikoto
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 5 (variant account)
scenes.text: When Izanagi-no-Mikoto took leave of his wife in the Land of Yomi, Hayatama-no-O came into being from his spittle, and Yomotsu-kotosaka-no-O from the act of sweeping away.

hayatamano.note_full: Deity enshrined in the Second Hall of Kumano Hongū Taisha (official). The official site's view on whether Hayatama-no-O of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki and the Hayatama-no-O-no-Kami of the official site are the same deity is not confirmed (to be confirmed).

izanami.name: Izanami-no-Mikoto
izanami.kojiki_where: Part 1, the sections known as 'Birth of the Gods' and 'Land of Yomi'
izanami.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), sections 4–5

scenes.title: The Birth of the Gods and the fire deity
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Birth of the Gods'
scenes.text: Izanami-no-Mikoto, who had given birth to many deities, suffered after giving birth to the fire deity. At that time, deities connected with food and water came into being from her urine and other matter.

takemikazuchi.name: Takemikazuchi-no-Ōkami
takemikazuchi.kojiki_where: Part 1, the sections known as 'Birth of the Gods' and 'Transfer of the Land'
takemikazuchi.nihonshoki_where: Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9 (Transfer of the Land)

scenes.title: Born from the blood on the sword
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Birth of the Gods'
scenes.text: One of the deities who came into being from the blood on the tip of the sword with which Izanagi-no-Mikoto cut down the fire deity.

scenes.title: Transfer of the Land
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Transfer of the Land'
scenes.text: Sent to Izumo with Ame-no-Torifune-no-Kami as his companion, he set a sword upside down on the beach, sat on its tip and pressed Ōkuninushi-no-Kami to hand over the land. It is told that Kotoshironushi-no-Kami agreed, Takeminakata-no-Kami was defeated in a trial of strength, and Ōkuninushi-no-Kami offered up the land and asked to dwell in a grand palace.

takemikazuchi.note_full: In the section on the Transfer of the Land, the Kojiki also records him as a child of Ame-no-Ohabari-no-Kami (Itsu-no-Ohabari-no-Kami). The Nihon Shoki records the lineage 'Mikahayahi-no-Kami → Hi-no-Hayahi-no-Kami → Takemikazuchi-no-Kami' (whether in the main text or a variant account is to be confirmed). The Kogo Shūi records him as 'the child of Mikahayahi-no-Kami; the present deity of Kashima in Hitachi Province'.

ajisuki.name: Ajisukitakahikone-no-Mikoto
ajisuki.kojiki_name: Ajisukitakahikone-no-Kami (also written two other ways, both read Ajishikitakahikone-no-Kami)
ajisuki.kojiki_where: Part 1, the sections known as 'The Genealogy of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami' and 'Ame-no-Wakahiko'
ajisuki.nihonshoki_name: Ajisukitakahikone-no-Kami (the edited main text in this file spells it 'Ajisukitakane-no-Kami'; to be confirmed)
ajisuki.nihonshoki_where: Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9, the funeral of Ame-no-Wakahiko

scenes.title: Child of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami and Takiri-bime
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'The Genealogy of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami'
scenes.text: The Kojiki notes that he was born to Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami and Takiri-bime-no-Mikoto, the deity of Okitsu-miya at Munakata, and that he is the later Kamo-no-Ōmikami.

scenes.title: Cuts down the mourning house at a friend's funeral
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Ame-no-Wakahiko'
scenes.text: Coming to mourn the dead Ame-no-Wakahiko, he was mistaken by the bereaved family for the man brought back to life because they looked alike; angered at being lumped in with a polluted corpse, he cut down the mourning house with his sword.

scenes.title: The same scene in the Nihon Shoki
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9
scenes.text: The Nihon Shoki also records that Ajisukitakahikone, who was close to Ame-no-Wakahiko, ascended to heaven to mourn him, was mistaken for him because they looked alike, and in anger cut the mourning house down with his sword.

ajisuki.note_full: The official site of Nikkō Futarasan Jinja says he is a child of Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto and Tagori-hime-no-Mikoto, but that his mother is written as Tagori-hime could not be confirmed in the Nihon Shoki texts obtained this time (Books 1 and 2). In the Kojiki his mother is Takiri-bime (one of the Three Munakata Goddesses, said to correspond to the Tagori-hime of the Nihon Shoki). For the mother in relations, the existing munakata3 was entered. The addition of children on the Ōkuninushi side is listed under uncertain.

amenokoyane.name: Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto
amenokoyane.kojiki_where: Part 1, the sections known as 'Heavenly Rock Cave' and 'Descent of the Heavenly Grandson'
amenokoyane.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 7 (Heavenly Rock Cave) / Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9 (Descent of the Heavenly Grandson)

scenes.title: Prays at the Heavenly Rock Cave
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Heavenly Rock Cave'
scenes.text: When Amaterasu-Ōmikami shut herself in the Heavenly Rock Cave, he took, together with Futodama-no-Mikoto, the role concerned with divination and norito prayers.

scenes.title: Holds out the mirror
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Heavenly Rock Cave'
scenes.text: He appears in the scene where, together with Futodama-no-Mikoto, he held out the mirror and showed it to Amaterasu-Ōmikami.

scenes.title: Descends in attendance on the Heavenly Grandson
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Descent of the Heavenly Grandson'
scenes.text: He accompanied the descent of Ninigi-no-Mikoto as one of the five attendant chiefs (itsutomonoo).

scenes.title: Descends bearing the himorogi
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9 (variant account)
scenes.text: He is commanded to descend to Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni bearing the heavenly himorogi (sacred enclosure).

amenokoyane.note_full: The Kojiki notes him as the ancestor of the Nakatomi no Muraji and others. The official spelling at Kasuga Taisha is 天児屋根命 (Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto). The Nihon Shoki spelling is 天兒屋命, and the account of the Rock Cave scene in the Nihon Shoki differs between variant accounts.

futsunushi.name: Futsunushi-no-Ōkami
futsunushi.note: Child of Iwatsutsume-no-Kami in the Nihon Shoki
futsunushi.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
futsunushi.nihonshoki_where: Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9 (Transfer of the Land), main text and variant accounts

scenes.title: Envoy of the Transfer of the Land (Nihon Shoki)
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 9
scenes.text: Sent to Izumo as an envoy alongside Takemikazuchi-no-Kami, he subdued the deities who would not submit. One variant account records that Funato-no-Kami (a deity said to correspond to Kunado-no-Kami) guided the way. His character as a deity of warriors and swords is strong.

futsunushi.note_full: The Nihon Shoki (a variant account of section 5) and the Kogo Shūi make him the child of Iwatsutsume-no-Kami. In the Kojiki, Takemikazuchi-no-Kami is told of as the envoy for the Transfer of the Land, and this deity is not found. The official site of Katori Jingū gives 'Iwainushi-no-Mikoto' as an alternative name, but this has not been confirmed in the main texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.

himegami.name: Himegami (the Princess Deity)
himegami.note: Deity of the Fourth Hall at Kasuga Taisha
himegami.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki as a specific deity; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
himegami.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki as a specific deity; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
himegami.note_full: Deity enshrined in the Fourth Hall of Kasuga Taisha. The official site gives the deity's name only as 'Himegami', and it is not confirmed on the official site which deity this corresponds to. No identification with any particular deity of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki is made here.

jingu.name: Empress Jingū
aliases: Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto (spelling used at Sumiyoshi Taisha; to be confirmed)
jingu.nihonshoki_name: (Book 9, the Empress Jingū chronicle. Not confirmed, because the original text was not obtained this time)

scenes.title: Possessed by a deity, she learns the names of three great deities
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, Emperor Chūai
scenes.text: A deity possesses the empress Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto, and it becomes clear that the deity giving the oracle is the three great deities Sokotsutsu-no-O, Nakatsutsu-no-O and Uwatsutsu-no-O.

scenes.title: Making the aramitama of the Suminoe deity a deity that guards the land
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, Emperor Chūai
scenes.text: A staff was set up at the gate of the ruler of Silla, and the aramitama (rough spirit) of Suminoe-no-Ōkami was enshrined and pacified as a deity protecting the country.

scenes.title: The empress is possessed and receives an oracle
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section known as 'Emperor Chūai'
scenes.text: When Emperor Chūai was about to attack the Kumaso at the Kashihi Palace in Tsukushi, a deity possessed the empress Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto and announced the divine will to bestow a land in the west.

scenes.title: Enters the sacred hall and becomes the officiant herself
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 9, Empress Jingū, the account before the regency
scenes.text: After the death of her husband, the empress chose an auspicious day, entered the sacred hall (saigū) and became the kannushi (officiant) herself. She had Takeuchi-no-Sukune play the koto and asked the name of the deity.

scenes.title: Records her lineage
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 9, Empress Jingū
scenes.text: It records that she was a daughter of Prince Okinaga-no-Sukune and a great-granddaughter of Emperor Wakayamatoneko-hiko-ōhihi.

jingu.note_full: Consort of Emperor Chūai. At Sumiyoshi Taisha she is enshrined in the Fourth Main Shrine (confirmed on a sightseeing site; the relevant official page is to be confirmed). / In the Kojiki, the deeds of Empress Jingū are not in a separate Part but are included in the section on Emperor Chūai. In the Nihon Shoki, Book 9 is the book of Empress Jingū. Usa Jingū enshrines Empress Jingū in the Third Hall.

meijitenno.name: Emperor Meiji
meijitenno.note: The 122nd emperor, enshrined at Meiji Jingū
meijitenno.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki. A modern emperor, outside its period)
meijitenno.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki. A modern emperor, outside its period)

scenes.title: How the shrine was founded (the official explanation of Meiji Jingū)
scenes.where: Meiji Jingū, official page 'About Meiji Jingū'
scenes.text: Emperor Meiji, the 122nd emperor, passed away in 1912 (Meiji 45). By the wish of the people, he is enshrined together with his consort, Empress Dowager Shōken, at Meiji Jingū, founded in 1920 (Taishō 9) in Yoyogi, a place closely connected with them. He is a deity who is a modern historical figure, not a figure of the myths of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.

meijitenno.note_full: An enshrined deity who is a modern figure and does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki. The relations follow the official description (Emperor Meiji and his consort, Empress Dowager Shōken).

ojin.name: Emperor Ōjin
ojin.note: Known as Hachiman Ōkami at Usa Jingū
aliases: Hachiman Ōkami (a divine title that the official site of Usa Jingū gives as the divine spirit of Emperor Ōjin)
ojin.kojiki_where: Part 2, the section known as 'Emperor Chūai' (the birth of the child) and the section known as 'Emperor Ōjin'

scenes.title: Born as the child of Emperor Chūai and the empress
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section known as 'Emperor Chūai'
scenes.text: A child born between Emperor Chūai and the empress (Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto). It records that because he had flesh like a tomo (an archery tool) on his arm when he was born, he was named Ōtomowake.

scenes.title: Rules the realm from the Akira Palace at Karushima
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section known as 'Emperor Ōjin'
scenes.text: The opening of the Emperor Ōjin section: Homudawake-no-Mikoto dwelt at the Akira Palace at Karushima and ruled the realm.

scenes.title: His mother is Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 10, Emperor Ōjin
scenes.text: The fourth child of Emperor Tarashinakahiko (Emperor Chūai); his mother was Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto. It records that he was born in Tsukushi in the winter of the year his mother attacked Silla.

ojin.note_full: The official site of Usa Jingū says that Hachiman Ōkami is the divine spirit of Emperor Ōjin. A search of the obtained texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (Kojiki Part 2, Nihon Shoki Books 9 and 10) for 'Hachiman' found no match, and no description of him as the deity Hachiman is found in the main texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (the range checked is only the texts obtained).

sarutahiko.name: Sarutahiko-no-Kami
sarutahiko.note: Guide at the descent; deity of travel safety
aliases: Sata-hiko-no-Ōkami (name used at Fushimi Inari Taisha)
sarutahiko.kojiki_name: Sarutabiko-no-Kami (the original text uses variant characters and also 'Sarutabiko-no-Ōkami')
sarutahiko.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'The Descent of the Heavenly Grandchild'
sarutahiko.nihonshoki_where: Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9, variant account (guiding the descent of the heavenly grandchild)

scenes.title: Appears as the guide for the descent of the heavenly grandchild
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'The Descent of the Heavenly Grandchild'
scenes.text: When Ame-no-Uzume-no-Kami asks the deity at the eight-way crossroads of heaven (Ame-no-yachimata) for his name, he answers that he is Sarutabiko-no-Kami, an earthly deity (kunitsu-kami), and says he has come to meet the child of the heavenly deities, having heard of their descent.

scenes.title: Escorted by Ame-no-Uzume, who takes on his name
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'The Descent of the Heavenly Grandchild'
scenes.text: Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto is assigned to escort Sarutabiko-no-Ōkami home, and because she serves bearing that deity's name, she came to be called Sarume no Kimi.

scenes.title: Naming himself in a variant account of the Nihon Shoki
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9, variant account
scenes.text: The deity at the Ame-no-yachimata crossroads, asked by Ame-no-Uzume, himself says he is 'Saruta-no-Ōkami' and answers that he will go to the upper reaches of the Isuzu River in Ise.

sarutahiko.note_full: The official site of Fushimi Inari Taisha gives Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami as another name of Sata-hiko-no-Ōkami of the Middle Shrine and introduces him as a deity of traffic safety and safety on the road (see the shrine's deity_note). That 'Satahiko' and the Sarutabiko of the Kojiki are the same deity follows the official site's description.

shokenkotaigo.name: Empress Dowager Shōken
shokenkotaigo.note: Consort of Emperor Meiji, enshrined at Meiji Jingū
shokenkotaigo.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki. A modern empress, outside its period)
shokenkotaigo.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki. A modern empress, outside its period)

scenes.title: How the shrine was founded (the official explanation of Meiji Jingū)
scenes.where: Meiji Jingū, official page 'About Meiji Jingū'
scenes.text: Empress Dowager Shōken, the consort of Emperor Meiji, passed away in 1914 (Taishō 3). By the wish of the people, she is enshrined together with Emperor Meiji at Meiji Jingū, founded in 1920 (Taishō 9) in Yoyogi, a place closely connected with them. She is a deity who is a modern historical figure, not a figure of the myths of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.

shokenkotaigo.note_full: An enshrined deity who is a modern figure and does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki.

ukanomitama.name: Ukanomitama-no-Kami
ukanomitama.note: Also called Ukemochi-no-Kami at Fushimi Inari
aliases: Ukanomitama-no-Ōkami (name used at Fushimi Inari Taisha)
Ukanomitama-no-Kami (spelling at Nagayama Inari-sha, Kashihara Jingū)
ukanomitama.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'The Genealogy of Susanoo-no-Mikoto' (the passage on the genealogy of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami after the Yamata no Orochi)
ukanomitama.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 5, variant account (the passage in which Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto give birth to lands and deities)

scenes.title: Named as a child of Susanoo-no-Mikoto
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'The Genealogy of Susanoo-no-Mikoto'
scenes.text: In the genealogy, the name appears just once: Susanoo-no-Mikoto took Kamuōichi-hime, daughter of Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami, as his wife, and Ōtoshi-no-Kami and his younger brother Ukanomitama (two deities) were born.

scenes.title: Appears as Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 5, variant account
scenes.text: A variant account of the Nihon Shoki records that after Izanagi-no-Mikoto gave birth to the wind deity, he gave birth to Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto 'when hungry'. A note in the original text gives the reading as 'Ukanomitama'.

ukanomitama.note_full: In the Kojiki he is a child of Susanoo-no-Mikoto; in a variant account of the Nihon Shoki he is a deity born of Izanagi-no-Mikoto; the descriptions of his parentage differ. Regarding the Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto of the Nihon Shoki and the Ukanomitama of the Kojiki as the same deity is the generally accepted understanding, but the texts of this survey do not state that they are 'the same' (to be confirmed). Here no deity ID has been made for his mother, Kamuōichi-hime (relations has only the father of the Kojiki). The official site of Fushimi Inari Taisha introduces Ukanomitama-no-Ōkami as also called Ukemochi-no-Kami and as having the virtue of prosperity (see the shrine's deity_note).

kamotakeru.name: Kamotaketsunumi-no-Mikoto
kamotakeru.note: Ancestral deity of the Kamo clan
aliases: Kamotaketsunumi-no-Mikoto (spelling in the Shinsen Shōjiroku; checked in a reference dictionary, to be confirmed)
kamotakeru.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
kamotakeru.kojiki_where: The 'Yatagarasu' appears in Kojiki Part 2 (the eastern expedition of Emperor Jinmu), but it is not written that it is Kamotaketsunumi-no-Mikoto
kamotakeru.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
kamotakeru.nihonshoki_where: The 'Yatagarasu' appears in Book 3, the account before the accession of Emperor Jinmu, but it is not written that it is Kamotaketsunumi-no-Mikoto

scenes.title: The Yatagarasu guides Emperor Jinmu (Kojiki)
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section known as 'The Eastern Expedition of Emperor Jinmu (from Kumano to Uda)'
scenes.text: When Emperor Jinmu was unable to advance at Kumano, Takagi-no-Ōkami told him that he would send a Yatagarasu from heaven and taught him to follow behind it. That this Yatagarasu is Kamotaketsunumi-no-Mikoto is not the account of the Kojiki but a theory from later materials.

scenes.title: Guidance of the Yatagarasu (Nihon Shoki)
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 3, the account before the accession of Emperor Jinmu, the section known as 'From Kumano to Uda'
scenes.text: In a dream, Amaterasu-Ōmikami said she would send a Yatagarasu to guide the way, and following where the crow flew he arrived at Uda. The Nihon Shoki does not give the name Kamotaketsunumi-no-Mikoto.

scenes.title: The Yatagarasu as distant ancestor of the Kamo Agatanushi (Kogo Shūi)
scenes.where: Kogo Shūi (the section on Emperor Jinmu)
scenes.text: The Kogo Shūi records the Yatagarasu who led the way in Emperor Jinmu's eastern expedition as the distant ancestor of the Kamo Agatanushi. One of the old accounts linking the Yatagarasu of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki to the Kamo clan.

scenes.title: Accounts in the lost passages of the Yamashiro no Kuni Fudoki and the Shinsen Shōjiroku (outside the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki)
scenes.where: Lost passages of the Yamashiro no Kuni Fudoki and the Shinsen Shōjiroku (materials other than the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki)
scenes.text: Apart from the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, the lost passages of the Yamashiro no Kuni Fudoki and others tell the story of Tamayori-hime, daughter of Kamotaketsunumi-no-Mikoto, and the red-painted arrow, and the Shinsen Shōjiroku is said to link the Yatagarasu that guided Emperor Jinmu with Takeru-tsunumi. This item is based on the official site of Shimogamo Jinja and a reference dictionary, and the original texts are not confirmed.

kamotakeru.note_full: A deity whose name does not appear in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, and who is spoken of as the ancestral deity of the Kamo clan on the basis of the lost passages of the Fudoki, the Shinsen Shōjiroku and the Kogo Shūi. The identification with the Yatagarasu is not an account of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki but a theory from later materials, and there are various views. The official site cites the theory of Ban Nobutomo's 'Semi no Ogawa' that 'the Yatagarasu is none other than Takeru-tsunumi-no-Mikoto' (the original text is not confirmed). The original texts of the lost passages of the Yamashiro no Kuni Fudoki and the Shinsen Shōjiroku could not be checked this time and are to be confirmed.

kamowakeikazuchi.name: Kamowake-ikazuchi-no-Ōkami
kamowakeikazuchi.note: Deity of warding off misfortune and thunder
kamowakeikazuchi.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
kamowakeikazuchi.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)

scenes.title: Born from a red-lacquered arrow and descending on Mount Kōyama (a tradition not in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki)
scenes.where: Surviving fragment of the Yamashiro-no-kuni Fudoki and the Kamo Kyūki (sources other than the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki)
scenes.text: It is said that Kamo-tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto took home a red-lacquered arrow that had floated down the Semi-no-Ogawa stream, placed it by her bed and worshipped it, became pregnant and gave birth to a child. At the feast celebrating his coming of age he said 'My father is a heavenly deity', threw his cup toward heaven and rose to heaven with a peal of thunder; later, when a rite to welcome the deity was held as his mother's dream had instructed, he descended on Mount Kōyama. This child deity is regarded as Kamowake-ikazuchi-no-Ōkami. This is a summary of the official site's sacred tale; the original text has not been checked.

virtues: Warding off misfortune, protection against bad directions, good fortune, protection in all eight directions, protection from lightning, protection from calamity, certain victory and protection of the electrical industry (the wording of the divine virtues on the official site of Kamowake-ikazuchi Jinja)
kamowakeikazuchi.note_full: He does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki; he is a deity based on the traditions of a surviving fragment of the Yamashiro-no-kuni Fudoki (quoted in the Shaku Nihongi) and the Kamo Kyūki. His relationships with Kamotaketsunumi-no-Mikoto (existing ID kamotakeru), said to be his grandfather, and Kamo-tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto, said to be his mother, also rest on the same traditions, not on the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki. Kamo-tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto is a different deity from Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto (existing ID tamayori), the mother of Emperor Jinmu, and the two must not be confused.

miyazuhime.name: Miyazu-hime-no-Mikoto
miyazuhime.kojiki_name: Miyazu-hime (ancestor of the Owari no Kuni no Miyatsuko)
miyazuhime.kojiki_where: Part 2, Emperor Keikō, the section known as 'Yamato Takeru's Eastern Expedition'
miyazuhime.nihonshoki_where: Book 7, Emperor Keikō, the Eastern Expedition of Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto (entries from year 40 onward)

scenes.title: Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto enters her house in Owari
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section known as 'Yamato Takeru's Eastern Expedition'
scenes.text: On his way to the eastern provinces, Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto entered the house of Miyazu-hime, ancestor of the Owari no Kuni no Miyatsuko. Leaving a promise to marry her on his return, he went east, and visited again after returning.

scenes.title: Takes the daughter of the Owari clan as his wife and leaves the sword at her house
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 7, Emperor Keikō, the Eastern Expedition of Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto
scenes.text: Back in Owari, Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto took Miyazu-hime, daughter of the Owari clan, as his wife and stayed for more than a month; when he set out for Mount Ibuki he left the sword at her house and went on foot.

miyazuhime.note_full: The Miyazu-hime of the Kojiki and the Miyazu-hime of the Nihon Shoki are regarded as the same person (the accepted view). The Atsuta Jingū official site explains that she was the daughter of Otoyo-no-Mikoto, the Owari no Kuni no Miyatsuko, and the consort of Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto, and that after his death she enshrined the sacred sword at Atsuta (the name Otoyo-no-Mikoto has not been confirmed in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki).

omonushi.name: Ōmononushi-no-Kami
omonushi.note: Guardian of nation-building, healing, sake brewing and more
omonushi.kojiki_name: Ōmononushi-no-Kami ('Miwa-no-Ōmononushi-no-Kami' in the record of Emperor Jinmu) / Ōmononushi-no-Ōkami (record of Emperor Sujin). In the section on Building the Land in Part 1, no deity name is written; it records only 'the deity who dwells on Mount Mimoro'
omonushi.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'Ōkuninushi's Building of the Land' / Part 2, Emperor Jinmu, the section known as 'Choosing the Empress' / Part 2, Emperor Sujin, the section known as 'Ōtataneko'
omonushi.nihonshoki_name: Ōmononushi-no-Kami (in a variant account of section 8 he is made an alternative name of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, and in the same variant account the sakimitama-kushimitama (auspicious and wondrous spirit) becomes 'Ōmiwa-no-Kami')
omonushi.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 8, variant account (6) / Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9, variant account (2)

scenes.title: The deity who helps build the land, enshrined on Mount Mimoro
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Ōkuninushi's Building of the Land'
scenes.text: Before Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, at a loss after Sukunabikona-no-Kami had gone, a deity appeared, approaching and lighting up the sea, and declared, 'Enshrine me on the mountain to the east of the green fence of Yamato.' The Kojiki writes this deity as 'the deity who dwells on Mount Mimoro' and does not record the name as Ōmononushi.

scenes.title: Dwells on Mount Mimoro as the sakimitama-kushimitama
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, section 8, variant account (6)
scenes.text: A deity who appeared before Ōnamuchi-no-Kami declared, 'I am your sakimitama-kushimitama (auspicious and wondrous spirit),' and wished to dwell on Mount Mimoro in the land of Japan. The variant account of the Nihon Shoki makes this the deity of Ōmiwa, and also records Ōkuninushi-no-Kami as an alternative name of Ōmononushi-no-Kami.

scenes.title: The red-lacquered arrow and the birth of Isukeyori-hime
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section known as 'Choosing the Empress'
scenes.text: The Kojiki tells that Ōmononushi-no-Kami changed into a red-lacquered arrow and visited Seyadatara-hime, daughter of Mishima-no-Mizokui, and that their child was Hototatara-isusuki-hime-no-Mikoto (Hime-tatara-isukeyori-hime), who became the empress of Emperor Jinmu.

scenes.title: The plague and Ōtataneko
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section known as 'Ōtataneko'
scenes.text: When plague spread in the reign of Emperor Sujin, Ōmononushi-no-Ōkami appeared in the emperor's dream and told him to have Ōtataneko enshrine him. When Ōtataneko enshrined him on Mount Mimoro, it is said, the realm was at peace and the people prospered.

scenes.title: The first to submit in the Transfer of the Land
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 9, variant account (2)
scenes.text: A variant account of the Nihon Shoki records that, in the pacification by Futsunushi-no-Kami and Takemikazuchi-no-Kami, Ōmononushi-no-Kami and Kotoshironushi-no-Kami were the first to submit, and showed their sincerity by leading the eighty myriad deities up to heaven.

virtues: Revered as a guardian deity of nation-building, industrial development, protection from ill directions, healing of illness, sake brewing, medicine-making, charms, transport, seafaring, matchmaking and more (as explained on the Ōmiwa Jinja official site)
omonushi.note_full: His relationship with Ōkuninushi-no-Kami differs between sources. The Kojiki depicts the deity who cooperated in building the land as a deity distinct from Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, while a variant account of the Nihon Shoki makes him an alternative name of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, his sakimitama-kushimitama (auspicious and wondrous spirit). The Kogo Shūi records: 'Ōnamuchi-no-Kami, also named Ōmononushi-no-Kami, also named Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, also named Ōkunitama-no-Kami; this is the present Ōmiwa-no-Kami of Shiki-no-Kami District, Yamato Province.' The Ōmiwa Jinja official site also explains Ōmononushi-no-Ōkami as a deity manifested as a separate spirit (sakimitama and kushimitama) of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami. There are various views on the degree of identification.

sugawaranomichizane.name: Sugawara no Michizane
sugawaranomichizane.note: Deity of learning, culture and protection from misfortune
sugawaranomichizane.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; a figure of the Heian period, so the name is not in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki)
sugawaranomichizane.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; a figure of the Heian period, so the name is not in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki)
virtues: Revered as the deity of learning, culture and the arts, and protection from misfortune (explanation on the official site of Dazaifu Tenmangū)
sugawaranomichizane.note_full: Not a deity of the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki, but a real nobleman and scholar of the Heian period. According to the official site of Dazaifu Tenmangū, he was demoted to Dazai no Gon-no-sochi in 901 (Shōtai 4) and died at Dazaifu in 903 (Engi 3) at the age of 59. Later, after Emperor Daigo restored him to Minister of the Right and Emperor Ichijō granted him the Senior First Rank, Minister of the Left and Chancellor (Daijō-daijin), among other events, he came to be revered as 'Tenman Daijizai Tenjin' (official). His divine status as 'Tenjin' is a tradition that arose after his death, separate from the myths of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.

takeinadane.name: Takeinadane-no-Mikoto
takeinadane.note: Distant ancestor of the Owari clan (official)
takeinadane.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
takeinadane.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
takeinadane.note_full: The Atsuta Jingū official site explains that he was the child of Otoyo-no-Mikoto and the elder brother of Miyazu-hime-no-Mikoto, that he accompanied Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto on the pacification of the eastern provinces and died on the way, and that he is revered as a distant ancestor of the Owari clan. The obtained texts of the Kojiki (Parts 1 and 2) and the Nihon Shoki (Books 1–3, 7 and 14) were searched, but the name does not appear. Part 3 of the Kojiki has not been checked. The 'Takeinada no Sukune' of the Kojiki is regarded as a different person and has not been identified with him.

tamayori.name: Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto
tamayori.note: Raised her sister's child and later married him
tamayori.kojiki_name: Tamayori-bime-no-Mikoto (written 玉依毗賣 in the original text)
tamayori.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'Umisachi and Yamasachi'
tamayori.nihonshoki_where: Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 10 (Umisachi and Yamasachi). Also in Book 3, the pre-accession annals of Emperor Jinmu: 'his mother was called Tamayori-hime'

scenes.title: Raises the child born to her elder sister
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Umisachi and Yamasachi'
scenes.text: Toyotama-bime, daughter of the sea deity, gives birth to a child and returns to the sea, and sends her younger sister Tamayori-bime to raise that child.

scenes.title: Marries the child she raised and becomes the mother of Emperor Jinmu
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the end of the section known as 'Umisachi and Yamasachi'
scenes.text: Grown up, Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto took his aunt Tamayori-bime as his wife, and four children were born: Itsuse-no-Mikoto, Inahi-no-Mikoto, Mikenu-no-Mikoto and Wakamikenu-no-Mikoto (later Kamu-yamato-iwarebiko-no-Mikoto).

scenes.title: The account in the Nihon Shoki
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 10
scenes.text: The main text of the Nihon Shoki also records that Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto took his aunt Tamayori-hime as his consort and four sons were born. Book 3 gives the mother of Kamu-yamato-iwarebiko (Emperor Jinmu) as Tamayori-hime, the younger daughter of the sea deity (Watatsumi).

scenes.title: Raises the child in place of her elder sister
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 10, variant account
scenes.text: After her elder sister Toyotama-hime returned to the sea, the younger sister Tamayori-hime stayed and raised the child.

scenes.title: Delivers a song
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the end
scenes.text: Toyotama-bime entrusted a song to her younger sister Tamayori-bime, by way of her raising the child, and presented it to her husband.

tamayori.note_full: In both the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki she is depicted as 'the younger sister who raises the child and later marries him'. The Tamasaki Jinja official site gives the enshrined deity as Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto, but states that her relationship with Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto is under examination. IDs for the deities who are the parent (the sea deity) and children (Emperor Jinmu and others) of Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto were not created in this survey. / In the Kojiki she is the 'younger sister' (弟) of Toyotama-bime, and in a variant account of the Nihon Shoki the 'younger sister' (女弟).

yamatotakeru.name: Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto
yamatotakeru.kojiki_name: Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto (first name Ousu-no-Mikoto, also called Yamato Oguna-no-Mikoto)
yamatotakeru.kojiki_where: Part 2, Emperor Keikō, the section known as 'Yamato Takeru's Eastern Expedition'
yamatotakeru.nihonshoki_name: Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto (first name Ousu-no-Mikoto, also called Yamato Oguna)
yamatotakeru.nihonshoki_where: Book 7, Emperor Keikō, the Eastern Expedition of Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto (entries from year 40 onward, and year 51)

scenes.title: Receives the sword Kusanagi from Yamatohime-no-Mikoto
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section known as 'Yamato Takeru's Eastern Expedition'
scenes.text: To Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto, who laments at being ordered to pacify the eastern provinces, his aunt Yamatohime-no-Mikoto gives the sword Kusanagi and a bag.

scenes.title: The peril of the grass fire and the sword that cleared the grass
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section known as 'Yamato Takeru's Eastern Expedition'
scenes.text: When fire was set against him, Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto cut away the surrounding grass with the sword, lit a counter-fire with the flint from the bag and escaped the peril. The Kojiki records that the place is still called Yaizu.

scenes.title: Origin of the name Kusanagi
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 7, Emperor Keikō, the Eastern Expedition of Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto
scenes.text: When fire was set to the field in Suruga, the sword drew itself and mowed down the grass beside him so that he escaped the peril, and so, it is said, the sword came to be called Kusanagi.

scenes.title: Leaves the sword with Miyazu-hime
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section known as 'Yamato Takeru's Eastern Expedition'
scenes.text: On his way home, Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto was joined with Miyazu-hime in Owari, left the sword Kusanagi with her and set off for the deity of Mount Ibuki.

scenes.title: The sword Kusanagi is at the shrine of Atsuta
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 7, Emperor Keikō, year 51, 8th month
scenes.text: The Kusanagi sword that Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto wore is recorded as being, at the time the Nihon Shoki was compiled, at the shrine of Atsuta in Ayuchi District, Owari Province.

yamatotakeru.note_full: Prince of Emperor Keikō. Written 倭建命 (Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto) in the Kojiki and 日本武尊 (Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto) in the Nihon Shoki. A deity enshrined in the same hall (aidono) at Atsuta Jingū (official).

konohanasakuya.name: Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto
konohanasakuya.kojiki_name: Konohanasakuya-bime (written 木花之佐久夜毗賣 in the original text), also called Kamu-atatsu-hime
konohanasakuya.kojiki_where: Part 1, the latter part of the section known as 'Descent of the Heavenly Grandson' (Ninigi-no-Mikoto and Konohanasakuya-bime)
konohanasakuya.nihonshoki_where: Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9, main text and variant accounts

scenes.title: Meeting Ninigi-no-Mikoto
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the latter part of the section known as 'Descent of the Heavenly Grandson'
scenes.text: When Ninigi-no-Mikoto met a beautiful maiden at Cape Kasasa and asked her name, she answered that she was the daughter of Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami. She had an elder sister, Iwanaga-hime.

scenes.title: Giving birth in the fire
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the latter part of the section known as 'Descent of the Heavenly Grandson'
scenes.text: Suspected because she had conceived in a single night, Sakuya-bime built a hall without doors, set fire to it, and inside it gave birth to Hoderi-no-Mikoto, Hosuseri-no-Mikoto and Hoori-no-Mikoto.

scenes.title: The account in the Nihon Shoki
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9, variant account 2
scenes.text: In a variant account of the Nihon Shoki, she is Kamu-ata-kashitsu-hime, child of Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami, also called Konohanasakuya-hime.

scenes.title: A single night's marriage with Ninigi-no-Mikoto
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Konohanasakuya-bime and Iwanaga-hime'
scenes.text: Daughter of Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami. Her elder sister Iwanaga-hime was sent back, and only the younger sister Konohanasakuya-bime had a single night's marriage with Ninigi-no-Mikoto.

scenes.title: Conceives in a single night
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9
scenes.text: Kashitsu-hime, summoned by the Imperial Grandson, conceives in a single night. It records that when the Imperial Grandson doubted her, the princess entered a chamber without doors, set fire to it, and safely gave birth to her children.

konohanasakuya.note_full: In the Kojiki, a story is attached in which, because her elder sister Iwanaga-hime was sent back, the lifespan of the emperors became short like the flowers. Her identification with 'Asama-no-Ōkami' at Asama shrines is the shrines' own tradition, with no direct statement in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki. Her virtues (safe childbirth, protection from fire, etc.) have only been confirmed in official summaries and are not entered in virtues. / Her father Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami (written 大山祇神 in the Nihon Shoki) has no existing ID, so the parent is left empty.

sumiyoshi3.name: The Three Sumiyoshi Deities
sumiyoshi3.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, a variant account of section 5

scenes.title: Born at the bottom, middle and surface of the purifying water
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Purification'
scenes.text: Three deities born at the bottom, middle and surface of the sea when Izanagi-no-Mikoto purified himself to wash away the pollution of Yomi. They are enshrined as guardian deities of the sea and seafaring.

sumiyoshi3.note_full: The Ikisu Jinja official site records only 'the Three Sumiyoshi Deities'. The breakdown (Uwatsutsu, Nakatsutsu and Sokotsutsu) is from a reference dictionary (to be confirmed).

izanagi.name: Izanagi-no-Mikoto
izanagi.note: A 'linking' deity, parent of later gods
izanagi.kojiki_where: Part 1, the sections known as 'Birth of the Gods', 'Land of Yomi' and 'Purification'
izanagi.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), sections 4–5

scenes.title: Purification and the birth of the Three Noble Children
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Purification'
scenes.text: When Izanagi-no-Mikoto, back from the Land of Yomi, purified himself in water, deities such as the Three Sumiyoshi Deities, Amaterasu-Ōmikami and Susanoo-no-Mikoto came into being one after another.

izanagi.note_full: In this work, this deity is placed as a 'link', the parent of the deities that appear after this.

wakumusubi.name: Wakumusubi-no-Kami
wakumusubi.note: Identified with the Nihon Shoki's Wakumusubi-no-Mikoto
wakumusubi.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'Birth of the Gods'
wakumusubi.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), a variant account of section 5

scenes.title: Comes into being as a deity of food and production
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Birth of the Gods'
scenes.text: A deity connected with food and production, who came into being from the urine of Izanami-no-Mikoto as she suffered after giving birth to the fire deity. Her child is said to be Toyouke-bime-no-Kami (the deity of the Outer Shrine).

scenes.title: Origin of silkworms and the five grains (Nihon Shoki)
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, a variant account of section 5
scenes.text: In a variant account of the Nihon Shoki, Wakumusubi is born as the child of Kagutsuchi and Haniyama-hime, and silkworms and mulberry grew from the head and the five grains from the navel. The parentage differs from the Kojiki.

wakumusubi.note_full: The official site of Makata Jinja (Kaburagi-chō, Sakura City) explains that 'the Wakumusubi-no-Kami of the Kojiki is the Wakumusubi-no-Mikoto of the Nihon Shoki', which does not contradict the main texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (deity name and parent–child relationship). The 'Wakahirume-no-Mikoto' of the inner shrine (Okumiya) of Makata Jinja in Narita City belongs to the Wakahirume-no-Mikoto line of the Nihon Shoki and is treated as a different deity (as described in a reference dictionary; to be confirmed).

oshihomimi.name: Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto
oshihomimi.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'the Oath'

scenes.title: Child of Amaterasu-Ōmikami
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'the Oath'
scenes.text: One of the deities born in the oath between Amaterasu-Ōmikami and Susanoo-no-Mikoto. The Heavenly Grandson descends from him.

kunado.name: Kunado-no-Kami
kunado.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, a variant account of section 5 / Book 2, a variant account of section 9

scenes.title: Born from the thrown staff
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Purification'
scenes.text: A deity who came into being from the staff that Izanagi-no-Mikoto, back from Yomi, threw away. He is regarded as a deity who guards the boundaries of roads and blocks the entry of evil things.

scenes.title: Guide in the Transfer of the Land (Nihon Shoki)
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, a variant account of section 9
scenes.text: It records that Funato-no-Kami, recommended to the two deities by Ōnamuchi-no-Kami, took the role of guide, and the pacification of the various regions went forward.

kunado.note_full: The correspondence by which the 'Kunado-no-Kami' of the Ikisu Jinja official site matches the 'Tsukitatsu-Funado-no-Kami' of the Kojiki and the 'Funato-no-Kami' of the Nihon Shoki is an understanding found in reference dictionaries and shrine tradition. The main texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki do not themselves use the spelling 'Kunado' (to be confirmed).

amenotorifune.name: Ame-no-Torifune-no-Kami
amenotorifune.note: Deity name not confirmed in Nihon Shoki
amenotorifune.kojiki_where: Part 1, the sections known as 'Birth of the Gods' and 'Transfer of the Land'
amenotorifune.nihonshoki_name: (Not confirmed as a deity name; to be confirmed)

scenes.title: Deputy envoy in the Transfer of the Land
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Transfer of the Land'
scenes.text: Born as a deity of boats, in the Transfer of the Land he accompanied Takemikazuchi-no-Kami to Izumo as deputy envoy, and also served as the messenger sent to summon Kotoshironushi-no-Kami.

amenotorifune.note_full: In the Nihon Shoki the term 'Ame-no-Torifune' appears as the name of a boat, but its appearance as a deity name has not been confirmed.

futotama.name: Ame-no-Futodama-no-Mikoto
futotama.note: Child of Takamimusubi-no-Kami in the Kogo Shūi
futotama.kojiki_where: Part 1, the sections known as 'Heavenly Rock Cave' and 'Descent of the Heavenly Grandson'
futotama.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, section 7 (Heavenly Rock Cave), variant accounts and elsewhere

scenes.title: The rite at the Heavenly Rock Cave
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Heavenly Rock Cave'
scenes.text: Ancestral deity of the Inbe clan, who prepared the mirror and offerings and directed the rite before the rock cave where Amaterasu-Ōmikami had hidden.

scenes.title: Accompanies the Descent of the Heavenly Grandson
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Descent of the Heavenly Grandson'
scenes.text: He descends as one of the five attendant chiefs (itsutomonoo) who accompany the Heavenly Grandson. A note reads 'Futodama-no-Mikoto is the ancestor of the Inbe no Obito and others'.

futotama.note_full: The Kogo Shūi makes him the child of Takamimusubi-no-Kami. In the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, an explicit statement of his parent has not been confirmed (to be confirmed). The Awa Jinja official site gives his consort as Ame-no-Hiritome-no-Mikoto, but she does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki.

amenohiri.name: Ame-no-Hirinome-no-Mikoto
amenohiri.note: Not confirmed in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki
amenohiri.kojiki_name: (Not confirmed within the obtained range of the Kojiki, Nihon Shoki and Kogo Shūi; to be confirmed)

scenes.title: No myth in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki
scenes.where: Shrine tradition of Sunosaki Jinja
scenes.text: No myth is confirmed in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki. By shrine tradition, Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto is said to have enshrined the mirror of his grandmother deity, Ame-no-Hirinome-no-Mikoto, as the sacred object (tradition).

amenohiri.note_full: A reference dictionary summarizes that the Engishiki register of shrines lists 'Kisaki-gami Ame-no-Hirinome-no-Mikoto Jinja (Major), former name Su-no-Kami', and that the Six National Histories have entries on 'Ame-no-Hiritome-no-Mikoto', but the original texts are not confirmed. Rather than stating 'not in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki', this is marked 'to be confirmed'. There are two lines of spelling, with 乃 (no) and 刀 (to).

amenofuyuginu.name: Ame-no-Fuyukinu-no-Kami
amenofuyuginu.note: Father of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami in the Kojiki
amenofuyuginu.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'Genealogy of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami'
amenofuyuginu.note_full: The deity the Kojiki makes the father of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami. Placed as a 'link'.

sashikuniwakahime.name: Sashikuni-wakahime
sashikuniwakahime.note: Mother of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami in the Kojiki
sashikuniwakahime.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'Genealogy of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami'
sashikuniwakahime.note_full: The deity the Kojiki makes the mother of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami. Placed as a 'link'.

kotoshironushi.name: Kotoshironushi-no-Kami
kotoshironushi.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'Transfer of the Land'

scenes.title: Agrees to the Transfer of the Land
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Transfer of the Land'
scenes.text: Child of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami. Summoned by Ame-no-Torifune-no-Kami, he agreed to the transfer of the land.

takeminakata.name: Takeminakata-no-Kami
takeminakata.note: Placed as a 'link'; mother not confirmed
takeminakata.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'Transfer of the Land'

scenes.title: Defeated in a trial of strength
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Transfer of the Land'
scenes.text: Child of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami. It is told that he competed with Takemikazuchi-no-Kami in a trial of strength and was defeated.

takeminakata.note_full: Placed as a 'link'. An explicit statement of his mother deity is not found in the Kojiki (to be confirmed).

amenotomi.name: Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto
amenotomi.note: Enshrined at the Lower Shrine of Awa Jinja
amenotomi.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)

scenes.title: Opening up Bōsō (Kogo Shūi)
scenes.where: Kogo Shūi
scenes.text: He is regarded as the grandson of Futodama-no-Mikoto. It is told that in the reign of Emperor Jinmu he led the Inbe of Awa (Tokushima) eastward, opened up Bōsō by planting hemp and other crops, and founded the shrine of Futodama-no-Mikoto (Awa-sha). Historical corroboration requires separate examination.

amenotomi.note_full: The enshrined deity of the Lower Shrine (Shimo-no-Miya) of Awa Jinja. The Kogo Shūi is a record of clan traditions compiled in 807 and differs in character from the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.

ugayafukiaezu.name: Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto
ugayafukiaezu.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'Umisachi and Yamasachi'
ugayafukiaezu.nihonshoki_where: Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 10 (Umisachi and Yamasachi)

scenes.title: Born before the roof of the birthing hall was finished
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Umisachi and Yamasachi'
scenes.text: His mother Toyotama-bime began thatching the roof of a birthing hall on the seashore with cormorant feathers, but the child was born before the thatching was finished, and so he was given this name.

scenes.title: Takes his aunt Tamayori-bime as his wife
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the end of the section known as 'Umisachi and Yamasachi'
scenes.text: Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto took his aunt Tamayori-bime as his wife and had four children. The youngest was Kamu-yamato-iwarebiko-no-Mikoto.

scenes.title: Born in a birthing hut by the sea
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the end, the section known as 'Birth of Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto'
scenes.text: It gives the origin of the name: he was born before the roof of the birthing hut had been finished with cormorant feathers, and so was given this name.

ugayafukiaezu.note_full: His father is Hoori-no-Mikoto (Yamasachi-hiko) and his mother Toyotama-bime-no-Mikoto (Kojiki). IDs for each were not created this time. The Tamasaki Jinja official site lists only Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto as the enshrined deity and notes that this deity's name is recorded alongside in old shrine records. / His children Itsuse-no-Mikoto, Inahi-no-Mikoto and Kamu-yamato-iwarebiko-no-Mikoto (Emperor Jinmu) were not created this time (only Mikeirino-no-Mikoto was entered in children).

inadahime.name: Inada-hime-no-Mikoto
inadahime.note: Spelling follows the Nihon Shoki's Kushi-inada-hime
inadahime.kojiki_name: Kushinada-hime (written 櫛名田比賣 in the original text)
inadahime.nihonshoki_name: Kushi-inada-hime (written 奇稻田姬 in the original text)
inadahime.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 8 (Yamata-no-Orochi)

scenes.title: The daughter about to be swallowed by Yamata-no-Orochi
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Yamata-no-Orochi'
scenes.text: On the upper reaches of the Hi River in Izumo, an old couple, Ashinazuchi and Tenazuchi, were weeping. One of their eight daughters had been eaten by the great serpent each year, and it was the turn of the youngest, Kushinada-hime, to be swallowed.

scenes.title: Becomes the wife of Susanoo-no-Mikoto
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Yamata-no-Orochi'
scenes.text: Susanoo-no-Mikoto slew the great serpent, took Kushinada-hime as his wife and built a palace at Suga. From the two was born Yashimajinumi-no-Kami, whose descendants lead to Ōkuninushi-no-Kami.

scenes.title: The account in the Nihon Shoki
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 8
scenes.text: In the main text of the Nihon Shoki she appears as 'Kushi-inada-hime', daughter of Ashinazuchi and Tenazuchi. Susanoo-no-Mikoto changes her into a comb, puts it in his hair and fights the great serpent.

inadahime.note_full: The spelling Inada-hime owes much to the Nihon Shoki's 'Kushi-inada-hime'; the Kojiki writes 'Kushinada-hime'. IDs for Yashimajinumi-no-Kami, Ashinazuchi and Tenazuchi were not created this time.

ooyamatsumi.name: Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami
ooyamatsumi.note: Father of Konohanasakuya-bime; also of Ashinazuchi
ooyamatsumi.kojiki_where: Part 1, the latter part of the section known as 'Descent of the Heavenly Grandson', and 'Yamata-no-Orochi'
ooyamatsumi.nihonshoki_where: Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9

scenes.title: Offers his two daughters to Ninigi-no-Mikoto
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the latter part of the section known as 'Descent of the Heavenly Grandson'
scenes.text: At the proposal of Ninigi-no-Mikoto, Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami was greatly pleased and offered Konohanasakuya-bime together with her elder sister Iwanaga-hime.

ooyamatsumi.note_full: The Kojiki also records Ashinazuchi, father of Susanoo-no-Mikoto's wife Kushinada-hime, as 'a child of Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami'. His parent deities (the point that he is regarded as a child of Izanagi and Izanami) were not checked in the text this time and are not entered in relations.

ninigi.name: Ninigi-no-Mikoto
ninigi.note: Grandson of Amaterasu-Ōmikami; husband of Konohanasakuya-hime
ninigi.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'Descent of the Heavenly Grandson'
ninigi.nihonshoki_where: Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9 (Descent of the Heavenly Grandson)

scenes.title: Meets Konohanasakuya-bime at Kasasa in Hyūga
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the latter part of the section known as 'Descent of the Heavenly Grandson'
scenes.text: Having descended from heaven, Ninigi-no-Mikoto met a beautiful maiden at Cape Kasasa and wished to marry her.

scenes.title: Sent down to become lord of Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9
scenes.text: In the main text of the Nihon Shoki, Takamimusubi-no-Mikoto sends down his grandson Ninigi-no-Mikoto to make him lord of Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni.

scenes.title: Descends from heaven to Takachiho
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Descent of the Heavenly Grandson'
scenes.text: At the command of Amaterasu-Ōmikami and others, Ninigi-no-Mikoto descended from the Floating Bridge of Heaven to Kujifuru-take of Takachiho in Hyūga of Tsukushi.

scenes.title: Descends to Takachiho Peak in Hyūga
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9 (Descent of the Heavenly Grandson)
scenes.text: In the Nihon Shoki, Takamimusubi-no-Mikoto covers the Imperial Grandson with the madoko-ofusuma (sacred coverlet) and sends him down, and the Imperial Grandson descends to Takachiho Peak in So of Hyūga.

ninigi.note_full: Husband of Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto. Grandson of Amaterasu-Ōmikami (child of Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto). An ID for his child Hoori-no-Mikoto was not created this time. / As for the site of the descent at Takachiho, the Kojiki writes 'Kujifuru-take of Takachiho in Hyūga of Tsukushi', and the Nihon Shoki 'Takachiho Peak in So of Hyūga' and 'Kushifuru Peak of Takachiho in Hyūga of Tsukushi'. What the Takachiho Jinja official site says about the site of the descent has not been confirmed. In the Kojiki he has an elder brother, Ame-no-Hoakari-no-Mikoto (Hoderi-no-Mikoto and Hosuseri-no-Mikoto are recorded separately as his children).

yasakatome.name: Yasakatome-no-Kami
yasakatome.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
yasakatome.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
yasakatome.note_full: The Suwa Taisha official site gives the enshrined deity of the Maemiya as Yasakatome-no-Kami, and the enshrined deities of the Shimosha Harumiya and Akimiya as Takeminakata-no-Kami, Yasakatome-no-Kami and Yaekotoshironushi-no-Kami, and records that 'he opened up Shinano Province together with his consort deity, his elder brother deity and his child deities'. The name does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki (Parts 1 and 2 of the Kojiki and Books 1–3 and 14 of the Nihon Shoki, as obtained), and the marital relationship with Takeminakata-no-Kami cannot be confirmed in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki either (a Suwa tradition; Part 3 of the Kojiki has not been checked).

takeuchi.name: Takeuchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto
takeuchi.note: Deity of longevity and fortune in war
aliases: Takeuchi-no-Sukune (Nihon Shoki, variant characters 武內宿禰)
takeuchi.kojiki_where: Part 2, sections commonly called 'Emperor Chūai' and 'Emperor Ōjin and Kehi-no-Ōkami'
takeuchi.nihonshoki_where: Book 9, Empress Jingū, the account before her regency and the 13th year of the regency

scenes.title: Attending the sacred court for calling down the deity
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called 'Emperor Chūai'
scenes.text: When Emperor Chūai played the koto and Takeuchi-no-Sukune, seated in the saniwa (sacred court), asked for the will of the deity, the empress became possessed and delivered the oracle.

scenes.title: Playing the koto for the empress
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 9, Empress Jingū, the account before her regency
scenes.text: It records that when the empress entered the purification hall and herself became the officiant, she had Takeuchi-no-Sukune play the koto.

scenes.title: Taking the crown prince to Tsunuga
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called 'Emperor Ōjin and Kehi-no-Ōkami'
scenes.text: Takeuchi-no-Sukune took the crown prince (the future Emperor Ōjin) out for purification, and passing through Ōmi and Wakasa, built a temporary palace at Tsunuga in Koshi.

scenes.title: Becoming chief minister
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called 'Emperor Seimu'
scenes.text: It is recorded that in the reign of Emperor Seimu, Takeuchi-no-Sukune became chief minister (ōomi) and took charge of the work of appointing the greater and lesser kuni-no-miyatsuko and agata-nushi.

scenes.title: Asking for the deity's oracle
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called 'Emperor Chūai'
scenes.text: When Emperor Chūai played the koto and Takeuchi-no-Sukune waited in the saniwa (the place for hearing the words of the deity) and asked for the deity's will, the deity descended on the empress and delivered the oracle.

scenes.title: The possession of Empress Jingū
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 9, Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto (Empress Jingū)
scenes.text: The empress entered the purification hall and herself became the officiant. Takeuchi-no-Sukune played the koto, and Nakatomi-no-Ikatsu-no-Omi served as saniwa (interpreter of the deity) and asked the deity's name.

scenes.title: Defeating Prince Oshikuma
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 9, Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto (Empress Jingū)
scenes.text: On the empress's orders, Takeuchi-no-Sukune, together with Takefurukuma, ancestor of the Wani-no-Omi, led tens of thousands of soldiers and defeated Prince Oshikuma.

scenes.title: The tradition of his long life and Inaba (not in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki)
scenes.where: The origin story told on the official site of Ube Jinja (outside the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki)
scenes.text: Ube Jinja says that Takeuchi-no-Sukune served five reigns from Emperor Keikō to Emperor Nintoku and passed away in Inaba at the age of over 360. This age and the story of his end in Inaba are not confirmed in the Kojiki Part 2 and Nihon Shoki Book 9 obtained for this survey.

virtues: Long life, freedom from illness, and lasting fortune in war (the divine virtues listed on the official site of Kehi Jingū)
takeuchi.note_full: One of the deities enshrined at Kehi Jingū. The Kojiki records him as the child of Yamashita-kage-hime. The relationship with the parent deity is not included in the diagram in this survey. / In the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki he appears only as far as his activity as a minister. The stories of his long life (over 360 years) and his death in Inaba are the shrine's tradition and are not confirmed in the main text of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. The Kojiki lists Takeuchi-no-Sukune in the genealogy of Emperor Kōgen.

ookibitsuhiko.name: Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto
ookibitsuhiko.note: Prince who pacified the land of Kibi
aliases: Kibitsuhiko (Nihon Shoki, the passage on the Four Generals / to be confirmed)
ookibitsuhiko.nihonshoki_name: Kibitsuhiko (said to appear in the passage on the Four Generals in the annals of Emperor Sujin; word-by-word checking not yet done, to be confirmed)

scenes.title: A child of Emperor Kōrei
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called 'Emperor Kōrei'
scenes.text: Among the children of Emperor Kōrei is listed Hikoisaseribiko-no-Mikoto, also called Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto. In the same passage, Wakahiko-Takekibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto also appears as a younger brother by a different mother.

scenes.title: Pacifying Kibi by persuasion
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called 'Emperor Kōrei'
scenes.text: It is recorded that Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto and Wakatake-Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto, the two deities joining forces, entered from Harima and brought the land of Kibi into submission (pacified it by persuasion). The phrase used is 'pacify by persuasion' (kotomuke-yawasu), not subjugation by force of arms.

scenes.title: The tradition of defeating Ura (not in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki)
scenes.where: The origin story told on the official site of Kibitsu Jinja (outside the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki)
scenes.text: Kibitsu Jinja tells as its origin story that Kibitsuhiko defeated Ura, said to be a prince of Baekje. The name Ura is not found in the original texts of the Kojiki Part 2 and the Nihon Shoki obtained for this survey, and it is considered a tradition shaped in later times.

ookibitsuhiko.note_full: The Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto of the Kojiki, the Kibitsuhiko of the Nihon Shoki and the Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto enshrined at the shrine are regarded as the same, but the original text on the Nihon Shoki side has not been checked, so this is to be confirmed. The defeat of Ura is a tradition not found in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki.

takeiwatatsu.name: Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto
takeiwatatsu.note: Grandson of Emperor Jinmu, per Aso Jinja
takeiwatatsu.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
takeiwatatsu.kojiki_where: Does not appear. In the section on Emperor Jinmu, 'Aso-no-Kimi' appears in an interlinear note as a descendant of Kamuyaimimi-no-Mikoto (the name Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto is absent)
takeiwatatsu.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
takeiwatatsu.nihonshoki_where: Does not appear. In Book 7, the 18th year of Emperor Keikō, the two deities of the land of Aso, Asotsuhiko and Asotsuhime, appear (different names)

scenes.title: Grandson deity of Emperor Jinmu who opened up Aso (the official explanation of Aso Jinja)
scenes.where: Aso Jinja, official page 'About Aso Jinja'
scenes.text: The official site of Aso Jinja explains that Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto is a grandson deity of Emperor Jinmu and the deity who opened up Aso, enshrined at the center of the twelve family deities. He is a deity based on shrine tradition and later lore, not on the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki.

scenes.title: The two deities of the land of Aso (Nihon Shoki)
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 7, the 18th year of Emperor Keikō, sixth month
scenes.text: It records that when Emperor Keikō visited the land of Aso and asked 'Is anyone here?' on a plain where no person could be seen, two deities appeared in human form, and this became the origin of the land's name. The deity names given here are Asotsuhiko and Asotsuhime; Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto is not written.

takeiwatatsu.note_full: A deity whose name is absent from the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki and who is based on the shrine tradition of Aso Jinja. The official site calls him 'a grandson deity of Emperor Jinmu'. The explanation that his father is Kamuyaimimi-no-Mikoto is commonly seen, but it is not written on the official page checked and is to be confirmed, so it is not recorded in the relations (Kamuyaimimi-no-Mikoto is, in the Kojiki, a child of Emperor Jinmu and one of the ancestors of the Aso-no-Kimi).

kamuyaimimi.name: Kamuyaimimi-no-Mikoto
kamuyaimimi.note: Son of Emperor Jinmu who yielded the throne
kamuyaimimi.kojiki_name: Kamuyaimimi-no-Mikoto (the original text has both 'Kamuyaimimi-no-Mikoto' and 'Kamuyai-no-Mikoto')
kamuyaimimi.kojiki_where: Part 2, the final part of the section commonly called 'Emperor Jinmu' (the revolt of Tagishimimi-no-Mikoto)
kamuyaimimi.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in Book 3, which has been obtained. Appears in Book 4, Emperor Suizei, but that book has not been obtained; to be confirmed)

scenes.title: Yielding the throne to his younger brother (the revolt of Tagishimimi-no-Mikoto)
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the final part of the section commonly called 'Emperor Jinmu'
scenes.text: After the death of Emperor Jinmu, his half-brother Tagishimimi-no-Mikoto tried to kill the three younger brothers. Kamuyaimimi-no-Mikoto went in with weapons, but his hands and feet trembled and he could not kill him, and his younger brother Kamununakawamimi-no-Mikoto struck him down. Kamuyaimimi-no-Mikoto then yielded the throne to his younger brother and said he would serve in the role of worshipping the deities. An interlinear note says this deity is the ancestor of the Ō-no-Omi, the Chiisakobe-no-Muraji, the Aso-no-Kimi and others.

kamuyaimimi.note_full: The parent-child relationship with Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto, the deity of Aso Jinja, is not written in the materials checked and is to be confirmed. The 'Aso-no-Kimi' in the Kojiki's interlinear note is the name of the Aso clan, and is distinct from Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto.

hitokotonushi.name: Hitokotonushi-no-Kami
hitokotonushi.note: Deity who settles matters with one word
hitokotonushi.kojiki_where: Part 3, section commonly called 'Emperor Yūryaku' (the encounter on Mount Katsuragi)
hitokotonushi.nihonshoki_where: Book 14, the 4th year of Emperor Yūryaku, spring, second month

scenes.title: Meeting Emperor Yūryaku on Mount Katsuragi (Kojiki)
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 3, section commonly called 'Emperor Yūryaku'
scenes.text: When Emperor Yūryaku climbed Mount Katsuragi, a procession exactly like the emperor's own was climbing the mountain opposite. When asked its name, the other party gave its own name first, saying it was 'the deity who pronounces bad things in one word and good things in one word, Hitokotonushi-no-Ōkami of Katsuragi'. The emperor was awestruck, offered the clothing, swords, bows and arrows of all his officials and worshipped, and the deity is said to have escorted the emperor to the mountain entrance at Hatsuse.

scenes.title: Hunting together with the emperor on Mount Katsuragi (Nihon Shoki)
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 14, the 4th year of Emperor Yūryaku, spring, second month
scenes.text: When Emperor Yūryaku hunted on Mount Katsuragi, a tall person resembling the emperor appeared and called himself 'a deity in visible human form (arahito-gami)'. When the emperor gave his name, the other replied 'I am Hitokotonushi-no-Kami', and the two enjoyed the hunt side by side. It records that at dusk the deity escorted the emperor to the Kume River, and the people said he was 'an emperor of virtue'.

virtues: A deity of harmony and cooperation, said to be the object of a special belief that matters are settled with a single word (the official explanation of Tosa Jinja).
hitokotonushi.note_full: In both the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki the setting is Mount Katsuragi in Yamato, and no mention of a connection with Tosa can be read in the original texts obtained. The official site of Tosa Jinja explains that in a surviving fragment of the Tosa-no-kuni Fudoki, Hitokotonushi-no-Mikoto appears as the deity of the great shrine of Takakamo in Tosa (the original text of the Fudoki fragment has not been checked here). The Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki differ in how Hitokotonushi-no-Kami is portrayed (the emperor is awestruck / the deity enjoys the hunt as the emperor's equal).

utsushikunitama.name: Utsushikunitama-no-Kami
utsushikunitama.note: Deity of Iwakiyama Jinja; identity to be confirmed
utsushikunitama.kojiki_name: Utsushikunitama-no-Kami (appears as one of the alternative names of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami)
utsushikunitama.kojiki_where: Part 1, section commonly called 'The descendants of Susanoo-no-Mikoto'
utsushikunitama.nihonshoki_name: Utsushikunitama-no-Kami (appears in a variant account of the Nihon Shoki as an alternative name of Ōnamuchi-no-Kami)
utsushikunitama.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1 (variant account) / Book 2, Age of the Gods Part 2

scenes.title: One of the alternative names of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called 'The descendants of Susanoo-no-Mikoto'
scenes.text: The Kojiki lists the names of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami as 'Ōnamuji-no-Kami', 'Ashiharashikoo-no-Kami', 'Yachihoko-no-Kami', 'Utsushikunitama-no-Kami' and so on, and records that there are five in all.

utsushikunitama.note_full: The official site of Iwakiyama Jinja lists 'Utsushikunitama-no-Kami' as one of its enshrined deities. The name sounds the same as the names in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, but it has not been confirmed whether the official site explains it as the same deity, so no identification with Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami is made here (it is also treated separately from Ōkunitama-no-Kami).

omoikane.name: Yagokoro-omoikane-no-Mikoto
omoikane.note: Ancestral deity of politics, learning and industry
omoikane.kojiki_where: Part 1, sections commonly called 'The Heavenly Rock Cave' and 'The Descent of the Heavenly Grandson'
omoikane.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 7, main text and variant accounts

scenes.title: Devising a plan before the rock cave door
