scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called 'The Heavenly Rock Cave'
scenes.text: When Amaterasu-Ōmikami shut herself in the rock cave, among the myriad deities who gathered, Omoikane-no-Kami, child of Takamimusubi-no-Kami, was given the task of thinking, and measures such as making the long-crowing birds of Tokoyo crow were taken.

scenes.title: Making a plan to bring out Amaterasu-Ōmikami
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 7, main text
scenes.text: When Amaterasu-Ōmikami shut herself in the heavenly rock cave, the eighty myriad deities gathered to consult on a method, and Omoikane-no-Kami thought deeply and had the long-crowing birds gathered.

scenes.title: Conducting affairs of state at the Descent of the Heavenly Grandson
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called 'The Descent of the Heavenly Grandson'
scenes.text: Amaterasu-Ōmikami presented the mirror and commanded Omoikane-no-Kami to 'take charge of the matters before you and conduct the affairs of state'.

virtues: Ancestral deity of politics, learning, industry and good fortune (the official explanation of Chichibu Jinja)
omoikane.note_full: The Kojiki records him as a child of Takamimusubi-no-Kami. The spelling 'Yagokoro-omoikane-no-Mikoto' is the shrine's official one; the word 'Yagokoro' does not occur in the texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki obtained for this survey (the spelling in other classical texts has not been checked). As the parent, Takamimusubi-no-Kami, has no existing deity ID, the parents in the relations are left empty.

chichibuhiko.name: Chichibuhiko-no-Mikoto
chichibuhiko.note: Ancestral deity who opened the Chichibu region
chichibuhiko.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by searching Parts 1 and 2 at hand / Part 3 not checked, to be confirmed)
chichibuhiko.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by searching the books obtained at hand / other books not checked, to be confirmed)

scenes.title: Becoming the first kuni-no-miyatsuko of the land of Chichibu
scenes.where: Sendai Kuji Hongi, 'Kokuzō Hongi' (according to the official description of Chichibu Jinja; original text not checked)
scenes.text: The official site of Chichibu Jinja records that in the reign of Emperor Sujin he was appointed the first kuni-no-miyatsuko of the land of Chichibu as a descendant of Yagokoro-omoikane-no-Mikoto in the tenth generation, and worshipped his ancestral deity.

virtues: Ancestral deity who opened up the Chichibu region (the official explanation of Chichibu Jinja)
chichibuhiko.note_full: He does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki; the official site of Chichibu Jinja relies on the 'Kokuzō Hongi' of the Sendai Kuji Hongi. The blood relationship with Yagokoro-omoikane-no-Mikoto (a descendant in the tenth generation) is not a statement of the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki but the official site's explanation, and the original text has not been checked.

amenominakanushi.name: Ame-no-Minakanushi-no-Kami
amenominakanushi.note: First deity to appear; guardian of directions
amenominakanushi.kojiki_where: Part 1, opening, section commonly called 'The Beginning of Heaven and Earth'
amenominakanushi.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 1, variant account (does not appear in the main text)

scenes.title: Appearing at the beginning of heaven and earth
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, opening, 'The Beginning of Heaven and Earth'
scenes.text: He is recorded as the first deity to come into being in Takamagahara when heaven and earth first opened. Takamimusubi-no-Kami and Kamimusubi-no-Kami come into being after him.

scenes.title: Appearing in a variant account
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 1, variant account
scenes.text: In the Nihon Shoki his name is given, not in the main text but in one of the variant accounts, as a deity born in Takamagahara.

virtues: Worshipped as a guardian deity of directions and bearings (the official explanation of Chichibu Jinja, which enshrines him as the same deity as Myōken-sama, Hokushin Myōken)
amenominakanushi.note_full: In the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki the name appears only as the deity of the beginning of heaven and earth, and no deeds are told. The official site of Chichibu Jinja records that in the Kamakura period he was enshrined together with the Myōken faith, which takes the North Star (Hokushin) as its divine seat. This is a later current of belief, separate from the myths of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. The variant account number in the Nihon Shoki is thought to be 'Section 1, variant account 4', but checking of the section and variant account against the original text is not complete and is to be confirmed.

futsunomitama.name: Futsunomitama-no-Ōkami
futsunomitama.note: Divine power of the sacred sword Futsunomitama
futsunomitama.kojiki_name: Futsunomitama (name of a sword; also Sajifutsu-no-Kami and Mikafutsu-no-Kami; appears in a small note)
futsunomitama.kojiki_where: Part 2, Emperor Jinmu, section commonly called 'Takakuraji of Kumano'
futsunomitama.nihonshoki_where: Book 3, Emperor Jinmu, the account before his accession (Takakuraji of Kumano)

scenes.title: The sword sent down into Takakuraji's storehouse
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called 'Takakuraji of Kumano'
scenes.text: When Emperor Jinmu's army collapsed at Kumano, Takakuraji was told in a dream that the sword with which Takemikazuchi-no-Ōkami had pacified the land would be sent down. In the morning the sword was standing inside the storehouse; when he presented it, the emperor awoke and the army rose too. A small note records that the sword is called Sajifutsu-no-Kami, Mikafutsu-no-Kami and Futsunomitama, and that it resides at Isonokami Jingū.

scenes.title: The sword named Futsunomitama
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 3, Emperor Jinmu, the account before his accession
scenes.text: The army that had fallen to poisonous vapors at Kumano was saved by the sword Takakuraji found in his storehouse through the teaching of a dream. In the dream, Takemikazuchi-no-Ōkami gives the name of his own sword as Futsunomitama.

futsunomitama.note_full: Futsunomitama is the name of a sword and is distinct from the deity name Futsunushi-no-Ōkami (existing ID futsunushi). The official site of Isonokami Jingū explains that the divine power dwelling in the sacred sword 'Futsunomitama' is Futsunomitama-no-Ōkami, and that Futsunomitama is the sword Takemikazuchi-no-Ōkami held at the transfer of the land and the sword that aided Emperor Jinmu's eastern expedition. The Kojiki gives the sword's name in a small note.

furunomitama.name: Furunomitama-no-Ōkami
furunomitama.note: Divine power of the ten sacred treasures
aliases: The divine power dwelling in the ten sacred heavenly treasures (Amatsushirushi Tokusa-no-Mizutakara) (official site of Isonokami Jingū)
furunomitama.kojiki_name: (The name 'Furunomitama' is not found in the range of the Kojiki checked / to be confirmed)
furunomitama.kojiki_where: (In Part 2, Emperor Jinmu, section commonly called 'The submission of Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto', the presentation of the 'heavenly tokens' (amatsushirushi) appears)
furunomitama.nihonshoki_name: (The name 'Furunomitama' is not found in the range of the Nihon Shoki checked / to be confirmed)
furunomitama.nihonshoki_where: (In Book 3, Emperor Jinmu, the account before his accession, Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto appears as the distant ancestor of the Mononobe clan)

scenes.title: Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto presents the heavenly tokens
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called 'The submission of Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto'
scenes.text: Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto came before Emperor Jinmu, who had come down from heaven, presented the heavenly tokens and served him. The official site of Isonokami Jingū takes the ten sacred heavenly treasures granted to Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto to be the divine power of Furunomitama-no-Ōkami. The phrase 'ten sacred treasures' is not confirmed in the main text of the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki, and this connection is the official site's tradition.

furunomitama.note_full: The official site of Isonokami Jingū explains that the ten sacred treasures hold the power to bring even the dead back to life, and that the first chinkon-sai (spirit-pacifying rite) was when Umashimaji-no-Mikoto performed the pacification of spirits (mitamafuri) with these treasures. This is not confirmed in the main text of the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki (possibly a tradition from the Kuji Hongi or similar; to be confirmed).

futsushimitama.name: Futsushimitama-no-Ōkami
futsushimitama.note: Divine power of the sword that slew Orochi
aliases: The divine power dwelling in the Ame-no-Totsuka-no-Tsurugi (official site of Isonokami Jingū)
futsushimitama.kojiki_name: (The name 'Futsushimitama' is not found in the range of the Kojiki checked / to be confirmed)
futsushimitama.kojiki_where: (The ten-span sword (totsuka-no-tsurugi) is mentioned in Part 1, section commonly called 'The Eight-Headed Serpent')
futsushimitama.nihonshoki_name: Orochi-no-Aramasa (name of a sword; the name 'Futsushimitama' is not found)
futsushimitama.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 8, main text

scenes.title: The sword that cut the serpent is at Isonokami
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 8, main text
scenes.text: The Nihon Shoki calls the sword with which Susanoo-no-Mikoto cut the eight-headed serpent Orochi-no-Aramasa, and records that it is now at Isonokami. The official site of Isonokami Jingū takes the divine power dwelling in this Ame-no-Totsuka-no-Tsurugi to be Futsushimitama-no-Ōkami.

futsushimitama.note_full: The deity name 'Futsushimitama' is not found in the range of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki checked and is the official designation of Isonokami Jingū. Taking Orochi-no-Aramasa to be the Ame-no-Totsuka-no-Tsurugi is the official site's explanation, and the correspondence of sword names in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki is to be confirmed.

umashimaji.name: Umashimaji-no-Mikoto
umashimaji.note: Ancestral deity of the Mononobe clan
aliases: Umashimade-no-Mikoto (Nihon Shoki; regarded as the same / to be confirmed)
umashimaji.kojiki_where: Part 2, Emperor Jinmu, section commonly called 'The submission of Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto'
umashimaji.nihonshoki_where: Book 3, Emperor Jinmu, the account before his accession (the words of Nagasunehiko)

scenes.title: Child of Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called 'The submission of Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto'
scenes.text: The child born when Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto married Tomiyabime, younger sister of Tomibiko. A small note records him as the ancestor of the Mononobe-no-Muraji, the Hozumi-no-Omi and the Uneme-no-Omi.

umashimaji.note_full: The Kojiki gives his father as Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto (no ID has been made for this deity this time). The main text of the Nihon Shoki, in the words of Nagasunehiko, records the child of Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto and Mikashikiyahime as Umashimade-no-Mikoto, and makes Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto the distant ancestor of the Mononobe clan. The identification of Umashimade-no-Mikoto with Umashimaji-no-Mikoto is the general understanding and is not stated explicitly in the texts obtained (to be confirmed). The official site of Isonokami Jingū explains that he is the ancestral deity of the Mononobe clan and performed the divine rite of pacifying spirits.

ooyamakui.name: Ōyamakui-no-Kami
ooyamakui.note: Deity of Mount Hie, enshrined at Hiyoshi Taisha
ooyamakui.kojiki_where: Part 1, section commonly called 'The genealogy of Ōtoshi-no-Kami'
ooyamakui.nihonshoki_name: (Not found in the range of the Nihon Shoki checked / to be confirmed)
ooyamakui.nihonshoki_where: (Not in the range of Books 1 and 2 checked)

scenes.title: The deity residing on Mount Hie in the land of Chikatsu-Ōmi
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called 'The genealogy of Ōtoshi-no-Kami'
scenes.text: One of the children of Ōtoshi-no-Kami, also called Yamasue-no-Ōnushi-no-Kami. It records that he resides on Mount Hie in the land of Chikatsu-Ōmi, and also at Matsuo in Kadono, and that he is a deity who uses a whistling arrow (narikabura). The official site of Hiyoshi Taisha makes Ōyamakui-no-Kami the deity of the East Main Shrine, but the official page obtained does not cite the Kojiki.

ooyamakui.note_full: The Kojiki makes him a child of Ōtoshi-no-Kami (no existing ID). The official site of Hiyoshi Taisha records that Ōyamakui-no-Kami is enshrined at the East Main Shrine (Higashi Hongū) and the aramitama (rough spirit) of Ōyamakui-no-Kami at Ushio-gū.

niutsuhime.name: Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami
niutsuhime.note: Goddess of cinnabar who wards off misfortune
aliases: Also called Wakahirume-no-Mikoto (official site of Niutsuhime Jinja)
niutsuhime.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
niutsuhime.nihonshoki_name: (The name 'Niutsuhime' is absent from the Nihon Shoki. Wakahirume-no-Mikoto appears as a separate name / the identification is the official site's explanation)
niutsuhime.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, Section 7, variant account 1 / Book 9, Empress Jingū, the account before her regency (Wakahirume-no-Mikoto)

scenes.title: Wakahirume-no-Mikoto gives an oracle to Empress Jingū
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 9, Empress Jingū, the account before her regency
scenes.text: Wakahirume-no-Mikoto told Empress Jingū that she wished to dwell in the land of Ikuta-no-Nagao, and had Unakami-no-Isachi enshrine her. Taking Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami to be Wakahirume-no-Mikoto is the official site's explanation; the name Niu is absent from the Nihon Shoki.

niutsuhime.note_full: A deity absent from the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. The official site explains that she is the younger sister of Amaterasu-Ōmikami, a goddess who governs cinnabar (mercury vermilion) and wards off misfortune. The official site states that the Harima-no-kuni Fudoki has a passage in which she granted cinnabar to Empress Jingū, but this survey has not checked the original text of the Fudoki (to be confirmed).

takanomiko.name: Takanomiko-no-Ōkami
takanomiko.note: Deity of guidance, child of Niutsuhime
takanomiko.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
takanomiko.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)

scenes.title: Guiding Kōbō Daishi to Amano
scenes.where: Tradition of Niutsuhime Jinja (not in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki)
scenes.text: The official site explains that Takanomiko-no-Ōkami appeared before Kōbō Daishi in the form of a hunter with a white dog and a black dog, and led the Daishi to the land of Amano with the dogs as guides. He is worshipped as a deity of guidance and of opening the way (michihiraki).

takanomiko.note_full: Absent from the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. The official site makes him the child deity of Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami and explains that the origin legend of Mount Kōya is depicted in the Konjaku Monogatari and other works.

ookegetsuhime.name: Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami
ookegetsuhime.note: Goddess of the five grains and food
aliases: Kehi Myōjin (official site of Niutsuhime Jinja)
ookegetsuhime.kojiki_name: Ōgetsuhime-no-Kami (the official site does not state the identification explicitly; to be confirmed)
ookegetsuhime.nihonshoki_name: (Possibly under another name such as Ukemochi-no-Kami. Unclear within the range checked / to be confirmed)

scenes.title: The goddess of food is killed
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called 'Ōgetsuhime'
scenes.text: When the banished Susanoo-no-Mikoto asked for food, Ōgetsuhime took out food from her nose, mouth and rear and offered it. Susanoo-no-Mikoto, thinking she had defiled it, killed her. The official site of Niutsuhime Jinja makes the shrine's Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami the goddess of the five grains and food, but does not state explicitly that she is the same as the deity of the Kojiki.

ookegetsuhime.note_full: The official site of Niutsuhime Jinja says she is a deity invited (kanjō) from Kehi Jingū in Echizen by an oracle in the Kamakura period, and the 'friend of old (old friend)' of Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami. Whether she is the same as the Ōgetsuhime-no-Kami of the Kojiki is to be confirmed.

kotosakao.name: Yomotsu-Kotosaka-no-O
kotosakao.note: Deity from the Yomi scene (Nihon Shoki)
kotosakao.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
kotosakao.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 5 (variant account; the scene in the land of Yomi. The number of the variant account is to be confirmed)

scenes.title: Coming into being from Izanagi-no-Mikoto's sweeping
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 5 (variant account)
scenes.text: In the scene where Izanagi-no-Mikoto bids farewell to his wife in the land of Yomi, Hayatama-no-O-no-Kami came into being from his spittle, and then Yomotsu-Kotosaka-no-O from his sweeping (brushing away).

kotosakao.note_full: The official site of Naminoue-gū in Naha lists 'Kotosaka-no-O-no-Mikoto' among its enshrined deities. Whether the 'Yomotsu-Kotosaka-no-O' of the Nihon Shoki and the official site's Kotosaka-no-O-no-Mikoto are the same deity has not been confirmed from the official site's view (to be confirmed).

obiko.name: Ōbiko-no-Mikoto
obiko.note: One of the Four Generals, sent to Koshi
obiko.kojiki_where: Part 2, the sections on Emperor Kōgen and Emperor Sujin
obiko.nihonshoki_where: Book 5, the 10th year of Emperor Sujin, 9th month, the Four Generals

scenes.title: Sent to the Koshi road
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section on Emperor Sujin
scenes.text: In the reign of Emperor Sujin, Ōbiko-no-Mikoto is sent to the Koshi road and his son Takenunakawawake-no-Mikoto to the twelve roads of the east, to pacify those who would not submit.

scenes.title: Father and son meet at Aizu
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section on Emperor Sujin
scenes.text: Ōbiko-no-Mikoto, who went toward the land of Koshi, and his son Takenunakawawake-no-Mikoto, sent from the east, met at Aizu, and the place came to be called Aizu; so the origin of the place name is told.

scenes.title: To Hokuriku as one of the Four Generals
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 5, the 10th year of Emperor Sujin, 9th month
scenes.text: In the Nihon Shoki he is written Ōhiko-no-Mikoto and is sent to Hokuriku as one of the Four Generals (Takenunakawawake to Tōkai).

obiko.note_full: The Kojiki has Ōbiko, the Nihon Shoki Ōhiko. Isasumi Jinja tells, as shrine tradition, that father and son were involved in its founding (see the shrine's deity_note). The word 'Aizu' was not found in the same book of the Nihon Shoki.

takenunakawawake.name: Takenunakawawake-no-Mikoto
takenunakawawake.note: One of the Four Generals, sent east
takenunakawawake.kojiki_where: Part 2, the sections on Emperor Kōgen and Emperor Sujin
takenunakawawake.nihonshoki_where: Book 5, the 10th year of Emperor Sujin, 9th month, the Four Generals

scenes.title: Recorded as the child of Ōbiko
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section on Emperor Kōgen
scenes.text: Takenunakawawake-no-Mikoto is named as the child of Ōbiko-no-Mikoto, child of Emperor Kōgen (noted as the ancestor of the Abe-no-Omi and others).

scenes.title: Sent to the twelve roads of the east
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section on Emperor Sujin
scenes.text: In the reign of Emperor Sujin, his father Ōbiko-no-Mikoto is sent to the Koshi road and Takenunakawawake-no-Mikoto to the twelve roads of the east.

scenes.title: Meeting his father at Aizu
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section on Emperor Sujin
scenes.text: Takenunakawawake-no-Mikoto, sent from the east, met his father Ōbiko-no-Mikoto at Aizu, and this is said to be the origin of the place name.

takenunakawawake.note_full: In the Nihon Shoki he is written Takenunakawawake and is sent to Tōkai as one of the Four Generals (Book 5).

takamimusubi.name: Takamimusubi-no-Kami
takamimusubi.kojiki_where: Part 1, section commonly called 'The Beginning of Heaven and Earth'
takamimusubi.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 1, variant account and elsewhere

scenes.title: Appearing at the beginning of heaven and earth
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called 'The Beginning of Heaven and Earth'
scenes.text: When heaven and earth first opened, following Ame-no-Minakanushi-no-Kami, Takamimusubi-no-Kami and Kamimusubi-no-Kami appear in Takamagahara. They are said to be single deities who did not show their forms.

scenes.title: Gathering the deities together with Amaterasu-Ōmikami
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called 'The pacification of Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni'
scenes.text: Takamimusubi-no-Kami, together with Amaterasu-Ōmikami, gives the command, gathers the myriad deities on the riverbed of the Ame-no-Yasukawa, and has them consult Omoikane-no-Kami.

takamimusubi.note_full: In the Kojiki, the father of Omoikane-no-Kami. In the Nihon Shoki he is made the father of Takuhatachijihime (Book 2, Section 9).

amenouzume.name: Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto
amenouzume.note: Goddess who danced before the rock cave
amenouzume.kojiki_where: Part 1, sections commonly called 'The Heavenly Rock Cave' and 'The Descent of the Heavenly Grandson'
amenouzume.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 7, variant account / Book 2, Age of the Gods Part 2, Section 9, variant account

scenes.title: Dancing at the Heavenly Rock Cave
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called 'The Heavenly Rock Cave'
scenes.text: When Amaterasu-Ōmikami hid in the rock cave, Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto hung vines from Mount Ame-no-Kaguyama as a sash and danced a dance that made the deities laugh.

scenes.title: Leading the way at the Descent of the Heavenly Grandson
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called 'The Descent of the Heavenly Grandson'
scenes.text: She is given the task of asking the name of the deity at the eight crossroads of heaven, and later is also commanded to escort Sarutahiko-no-Kami home.

scenes.title: Attending and escorting Sarutahiko (Nihon Shoki)
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, Age of the Gods Part 2, Section 9, variant account
scenes.text: As Saruta-no-Kami wished, Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto accompanied him and escorted him to the upper reaches of the Isuzu River at Sanagata in Ise.

amenouzume.note_full: The Kojiki notes her as the ancestor of the Sarume-no-Kimi and others. The chief deity of Tsubakigishi Jinja, an auxiliary shrine (betsugū) of Tsubaki Ōkamiyashiro (see the shrine's deity_note).

takuhatachijihime.name: Takuhatachijihime-no-Mikoto
takuhatachijihime.note: Mother of Ninigi in the Nihon Shoki
aliases: Takuhatachijihime-Yorozuhatahime-no-Mikoto (a variant tradition in the Nihon Shoki)
takuhatachijihime.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search. In the Kojiki the mother of Ninigi-no-Mikoto is Yorozuhata-toyoakitsushi-hime-no-Mikoto)
takuhatachijihime.nihonshoki_where: Book 2, Age of the Gods Part 2, Section 9, main text and variant accounts

scenes.title: As the mother of Ninigi-no-Mikoto
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, Age of the Gods Part 2, Section 9, main text
scenes.text: Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto marries Takuhatachijihime, daughter of Takamimusubi-no-Mikoto, and she gives birth to Amatsuhiko-Hononinigi-no-Mikoto.

scenes.title: How the Kojiki records it
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called 'The Descent of the Heavenly Grandson'
scenes.text: In the Kojiki it is written that Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto united with Yorozuhata-toyoakitsushi-hime-no-Mikoto, daughter of Takagi-no-Kami, and fathered Ame-no-Hoakari-no-Mikoto and Ninigi-no-Mikoto; the name Takuhatachijihime does not appear.

takuhatachijihime.note_full: The spelling of the Nihon Shoki. Whether she is the same deity as the Kojiki's Yorozuhata-toyoakitsushi-hime-no-Mikoto cannot be settled from the main texts alone and is to be confirmed.

wakahirume.name: Wakahirume-no-Mikoto
wakahirume.note: Deity who blesses the growth of all things
wakahirume.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
wakahirume.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 7 (variant account) / Book 9, Empress Jingū

scenes.title: Weaving the divine garments in the sacred weaving hall
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 7, variant account
scenes.text: In a variant account telling the circumstances of Amaterasu-Ōmikami shutting herself in the heavenly rock cave, Wakahirume-no-Mikoto was weaving the divine garments in the sacred weaving hall. There Susanoo-no-Mikoto threw in a piebald horse; startled, she fell from the loom, injured herself with the shuttle and, it is recorded, 'departed as a deity' (it is not written that she was weaving the garments of Amaterasu-Ōmikami).

scenes.title: Declaring the wish to dwell in the land of Ikuta-no-Nagao
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 9, Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto (Empress Jingū)
scenes.text: On the return from the expedition to Silla, the empress's ship would not move forward, and when the divine will was asked, Wakahirume-no-Mikoto declared 'I wish to dwell in the land of Ikuta-no-Nagao', and had Unakami-no-Isachi enshrine her. The passage regarded as the origin of Ikuta Jinja.

virtues: Revered as a deity who blesses the growth of all things (the official explanation of Ikuta Jinja)

Said to have the divine virtues of peace in family life, the prosperity and health of companies and organizations, and warding off misfortune, and is widely worshipped (the official explanation of Ikuta Jinja)
wakahirume.note_full: The official site of Ikuta Jinja explains Wakahirume-no-Mikoto as 'said to be the nigimitama (gentle spirit) or the younger sister of Amaterasu-Ōmikami', but this is the official site's tradition, not something written in the main text of the Nihon Shoki. Treating the weaving deity in the variant account of Section 7 of the Nihon Shoki and the deity in the section on Empress Jingū as the same deity also follows the official site's explanation. The name Wakahirume-no-Mikoto could not be confirmed in the Kojiki.

kumanookami.name: Kaburogi-Kumano-no-Ōkami-Kushimikenu-no-Mikoto
kumanookami.note: Deity of industry, good fortune and matchmaking
kumanookami.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
kumanookami.kojiki_where: — (checked in the main text of Kojiki Parts 1 and 2. Part 3 not checked)
kumanookami.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
kumanookami.nihonshoki_where: — (checked in Books 1 to 3, 9, 10 and 14. Other books not checked)

scenes.title: Kumano-no-Ōkami in the sources cited by the official site
scenes.where: The sources section of the official site of Kumano Taisha (Nihon Shoki, Izumo-no-kuni Fudoki, Engishiki and others)
scenes.text: The official site records that Kumano-no-Ōkami appears in the Fudoki, Kumano-no-Ōkami and Kumano Taisha in the Engishiki, and that the Nihon Shoki has an entry about having the kuni-no-miyatsuko of Izumo build the 'Itsu-no-kami-no-miya' (palace of the solemn deity). The original texts could not be checked this time, and no mythological scene in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki has been confirmed from the main texts.

virtues: A great deity of industry, good fortune and matchmaking, and warding off misfortune, deeply worshipped by the common people (the official explanation of Kumano Taisha)
kumanookami.note_full: The official site of Kumano Taisha records the chief deity as 'Susanoo-no-Mikoto, honored as Kaburogi-Kumano-no-Ōkami-Kushimikenu-no-Mikoto'. Whether he is the same deity as the Susanoo-no-Mikoto of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (existing ID susanoo) is left at the official site's form of honoring and is not asserted. He is distinct from the deity of Kumano Hongū Taisha in Kii.

komagataookami.name: Komagata-Ōkami
komagataookami.note: Mountain deity of Komagatake, linked to horses
komagataookami.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search)
komagataookami.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by search)
komagataookami.note_full: The official site of Komagata Jinja (Ōshū City, Iwate) tells that Kamitsukeno-no-Isawa-no-Kimi invited (kanjō) Komagata-Ōkami to the summit of Komagatake, and records that, while the enshrined deity is unknown, the six deities written on the ridge tablet (munafuda) of the inner shrine are revered as the enshrined deities. A separate tradition, absent from the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, handed down as worship of a mountain deity (also linked with a deity of horses). The official site's explanations of the relationship with other Komagata shrines and of the origin of the name do not settle the enshrined deity of the main hall.

amenotokotachi.name: Ame-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto
amenotokotachi.note: Deity of the beginning of heaven and earth
amenotokotachi.kojiki_where: Part 1, section commonly called 'The Beginning of Heaven and Earth'
amenotokotachi.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 1, variant account

scenes.title: One of the Separate Heavenly Deities who appeared at the beginning of heaven and earth
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called 'The Beginning of Heaven and Earth'
scenes.text: A deity who came into being, after Umashiashikabihikoji-no-Kami, from something sprouting up like a reed shoot around the time heaven and earth separated, and who hid his form as a single deity. The Kojiki calls the five deities up to this point the Separate Heavenly Deities (Kotoamatsukami).

scenes.title: Ame-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto in a variant account of the Nihon Shoki
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 1, variant account
scenes.text: The Nihon Shoki, in one of the variant accounts of Section 1, names Ame-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto as a deity transformed from something like a reed shoot that arose in the air, followed next by Umashiashikabihikoji-no-Mikoto. He does not appear in the main text.

amenotokotachi.note_full: The official site of Komagata Jinja (Ōshū City, Iwate) explains Ame-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto as 'the deity who governs the universe'. This explanation is the official site's; the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki record no deeds beyond his being a deity of the beginning of heaven and earth.

kunisatsuchi.name: Kuni-no-Sazuchi-no-Mikoto
kunisatsuchi.note: Deity who came into being after Kuni-no-Tokotachi
aliases: Kuni-no-Satachi-no-Mikoto (variant account in the Nihon Shoki)
kunisatsuchi.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search)
kunisatsuchi.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 1, main text and variant account

scenes.title: The deity who came into being after Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 1, main text
scenes.text: Following Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto, who was transformed from something like a reed shoot that arose between heaven and earth, Kuni-no-Sazuchi-no-Mikoto is named as the next deity to come into being. The main text records that the three deities Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto, Kuni-no-Sazuchi-no-Mikoto and Toyokumunu-no-Mikoto came into being alone as male deities.

scenes.title: The alternative name Kuni-no-Satachi-no-Mikoto
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 1, variant account
scenes.text: One of the variant accounts names Kuni-no-Sazuchi-no-Mikoto as the deity who came into being after Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto, and gives his alternative name as Kuni-no-Satachi-no-Mikoto.

kunisatsuchi.note_full: The official site of Komagata Jinja (Ōshū City, Iwate) calls Kuni-no-Sazuchi-no-Mikoto 'the deity who protects the earth' and explains that he is also called Kuni-no-Satachi-no-Mikoto. This explanation is the official site's; the Nihon Shoki records only the deity's name and order.

otorimurajioya.name: Ōtori-no-Muraji-no-Oyagami
otorimurajioya.note: Ancestral deity of the Ōtori clan
otorimurajioya.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
otorimurajioya.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki either; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
otorimurajioya.note_full: The ancestral deity of a clan, which the official site of Ōtori Taisha explains as the deity enshrining the ancestors of the Ōtori clan, which flourished in Izumi Province. The official site records that, according to the Shinsen Shōjiroku, Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto (existing ID amenokoyane) is said to be the ancestor, but the main text of the Shinsen Shōjiroku has not been checked this time, so the parent-child relationship is not entered in the relations. The word 'Ōtori' is not found in the main texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki obtained, and the deity does not appear in them (a separate tradition).

wakahikotakekibitsuhiko.name: Wakahiko-Takekibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto
aliases: Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto (name used for the co-enshrined deity at Kibitsuhiko Jinja)
Wakatakehiko-no-Mikoto (Nihon Shoki; identification as the same deity to be confirmed)
wakahikotakekibitsuhiko.nihonshoki_name: Wakatakehiko-no-Mikoto (a prince in the entry for the 2nd year of Emperor Kōrei. Whether this is the same deity is not confirmed in this note; to be confirmed)
wakahikotakekibitsuhiko.nihonshoki_where: Book 4, 2nd year of Emperor Kōrei (to be confirmed)

scenes.title: Child of Emperor Kōrei
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called "Emperor Kōrei"
scenes.text: Among the children Emperor Kōrei had with Haeirodo, the name Wakahiko-Takekibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto is listed together with Hikosamema-no-Mikoto. He is a younger brother of Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto by a different mother.

scenes.title: Subdues Kibi together with his brother
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called "Emperor Kōrei"
scenes.text: It is recorded that he and his elder brother Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto joined forces and, using Harima (Harima Province) as the entry point, brought the land of Kibi into submission.

scenes.title: Wakatakehiko-no-Mikoto is the ancestor of the Kibi no Omi
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 4, 2nd year of Emperor Kōrei (to be confirmed)
scenes.text: The Nihon Shoki records that the younger sister of Emperor Kōrei's consort bore Hikosashima-no-Mikoto and Wakatakehiko-no-Mikoto, and that Wakatakehiko-no-Mikoto was the ancestor of the Kibi no Omi. He is thought to be the prince corresponding to the Kojiki's Wakahiko-Takekibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto, but this note has not confirmed that they are the same.

wakahikotakekibitsuhiko.note_full: The official site of Kibitsuhiko Jinja explains that the co-enshrinement hall enshrines 'Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto (a prince of Emperor Kōrei, Wakatake-Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto)'. The official name 'Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto' is the same as the name the Nihon Shoki uses as another name of Hiko-Isaserihiko-no-Mikoto (who corresponds to Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto), so to avoid confusion the Kojiki spelling is used as the name here. The parent, Emperor Kōrei, is not among the existing deities, so parents is left empty.

hinokuma.name: Hinokuma-no-Ōkami
hinokuma.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by text search / to be confirmed)
hinokuma.kojiki_where: (No entry. The making of a mirror appears in the Rock Cave section, but the name Hinokuma does not)
hinokuma.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 7, a variant account (the number of the variant account is not checked; to be confirmed)

scenes.title: The deity who made the sun-spear is Hinokuma-no-Kami
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 7, a variant account (number to be confirmed)
scenes.text: Before the heavenly rock cave, by the plan of Omoikane-no-Kami, Ishikoridome was made smith and had the 'sun-spear' (hihoko) made from the metal of Mt. Ame-no-Kaguyama. It is recorded that the deity who made and presented it is Hinokuma-no-Kami, who is in Kii Province.

scenes.title: The first-cast mirror of the sun's image
scenes.where: Kogo Shūi, the Heavenly Rock Cave section
scenes.text: When Ishikoridome-no-Kami was made to cast a mirror of the sun's image, the first result was not satisfactory. An interlinear note says that this first mirror is Hinokuma-no-Kami of Kii Province (and that the beautiful mirror cast next is the great deity of Ise).

hinokuma.note_full: Chief deity of Hinokuma Jingū. The official site of Hinokuma Jingū and Kunikakasu Jingū explains that the sacred object of Hinokuma-gū is the Higata-no-Kagami (mirror of the sun's image), a mirror of Amaterasu-Ōmikami. Because a variant account in the Nihon Shoki links the sun-spear to Hinokuma-no-Kami, and the Kogo Shūi makes the first casting of the mirror of the sun's image Hinokuma-no-Kami, the accounts in the Kojiki, Nihon Shoki and Kogo Shūi do not match the shrine's explanation in detail (sun's image or sun-spear). The relation to the shrine's explanation that Hinokuma-Kunikakasu-no-Ōkami is another name of Amaterasu-Ōmikami is also to be confirmed.

kunikakasu.name: Kunikakasu-no-Ōkami
kunikakasu.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by text search / to be confirmed)
kunikakasu.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki either; confirmed by text search / to be confirmed)
kunikakasu.note_full: Chief deity of Kunikakasu Jingū. The official site says its sacred object is the Hiboko-no-Kagami (sun-spear mirror) and that, together with Hinokuma-no-Ōkami, it derives from the mirror of Amaterasu-Ōmikami. The name 'Kunikakasu' is not found in the texts of the Kojiki, Nihon Shoki and Kogo Shūi obtained so far (in the variant account of the Nihon Shoki, it is Hinokuma-no-Kami who is linked to the sun-spear). Treated as absent from the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki / a separate tradition.

ishikoridome.name: Ishikoridome-no-Mikoto
ishikoridome.note: Ancestor of the Kagami-tsukuri; co-enshrined at Hinokuma Jingū
aliases: Ishikoridome-no-Mikoto (Kojiki, written 伊斯許理度売命)
ishikoridome.kojiki_where: Part 1, sections commonly called "the Heavenly Rock Cave" and "the Descent of the Heavenly Grandson"
ishikoridome.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 7, a variant account / Book 2, Age of the Gods Part 2, Section 9, a variant account

scenes.title: Makes the mirror at the Heavenly Rock Cave
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called "the Heavenly Rock Cave"
scenes.text: When Amaterasu-Ōmikami shut herself in the rock cave, it is recorded that, following the arrangement to summon Amatsumara, Ishikoridome-no-Mikoto was made to make a mirror.

scenes.title: Makes the sun-spear as smith
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 7, a variant account (number to be confirmed)
scenes.text: It is recorded that by the plan of Omoikane-no-Kami, Ishikoridome, as smith, was made to take metal from Mt. Ame-no-Kaguyama and make the sun-spear.

scenes.title: Accompanies the Descent of the Heavenly Grandson
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called "the Descent of the Heavenly Grandson"
scenes.text: She is listed as one of the five attendant deities (itsutomo-no-o) who accompanied the descent of Ninigi-no-Mikoto, together with Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto, Futodama-no-Mikoto and Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto.

ishikoridome.note_full: The Kojiki, in a note, makes her the ancestor of the Kagami-tsukuri no Muraji and others. At Hinokuma Jingū and Kunikakasu Jingū she is enshrined in the co-enshrinement hall of Hinokuma Jingū (official).

tamaoya.name: Tamanooya-no-Mikoto
tamaoya.note: Ancestor of the Tamanooya; co-enshrined at Kunikakasu Jingū
aliases: Tamanooya-no-Mikoto (Nihon Shoki, a variant account in Book 2. Identification as the same deity to be confirmed)
tamaoya.kojiki_where: Part 1, sections commonly called "the Heavenly Rock Cave" and "the Descent of the Heavenly Grandson"
tamaoya.nihonshoki_name: Tamanooya-no-Mikoto (founding ancestor of the jewel-makers. Identification as the same deity to be confirmed)
tamaoya.nihonshoki_where: Book 2, Age of the Gods Part 2, Section 9, a variant account (to be confirmed)

scenes.title: Makes the string of yasaka curved beads
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called "the Heavenly Rock Cave"
scenes.text: Tamanooya-no-Mikoto took on the task of making the jewel ornament, a string of five hundred yasaka curved beads (magatama), to hang before the rock cave door.

scenes.title: Accompanies the Descent of the Heavenly Grandson
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called "the Descent of the Heavenly Grandson"
scenes.text: He is listed as one of the five attendant deities (itsutomo-no-o) who accompanied the descent of Ninigi-no-Mikoto.

tamaoya.note_full: The Kojiki, in a note, makes him the ancestor of the Tamanooya no Muraji and others. At Hinokuma Jingū and Kunikakasu Jingū he is enshrined in the co-enshrinement hall of Kunikakasu Jingū (official). Whether he may be regarded as the same deity as the Nihon Shoki's 'Tamanoya-no-Mikoto' (founding ancestor of the jewel-makers) is not confirmed in this note.

akedatsuamenomikage.name: Aketatsu-Ame-no-Mikage-no-Mikoto
akedatsuamenomikage.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by text search / to be confirmed)
akedatsuamenomikage.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki either; confirmed by text search / to be confirmed)
akedatsuamenomikage.note_full: A deity enshrined in the co-enshrinement hall of Kunikakasu Jingū at Hinokuma Jingū and Kunikakasu Jingū (official). The name 'Aketatsu-Ame-no-Mikage' is not found in the texts of the Kojiki, Nihon Shoki and Kogo Shūi obtained so far. The Kojiki has 'Ame-no-Mikage-no-Kami' in the Emperor Kaika section, but this is thought to be a different deity and is not identified with him.

amenomichine.name: Ame-no-Michine-no-Mikoto
amenomichine.note: Ancestor of the Ki clan of Kii Province
amenomichine.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by text search / to be confirmed)
amenomichine.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki either; confirmed by text search / to be confirmed)
amenomichine.note_full: The official site of Hinokuma Jingū and Kunikakasu Jingū explains that he served as an attendant at the Descent of the Heavenly Grandson together with the two sacred mirrors, that in the spring, 2nd month of the 2nd year of Emperor Jinmu he was granted Kii Province and appointed its first kuni-no-miyatsuko (provincial governor), and that he is the ancestor of the Ki clan. He is enshrined in an auxiliary shrine (sessha) in the precincts. He is not found in the texts of the Kojiki, Nihon Shoki and Kogo Shūi obtained so far, and is absent from the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (a shrine tradition).

iwatsuchibiko.name: Iwatsuchibiko-no-Kami
iwatsuchibiko.note: Deity of household safety and protection from misfortune
iwatsuchibiko.kojiki_name: Iwatsuchibiko-no-Kami (the original text writes 石土毗古神; a note says the characters 毗古 represent the sound)
iwatsuchibiko.kojiki_where: Part 1, section commonly called "the Birth of the Deities" (born after the birth of the land, next after Ōkotooshio-no-Kami)
iwatsuchibiko.nihonshoki_name: (The name 'Iwatsuchibiko' cannot be confirmed in the Nihon Shoki. A different deity name, 'Iwatsuchi-no-Mikoto', appears in a variant account of Book 1, Section 5, but whether it is the same deity is to be confirmed)

scenes.title: The birth of the deities after the birth of the land
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called "the Birth of the Deities"
scenes.text: After Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto had finished giving birth to the land (the islands), they first gave birth to Ōkotooshio-no-Kami, and then to Iwatsuchibiko-no-Kami as one of the deities connected with houses and land.

virtues: Worshipped as a deity of household safety, protection from misfortune and good fortune, and recovery from illness (explanation on the official site of Ishizuchi Jinja)
iwatsuchibiko.note_full: The Kojiki records that, alongside Iwatsuchibiko-no-Kami, Iwasuhime-no-Kami, Ōtohiwake-no-Kami, Ame-no-Fukio-no-Kami, Ōyabiko-no-Kami and others were born. The official site of Ishizuchi Jinja explains that its deity Ishizuchihiko-no-Mikoto is also called Iwatsuchibiko-no-Mikoto, and this note treats them as the same deity. A corresponding name cannot be confirmed in the Nihon Shoki (to be confirmed).

yamatototohimomoso.name: Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime-no-Mikoto
yamatototohimomoso.note: Daughter of Emperor Kōrei, enshrined at Tamura Jinja
yamatototohimomoso.kojiki_where: Part 2, section commonly called "Emperor Kōrei" (genealogy of Emperor Kōrei's children)
yamatototohimomoso.nihonshoki_where: Book 4, Emperor Kōrei (genealogy of his children) / Book 5, Emperor Sujin (the oracle of Ōmononushi-no-Kami, foreseeing the rebellion of Takehaniyasuhiko, and the Hashihaka tomb)

scenes.title: Genealogy of Emperor Kōrei's children
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called "Emperor Kōrei"
scenes.text: The Kojiki lists Yamato-tomomoso-bime-no-Mikoto as one of the children born to Emperor Kōrei by Ōyamato-kuni-arehime-no-Mikoto, followed by Hikoisaseribiko-no-Mikoto (also named Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto).

scenes.title: Child of Emperor Kōrei
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 4, Emperor Kōrei
scenes.text: The Nihon Shoki records that Emperor Kōrei's consort Yamato-no-Kunikahime bore Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime-no-Mikoto and Hiko-Isaserihiko-no-Mikoto (also named Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto) and others. The mother's name differs from the Kojiki.

scenes.title: The oracle of Ōmononushi-no-Kami and the Hashihaka tomb
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 5, Emperor Sujin
scenes.text: When plague spread in the reign of Emperor Sujin, a deity possessed the princess and named itself Ōmononushi-no-Kami. Later the princess became the wife of Ōmononushi-no-Kami, but she was startled to find that her husband, who visited only at night, was in truth a small snake, cried out, and in remorse died and was buried at Ōichi (the Hashihaka tomb).

scenes.title: Foreseeing the rebellion of Takehaniyasuhiko
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 5, Emperor Sujin
scenes.text: The princess, who was an aunt of Emperor Sujin, was wise and had the power to see the future; hearing a young girl's song, she saw through it as a sign of the rebellion of Takehaniyasuhiko and told the emperor.

yamatototohimomoso.note_full: In the Kojiki her name is listed only as a child of Emperor Kōrei; the marriage to Ōmononushi-no-Kami and the Hashihaka story are not in the Kojiki but are recorded in the Nihon Shoki, in the chronicle of Emperor Sujin. The Tamura Jinja official site's 'founding deity of agriculture and industry' and 'went down to Sanuki Province on the order to pacify the western seas' are shrine traditions and are not written in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki.

amenokakureyama.name: Ame-no-Kakureyama-no-Mikoto
amenokakureyama.note: Identified with Takakuraji by Tamura Jinja
aliases: Takakuraji-no-Mikoto (the official site of Tamura Jinja regards him as the same deity)
amenokakureyama.kojiki_name: (The name 'Ame-no-Kakureyama-no-Mikoto' does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by text search / to be confirmed). 'Takakuraji', whom the official site of Tamura Jinja regards as the same deity, appears in the Jinmu chapter as 'Takakuraji of Kumano'
amenokakureyama.kojiki_where: Part 2, section commonly called "Emperor Jinmu" (the presentation of the sword at Kumano)
amenokakureyama.nihonshoki_name: (The name 'Ame-no-Kakureyama-no-Mikoto' does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by searching the obtained text). Takakuraji appears in the Jinmu chronicle as 'Kumano no Takakuraji'

scenes.title: Takakuraji of Kumano presents the sword
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called "Emperor Jinmu"
scenes.text: When Emperor Jinmu's army was in danger at Kumano, Takakuraji of Kumano came bearing a single sword and presented it. The Kojiki attaches a note to this name: 'this is the name of a person'. Takakuraji tells that he obtained the sword after receiving instruction in a dream from Amaterasu-Ōmikami and Takemikazuchi-no-Kami.

amenokakureyama.note_full: The official site of Tamura Jinja describes Ame-no-Kakureyama-no-Mikoto (Takakuraji-no-Mikoto) as 'the deity who rescued the imperial ancestor Emperor Jinmu from peril during his eastern expedition', and explains that, together with his child Ame-no-Itane-no-Mikoto, he crossed from Kii Province to Sanuki, divided the boundaries of the districts by mountains and rivers, and laid the foundations of land development and irrigation. This story of the move to Sanuki and the development is a shrine tradition and is not written in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki. The identification of the name Ame-no-Kakureyama-no-Mikoto with Takakuraji is also the official site's explanation and cannot be confirmed from the texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. He is treated separately from the existing Ame-no-Kaguyama-no-Mikoto (amenokaguyama) (whether they are the same is to be confirmed).

amenoitane.name: Ame-no-Itane-no-Mikoto
amenoitane.note: Child of Ame-no-Kakureyama-no-Mikoto, enshrined at Tamura Jinja
aliases: Ame-no-Murakumo-no-Mikoto (the official site of Tamura Jinja regards him as the same deity)
amenoitane.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by text search / to be confirmed)
amenoitane.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by searching the obtained text / to be confirmed)
amenoitane.note_full: The official site of Tamura Jinja explains that he is the child of Ame-no-Kakureyama-no-Mikoto, and that he crossed from Kii Province to Sanuki together with Ame-no-Kakureyama-no-Mikoto and laid the foundations of land development and irrigation. In the obtained texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (Books 1–5, 7, 9, 10 and 14), neither 'Ame-no-Murakumo' nor 'Ame-no-Itane' can be confirmed, and this is thought to be a tradition based on other sources (to be confirmed).

kanmu.name: Emperor Kanmu
kanmu.note: Emperor who moved the capital to Heian-kyō
kanmu.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki)
kanmu.note_full: A historical emperor (the 50th; 737–806). The official site explains that he is the emperor who moved to the new capital (Heian-kyō) in 794 (Enryaku 13). A figure later than the age of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, he does not appear in them. Not a deity of myth, but listed as a deity enshrined at Heian Jingū.

komei.name: Emperor Kōmei
komei.note: Emperor co-enshrined at Heian Jingū in 1940
komei.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki)
komei.note_full: A historical emperor (the 121st; 1831–1866). The official site explains that he is the emperor who laid the foundations of the Meiji Restoration in the difficult final years of the shogunate, and he was co-enshrined at Heian Jingū in 1940 (Shōwa 15). A figure later than the age of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, he does not appear in them.

nakatsuhime.name: Nakatsuhime-no-Mikoto
nakatsuhime.note: Empress of Emperor Ōjin, co-enshrined at Kagoshima Jingū
nakatsuhime.kojiki_name: Nakatsuhime-no-Mikoto (the original text writes 中日賣命)
nakatsuhime.nihonshoki_where: Book 10, Emperor Ōjin, 2nd year, spring, 3rd month

scenes.title: One of the three sisters Emperor Ōjin married
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called "Emperor Ōjin"
scenes.text: The Kojiki records that Emperor Ōjin married the three daughters of Homuda-no-Mawaka-no-Miko (Takagi-no-Irihime-no-Mikoto, Nakatsuhime-no-Mikoto and Otohime-no-Mikoto), and lists as the children of Nakatsuhime-no-Mikoto Ki-no-Arata-no-Iratsume, Ōsazaki-no-Mikoto and Netori-no-Mikoto.

scenes.title: Made empress
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 10, Emperor Ōjin, 2nd year, spring, 3rd month
scenes.text: The Nihon Shoki records that in the 2nd year of Emperor Ōjin, Nakatsuhime was made empress, and that Princess Arata, Emperor Ōsazaki and Prince Netori were born. Her elder sister Takagi-no-Irihime and younger sister Otohime are made consorts.

nakatsuhime.note_full: The official site of Kagoshima Jingū says that the co-enshrinement hall enshrines 'Nakatsuhime-no-Mikoto (empress of Emperor Ōjin)'. The Kojiki records her as one of three sisters but does not explicitly call her 'great consort' (within the range of the obtained text). The Nihon Shoki makes her empress. No deity ID has been made for her father, Homuda-no-Mawaka-no-Miko.

akihayatama.name: Akihayatamao-no-Mikoto
akihayatama.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by searching the obtained Parts 1 and 2 / to be confirmed)
akihayatama.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by searching the obtained books / to be confirmed)

scenes.title: Appointed kuni-no-miyatsuko of Aki (Sendai Kuji Hongi)
scenes.where: Sendai Kuji Hongi, Book 10, Kokuzō Hongi (not the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki)
scenes.text: The Kokuzō Hongi records that in the reign of the Shiga-no-Takaanaho court (the time of Emperor Seimu), Akihayatama-no-Mikoto, a fifth-generation descendant of Ame-no-Yutsuhiko-no-Mikoto, was appointed kuni-no-miyatsuko of Aki. This account is not found in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki.

akihayatama.note_full: Deity of Hayatani Jinja. The name is not found in the texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki; the only place the name could be confirmed is the Kokuzō Hongi of the Sendai Kuji Hongi (a book separate from the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki). Treated as a different deity from Hayatama-no-O-no-Kami of Kumano Hayatama Taisha (ID hayatamano).

samukawahiko.name: Samukawahiko-no-Mikoto
samukawahiko.note: Guardian deity of happō-yoke at Samukawa Jinja
aliases: Samukawa Daimyōjin (collective name for the two deities Samukawahiko-no-Mikoto and Samukawahime-no-Mikoto)
samukawahiko.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by text search / to be confirmed)
samukawahiko.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by text search / to be confirmed)
virtues: Said to be the guardian deity of happō-yoke and hōi-yoke (protection from misfortune from all directions), removing evil and calamity and bringing good fortune (explanation on the official site of Samukawa Jinja)
samukawahiko.note_full: One of the deities of Samukawa Jinja. The official site says that together with Samukawahime-no-Mikoto he is revered as Samukawa Daimyōjin, and explains him as the deity who developed the Kantō region, centred on Sagami Province, and opened up and guided the foundations of people's lives. The word 'Samukawa' was not found in the obtained Kojiki Parts 1 and 2, Nihon Shoki Books 1–3 and 14, or the Kogo Shūi, and his place in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki cannot be confirmed (other sources such as the Fudoki and Engishiki are not checked). The relation to Samukawahime-no-Mikoto (whether they are regarded as a married pair) is not stated on the official site, and is not written in relations.

samukawahime.name: Samukawahime-no-Mikoto
samukawahime.note: Guardian deity of happō-yoke at Samukawa Jinja
aliases: Samukawa Daimyōjin (collective name for the two deities Samukawahiko-no-Mikoto and Samukawahime-no-Mikoto)
samukawahime.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by text search / to be confirmed)
samukawahime.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by text search / to be confirmed)
virtues: Said to be the guardian deity of happō-yoke and hōi-yoke (protection from misfortune from all directions), removing evil and calamity and bringing good fortune (explanation on the official site of Samukawa Jinja)
samukawahime.note_full: One of the deities of Samukawa Jinja. Together with Samukawahiko-no-Mikoto she is revered as Samukawa Daimyōjin. As with Samukawahiko-no-Mikoto, the name does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki, and other sources such as the Fudoki are not checked.

masakado.name: Taira no Masakado-no-Mikoto
masakado.note: Deity of the third shrine of Kanda Jinja
aliases: Masakado-sama (name used on the official site of Kanda Jinja)
masakado.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki. A figure of the Heian period)
masakado.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki. A figure of the Heian period)
virtues: Revered as a deity of removing calamity and protection from misfortune (explanation on the official site of Kanda Jinja)
masakado.note_full: Deity of the third shrine (San-no-miya) of Kanda Jinja. The official site records that he was enshrined in 1309 (Enkyō 2), temporarily moved in 1874 (Meiji 7) to the auxiliary Masakado Jinja, and enshrined again in the main sanctuary in 1984 (Shōwa 59), and describes him as 'one who, as a forerunner of the warriors in the Jōhei and Tengyō eras, sought political reform in the Kantō and protected the people at the cost of his life'. A real figure of the Heian period, not a deity of the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki. The official site records that the Masakado-zuka (a Tokyo Metropolitan designated cultural property), where Masakado's head is enshrined, is in Ōtemachi.

minashinokami.name: Minashi-no-Ōkami
minashinokami.note: Central deity of Hida, lord of water
aliases: Hida-no-Kunitama-no-Kami (the official site says 'there is a theory')
minashinokami.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed because the word 'Minashi' was not found by searching the obtained Parts 1 and 2 / Part 3 is not searched, so to be confirmed)
minashinokami.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki either; confirmed by searching the obtained books (Books 1–7, 9, 10 and 14) / other books are not searched, so to be confirmed)
virtues: The official site of Minashi Jinja writes that he is revered as the lord of water and Sakugami-sama (ancestral deity of agriculture, guardian deity of livestock and sericulture, guardian deity of long life)

The official site lists good health, good fortune and protection from misfortune, household safety, prosperity in business, abundant harvests, traffic safety, travel safety, the blessing of children, safe childbirth and child-rearing (as a deity of child protection and water distribution)
minashinokami.note_full: The official site of Minashi Jinja (Hida Ichinomiya) explains that Minashi-no-Ōkami is the central deity of Hida and is thought to also have the character of the kunitama (land-spirit) deity of Hida. The sacred mountain Mt. Kurai is the watershed dividing the Miya River (to the Sea of Japan) from the Hida River (to the Pacific), and the deity has been revered as the 'Minushi-no-Kami' (lord of water) who grants the blessings of water. The official site writes that there are two theories on the origin of the word 'Minashi': that it changed from 'minushi' (lord of water) and that it changed from 'minashi' written as 'formed by water'. There is a theory that the chief deity Mitoshi-no-Ōkami is Minashi-no-Ōkami, and a theory that it is a collective name for 15 deities. As the name does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki, no relation to their deities is written.

ootoshi.name: Ōtoshi-no-Kami
ootoshi.note: Child of Susanoo; co-enshrined at Minashi Jinja
aliases: Ōtoshi-no-Ōkami (spelling used for the co-enshrined deity at Minashi Jinja)
ootoshi.kojiki_name: Ōtoshi-no-Kami (the original text writes 大年神)
ootoshi.kojiki_where: Part 1, section commonly called "the Genealogy of Susanoo-no-Mikoto"
ootoshi.nihonshoki_name: (Not found by searching the obtained text of the Nihon Shoki / to be confirmed)

scenes.title: Child of Susanoo-no-Mikoto and Kamuōichi-hime
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called "the Genealogy of Susanoo-no-Mikoto"
scenes.text: The Kojiki records that Susanoo-no-Mikoto married Kamuōichi-hime, daughter of Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami, and that two deities, Ōtoshi-no-Kami and Ukanomitama, were born.

scenes.title: The children of Ōtoshi-no-Kami
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called "the Genealogy of Susanoo-no-Mikoto"
scenes.text: The Kojiki records that Ōtoshi-no-Kami married Inohime, daughter of Kamu-Ikusubi-no-Kami, and bore Ōkunimitama-no-Kami, Karakami, Sohori-no-Kami, Shirahi-no-Kami and Hijiri-no-Kami, and further bore Ōkaguyamatomi-no-Kami and Mitoshi-no-Kami with Kaguyohime, and counts the children of Ōtoshi-no-Kami as sixteen deities in all.

ootoshi.note_full: The official site of Minashi Jinja lists 'Ōtoshi-no-Ōkami' among the co-enshrined deities. Whether this corresponds to the Ōtoshi-no-Kami of the Kojiki is not stated on the official site (to be confirmed). The Kojiki's 'Ōkunimitama-no-Kami' is a child of Ōtoshi-no-Kami and is treated as a different deity from the 'Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Ōkami' of Ōyamato Jinja (the Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Kami of the Nihon Shoki).

mitoshi.name: Mitoshi-no-Kami
mitoshi.note: Deity of the fields and the year's harvest
aliases: Mitoshi-no-Ōkami (spelling 御歳大神 used at Minashi Jinja)
Mitoshi-no-Ōkami (spelling 御年大神 used at Ōyamato Jinja and Minashi Jinja)
Toshimikami (spelling 年御神 in the collated text of the Kojiki)
Toshigami (written 歳神 or 年神; other names at Minashi Jinja)
mitoshi.kojiki_name: Toshimikami (spelling 年御神 in the obtained collated text. Generally written 御年神, Mitoshi-no-Kami)
mitoshi.kojiki_where: Part 1, section commonly called "the Genealogy of Susanoo-no-Mikoto" (entry on the children of Ōtoshi-no-Kami)
mitoshi.nihonshoki_name: (Not found by searching the obtained text of the Nihon Shoki / to be confirmed)

scenes.title: Child of Ōtoshi-no-Kami and Kaguyohime
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called "the Genealogy of Susanoo-no-Mikoto"
scenes.text: The Kojiki records that Ōtoshi-no-Kami married Kaguyohime and that two deities, Ōkaguyamatomi-no-Kami and Toshimikami (Mitoshi-no-Kami), were born.

virtues: The official site of Ōyamato Jinja explains him as the deity who protects the fields and brings the grain to ripen, and makes the Otaue Festival on 10 February the annual festival of Mitoshi-no-Ōkami

The official site of Minashi Jinja lists, for the chief deity Mitoshi-no-Ōkami (Toshigami), the divine virtues of granting each year's happiness, prosperity and good harvest (good fortune and protection from misfortune, household safety, prosperity in business, abundant harvests)
mitoshi.note_full: Neither the official site of Minashi Jinja (chief deity Mitoshi-no-Ōkami) nor that of Ōyamato Jinja (Mitoshi-no-Ōkami) states the deity's name as given in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki. He is generally explained as the same deity as 'Mitoshi-no-Kami', the child of Ōtoshi-no-Kami in the Kojiki, but it is not confirmed whether the official sites say so (to be confirmed). The name is not found in the obtained text of the Nihon Shoki.

yamatookunitama.name: Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Ōkami
aliases: Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Kami (Nihon Shoki, written 倭大国魂神)
Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Kami (Nihon Shoki, written 日本大国魂神)
Ōtokonushi-no-Ōkami (explanation on the official site of Ōyamato Jinja)
yamatookunitama.kojiki_name: (The name 'Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Kami' does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by searching the obtained Parts 1 and 2. A different deity, 'Ōkunimitama-no-Kami' (child of Ōtoshi-no-Kami), appears in Part 1 / Part 3 is not searched, so to be confirmed)
yamatookunitama.nihonshoki_name: Yamato-Ōkunitama (in the text of the Sujin chronicle written variously as 倭大國魂, 日本大國魂神 and 倭大國魂神)

scenes.title: Enshrined in the palace alongside Amaterasu-Ōmikami
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 5, Emperor Sujin, 6th year
scenes.text: The Nihon Shoki records that in the 6th year of Emperor Sujin the two deities Amaterasu-Ōmikami and Yamato-Ōkunitama had been enshrined together inside the emperor's great hall, but the emperor feared the power of the deities and was uneasy living together with them.

scenes.title: Entrusted to Nunakiirihime to enshrine
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 5, Emperor Sujin, 6th year
scenes.text: The Nihon Shoki records that Amaterasu-Ōmikami was entrusted to Toyosukiirihime-no-Mikoto and enshrined at Kasanui Village in Yamato, and Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Kami was entrusted to Nunakiirihime-no-Mikoto to enshrine, but Nunakiirihime-no-Mikoto lost her hair and grew thin and could not perform the rites.

scenes.title: Ichishi no Nagaochi appointed as priest
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 5, Emperor Sujin, 7th and 8th years
scenes.text: The Nihon Shoki records that, by instruction in a dream, it was told that if Ōtataneko were made priest of Ōmononushi-no-Ōkami and Ichishi no Nagaochi priest of Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Kami, the realm would be at peace, and that in the 8th year Nagaochi was appointed priest.

scenes.title: 'Ōyamato-no-Ōkami' in a variant account in the Suinin chronicle
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 6, Emperor Suinin, 25th year, 3rd month (a variant account)
scenes.text: In a variant account in the Suinin chronicle, Yamato-no-Ōkami possessed Ōmikuchi-no-Sukune and admonished that the rites of the previous emperor had been insufficient; divination was made as to whom to have enshrine Ōyamato-no-Ōkami, and Nunaki-Wakahime-no-Mikoto was ordered, but her body weakened and she could not perform the rites, so Nagaochi-no-Sukune, ancestor of the Yamato no Atai, was made to perform them. Whether this refers to the same deity as Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Kami cannot be determined from the text.

virtues: The official site of Ōyamato Jinja explains that envoys to Tang China visited this shrine before departure to pray for safe travel
yamatookunitama.note_full: The official site of Ōyamato Jinja explains Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Ōkami as Ōtokonushi-no-Ōkami, and links the founding to the entry of the 6th year of Emperor Sujin (the official site writes 'it is handed down'). The Kojiki does not have this name. The relation to 'Ōkunitama-no-Kami' (existing ID okunitama), which a variant account of the Nihon Shoki gives as another name of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, and to the Ōkunitama-no-Kami that the Kogo Shūi lists as one name of Ōnamuchi-no-Kami with the note 'the present Ōmiwa-no-Kami of Shikijō District, Yamato Province', cannot be settled from the texts of the Kojiki, Nihon Shoki and Kogo Shūi, and the shrine's official site does not address this point either (to be confirmed). For that reason a separate ID was made.

oshikuma.name: Oshikuma-no-Miko
oshikuma.note: Prince of Emperor Chūai enshrined at Tsurugi Jinja
oshikuma.kojiki_name: Oshikuma-no-Miko (the original text writes 忍熊王)
oshikuma.kojiki_where: Part 2, sections commonly called "Emperor Chūai" and "Empress Jingū" (the rebellion of Kagosaka-no-Miko and Oshikuma-no-Miko)
oshikuma.nihonshoki_where: Book 9, Empress Jingū, 1st year of the regency

scenes.title: Child of Emperor Chūai
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called "Emperor Chūai"
scenes.text: The Kojiki records that Emperor Tarashinakatsuhiko (Emperor Chūai) married Ōnakatsuhime-no-Mikoto, daughter of Ōe-no-Miko, and that two children, Kagosaka-no-Miko and Oshikuma-no-Miko, were born.

scenes.title: Defeated by Empress Jingū and goes into the sea
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called "Empress Jingū"
scenes.text: When Empress Jingū returned from Tsukushi to Yamato, Kagosaka-no-Miko and Oshikuma-no-Miko raised an army to lie in wait. Even after Kagosaka-no-Miko was eaten by a boar during a hunting divination, Oshikuma-no-Miko advanced his army, but, the Kojiki records, he was driven into a corner and went into the sea with Isahi-no-Sukune and died.

scenes.title: Sinks at the Seta crossing
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 9, Empress Jingū, 1st year of the regency
scenes.text: The Nihon Shoki records that Oshikuma-no-Miko was deceived and defeated by the army of Takenouchi-no-Sukune and others, and, with no way of escape, sank with Isachi-no-Sukune at the Seta crossing and died.

oshikuma.note_full: The official site of Tsurugi Jinja writes that Oshikuma-no-Miko was the second prince of Emperor Chūai and that the shrine records tell he built the shrine in gratitude for governing this region (Koshi) through the divine power of Tsurugi-no-Ōkami. This story of pacifying Koshi is not in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki (a separate tradition). In the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki he is depicted as the rebel prince defeated and killed by Empress Jingū. In the Kojiki his mother is Ōnakatsuhime-no-Mikoto, but no deity ID has been made for the mother.

miyoshiookami.name: Miyoshi-no-Ōkami
miyoshiookami.note: Deity of strength, victory and success
aliases: Miyoshi-no-Ōkami (spelling 三吉大神 on the shrine's stone monuments and elsewhere)
miyoshiookami.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; checked against the original text at hand / to be confirmed)
miyoshiookami.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; checked against the original text at hand / to be confirmed)
virtues: Deity of strength and of contests
Victory and success, prosperity in business
miyoshiookami.note_full: The official site of Taiheizan Miyoshi Jinja describes Miyoshi-no-Ōkami as 'a guardian deity born in Akita', and records the tradition that Fujiwara Tsurujumaru Miyoshi, lord of Taihei Castle, renounced the world and secluded himself on Mt. Taihei, trained in deep faith in Ōnamuchi-no-Ōkami and Sukunahikona-no-Kami, gained strength and came to be enshrined as a deity: a local deity. He is held to be a deity of strength, of contests, and of crushing evil and revealing the right. A deity of Akita tradition who does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki.

toyokiirihiko.name: Toyokiirihiko-no-Mikoto
toyokiirihiko.note: Founder of Utsunomiya, deity of good fortune
aliases: Toyokiirihiko-no-Mikoto (Kojiki, written 豊木入日子命)
Toyoki-no-Mikoto (Nihon Shoki, spelling in the 48th year of the Sujin chronicle)
toyokiirihiko.kojiki_where: Part 2, section commonly called "Emperor Sujin" (consorts and children)
toyokiirihiko.nihonshoki_name: Toyokiirihiko-no-Mikoto (Sujin chronicle, 1st year) / Toyoki-no-Mikoto (Sujin chronicle, 48th year)

scenes.title: Listed as a child of Emperor Sujin
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called "Emperor Sujin"
scenes.text: Toyokiirihiko-no-Mikoto is listed as a child born to Emperor Sujin by Tōtsu-Ayumemakuwashi-hime, daughter of the kuni-no-miyatsuko of Ki. Later, in the list of children, a note makes him the ancestor of the Kamitsukeno no Kimi, the Shimotsukeno no Kimi and others.

scenes.title: Rules the eastern provinces by dream divination
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 5, Emperor Sujin, 48th year
scenes.text: Emperor Sujin could not decide which of his sons, the elder Toyoki-no-Mikoto or the younger Ikume-no-Mikoto (later Emperor Suinin), should succeed him, so he had the two dream and divined by their dreams. Toyoki-no-Mikoto reported a dream of climbing Mt. Mimoro and brandishing spear and sword toward the east; Ikume-no-Mikoto reported a dream of stretching ropes on all four sides and chasing away sparrows. The emperor judged that the elder should rule the eastern provinces.

scenes.title: Rules the eastern provinces and becomes founder of the Kamitsukeno no Kimi and Shimotsukeno no Kimi
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 5, Emperor Sujin, 48th year
scenes.text: Ikume-no-Mikoto was made crown prince, and Toyoki-no-Mikoto was to rule the eastern provinces. The Nihon Shoki makes him the founding ancestor of the Kamitsukeno no Kimi and the Shimotsukeno no Kimi.

virtues: Good fortune (the official site of Utsunomiya Futaarayama Jinja writes 'his divine virtue is said to bring good fortune…')
Prayers for victory in battle (the same official site writes 'he has also been revered as a deity of prayers for victory in battle')
toyokiirihiko.note_full: In the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki he is recorded as a prince (a person) of Emperor Sujin, not a deity of myth. The official site of Utsunomiya Futaarayama Jinja says it enshrines him as the founder of Utsunomiya, who developed Keno Province (present-day Tochigi and Gunma Prefectures) and encouraged industry. The Nihon Shoki, in the 1st year of the Sujin chronicle, records 'bore Toyokiirihiko-no-Mikoto' as the child of the consort Tōtsu-Ayumemakuwashi-hime.

tokugawaieyasu.name: Tokugawa Ieyasu (Tōshō Daigongen)
tokugawaieyasu.note: Deified founder of the Edo shogunate
tokugawaieyasu.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki. A historical figure, born 1542 (Tenbun 11), died 1616 (Genna 2))
tokugawaieyasu.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki)
virtues: Deity of peace and compassion (wording in the prayer guide on the official site of Kunōzan Tōshōgū)
tokugawaieyasu.note_full: Not in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki. A historical figure who founded the Edo shogunate, enshrined after his death with the divine title 'Tōshō Daigongen' (according to the chronology on the official site of Kunōzan Tōshōgū, the divine title and the Senior First Rank were granted in 1617 (Genna 3)). He has no connection to the myths or divine genealogies of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.

omonoimi.name: Ōmonoimi-no-Kami
omonoimi.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by searching the obtained texts of Parts 1, 2 and 3 / to be confirmed)
omonoimi.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by searching the texts that could be obtained / some books may not be complete, so to be confirmed)
omonoimi.note_full: An encyclopedia (Wikipedia) says this is a deity who does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki and about whom much is unclear, and that works such as the Dainihonkoku Ichinomiya-ki identify the deity with Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto (the original sources are not checked; to be confirmed). For the deity's name, a Yamagata Prefecture tourism site gives the enshrined deity as 'Ōmonoimi-no-Ōkami', while the text of the 'Enshrined Deity' page on the official site of Chōkaisan Ōmonoimi Jinja does not give the name.

amenohiboko.name: Ame-no-Hiboko-no-Mikoto
amenohiboko.note: Prince of Silla, deity of Izushi Jinja
amenohiboko.kojiki_where: Part 2, Emperor Ōjin, section commonly called "Ame-no-Hiboko"
amenohiboko.nihonshoki_where: Book 6, Emperor Suinin, 3rd year, spring, 3rd month (including a variant account)

scenes.title: Ame-no-Hiboko stays in Tajima
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called "Ame-no-Hiboko"
scenes.text: Ame-no-Hiboko, son of the ruler of Silla, crossed over in pursuit of his wife who had fled, but was blocked by the deity of the Naniwa crossing and could not go on; he returned to Tajima Province and stayed there, married the daughter of Matao of that land, and his descendants continued.

scenes.title: The prince of Silla comes
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 6, Emperor Suinin, 3rd year, spring, 3rd month
scenes.text: Ame-no-Hiboko, prince of Silla, came to the court, and the articles he brought were stored in Tajima Province and always treated as sacred objects.

scenes.title: The brought treasures stored in Tajima as sacred objects
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 6, Emperor Suinin, 3rd year, spring, 3rd month
scenes.text: The brought treasures were stored in Tajima Province, and among them were a small sword and a spear bearing the name 'Izushi'. A connection with the name of Izushi Jinja is surmised, but the Nihon Shoki does not describe the founding of the shrine.

amenohiboko.note_full: The official site of Izushi Jinja explains that Ame-no-Hiboko-no-Mikoto is revered as the deity who opened the rocky hills at the mouth of the Maruyama River to reveal the Tajima plain, and who left achievements in flood control and the promotion of industry (the official site also calls him 'the deity of civil engineering'). These achievements in development are not written in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki.

izushiyamae.name: Izushi-Yamae-no-Ōkami
izushiyamae.note: Deity of Izushi Jinja, the eight treasures
izushiyamae.kojiki_where: Part 2, Emperor Ōjin, section commonly called "Ame-no-Hiboko"
izushiyamae.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear as a deity name. The entry for the 3rd year of Emperor Suinin on the seven brought articles (eight in a variant account))
izushiyamae.nihonshoki_where: Book 6, Emperor Suinin, 3rd year, spring, 3rd month

scenes.title: The eight treasures Ame-no-Hiboko brought across
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, section commonly called "Ame-no-Hiboko"
scenes.text: The treasures Ame-no-Hiboko brought across were eight in kind: two strings of beads, two kinds each of scarves (hire) for waves and for wind, the mirror of the offing and the mirror of the shore; the small note makes these Izushi-no-Yamae-no-Ōkami. In the story that follows, his daughter Izushi-otome-no-Kami appears.

izushiyamae.note_full: The deity page on the official site of Izushi Jinja gives only the deity name 'Izushi-Yamae-no-Ōkami', and the obtained page has no explanation about the eight sacred treasures. The correspondence with the small note in the Kojiki is a confirmation from the text of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, not the official site's explanation (to be confirmed).

takaokami.name: Takaokami-no-Kami
takaokami.note: Water deity, dragon deity of rain
aliases: Takaokami-no-Kami (Kojiki spelling 高淤加美神; not confirmed in the text of the Kojiki)
takaokami.kojiki_name: (The spellings 高龗 and 高淤加美 are not confirmed in the Kojiki; to be confirmed. Kuraokami-no-Kami appears in the same scene)
takaokami.kojiki_where: Part 1, section commonly called "the Birth of the Deities" (Kuraokami-no-Kami; whether the same deity is to be confirmed)
takaokami.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 5, a variant account (the variant account in which the fire deity is cut down; the number of the variant account is to be confirmed)

scenes.title: A piece of the slain fire deity becomes the deity (Nihon Shoki)
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 5, a variant account
scenes.text: It is told that when Izanagi-no-Mikoto cut the fire deity Kagutsuchi into three pieces, one piece became the thunder deity, one became Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami, and one became Takaokami.

scenes.title: Kuraokami-no-Kami formed from the blood on the sword hilt (Kojiki, for reference)
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called "the Birth of the Deities"
scenes.text: In the Kojiki, from the blood on the hilt of the sword with which Izanagi-no-Mikoto cut down the fire deity, Kuraokami-no-Kami and Kuramitsuha-no-Kami are formed. The relation to Takaokami-no-Kami is not mentioned on the official site and has not been confirmed here either.

takaokami.note_full: The official site of Ōyama Afuri Jinja explains that this is a water deity recorded in the Nihon Shoki, said to be a dragon deity ('taka' meaning mountain and 'okami' meaning dragon), worshipped since ancient times as a deity of praying for rain and for its cessation, and also called Kotengu (the Lesser Tengu) at Ōyama (the explanation of divine virtues is the shrine's belief, not a description from the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki). As there is no existing ID for the fire deity Kagutsuchi-no-Kami, he is not included in relations.

ooikazuchi.name: Ōikazuchi-no-Kami
ooikazuchi.note: Thunder deity, protection from fire and theft
ooikazuchi.kojiki_where: Part 1, section commonly called "the Land of Yomi" (one of the eight thunder deities)
ooikazuchi.nihonshoki_where: Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 5, a variant account (the scene in the Land of Yomi; the number of the variant account is to be confirmed)

scenes.title: The thunder on his wife's head in the Land of Yomi
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, section commonly called "the Land of Yomi"
scenes.text: When Izanagi-no-Mikoto lit a light in the Land of Yomi and looked inside the hall, eight thunder deities were on the body of Izanami-no-Mikoto, and the one on her head was Ōikazuchi.

scenes.title: Among the eight thunders, the thunder on the neck (Nihon Shoki)
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, Age of the Gods Part 1, Section 5, a variant account
scenes.text: A variant account of the Nihon Shoki also lists the eight thunders on various parts of the body, and makes the one on the neck Ōikazuchi.
