ooikazuchi.note_full: The official site of Ōyama Afuri Jinja calls him 'the thunder deity recorded in the Nihon Shoki', and explains that he has been worshipped since ancient times as a deity of protection from fire and theft, and is also called Ōtengu (the Great Tengu) at Ōyama. Because the official site does not indicate which passage of the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki, whether he is the same deity as the 'Ōikazuchi' of the eight thunders is to be confirmed. In the texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki he is told of as a thunder dwelling in the body of Izanami-no-Mikoto, and no parent–child relation is stated.

hikohohodemi.name: Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto
hikohohodemi.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'Umisachihiko and Yamasachihiko'
hikohohodemi.nihonshoki_where: Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 10 (Umisachi and Yamasachi)

scenes.title: The younger brother who takes the game of the mountains
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Umisachihiko and Yamasachihiko'
scenes.text: The elder brother Hoderi-no-Mikoto was in charge of the bounty of the sea and the younger brother Hoori-no-Mikoto of the bounty of the mountains. Later they exchanged tools, and this leads to the tale of going to the palace of the sea deity.

scenes.title: Takes the sea deity's daughter as his wife
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 10 (Umisachi and Yamasachi)
scenes.text: After finding the lost fishhook, Hohodemi-no-Mikoto took Toyotama-hime, the daughter of the sea deity, as his wife.

scenes.title: Dwells in the Takachiho Palace
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the end (the genealogy of Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto)
scenes.text: It records that Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto dwelt in the Takachiho Palace and that his mausoleum is also west of Mt. Takachiho.

hikohohodemi.note_full: In the Nihon Shoki main text the elder brother is written Honosusori-no-Mikoto, and in a variant account Honosuseri-no-Mikoto. The Nihon Shoki says that after his death Hohodemi-no-Mikoto was buried in the mausoleum on Mt. Takaya in Hyūga (Takaya-no-yama-no-ue no Misasagi).

toyotama.name: Toyotama-hime
toyotama.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'Umisachihiko and Yamasachihiko'
toyotama.nihonshoki_where: Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 10 (Umisachi and Yamasachi)

scenes.title: Gives birth to a child by the sea
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 10
scenes.text: At the birth, Toyotama-hime asked her husband, 'Please do not look', but he peeped and saw her in the form of a dragon; ashamed, she returned to the land of the sea.

scenes.title: Daughter of the sea deity
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Umisachihiko and Yamasachihiko'
scenes.text: Their meeting began when a maidservant of Toyotama-bime, the daughter of the sea deity, found Hoori-no-Mikoto, who had climbed the tree beside the well of the palace of the sea deity.

toyotama.note_full: Her father is the sea deity (no existing ID). Her younger sister is Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto.

mikenu.name: Mikeirino-no-Mikoto
mikenu.kojiki_where: Part 1, the end, the section known as 'The Birth of Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto'
mikenu.nihonshoki_where: Book 3, Emperor Kamuyamato-iwarehiko (Emperor Jinmu), the eastern expedition

scenes.title: Crosses to the Land of Tokoyo
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the end, the section known as 'The Birth of Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto'
scenes.text: It records that Mikenu-no-Mikoto, the elder brother of Emperor Jinmu, leapt over the waves and went to the Land of Tokoyo.

scenes.title: A storm during the eastern expedition
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 3, the eastern expedition of Emperor Jinmu
scenes.text: In the storm during the voyage to Kumano, Mikeirino-no-Mikoto, resenting that waves were raised though his mother and aunt were sea deities, trod on the waves and departed for the land of Tokoyo, it records.

mikenu.note_full: At Takachiho Jinja, the Jissha Daimyōjin are said to be Mikeirino-no-Mikoto, his wife Unome-hime-no-Mikoto and their eight children. The names of Unome-hime-no-Mikoto and the child deities were not found in the search range of the obtained texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (Kojiki Parts 1 and 2, Nihon Shoki Books 2 and 3), and cannot be confirmed in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. The relationship between the account of Mikeirino-no-Mikoto in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (crossing to Tokoyo) and the worship at Takachiho is not confirmed.

okunitama.name: Ōkunitama-no-Kami
okunitama.note: Land deity of Hokkaidō at Hokkaidō Jingū
aliases: Ōkunitama-no-Kami (variant account of the Nihon Shoki)
okunitama.kojiki_name: (The name 'Ōkunitama-no-Kami' does not appear in the Kojiki. 'Utsushikunitama-no-Kami', one of the other names of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami, does appear; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
okunitama.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'The Genealogy of Susanoo-no-Mikoto' (the passage on the five names of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami)
okunitama.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 8, variant account (a variant account listing the other names of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami; said to be the sixth; to be confirmed)

scenes.title: One of the other names of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 8, variant account
scenes.text: A variant account of the Nihon Shoki lists 'Ōkunitama-no-Kami' and 'Utsushikunitama-no-Kami' among the other names of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami.

scenes.title: 'Utsushikunitama-no-Kami' in the Kojiki
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'The Genealogy of Susanoo-no-Mikoto'
scenes.text: The Kojiki records that Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami has five names, including Ōanamuji-no-Kami, Ashihara-shikoo-no-Kami, Yachihoko-no-Kami and Utsushikunitama-no-Kami. The name 'Ōkunitama-no-Kami' does not appear.

okunitama.note_full: The official site of Hokkaidō Jingū counts Ōkunitama-no-Kami, as the 'deity of the land of Hokkaidō', as a deity separate from Ōnamuji-no-Kami (the same deity as Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami). In the Kojiki, Nihon Shoki and Kogo Shūi this is a name that appears as another name of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami (Ōnamuchi-no-Kami), and how the official site regards the relationship between the two is not confirmed from the official pages (to be confirmed). Yamato-no-Ōkunitama-no-Kami appears in the book of Emperor Sujin of the Nihon Shoki and elsewhere, but that book was not obtained this time (to be confirmed).

sukunahikona.name: Sukunahikona-no-Kami
sukunahikona.note: Partner of Ōanamuji-no-Kami in building the land
sukunahikona.kojiki_name: Sukunabikona-no-Kami (the original text uses variant characters)
sukunahikona.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'Sukunabikona (Ōkuninushi's Building of the Land)'
sukunahikona.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 8, variant account (said to be the sixth; to be confirmed)

scenes.title: His name is revealed as a child of Kamimusubi-no-Kami
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Sukunabikona'
scenes.text: Kuebiko answers the name of the small deity who came from beyond the sea: 'He is Sukunabikona-no-Kami, a child of Kamimusubi-no-Kami.' Kamimusubi-no-Kami acknowledges the child and commands him to become a brother of Ōanamuji-no-Kami and make the land firm.

scenes.title: Making and firming the land with Ōanamuji-no-Kami
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Sukunabikona'
scenes.text: The two deities, Ōanamuji-no-Kami (Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami) and Sukunabikona-no-Kami, made and firmed the land side by side, but later Sukunabikona-no-Kami crossed over to the Land of Tokoyo.

scenes.title: A variant account of the Nihon Shoki: managing the realm
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 8, variant account
scenes.text: A variant account records that Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto and Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto joined forces to manage the realm under heaven, and also fixed methods of curing illness for people and livestock.

sukunahikona.note_full: In the Kojiki he is a child of Kamimusubi-no-Kami, but since a deity ID for Kamimusubi-no-Kami was not made this time, the parent in relations was left empty. The official site of Hokkaidō Jingū describes Sukunahikona-no-Kami as a 'deity of land management, medicine and sake brewing', and at Dewa Sanzan Jinja he is regarded as one of the deities of Mt. Yudono.

shiotsuchi.name: Shiotsuchi-no-Oji-no-Kami
shiotsuchi.note: Said to have taught salt-making at Shiogama
aliases: Shiotsutsu-no-Oji (variant account of the Nihon Shoki)
shiotsuchi.kojiki_name: Shiotsuchi-no-Kami (regarding him as the same deity as Shiotsuchi-no-Oji is the generally accepted understanding, but this is not stated explicitly in the text obtained; to be confirmed)
shiotsuchi.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'Umisachi and Yamasachi'
shiotsuchi.nihonshoki_where: A variant account of Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 10 (Umisachi and Yamasachi); Book 3, the account before the accession of Emperor Jinmu. The name also appears in a variant account of section 9

scenes.title: Gives wisdom to the younger brother weeping by the sea
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Umisachi and Yamasachi'
scenes.text: Shiotsuchi-no-Kami comes to the younger brother Yamasachihiko, who is weeping by the sea after losing his elder brother's fishhook, asks the reason, makes a tightly woven small boat, and teaches him the way to the palace of the sea deity.

scenes.title: A variant account of the Nihon Shoki: appears as an old man
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 10, variant account
scenes.text: In a variant account, as Hohodemi-no-Mikoto wanders by the sea, Shiotsuchi-no-Oji appears, asks about his circumstances, says 'I will plan for you', and makes a small boat.

scenes.title: Tells of a good land in the east
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 3, the account before the accession of Emperor Jinmu
scenes.text: Speaking to his elder brothers and children, Emperor Jinmu says that he heard from Shiotsuchi-no-Oji that in the east there is a beautiful land surrounded by green mountains.

shiotsuchi.note_full: A variant account of section 9 of the Nihon Shoki writes that Kotokatsu-kunikatsu-no-Kami is a 'child of Izanagi-no-Mikoto, also named Shiotsuchi-no-Oji' (which variant account is to be confirmed). The official site of Shiogama Jinja says that Shiotsuchi-no-Oji-no-Kami remained at Shiogama and taught the people how to make salt, but this is not written in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.

tsukuyomi.name: Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto
aliases: Tsukuyumi-no-Mikoto (variant account of the Nihon Shoki)
tsukuyomi.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'Purification and the Three Noble Children'
tsukuyomi.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 5

scenes.title: Born when the right eye is washed
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Purification and the Three Noble Children'
scenes.text: When Izanagi-no-Mikoto purified himself, Amaterasu-Ōmikami was born as he washed his left eye, Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto as he washed his right eye, and Takehaya-Susanoo-no-Mikoto as he washed his nose.

scenes.title: Commanded to rule the realm of the night
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Purification and the Three Noble Children'
scenes.text: Izanagi-no-Mikoto divided the realms among the three noble children and commanded Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto to rule the world of the night.

scenes.title: Nihon Shoki main text: born as the moon deity
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 5, main text
scenes.text: The main text records that the moon deity was born next after the sun deity, and says that, because its radiance was second only to the sun's, it was sent to heaven to rule the heavens as a pair with the sun.

scenes.title: A variant account of the Nihon Shoki: slays Ukemochi-no-Kami
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 5, variant account
scenes.text: Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto, sent by Amaterasu-Ōmikami to Ukemochi-no-Kami in the Central Land of Reed Plains, was angered at being entertained with food brought out of the mouth and slew Ukemochi-no-Kami; Amaterasu-Ōmikami was angry, and it is told that from then on the two would live apart, in day and night.

tsukuyomi.note_full: The official site of Dewa Sanzan Jinja gives Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto as the deity of Mt. Gassan. The link between Mt. Gassan and Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto is not written in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (the word 'Gassan' is not in the texts obtained). The story of Ukemochi-no-Kami in a variant account of the Nihon Shoki is one of the variant accounts of section 5, and which one is to be confirmed.

idewa.name: Ideha-no-Kami
aliases: Ideha-no-Kami (spelling in the official history of the shrine; from a summary of search results)
Kunitama (land spirit) of Dewa Province (so called)
idewa.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
idewa.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the volumes of the Nihon Shoki obtained; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
idewa.note_full: A deity listed as enshrined at Dewa Sanzan Jinja (Dewa Jinja on Mt. Haguro). According to the official history of the shrine (a summary of search results), Prince Hachiko worshipped the appearance of Haguro-no-Ōkami and Ideha-no-Kami on Mt. Haguro. Because the deity does not appear in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, no scenes from them are attached. The relationship with the shrines of Dewa Province in the Engishiki register of shrines has not been checked this time.

kukurihime.name: Kukuri-hime-no-Kami
kukurihime.note: Appears only once, in the Nihon Shoki
kukurihime.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
kukurihime.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 5, variant account (the Yomotsu-hirasaka passage)

scenes.title: A statement at Yomotsu-hirasaka
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 5, variant account
scenes.text: At the scene where Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto, who had fled back from the Land of Yomi, argued, Kukuri-hime-no-Kami said something, and Izanagi-no-Mikoto approved it and withdrew. What she said is not written.

kukurihime.note_full: Her only appearance in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki is this one, and no genealogy is given. The identification with Shirayama-hime-no-Ōkami is a tradition of the shrines, such as Shirayama-hime Jinja.

tajikarao.name: Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Kami
tajikarao.note: Drew Amaterasu-Ōmikami out of the rock cave
tajikarao.kojiki_where: Part 1, the sections known as 'The Heavenly Rock Cave' and 'The Descent of the Heavenly Grandchild'
tajikarao.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 7 (the Heavenly Rock Door)

scenes.title: Opens the door of the Heavenly Rock Cave
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'The Heavenly Rock Cave'
scenes.text: When Amaterasu-Ōmikami shut herself in the rock cave, Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Kami stood hidden beside the door, took the hand of the Great Deity as she showed her face, and pulled her outside.

scenes.title: Accompanies the descent of the heavenly grandchild
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'The Descent of the Heavenly Grandchild'
scenes.text: Tajikarao-no-Kami is listed among the deities who descend with Ninigi-no-Mikoto, and it is recorded that this deity dwells in the Sanana district.

scenes.title: Stands beside the rock door
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 7
scenes.text: Tajikarao-no-Kami stood beside the rock door, and when the sun deity opened the door a little, he pulled her out by the hand.

tajikarao.note_full: In the Kogo Shūi too, Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Kami pulls the door open. He is the deity enshrined in the inner shrine (Okusha) of Togakushi Jinja, but the place name 'Togakushi' does not appear in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.

amenokaguyama.name: Ame-no-Kagoyama-no-Mikoto
aliases: Ame-no-Kagoyama-no-Mikoto (spelling in the Sendai Kuji Hongi; name used by the shrine)
amenokaguyama.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki as a person; confirmed by search / to be confirmed. 'Ame-no-Kaguyama' is the name of a mountain)
amenokaguyama.nihonshoki_where: Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9, variant account (a child of Ame-no-Hoakari-no-Mikoto)

scenes.title: Distant ancestor of the Owari no Muraji and others
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9, variant account
scenes.text: The name 'Ame-no-Kaguyama' is given as a child of Ame-no-Hoakari-no-Mikoto, and he is said to be a distant ancestor of the Owari no Muraji and others.

amenokaguyama.note_full: Regarding the 'Ame-no-Kaguyama' of the Nihon Shoki as the same deity as Ame-no-Kagoyama-no-Mikoto, the deity of Yahiko Jinja, is an identification by the shrine and by later ages and cannot be confirmed from the main text alone. The spelling 天香語山命 ('Ame-no-Kagoyama-no-Mikoto', with an extra character) is of the Sendai Kuji Hongi line and is not in the text used this time.

jinmu.name: Emperor Jinmu
jinmu.note: Led the eastern expedition; enthroned at Kashihara
aliases: Hikohohodemi (personal name in the Nihon Shoki)
jinmu.kojiki_name: Kamu-yamato-iwarebiko-no-Mikoto (the original text uses variant characters)
jinmu.kojiki_where: Part 2, the section known as 'Emperor Jinmu' (the eastern expedition; the Kashihara Palace at Unebi)
jinmu.nihonshoki_where: Book 3, Emperor Jinmu (the eastern expedition; accession at the Kashihara Palace)

scenes.title: Sets out east from Hyūga
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section known as 'Emperor Jinmu'
scenes.text: At the Takachiho Palace he consulted his elder brother Itsuse-no-Mikoto, and thinking that a land further east would be better for ruling the realm, he set out east from Hyūga.

scenes.title: Sets out on the eastern expedition with a fleet
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 3, Emperor Jinmu
scenes.text: The Nihon Shoki records that in the winter of the Kōin year (a year of the sexagenary cycle) the emperor led the princes east with a fleet of ships.

scenes.title: Accedes to the throne at the Kashihara Palace
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 3, Emperor Jinmu
scenes.text: In the first month of spring in the Shin'yū year he took the imperial throne at the Kashihara Palace and made that year the first year. Kashihara Jingū was founded in the Meiji era on the site where this palace stood.

scenes.title: Rules the realm from the Unebi no Kashihara Palace
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section known as 'Emperor Jinmu'
scenes.text: The Kojiki records that after subduing the unruly deities and driving away those who did not submit, he ruled the realm from the Unebi no Kashihara Palace. It is understood to refer to the same palace as the Kashihara Palace of the Nihon Shoki, but the spelling differs.

jinmu.note_full: His father and mother are Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto and Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto of the Kojiki (based on the entries of the existing deities). The official site of Kashihara Jingū records a reign of 76 years and a long life of 127 years, and notes that 'in the Kojiki he is 137', but this figure of 137 was not checked against the texts obtained this time.

himetatara.name: Himetatara-isuzu-hime-no-Mikoto
himetatara.kojiki_name: Hotodatara-isusuki-hime-no-Mikoto (also called Hime-tatara-isukeyori-hime; the original text uses variant characters)
himetatara.kojiki_where: Part 2, the section known as 'Emperor Jinmu' (the choosing of the empress)
himetatara.nihonshoki_name: Himetatara-isuzu-hime-no-Mikoto (the main text uses variant characters)
himetatara.nihonshoki_where: Book 3, Emperor Jinmu, the Kōshin year (the passage on establishing the principal consort)

scenes.title: The 'child of a deity' born from a red-painted arrow
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section known as 'Emperor Jinmu'
scenes.text: Ōmononushi-no-Kami of Miwa changed into a red-painted arrow and visited Seyadatara-hime, and the child born was Hotodatara-isusuki-hime-no-Mikoto. There is a note that she later changed her name because she disliked the word 'hoto'.

scenes.title: Becomes the principal consort of Emperor Jinmu
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 3, Emperor Jinmu
scenes.text: The Nihon Shoki introduces her as a beautiful princess born between Kotoshironushi-no-Kami and Tamakushi-hime, and records that the emperor made her his principal consort.

himetatara.note_full: Her father is told differently: Ōmononushi-no-Kami (existing ID omonushi) in the Kojiki, and Kotoshironushi-no-Kami (existing ID kotoshironushi) in the Nihon Shoki. The official site of Kashihara Jingū notes that 'Kotoshironushi-no-Kami corresponds to Ōmononushi-no-Kami in the Kojiki'. The relations follow the Kojiki.

mihotsuhime.name: Mihotsu-hime-no-Mikoto
mihotsuhime.note: Wife of Ōmononushi-no-Kami in the Nihon Shoki
mihotsuhime.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
mihotsuhime.nihonshoki_where: Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9, variant account (after the transfer of the land, the scene in which Takamimusubi-no-Mikoto gives his daughter to Ōmononushi-no-Kami as wife)

scenes.title: Becomes the wife of Ōmononushi-no-Kami
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9, variant account
scenes.text: To Ōmononushi-no-Kami, who submitted at the transfer of the land, Takamimusubi-no-Mikoto gave his own daughter Mihotsu-hime as wife, and sent him back to earth with the command to lead the eighty myriad deities and protect the imperial grandchild.

mihotsuhime.note_full: The Nihon Shoki states that her father is Takamimusubi-no-Mikoto, but because Takamimusubi-no-Mikoto is not among the existing deity IDs, parents was left empty. At Miho Jinja she is enshrined together with Kotoshironushi-no-Kami, but in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki she is the wife of Ōmononushi-no-Kami, and her relationship with Kotoshironushi-no-Kami is not written in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.

tatsuhihime.name: Tatsuhi-hime-no-Kami
tatsuhihime.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
tatsuhihime.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
tatsuhihime.note_full: A deity enshrined at Iwakiyama Jinja. The official site gives only the name of the deity, and no identification with any particular deity of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki is made here. The name was not found in the search range of the texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki obtained.

ugamenokami.name: Uga-no-Me-no-Kami
ugamenokami.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
ugamenokami.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
ugamenokami.note_full: A deity enshrined at Iwakiyama Jinja. The official site gives only the name of the deity. The name suggests Ukanomitama-no-Kami (existing ID ukanomitama), a deity of food, but it is not confirmed whether the official site regards them as the same deity, so they are not identified (to be confirmed).

sakanouekaritamaro.name: Sakanoue-no-Karitamaro-no-Mikoto
sakanouekaritamaro.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
sakanouekaritamaro.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
sakanouekaritamaro.note_full: A name that the official site gives as an enshrined deity of Iwakiyama Jinja. It appears to be the name of a person rather than a deity of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. The official site records that Sakanoue no Tamuramaro rebuilt the shrine buildings, but the relationship between Karitamaro and Tamuramaro is not confirmed on the official site (to be confirmed).

kanayamahiko.name: Kanayamahiko-no-Ōkami
kanayamahiko.note: Deity of iron ore and mining
kanayamahiko.kojiki_where: Part 1, the section known as 'The Birth of the Deities (the birth of Hinokagutsuchi-no-Kami and the death of Izanami-no-Mikoto)'
kanayamahiko.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 5, variant account

scenes.title: Born from the suffering of Izanami-no-Mikoto
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'The Birth of the Deities'
scenes.text: It records that Kanayamabiko-no-Kami and Kanayamabime-no-Kami were born from the vomit of Izanami-no-Mikoto, who fell ill after giving birth to the fire deity.

scenes.title: A birth recorded in a variant account
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 5, variant account
scenes.text: It records that Kanayamahiko was born from the vomit of Izanami-no-Mikoto, who writhed in agony as she gave birth to the fire deity.

scenes.title: Helps Emperor Jinmu's eastern expedition (shrine tradition)
scenes.where: Shrine tradition of Nangū Taisha (not an account of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki)
scenes.text: Nangū Taisha tells that Kanayamahiko-no-Ōkami showed his power by helping the Yatagarasu during Emperor Jinmu's eastern expedition. The name Kanayamahiko does not appear in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki accounts of the eastern expedition (within the range searched).

kanayamahiko.note_full: Nangū Taisha (in Gifu) makes him its chief deity as the deity governing iron ore and mines. The official site of Nangū Taisha says that it is said he came to be revered as the deity of iron ore and mines because the form in which he was born resembled flowing iron.

minono.name: Mino-no-Mikoto
minono.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
minono.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
minono.note_full: A name that the official site gives as an aidono (co-enshrined) deity of Nangū Taisha. It was not found in the search range of the texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki obtained, and which deity it corresponds to is not explained on the official history page (to be confirmed).

izasawake.name: Izasawake-no-Mikoto
aliases: Izasawake-no-Kami (variant account of the Nihon Shoki)
izasawake.kojiki_where: Part 2, the section known as 'Emperor Ōjin and Kehi-no-Ōkami (the exchange of names)'
izasawake.nihonshoki_where: Book 10, Emperor Ōjin, the interlinear note at the opening (an 'other account')

scenes.title: Appears in a dream and exchanges names with the child
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section known as 'Emperor Ōjin and Kehi-no-Ōkami'
scenes.text: When Takeuchi-no-Sukune took the crown prince and built a temporary palace at Tsunuga, Izasawake-no-Ōkami appeared in a dream and said he wished to exchange his own name with the child's name.

scenes.title: Given fish, and the name becomes Mikeutsu-no-Ōkami
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section known as 'Emperor Ōjin and Kehi-no-Ōkami'
scenes.text: Taking the dolphins that washed up on the beach as a gift from the deity, the child praised the deity as Mikeutsu-no-Ōkami. It records that this is the present Kehi-no-Ōkami.

scenes.title: An exchange of names recorded in a variant account
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 10, Emperor Ōjin, the interlinear note at the opening
scenes.text: As a variant account, it records that when the crown prince worshipped Kehi-no-Ōkami of Tsunuga in Koshi Province, the deity and the prince exchanged names. It also adds a note that the mix-up over the original name is 'unknown'.

virtues: Clothing, food and housing, safety at sea, agriculture and fishing, and traffic safety (the virtues listed by the official site of Kehi Jingū)
izasawake.note_full: The chief deity of Kehi Jingū. The official site records that the deity is traditionally said to have descended on the peak of Amazutsu more than two thousand years ago. The names handed down in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki are spelled differently, and the interlinear note of the Nihon Shoki says that the original name is 'unknown'.

chuai.name: Emperor Chūai
chuai.kojiki_where: Part 2, the section known as 'Emperor Chūai'
chuai.nihonshoki_where: Book 8 (not obtained in this survey); the account of his death is in Book 9, Empress Jingū, the account before the regency

scenes.title: The empress and her children
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 2, the section known as 'Emperor Chūai'
scenes.text: It records that Emperor Tarashinakatsuhiko made Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto his empress and had two children, Homuyawake-no-Mikoto and Ōtomowake-no-Mikoto (also called Homudawake-no-Mikoto).

scenes.title: Dies in Tsukushi
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 9, Empress Jingū, the account before the regency
scenes.text: It records that the emperor, who did not follow the instruction of the deity, died at the Kashihi Palace in Tsukushi.

virtues: Freedom from illness, long life and lasting success in battle (the virtues listed by the official site of Kehi Jingū)
chuai.note_full: One of the deities of Kehi Jingū. Descriptions of his parent (said to be Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto) were not confirmed in the main texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki in this survey (to be confirmed).

tamahime.name: Tamahime-no-Mikoto
tamahime.note: Sister of Empress Jingū, per Kehi Jingū
tamahime.kojiki_name: (Does not appear in the Kojiki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
tamahime.nihonshoki_name: (Does not appear in the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by search / to be confirmed)
virtues: Music and dance (the virtue listed by the official site of Kehi Jingū)
tamahime.note_full: One of the deities of Kehi Jingū. The official site records that she is a younger sister of Empress Jingū and travelled from Tsukushi following the empress, but this cannot be confirmed in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (within the range searched of the texts obtained). She has a different name from Toyotama-hime (existing ID toyotama) and is not identified with her.

amenoikutama.name: Ame-no-Ikutama-no-Mikoto
amenoikutama.note: Co-enshrined at Takase Jinja; reading to be confirmed
aliases: Ikutama-no-Kami (notation on the official Takase Jinja site)
amenoikutama.kojiki_name: (The term 天活玉 could not be found in Part 1 of the Kojiki; confirmed by text-string search / to be confirmed)
amenoikutama.nihonshoki_name: (The term 天活玉 could not be found in Books 1 and 2 of the Nihon Shoki; confirmed by text-string search / to be confirmed)
virtues: Believed to be a deity of good health and well-being and of long life (notation on the official Takase Jinja site)
amenoikutama.note_full: A co-enshrined deity of Takase Jinja. The official site explains that he is also called Ikutama-no-Kami, that he attended the heavenly grandson at the descent, and that he is a deity who gives life to people. When the author searched the text strings of Part 1 of the Kojiki and Books 1 and 2 of the Nihon Shoki, the term 天活玉 could not be found. The official page does not name any book as the source of this explanation. It may rest on texts other than the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, but this is not confirmed (the author's conjecture).

itakeru.name: Itakeru-no-Mikoto
itakeru.note: Deity of tree planting; reading to be confirmed
itakeru.kojiki_name: (The term 五十猛 could not be found in Part 1 of the Kojiki; confirmed by text-string search / to be confirmed)
itakeru.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 8, variant account (the number of the variant account is to be confirmed)

scenes.title: Descends carrying tree seeds as a child of Susanoo-no-Mikoto
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 8, variant account
scenes.text: Susanoo-no-Mikoto took his child Itakeru-no-Kami down to the land of Silla, and later crossed east in a clay boat and reached Izumo. When Itakeru-no-Kami descended he was carrying many kinds of tree seeds. He did not plant them in the Korean lands but brought them back, and beginning from Tsukushi he sowed them throughout the Ōyashima country and turned it into green mountains. For this reason Itakeru-no-Mikoto is regarded as a deity of merit, and a variant account of the Nihon Shoki says he is the great deity who dwells in Kii Province.

virtues: Believed to be a deity of agriculture, forestry and the promotion of industry, traffic safety, warding off misfortune and recovery from illness (notation on the official Takase Jinja site)
itakeru.note_full: A co-enshrined deity of Takase Jinja. The official site explains him as a deity of especially great virtue in tree-planting work. A variant account of the Nihon Shoki treats Itakeru, a child of Susanoo-no-Mikoto, as the deity who sowed tree seeds, but the Nihon Shoki does not write of any relation to Takase Jinja. Another variant account of the Nihon Shoki also records that three deities — Itakeru-no-Mikoto, a child of Susanoo-no-Mikoto, and his younger sisters Ōyatsu-hime-no-Mikoto and Tsumatsu-hime-no-Mikoto (written 採津姫命; reading to be confirmed) — divided the tree seeds and sowed them (the number of the variant account is to be confirmed).

takehazuchi.name: Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto
takehazuchi.note: Ancestral deity of Shitoribe; deity of weaving
aliases: Takehazuchi-no-Kami (notation in the Jinjachō entry for Shitori Jinja in Kurayoshi City)
takehazuchi.kojiki_name: (Not found in the critical text of Part 1 of the Kojiki / to be confirmed)
takehazuchi.nihonshoki_where: Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9, interlinear note to the main text ('another account')

scenes.title: Sent to the star deity who would not submit
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9, interlinear note to the main text ('another account')
scenes.text: The interlinear note records that after Futsunushi-no-Ōkami and Takemikazuchi-no-Ōkami had put the disobedient deities to death, only the star deity Kagaseo did not submit; when Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto, the Shitori-no-Kami, was added and sent, he submitted. The note attaches a reading gloss, written 斯圖梨俄未, to the name Shitori-no-Kami.

virtues: The official Shitori Jinja site records that he is enshrined as the ancestral deity of the Shitoribe (a deity of woven cloth) (official, 'About the Shrine')
takehazuchi.note_full: The official Shitori Jinja site calls Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto the ancestral deity of the Shitoribe and says he was added to the enshrined deities because of the woven cloth called shizuori (倭文). This explanation, 'ancestral deity of the Shitoribe', comes from the official site and the prefectural shrine association (Jinjachō); the interlinear note of the Nihon Shoki only writes 'Shitori-no-Kami'. The names Shitori-no-Kami and Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto are not found in the critical text of Part 1 of the Kojiki (confirmed by text search of the pages obtained). The spelling of the deity's name divides: the Nihon Shoki, the official site and the Jinjachō (Yurihama entry) write 建葉槌命 (Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto), while the Jinjachō's Kurayoshi City entry writes 武葉槌神 (Takehazuchi-no-Kami). His relation to Ame-no-Hazuchio-no-Kami (天羽槌雄神) is not confirmed.

shitateruhime.name: Shitateru-hime-no-Mikoto
shitateruhime.note: Deity of safe childbirth; wife of Ame-no-Wakahiko
aliases: Taka-hime-no-Mikoto and Shitateru-hime-no-Mikoto (Kojiki, in the passage on Ōkuninushi's daughter)
Taka-hime and Waka-kunitama (Nihon Shoki, alternative names)
shitateruhime.kojiki_name: Shitateru-hime (wife of Ame-no-Wakahiko) / Taka-hime-no-Mikoto (also called Shitateru-hime-no-Mikoto)
shitateruhime.kojiki_where: Part 1, the sections known as 'Ame-no-Wakahiko' and 'The Genealogy of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami'
shitateruhime.nihonshoki_where: Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9, main text

scenes.title: Daughter of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami and Takiri-bime
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'The Genealogy of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami'
scenes.text: It records that among the children born when Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami married Takiri-bime-no-Mikoto, the deity of the Okitsu-miya of Munakata, were Ajisukitakahikone-no-Mikoto and his younger sister Taka-hime-no-Mikoto (also called Shitateru-hime-no-Mikoto).

scenes.title: Becomes the wife of Ame-no-Wakahiko
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Ame-no-Wakahiko'
scenes.text: Ame-no-Wakahiko, who had descended to Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni, married Shitateru-hime, a daughter of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami, and did not report back even after eight years. Later, when Ame-no-Wakahiko died, the sound of Shitateru-hime's weeping is recorded as having reached heaven along with the wind.

scenes.title: The same scene in the Nihon Shoki
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9, main text
scenes.text: The Nihon Shoki records that Ame-no-Wakahiko married Shitateru-hime (also called Taka-hime and Waka-kunitama), the daughter of Utsushikunitama, and stayed there. It also records that after her husband died, the sound of Shitateru-hime's grief reached heaven.

virtues: Revered as a deity of safe childbirth (description on the official Shitori Jinja site)

The official Shitori Jinja site records that she is praised as a goddess gifted with both talent and beauty, and that a 'Kahori-bukuro' (scent bag) associated with her virtue is given out as an amulet
shitateruhime.note_full: The official Shitori Jinja site and the prefectural shrine association (Jinjachō) say that Shitateru-hime-no-Mikoto, a daughter of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami, came by sea from Izumo to this place after the transfer of the land. This account of her arrival is not found in Part 1 of the Kojiki and Book 2 of the Nihon Shoki that were consulted (shrine tradition). The Kojiki names Taka-hime-no-Mikoto (also called Shitateru-hime-no-Mikoto) as a daughter of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami, and uses the name Shitateru-hime for the wife of Ame-no-Wakahiko. Some regard the two as the same deity, but the text of the Kojiki does not say so explicitly (to be confirmed). The Nihon Shoki writes the father of Shitateru-hime as 'Utsushikunitama'. Whether Utsushikunitama is another name of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami is not confirmed in this entry (the father shown under relations is based on the Kojiki).

amenowakahiko.name: Ame-no-Wakahiko-no-Mikoto
amenowakahiko.nihonshoki_name: Ame-no-Wakahiko (abbreviated to 'Ame-waka' (天稚) in the main text of the critical text obtained)
amenowakahiko.nihonshoki_where: Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9, main text

scenes.title: Sent to Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Ame-no-Wakahiko'
scenes.text: Because Ame-no-Hohi-no-Kami did not return, Ame-no-Wakahiko, a child of Amatsukunitama-no-Kami, was given a bow and arrows and sent. Having descended, Ame-no-Wakahiko married Shitateru-hime, a daughter of Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami, and did not report back even after eight years.

scenes.title: Killed by the returned arrow
scenes.where: Kojiki, Part 1, the section known as 'Ame-no-Wakahiko'
scenes.text: The arrow with which he had shot dead the messenger pheasant reached Takaki-no-Kami (another name of Takamimusubi-no-Kami), was thrown back, and struck Ame-no-Wakahiko in the chest as he lay asleep, and he died. The Kojiki notes that this is the origin of the 'returned arrow' (kaeshi-ya).

scenes.title: The same scene in the Nihon Shoki
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (Age of the Gods, second part), section 9, main text
scenes.text: The Nihon Shoki records that Takamimusubi-no-Kami sent 'Ame-waka, the child of Ame-kunitama' as a trial, and that Ame-waka was struck by the returned arrow and died.

amenowakahiko.note_full: The official Shitori Jinja site only names Ame-no-Wakahiko-no-Mikoto as one of the enshrined deities; the pages obtained give no explanation of why he is enshrined. In the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki he appears as the husband of Shitateru-hime.

ukemochi.name: Ukemochi-no-Kami
ukemochi.note: One of the enshrined deities at Ōhirumemuchi Jinja
ukemochi.nihonshoki_where: Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 5, variant account (the number of the variant account is to be confirmed)

scenes.title: Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto is sent to Ukemochi-no-Kami
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 5, variant account
scenes.text: Amaterasu-Ōmikami heard that Ukemochi-no-Kami was in Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni and sent Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto to look in on the deity. Ukemochi-no-Kami received the guest by producing rice, fish and animals from the mouth, but Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto, angered at the uncleanness, struck Ukemochi-no-Kami dead with a sword.

scenes.title: Cattle, horses and grains are born from the body
scenes.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 (Age of the Gods, first part), section 5, variant account
scenes.text: From the body of the slain Ukemochi-no-Kami, cattle and horses came into being, and crops such as millet, silkworm cocoons, barnyard millet, rice, wheat and beans grew. When Ame-no-Kumahito took them back and presented them, Amaterasu-Ōmikami was pleased.

ukemochi.note_full: The shrine search of the Akita prefectural shrine association (Jinjachō) lists Ukemochi-no-Kami as one of the enshrined deities of Ōhirumemuchi Jinja (the official site does not list which twelve deities there are). Neither the Jinjachō nor the official site records this deity's virtues. The name in the Kojiki is not confirmed (to be confirmed).

kichijohime.name: Kichijō-hime-no-Mikoto
kichijohime.note: Deity of matchmaking, safe birth and women's protection
aliases: 桂子 (reading to be confirmed; the name before she entered court service, in the legend on the Dainichidō Bugaku Preservation Society site)
kichijohime.kojiki_name: To be confirmed (whether she appears in the Kojiki is not confirmed. The official site and the Jinjachō do not describe any relation to the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki)
kichijohime.nihonshoki_name: To be confirmed (whether she appears in the Nihon Shoki is not confirmed. The official site and the Jinjachō do not describe any relation to the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki)
virtues: Matchmaking, blessing with children, safe childbirth and protection of women (official explanation)
kichijohime.note_full: The official Ōhirumemuchi Jinja site records that Kichijō-hime-no-Mikoto has been enshrined as a deity of matchmaking, children, safe childbirth and protection of women, in connection with the legend of Danburi Chōja. In the official legend, the daughter of the wealthy couple went into court service and became a consort of Emperor Keitai; she changed her name to Kichijō-hime and bore the fifth prince, and at her wish a shrine to the deity 大日神 (reading to be confirmed) was built in the 17th year of Emperor Keitai. How she is treated in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki is not confirmed (to be confirmed).

ise.name: Ise Jingū (Naikū, Inner Shrine)
ise.summary: Formally called simply "Jingū". The Inner Shrine (Kōtai Jingū) enshrines Amaterasu-Ōmikami and the Outer Shrine (Toyouke Daijingū) enshrines Toyouke-no-Ōmikami. The light on the map marks the Inner Shrine.
ise.deity_note: Amaterasu-Ōmikami appears in the Kojiki in scenes such as the purification rites and the Heavenly Rock Cave. Toyouke-no-Ōmikami corresponds to the Kojiki's "Toyoukebime / Toyuuke-no-Kami" and is regarded as the deity of the Outer Shrine.
history: The Inner Shrine is said to have been established about 2,000 years ago, in the reign of Emperor Suinin, on the bank of the Isuzu River (official site).
The Outer Shrine is said to have been established in the 22nd year of Emperor Yūryaku (encyclopedia only).
ise.address: Inner Shrine: 1 Ujitachi-chō, Ise, Mie. Outer Shrine: 279 Toyokawa-chō, Ise, Mie.
ise.access: The Outer Shrine is about a 5-minute walk from Iseshi Station. Between the Outer and Inner Shrines it is about 10 minutes by bus or taxi (official). The travel time to the Inner Shrine from a station has not been confirmed on the official site.
ise.parking: In busy periods the shrine promotes park-and-ride (official). Capacity and fees per lot are to be confirmed.

izumo.name: Izumo Taisha
izumo.summary: Enshrines Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami. The official site tells that, after building the land, he returned it to Amaterasu-Ōmikami and now rests in a grand sanctuary as the ruler of the unseen world.
izumo.deity_note: The central figure of the Kojiki's tales of "building the land" and "transferring the land". The Nihon Shoki calls him Ōnamuchi-no-Kami and gives other names including Ōkuninushi-no-Kami and Ōmononushi-no-Kami.
history: The official site explains that the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki describe the grandeur of the sanctuary, and that the Izumo no Kuni Fudoki (733) praises the deity as "the great deity who built all under heaven" and records the place name Kizuki.
Its shrine ranks (Shikinai Myōjin Taisha, Ichinomiya of Izumo, former Kanpei Taisha, Chokusai-sha) come from encyclopedias only and are not confirmed on the official site.
izumo.access: Ichibata Electric Railway: Izumo-taisha-mae Station. From JR Izumoshi Station, about 25 minutes by Ichibata Bus bound for Izumo Taisha (official).
izumo.hours: 6:00–19:00. Outside these hours, visitors pray at the bronze torii. Soga Shrine: 6:00–16:30 (notice dated 14 Oct 2024).
izumo.parking: Main lot 385 spaces, a second lot 360 spaces, and a third lot 20 spaces (official). Fees and opening hours are to be confirmed.

itsukushima.name: Itsukushima Jinja
itsukushima.summary: Located on Miyajima in the Seto Inland Sea, it enshrines the three Munakata goddesses. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996 and is known for its National Treasure halls and corridors.
itsukushima.deity_note: According to the official site, the enshrined deities are Ichikishima-hime, Tagori-hime and Tagitsu-hime, described as deities born from the oath between Amaterasu-Ōmikami and Susanoo-no-Mikoto. They are the same three goddesses as at Munakata Taisha and appear in the oath scene of the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki. The official site says they have been revered as protectors of the imperial family, the nation and the sea.
history: The official site says that in the year Empress Suiko took the throne (593), Saeki no Kuramoto of Aki Province received a divine command and, guided by a sacred crow, built the shrine on its present site.
The official site records that Taira no Kiyomori, after becoming governor of Aki, revered the shrine and rebuilt it in 1168 in the shinden-zukuri style.
It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.

The official list gives six National Treasure structures (the main sanctuary, offering hall, worship hall, Harae-den, the Marōdo shrine buildings, and the east and west corridors) and 11 buildings and 3 structures as Important Cultural Properties, including subsidiary shrines, the five-story pagoda, the Tahōtō and the Great Torii.
highlights: The Great Torii is an Important Cultural Property. The official site notes it comes at the end of the visiting route.
The east and west corridors are National Treasures. The official site explains the floorboards are spaced apart to cope with high tides.
The Noh stage is an Important Cultural Property and lies on the visiting route that runs from the west corridor over the arched bridge.
The Treasure Hall (8:00–17:00 all year) and the Senjōkaku (8:30–16:30) can be visited.
itsukushima.access: Take the ferry (about 10 minutes) from Miyajimaguchi Pier to Miyajima Pier and walk from there. Miyajimaguchi Pier can be reached from JR Miyajimaguchi Station or Hiroden Miyajimaguchi Station. By car, leave the Sanyo Expressway at Hatsukaichi IC or Ōno IC, drive to Miyajimaguchi and take the ferry.
itsukushima.hours: Open every day. Hours vary by season: 6:30–18:00 from 1 Mar to 14 Oct; 6:30–17:30 from 15 Oct to 30 Nov and from 4 Jan to the end of Feb; 6:30–17:00 in December (1 Jan: 0:00–18:30; 2–3 Jan: 6:30–18:30). Entry to the halls: adults 300 yen, high school students 200 yen, elementary and junior high students 100 yen.
itsukushima.parking: The shrine has no parking lot. The official site says public transport is essential.
itsukushima.goshuin: The availability, location and price of goshuin could not be confirmed on the official site.

kumano.name: Kumano Hongū Taisha
kumano.summary: In Hongū, Tanabe City, Wakayama. The official site calls it the center of the Three Kumano Shrines and the head shrine of more than 4,700 Kumano shrines across Japan. The chief deity is Ketsumiko-no-Ōkami.
kumano.deity_note: The official site identifies its chief deity Ketsumiko-no-Ōkami with Susanoo-no-Mikoto. A search of the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki finds no deity named "Ketsumiko", so this deity does not appear in either. One variant in Nihon Shoki volume 1 says Susanoo lived on "Kumanari Peak", but whether that is Kumano Hongū has not been confirmed (to confirm). So "Ketsumiko = Susanoo" is the official site's statement, not the Kojiki's or the Nihon Shoki's. The official site lists five enshrined deities: Ketsumiko-no-Ōkami, Kumano-musubi-no-Ōkami, Hayatama-no-O-no-Kami, Amaterasu-Ōmikami and Izanami-no-Ōkami.
history: The official site tells that, in the reign of Emperor Sujin, three moons descended on a great tree at the old shrine site, Ōyunohara, and the central moon declared "I am Shōjō Gongen" and ordered a shrine to be built.
The official site records that in the great flood of 1889 the middle and lower shrines collapsed, and now only the four upper shrines are enshrined.

The official site says it is registered as a World Heritage Site as part of the Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range. The year of registration has not been confirmed on the relevant official page.
highlights: The old shrine site, Ōyunohara, is near the present site (described in the official history; how to visit is to be confirmed).
kumano.address: Hongū, Hongū-chō, Tanabe, Wakayama 647-1731 (as written on the official top page; the street number has not been confirmed).
kumano.access: The official site refers visitors to the Kumano Hongū Tourist Association (https://www.hongu.jp/) for transport. Train and bus details have not been confirmed on the official site.
kumano.parking: The official site says there are free parking lots next to Zuihōden and by the riverbed, and a free lot near the main sanctuary for visitors with disabilities. The number of spaces has not been confirmed.
kumano.goshuin: The official site's goods page lists goshuin books (large 3,500 yen; 2,000 yen), but the price and hours for goshuin themselves have not been confirmed.

kashima.name: Kashima Jingū
kashima.summary: Ichinomiya of Hitachi Province. It enshrines Takemikazuchi-no-Ōkami and is one of the Three Shrines of the East.
kashima.deity_note: Takemikazuchi appears in the Kojiki in the birth of the deities and the transfer of the land. In the Nihon Shoki he is written Takemikazuchi-no-Kami.
history: Said to have been founded in the first year of Emperor Jinmu. The official site records a tradition that Emperor Jinmu, saved during his eastern expedition by the spiritual power of Takemikazuchi's sword, enshrined the deity in gratitude.
In the Nara and Heian periods imperial envoys were sent often and the shrine was rebuilt every 20 years (official). It is a Chokusai-sha and a Myōjin Taisha (official).
kashima.access: A 7-minute walk from Kashima-jingū Station on the JR Kashima Line and Kashima Rinkai Railway (official).
kashima.hours: The grounds have no gates or fences and are open 24 hours, 365 days a year. The amulet office and prayer reception are open 8:30–16:30 (official).
kashima.parking: No. 1 lot: 60 spaces (paid). No. 2 lot: 55 spaces (5-minute walk). Miyanaka-area lot: 150 spaces (3-minute walk; paid on weekends and holidays), and others. Please check fees on the official site.

meiji.name: Meiji Jingū
meiji.summary: A shrine founded in 1920 (Taishō 9) in Yoyogi, Shibuya, enshrining Emperor Meiji and his consort Empress Dowager Shōken. Its forest of about 700,000 square meters is an artificial forest made from about 100,000 trees donated from all over Japan. It is distinctive in enshrining a modern emperor and empress rather than deities of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki era.
meiji.deity_note: The enshrined deities are the 122nd emperor, Emperor Meiji, and his consort, Empress Dowager Shōken. Neither appears in the Kojiki or the Nihon Shoki. Emperor Meiji died in 1912 and Empress Dowager Shōken in 1914. The official site explains that the shrine was founded from the people's wish to "enshrine their spirits and forever respect and revere their virtue". Their deities belong to a modern foundation, separate from the mythology of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.
history: Emperor Meiji died in 1912 and Empress Dowager Shōken in 1914. The people's strong wish to enshrine their spirits and honor their virtue led to the founding of the shrine at Yoyogi, a place closely linked to them (official).

Founded in 1920. The forest of about 700,000 square meters around the sanctuary was made by planting about 100,000 trees donated from all over Japan, aiming for an "eternal forest". The official site says the area before construction was the Minami-Toshima imperial estate and, apart from the present Inner Garden, was mostly farmland.
In an air raid in April 1945, most of the buildings were lost to fire. The official site says the forest became a refuge for people and suffered no great damage.
It marked the 100th anniversary of its founding in 2020.
highlights: The grounds include the Inner Garden, which Emperor Meiji developed for his consort and had planted with iris, as well as the Treasure Museum, an Important Cultural Property, and the Meiji Jingu Museum (official).

The forest was planned with broadleaf evergreens such as shii, kashi and kusu as its main trees. The official site says the Inner Garden had about 120,000 trees of 365 species at the start, and about 36,000 trees of 234 species in the second comprehensive survey (reported in 2013), which also recorded about 3,000 kinds of living things.
meiji.address: 1-1 Yoyogi-Kamizono-chō, Shibuya, Tokyo 151-8557. Tel. 03-3379-5511 (main). For car navigation, the official site advises entering "Yoyogi 1-1-2".
meiji.access: Harajuku Entrance (south): JR Yamanote Line Harajuku Station, or Tokyo Metro Chiyoda and Fukutoshin Lines Meiji-jingūmae (Harajuku) Station. Yoyogi Entrance (north): JR Yamanote Line Yoyogi Station, or Toei Ōedo Line Yoyogi Station. Sangūbashi Entrance (west): Odakyū Line Sangūbashi Station. About 10 minutes on foot from each entrance to the main sanctuary (official).
meiji.hours: The gates open at sunrise and close at sunset. The official table of monthly hours gives October 5:40–16:40 and November 6:10–16:10 (January 6:40–16:20, July 5:00–18:20, and so on). Checked 12 Oct 2026.
meiji.parking: By car, enter from the Yoyogi Entrance (not from the Harajuku or Sangūbashi Entrances). Because the lot can be full, the official site recommends public transport. The number of spaces and fees are not given on the official page checked, so they are to be confirmed.
meiji.goshuin: Goshuin are given at "Nagadono" (the amulet office in front of the Kagura Hall) from 9:00 until closing (official). The fee is not given on the official page checked, so it is to be confirmed.

fushimi.name: Fushimi Inari Taisha
fushimi.summary: The head shrine of the Inari shrines, said to number about 30,000 across Japan. The whole of Mt. Inari, 233 m high at the southern end of the Thirty-Six Peaks of Higashiyama, is sacred ground. Tradition says the deity Inari-ōkami was enshrined on Mt. Inari on the first Horse Day of the second month in 711.
fushimi.deity_note: The official site says the main sanctuary houses five shrines in one building: the Lower, Middle and Upper Shrines, plus the subsidiary Tanaka Shrine and Shi-daijin. The five names express the wide virtues of Inari-ōkami. They are Ukanomitama-no-Ōkami (Lower), Sata-hiko-no-Ōkami (Middle), Ōmiyanome-no-Ōkami (Upper), and Tanaka-no-Ōkami and Shi-daijin (subsidiary). In the Kojiki, Ukanomitama is a child of Susanoo and Kamuōichi-hime; in the Nihon Shoki he appears as Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto in a variant account. The official site gives Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami as another name of Sata-hiko-no-Ōkami. For Ōmiyanome-no-Ōkami, Tanaka-no-Ōkami and Shi-daijin, the official site does not match them to deities of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki; its own history explains that Shi-daijin is described as four deities or one, so it is not certain. We therefore give them no deity entry here (to confirm). In the official prayer guide, Ukanomitama-no-Ōkami (also called Ukemochi-no-Kami) is introduced as the deity of prosperity, and Sata-hiko-no-Ōkami as the deity of traffic and travel safety.
history: The official site records a tradition that Inari-ōkami was enshrined on Mt. Inari on the first Horse Day of the second month in 711. The shrine records tell that Iroku no Hata no Kimi, a wealthy man of Fukakusa, received an imperial order and enshrined three deities on the three peaks of Mt. Inari; this is said to be the beginning.

The official site introduces a lost passage of the Yamashiro no Kuni Fudoki: a rice cake that Iroku no Hata no Kimi, ancestor of the Hata clan, used as an archery target turned into a white bird and flew off, and rice grew on the peak where it settled. This is said to be the origin of the name "Inari".
The official site explains that in 827 the shrine received the Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade, from Emperor Junna, and in 942 the Senior First Rank.

The official shrine chronology notes that the Engishiki register of 927 lists "Inari Shrine, three deities, all Myōjin Taisha", that the buildings were burned in war in 1468, and that the main sanctuary was rebuilt in 1499.
highlights: The main sanctuary, rebuilt in 1499 in the style called "Inari-zukuri", is an Important Cultural Property (official shrine map).
The Rōmon gate is said to have been built by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in 1589; an ink inscription of that year was found during dismantling and repair in 1973 (official shrine map).

About 10,000 torii line the paths of the mountain. The official site explains that the custom of donating a torii when a wish "comes through", or in thanks that it did, spread from the Edo period onward.

Mt. Inari is 233 m high, with three peaks (Ichinomine, Ninomine and Sannomine) running from west to east. The mountain holds what are said to be tens of thousands of otsuka stone memorials (official shrine map).
fushimi.address: 68 Fukakusa Yabunouchi-chō, Fushimi Ward, Kyoto 612-0882 (official site; checked 12 Oct 2026).
fushimi.access: By train: right next to JR Nara Line Inari Station (5 minutes from Kyoto Station), or a 5-minute walk east from Keihan Main Line Fushimi-Inari Station. By city bus: Minami 5 route, "Inari Taisha-mae", then a 7-minute walk east. By car: about 20 minutes from Meishin Expressway Kyoto-Minami IC, or about 10 minutes from Hanshin Expressway Kamitoba exit. The official site asks visitors to use public transport because the parking area gets very crowded (official: Access).
fushimi.hours: Visiting hours are not confirmed on the official pages.
fushimi.parking: The official site declines parking for anything other than worship, and asks visitors to follow staff instructions when the lot is full. The on-site lot is closed from 30 Dec to 6 Jan. The number of spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official access page (official: Access).
fushimi.goshuin: The official top page says that during the New Year period only pre-written goshuin sheets are given. Regular hours and fees are not confirmed.

kasuga.name: Kasuga Taisha
kasuga.summary: Located on Kasugano in Nara City, it enshrines four deities in its first to fourth sanctuaries: Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto, Futsunushi-no-Mikoto, Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto and Himegami. The official site says the precinct, including the sacred mountain, is a World Heritage Site, and that it is the head shrine of about 3,000 Kasuga shrines across Japan.
kasuga.deity_note: The official enshrined deities are Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto (first sanctuary), Futsunushi-no-Mikoto (second), Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto (third) and Himegami (fourth); the names are written as on the official site. Takemikazuchi is written Takemikazuchi-no-O-no-Kami and similar in the Kojiki, and in the Nihon Shoki he appears with Futsunushi-no-Kami in a variant of Volume 2, the ninth section of the Age of the Gods (second part). Ame-no-Koyane appears in both the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki in scenes such as the Heavenly Rock Cave and the descent of the heavenly grandson. In searches of the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki, Himegami could not be identified as a specific deity, so which deity of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki corresponds to the official Himegami is to be confirmed.
history: The official site records that in 768, by imperial order of Empress Shōtoku, a main sanctuary enshrining the four deities was built.

The official top page says that about 1,300 years ago Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto was welcomed from Kashima in Ibaraki to the summit of Mt. Mikasa (a founding tradition; support in historical records is to be confirmed).
The official site says the 20-year rebuilding cycle (Shikinen Zōtai) has continued 60 times, a record shared only with Ise Jingū and Kasuga Taisha.
The official site says the four main sanctuary buildings are National Treasures and 27 buildings are Important Cultural Properties.
highlights: Four main sanctuary buildings are National Treasures (official).
The grounds hold facilities such as the Kokuhō-den (National Treasure Hall) and the Manyō Botanical Garden (official top page and precinct guide).
kasuga.access: The official site says to take a bus bound for Kasuga Taisha Honden from JR Nara Station or Kintetsu Nara Station, or to walk about 10 minutes via the main approach. Bus routes and frequency are not confirmed on the official site.
kasuga.hours: Gates open 6:30–17:30 (as written on the official site; whether this changes by season is to be confirmed).
kasuga.parking: Not confirmed on the official site. To be confirmed.
kasuga.goshuin: The official top page has a notice about goshuin, and there are several kinds. The fee and hours are not confirmed on the official site.

futarasan.name: Nikkō Futarasan Jinja
futarasan.summary: A shrine whose sacred body is the mountain Nantai-san (Futarasan), and also the local guardian shrine of Nikkō. It stands in three places: the main shrine in the Nikkō temple-and-shrine area, Chūgūshi on the shore of Lake Chūzenji, and the Okumiya on the summit of Nantai-san. It enshrines three deities of one family: Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto, Tagori-hime-no-Mikoto and Ajisukitakahikone-no-Mikoto. The map marks the main shrine in the Nikkō Sannai area (just west of Tōshō-gū).
futarasan.deity_note: The official site calls the deity Futarasan-no-Ōkami and explains that the shrine enshrines a family of three: the father Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto, the mother Tagori-hime-no-Mikoto and the son Ajisukitakahikone-no-Mikoto. Ōnamuchi is another name of Ōkuninushi (in the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki); Tagorihime is one of the three Munakata goddesses of the Nihon Shoki (existing deity entry: munakata3); Ajisukitakahikone is "Ajishikitakahikone-no-Kami" in the Kojiki, a child of Ōkuninushi and Takiri-bime of Munakata, and appears in the funeral scene of Ame-no-Wakahiko in the Nihon Shoki. However, in the texts obtained for this work we could not confirm that the Kojiki or the Nihon Shoki names Tagorihime as Ajisuki's mother (to confirm).
history: The monk Shōdō, who opened the Nikkō mountains, is said to have crossed the Daiya River in 766, built a hermitage inside the Nikkō mountains, and the next year built a small shrine for Mt. Futarasan beside it. This is said to lead to today's Motomiya Shrine (a sub-shrine) (from a tourist guide article; not confirmed on the official pages).

Shōdō is said to have climbed Mt. Futarasan (Nantai-san) in 782 and built the Okumiya on the summit and then Chūgūshi on the shore of Lake Chūzenji (same article; not confirmed on the official pages).

In the Edo period, with the founding of Tōshō-gū, Futarasan Shrine is said to have moved to the west of Tōshō-gū, where a splendid shrine was built (same article; the year of the move cannot be read from the article and is not confirmed on the official site).

The two shrines and one temple (Futarasan Shrine, Tōshō-gū and Rinnō-ji) and their surroundings were designated a national historic site, "Nikkō Sannai", in 1998, and in 1999 were inscribed as the World Heritage site "Shrines and Temples of Nikkō" (same article).
highlights: The Shinkyō bridge, called "the front gate of Nikkō", is an Important Cultural Property and a World Heritage site, the official page introduces (the page's note "under repair" is an old statement from before March 2005).

Hōyū Shrine at the main shrine enshrines Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto, a deity of learning and wisdom, and is an Important Cultural Property and a World Heritage site according to the official page (annual festival on 15 May).

The official page introduces a great sword, "Tarōmaru" (total length 2.62 m, blade 1.8 m, weight 7.2 kg), in the Daikoku-den in the shrine garden. It is said to be the second largest sword at the shrine after "Nenekirimaru" in the Treasure Hall (photo taken in 2003).
Motomiya Shrine, a sub-shrine at the entrance to the Nikkō Sannai area, enshrines Ajisukitakahikone-no-Mikoto, the official page says.
futarasan.address: Main shrine: 2307 Sannai, Nikkō, Tochigi 321-1431 (tel. 0288-54-0535). Chūgūshi: 2484 Chūgūshi, Nikkō, Tochigi 321-1661 (tel. 0288-55-0017).
futarasan.access: The official parking page lists the bus stop "World Heritage Loop Bus (Taiyū-in / Futarasan Shrine-mae)". Travel times and how to ride from the station are not confirmed on the official site.
futarasan.hours: The official top page's note on the water-gathering ceremony gives the shrine garden's opening hours as 8:00–16:30 from April to October and 9:00–15:30 from November to March (a notice from around October 2021; the parking page currently says "opens at 8:00"). The garden admission fee and the hours of the main shrine's worship hall are not confirmed on the official site. Inquiries: main shrine 0288-54-0535.
futarasan.parking: Official main-shrine parking page: cars 700 yen (100 spaces), buses 20 spaces (4,000 yen, up to 3 hours), motorcycles 500 yen, no reservations. Hours: 8:00–17:00 from 1 Apr to 31 Oct, 9:00–16:00 from 1 Nov to 31 Mar (checked 12 Oct 2026).
futarasan.goshuin: Goshuin hours and fees are not confirmed on the official pages.

tsurugaoka.name: Tsurugaoka Hachimangū
tsurugaoka.summary: A shrine that the official site says Minamoto no Yoritomo moved to its present site, the same year he set up his shogunate base in Kamakura, from a Hachiman shrine linked to the Minamoto clan. It enshrines three deities, Emperor Ōjin, Empress Jingū and Himegami, and stands at the north end of Wakamiya Ōji, the main approach that forms the axis of the town of Kamakura.
tsurugaoka.deity_note: The official site names the enshrined deities as Emperor Ōjin, Empress Jingū and Himegami. It explains that Emperor Ōjin was the 15th emperor, son of Emperor Chūai and Empress Jingū (Emperor Ōjin and Empress Jingū appear in the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki). In the official account, Ōjin was enshrined here via Usa Jingū and Iwashimizu Hachimangū. Himegami is only named in the official description of the main hall, and which deity of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki she corresponds to is not confirmed on the official site, so it is to be confirmed.
history: The official site says it began when Minamoto no Yoriyoshi, an ancestor of Yoritomo, invited the deity of Iwashimizu Hachimangū in Kyoto and enshrined the Hachiman deity as the Minamoto clan's guardian at Yuigahama in Kamakura. The year is not given on this official page.
The official site says that in 1180 Yoritomo set up his shogunate base in Kamakura and in the same year moved the Hachiman shrine linked to his ancestors to its present location.

Yoritomo held the Hōjōe, Yabusame (horseback archery), sumo and bugaku dance in the grounds as important shogunate rites. The official site explains these are the beginnings of today's festivals. Yabusame is said to have begun in the Kamakura period.

The official site says that Wakamiya Ōji, the main approach, is said to have been built by Yoritomo as the first step in planning the town of Kamakura, and in prayer for the safe childbirth of his wife Hōjō Masako.
highlights: The Hongū (Upper Shrine) is the central hall enshrining Emperor Ōjin, Himegami and Empress Jingū, and, together with the Wakamiya (Lower Shrine), is an Important Cultural Property (official precinct guide).
The great stone stairway on the main approach is one of its symbols. The official site says it gives a view over the whole of Kamakura, and on clear days the Pacific Ocean and Izu-Ōshima can be seen.
A yabusame ritual is held at the yabusame field every year on 16 September (official precinct guide).
The official site says Genpei Pond was made by order of Yoritomo to Ōba Kageyoshi and the monk Ryōzen. The three-island Genji Pond and the four-island Heike Pond face each other.
Maruyama Inari Shrine, the oldest building in the grounds (Muromachi period), is a National Important Cultural Property (official precinct guide).
tsurugaoka.address: 2-1-31 Yukinoshita, Kamakura, Kanagawa 248-8588 (official visitor guide; checked 12 Oct 2026).
tsurugaoka.access: A 10-minute walk from the east exit of JR Kamakura Station, or 10 minutes from Enoden Kamakura Station. By car, about 5 km toward Kamakura on Prefectural Route 204 from Asahina IC on the Yokohama-Yokosuka Road (official visitor guide; checked 12 Oct 2026).
tsurugaoka.hours: Open 6:00–20:00 all year (official visitor guide; checked 12 Oct 2026). The Treasure Hall is open 9:00–16:00 with no regular closing day (it may close when exhibits are changed).
tsurugaoka.parking: The official table gives cars 9:00–19:30: 600 yen for the first hour, then 300 yen every 30 minutes; 40 car spaces and 10 large-vehicle spaces. Large buses 9:00–17:00 (reservation required; no reservations on weekends and holidays). No reservations for cars (official visitor guide; checked 12 Oct 2026).
tsurugaoka.goshuin: The goshuin hours and fee are not confirmed on the official visitor guide, precinct guide or amulet page.

kotohira.name: Kotohira-gū (Konpira-san)
kotohira.summary: A shrine resting halfway up Mt. Zōzu, enshrining Ōmononushi-no-Kami and Emperor Sutoku in its Main Hall (Gohongū). It has long been revered as a god of farming, industry, medicine and protection at sea. Visitors climb 785 stone steps from the old town at the foot to the Main Hall.
kotohira.deity_note: The official site names the deities of the Main Hall as "Ōmononushi-no-Kami and Emperor Sutoku". In the Kojiki, Ōmononushi appears in the middle volume as "Miwa no Ōmononushi-no-Kami" and "Ōmononushi-no-Ōkami". In the Nihon Shoki, a variant in Volume 1 gives "Ōmononushi-no-Kami" as another name of Ōkuninushi, and a variant in Volume 2 names the deity who submits at the transfer of the land. Emperor Sutoku is a historical emperor, not a deity of the Kojiki or the Nihon Shoki. The shrine's own account of its role (a god of farming, industry, medicine and protection at sea) rests on its history.
history: The shrine's history says it first enshrined Ōmononushi-no-Kami and was called "Kotohira Shrine". In the middle ages, under the influence of the honji-suijaku idea, it is said to have been called "Konpira Daigongen".
It is said that Emperor Sutoku was enshrined together in the same hall in the first year of Eiman.
The shrine's history records that it became an imperial prayer site in 1753 (Hōreki 3) and received an imperial edict naming it the foremost shrine of Japan in 1760 (Hōreki 10).
With the separation of Shinto and Buddhism it returned to the name "Kotohira Shrine", and in July of the same year it was renamed "Kotohira-gū".
highlights: Visitors climb 785 stone steps from the old town at the foot to the Main Hall.

In 2024 the Council for Cultural Affairs recommended that 12 buildings, including the Main Hall's worship hall, main sanctuary, middle hall, Minami-watari-dono and the separate shrine's worship hall, be designated Important Cultural Properties, and they were designated that year. They are said to be a group of buildings re-arranged as shrine architecture between 1874 and 1878.
kotohira.access: JR Kotohira Station is given as the destination. Visitors climb 785 stone steps from the old town to the Main Hall.
kotohira.hours: Daimon Gate: opens 6:00, closes 18:00. The Main Hall's doors: open 7:00, close 17:00. Amulet office: 8:30–17:00 (official site, checked 12 Oct 2026).
kotohira.parking: There is no dedicated parking lot. Visitors are asked to use car parks in the town and walk (the official site says the walk takes about one hour one way).
kotohira.goshuin: The official site announces seasonal goshuin paper, a cherry-blossom maki-e goshuin book and other items. The fee and hours are not confirmed on the official site.

atsuta.name: Atsuta Jingū
atsuta.summary: An ancient shrine in Nagoya enshrining the Kusanagi sacred sword, one of the Three Sacred Treasures. The official site explains that its chief deity is Atsuta-no-Ōkami, Amaterasu-Ōmikami with the Kusanagi sword as her spirit-vessel, and that it is a Myōjin Taisha of the Engishiki and a Chokusai-sha.
atsuta.deity_note: The official site explains that the chief deity, Atsuta-no-Ōkami, is Amaterasu-Ōmikami with the Kusanagi sword as her spirit-vessel, and that Amaterasu-Ōmikami, Susanoo-no-Mikoto, Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto, Miyazu-hime-no-Mikoto and Takeinadane-no-Mikoto are also enshrined. In the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki, the Kusanagi sword is the sword Susanoo took from the tail of the eight-forked serpent ("Kusanagi no Tachi" in the Kojiki; "Kusanagi no Tsurugi" in section 8 of the Nihon Shoki), and one of the three treasures that Amaterasu gives at the descent of the heavenly grandson (a variant of section 9 of the Nihon Shoki). Yamato Takeru (Yamato-takeru in the Kojiki) and Miyazu-hime (Miyazu-hime in the Kojiki) appear in the reign of Emperor Keikō, and the Nihon Shoki records that the Kusanagi sword is at the Atsuta shrine. The name Takeinadane does not appear in the Kojiki (upper and middle volumes) and the Nihon Shoki (volumes 1–3, 7 and 14) that we obtained (confirmed by search; the lower volume of the Kojiki is not confirmed).
history: The official site tells that in the reign of Emperor Keikō, Yamato Takeru died at Nobono, leaving the sacred sword behind, and his consort Miyazu-hime-no-Mikoto enshrined the sword at Atsuta. This is the founding, about 1,900 years ago. The chronology gives the 43rd year of Emperor Keikō.
The Nihon Shoki records that the Kusanagi sword Yamato Takeru wore is at the Atsuta shrine in Ayuchi District of Owari Province. The name "Atsuta shrine" appears in the Nihon Shoki.
The official site explains that it is ranked as a Myōjin Taisha of the Engishiki and a Chokusai-sha, and was revered as the most venerable shrine after Ise Jingū.
According to the official chronology, it received the title "Jingū" in 1868 and became Atsuta Jingū from Atsuta Shrine, was damaged by an air raid in 1945, and was rebuilt and re-enshrined in 1955.
highlights: The Main Sanctuary enshrines the Kusanagi sword. The buildings were changed in 1893 from the Owari style to the present Shinmei style (official).
Kusanagi-kan, the "Treasure House of Swords", was completed in June 2021 and opened that October. It is an exhibition hall for swords that holds about 450 donated Japanese swords (official).
The Treasure Hall holds more than 6,000 items, of which 177 are designated National Treasures, Important Cultural Properties or Aichi Prefecture cultural properties (official).
Nobunaga-bei is a tiled earthen wall that Oda Nobunaga dedicated in 1560 in thanks for victory before setting out to Okehazama. It is counted among the three great earthen walls of Japan (official).
The great camphor tree north of the hand-washing pavilion is said to have been planted by Kōbō Daishi, and is said to be over 1,000 years old (official).
atsuta.address: 1-1-1 Jingū, Atsuta Ward, Nagoya, Aichi 456-0031 (as shown on the official top page; the Treasure Hall page gives 456-8585).
atsuta.access: By train: 8 minutes on foot from JR Atsuta Station, or 7 minutes on foot from Tenma-chō or Jingū-nishi stations on the Meijō Subway Line (official).
atsuta.hours: Open for worship 24 hours (official). At night, use the west gate parking lot. The amulet office is open from about 7:00 until about sunset, and the prayer and kagura reception is open daily 8:30–16:00 (official).
atsuta.parking: About 400 spaces (east gate about 300, west gate about 40, south gate about 60), free. Gates basically close at 5 p.m. and access is restricted during festivals. The lot is often full on weekends and holidays. For the 2026 New Year visit, the visitors' lot was announced to be fully closed from year-end to 18 Jan (official).
atsuta.goshuin: Goshuin are not confirmed on the official page checked. To be confirmed.

dazaifu.name: Dazaifu Tenmangū
dazaifu.summary: A shrine in Dazaifu, Fukuoka, whose buildings stand over the grave of Sugawara no Michizane. The official site calls it the "head shrine of all Tenmangū shrines in Japan" and "the birthplace of Tenjin worship". The Main Hall is a national Important Cultural Property. The enshrined deity is a person of the Heian period who does not appear in the Kojiki or the Nihon Shoki, so it does not meet listing criterion 3.
dazaifu.deity_note: According to the official site, the enshrined deity Sugawara no Michizane was demoted in 901 to the post of Dazaifu Gon-no-sotsu, and died in the second month of 903 at the age of 59. He was a Heian-period figure and does not appear in the Kojiki or the Nihon Shoki (his name is not in the texts we obtained). He is not a deity derived from the Kojiki or the Nihon Shoki; the faith that honors Michizane as "Tenman Daijizai Tenjin", or Tenjin-sama, is a separate tradition that arose after his death through court honors such as posthumous ranks (the official site notes restoration of rank and posthumous honors by Emperor Daigo and Emperor Ichijō). We list the shrine while stating clearly that it does not meet criterion 3 of this survey (connection with the deities of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki).
history: The official site records that in 901 Michizane was demoted to Dazaifu Gon-no-sotsu through the scheming of the Fujiwara clan, and died at Dazaifu in 903.

The official site tells that, as he had wished, he was buried at Dazaifu: the ox pulling the funeral cart lay down and would not move, so his disciple Umasake no Yasuyuki buried him there and built a mausoleum. It records that a shrine building was built by imperial order in 919.

The official site records that the present Main Hall was built in 1591, a Azuchi-Momoyama-period building donated by Kobayakawa Takakage, lord of Chikuzen, and is designated a national Important Cultural Property.
highlights: The Main Hall (national Important Cultural Property): the official site says the shrine was built over Michizane's grave from the beginning and is praised as the only "Kansei-byō" in Japan.

Uso-kae and Oni-sube rites: held every year on 7 January. The official site explains that "Uso-kae" is a rite of exchanging the untruths one has told unknowingly in the past year for the sincerity of Tenjin-sama.
dazaifu.address: 4-7-1 Saifu, Dazaifu, Fukuoka 818-0195. The coordinates come from the Geospatial Information Authority address search (Saifu 4-7).
dazaifu.access: By public transport: from Nishitetsu Futsukaichi Station on the Nishitetsu Tenjin Ōmuta Line to Dazaifu Station on the Nishitetsu Dazaifu Line (official access page; walking time is not confirmed).
