By car: about 15 minutes from Dazaifu IC on the Kyushu Expressway, or about 20 minutes from Chikushino IC (official).
dazaifu.hours: Visiting hours: the gates open at 6:00 from the spring equinox day and at 6:30 from the autumn equinox day; they close at 19:00 in April–May and September–November, 19:30 in June–August, and 18:30 in December–March (official; subject to temporary changes). Prayer reception is from about 8:45 to about 17:00 (may change for festivals; no reservation needed). Individual hours for the amulet office are not confirmed (the official site says that during the New Year period amulets, prayers and goshuin are handled during gate hours).
dazaifu.parking: Parking inside the grounds is not confirmed on the official site. The official site refers to the nearby "Dazaifu Parking Center" (8:00–17:00, tel. 092-924-2843). For car purification, enter from the west gate and park in the dedicated space just inside on the right (official).
dazaifu.goshuin: At the amulet office in the grounds, your goshuin book is taken and written in on the spot, and an original goshuin book is also available. The goshuin of the subsidiary shrine Tenkai Inari Shrine is given at the same office. During the New Year period a special goshuin counter is set up outside the tower gate (official). The fee is not confirmed on the official site.

shimogamo.name: Kamomioya Jinja (Shimogamo Jinja)
shimogamo.summary: An ancient Kyoto shrine at the confluence of the Kamo and Takano Rivers, enshrining the ancestral deities of the Kamo clan. Kamotaketsunumi-no-Mikoto is enshrined in the West Hall and Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto in the East Hall. The two main halls are National Treasures, and it was inscribed as a World Heritage site in 1994.
shimogamo.deity_note: The official site describes Kamotaketsunumi-no-Mikoto as "the deity who turned into the Yatagarasu and led Emperor Jinmu to victory". In the Kojiki (middle volume), in Jinmu's eastern expedition a "Yatagarasu" guides the way on the order of Takagi-no-Ōkami, and in the Nihon Shoki (Volume 3) Amaterasu sends the "Yatagarasu", but neither identifies the Yatagarasu with Kamotaketsunumi-no-Mikoto (the Nihon Shoki names the descendants of the Yatagarasu as the Kadono Tonomo no Agatanushi-be). The Kogo Shūi has "Yatagarasu, remote ancestor of the Kamo Agatanushi", and lost passages of the Yamashiro no Kuni Fudoki and the Shinsen Shōjiroku (both sources outside the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki) link Kamotaketsunumi-no-Mikoto with the Yatagarasu. The name Kamotaketsunumi was not found in our searches of the upper and middle volumes of the Kojiki and volumes 1–3 of the Nihon Shoki. Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto is, on the official site, a child of Kamotaketsunumi and a female guardian of good matches, pregnancy and childbirth, and child-rearing. She comes from the red-painted arrow tradition in a lost passage of the Yamashiro no Kuni Fudoki (the mother of Kamowake-ikazuchi) and is thought to be a deity of a different tradition from Tamayori-bime of the Kojiki (the younger sister of Toyotama-bime and mother of Emperor Jinmu). Whether there is a theory identifying the two has not been confirmed on the official site (to be confirmed).
history: The official site says the exact time of its founding is unknown, but there is a record that the sacred fence was repaired in the 7th year of Emperor Sujin (90 BC), so worship is presumed to have begun earlier.

The official site introduces a passage of the Shoku Nihongi, in the second year of Emperor Monmu (698), ordering guards because crowds gathered to watch the Aoi Festival, and explains that a grand festival existed before the Nara period.

After the move of the capital to Heian-kyō (794) it was revered as a guardian of the state and the capital and the ancestral shrine of the imperial family. Following the Hyakurenshō, the system of periodic rebuilding was established with the first in 1036, and it is now held once every 21 years.

The two main halls are National Treasures and 53 buildings are Important Cultural Properties; it was inscribed as a World Heritage site in 1994. In the early Meiji period it was placed first among the Kanpei Taisha.
highlights: The official site introduces the Mikage Festival as the oldest divine procession in Japan.
The official site introduces shrines in the grounds: Aioi-sha for good matches, Kawai Shrine for beauty, Inshi-sha for contracts, Inoue-sha for purification, and Koto-sha for the zodiac.
shimogamo.address: 59 Shimogamo Izumikawa-chō, Sakyō Ward, Kyoto 606-0807 (official). Tel. 075-781-0010.
shimogamo.access: From Kyoto Station, take the Karasuma Line to Kitaōji Station and then city bus No. 1 or 205, or city bus No. 4 or 205, to "Shimogamo-jinja-mae" or "Tadasu-no-mori-mae". From Demachiyanagi Station it is a 12-minute walk (official).
shimogamo.hours: Inside the tower gate: opens 6:30, closes 17:00. Kawai Shrine: opens 6:30, closes 16:30 (may change for rites). Prayer reception 9:00–16:30 (official). Checked 12 Oct 2026.
shimogamo.parking: The West parking lot is open 24 hours (may change for festivals). 500 yen for the first hour, then 300 yen per 30 minutes, with no maximum. Height limit 2.3 m (official). The official site asks visitors to come by public transport.
shimogamo.goshuin: Available at the shrine front (as written on the official top page). The fee and hours are not confirmed on the official site.

kamigamo.name: Kamowake-ikazuchi Jinja (Kamigamo Jinja)
kamigamo.summary: Ichinomiya of Yamashiro Province. It enshrines Kamowake-ikazuchi-no-Ōkami; the Main Hall and the Gonden are National Treasures, and the entire grounds are inscribed as a World Heritage site (official).
kamigamo.deity_note: Kamowake-ikazuchi-no-Ōkami does not appear in the Kojiki or the Nihon Shoki (confirmed by search). The "red-painted arrow" story the official site gives as his origin is a tradition the official site attributes to a lost passage of the Yamashiro no Kuni Fudoki quoted in the Shaku Nihongi and to the Kamo Kyūki, not a myth of the Kojiki or the Nihon Shoki. In the official account, Kamo-tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto took home a red-painted arrow that floated down from upstream and became pregnant. At a banquet of her father Kamotaketsunumi, her child said "My father is a heavenly deity", threw his cup toward the sky and ascended; later, at the ritual to welcome the deity, he descended on Mt. Kamiyama. This child is said to be Kamowake-ikazuchi-no-Ōkami. The original texts of the lost Fudoki passage and the Kamo Kyūki could not be confirmed this time.
history: The shrine's official history says that in the reign of Emperor Jinmu, Kamowake-ikazuchi-no-Ōkami descended on Mt. Kamiyama and was enshrined.
The official site records that in 677 the Kamo shrine was built by Yamashiro Province, laying the foundations of buildings that have changed little to this day.

The official site records that after the move of the capital to Heian-kyō (794) successive emperors made visits and offerings to it as the guardian of the imperial city and Ichinomiya of Yamashiro, and in 1871 it was placed first among the Kanpei Taisha.

The official site records that the Main Hall and the Gonden were designated National Treasures in 1953, and that in 1994 the entire grounds were inscribed as one of the "Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto" World Heritage site.
highlights: The Main Hall and the Gonden (National Treasures) were rebuilt in 1863, and the official site explains that they are the prototype of the "nagare-zukuri" style, which accounts for about 60% of shrines in Japan. The official site records a 21-year periodic rebuilding, with the 42nd held in 2015.
The official site announces rites such as the Kamo Festival (Aoi Festival) on 15 May each year and the Kasagake rite on the third Sunday of October (18 October in 2026).
kamigamo.access: Get off right at the Kyoto city bus stop "Kamigamo-jinja-mae" (Route 4 from JR Kyoto Station, Route 4 from Kitayama Station on the subway, Route 4 from Keihan Demachiyanagi Station, Route 46 from Hankyū Ōmiya Station). About 25 minutes on foot from Kitaōji Station on the subway. By car, about 30 minutes from JR Kyoto Station (official).
kamigamo.hours: Second Torii: opens 5:30, closes 17:00. Tower gate and amulet office: open 8:00, close 16:45. Prayer reception 9:00–16:00 (no reservation needed). Special visit to the National Treasure Main Hall 10:00–16:00 (500 yen). Telephone reception at the shrine office 8:30–17:00 (official). The official page still has a note on shortened hours during the 2021 pandemic, so it is best to confirm the latest hours by phone.
kamigamo.parking: The visitors' lot is normally open 6:00–22:00 (exit possible 24 hours), 200 yen per 30 minutes (a donation for upkeep of the grounds). On busy days such as New Year and festival days, entry is 9:00–16:00, 1,000 yen per entry (official).
kamigamo.goshuin: The official top page announces a limited goshuin given only on the day of the Kasagake rite (18 October 2026). The place and hours for regular goshuin are not confirmed on the official site.

sengen.name: Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha
sengen.summary: Said to be the head shrine of the more than 1,300 Sengen shrines across Japan, it enshrines Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto (Asama-no-Ōkami). Ichinomiya of Suruga Province. Its origin is said to lie in the enshrinement of the deity to pacify the eruptions of Mt. Fuji.
sengen.deity_note: The official site names Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto (also called Asama-no-Ōkami) as the main deity, with Ninigi-no-Mikoto and Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami as the deities enshrined alongside. In the Kojiki she is a daughter of Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami; she is joined with Ninigi-no-Mikoto and gives birth to her children in the midst of fire (Hoderi-no-Mikoto, Hosuseri-no-Mikoto and Hoori-no-Mikoto). In the Nihon Shoki she appears as Kashitsu-hime and Konohanasakuya-hime.
history: The official account of the shrine's origin says that while the eruptions of Mt. Fuji continued, the 11th emperor, Suinin, was troubled; in the third year of his reign (27 BC) he enshrined Asama-no-Ōkami at the foot of the mountain to calm the spirit of the mountain.

The official site records that in the first year of Daidō (806), Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, by imperial order of Emperor Heizei, built the shrine buildings at the present Ōmiya site and moved the deity there from Yamamiya.

The present main sanctuary, offering hall, worship hall and Rōmon gate were built in 1604 (Keichō 9) by Tokugawa Ieyasu as a votive offering. The main sanctuary is a two-story tower-style building in the style called "Sengen-zukuri" and is a national Important Cultural Property (the worship hall and the gate are prefectural cultural properties).
highlights: Wakutama Pond is a pond where Mt. Fuji's snowmelt wells up through the lava; it is designated a Special Natural Monument (official page on the grounds and buildings).
sengen.access: Official: on foot, about 10 minutes from Fujinomiya Station on the Minobu Line; by taxi, about 30 minutes from Shin-Fuji Station on the Shinkansen. By car, about 20 minutes from Tōmei Fuji IC via the Nishi-Fuji Bypass, or about 15 minutes from Shin-Tōmei Shin-Fuji IC. Express buses (reservation required) run between Tokyo Station and Fujinomiya.
sengen.hours: Official top page: the gate is open 6:00–19:00 from November to February, 5:30–19:30 in March and October, and 5:00–20:00 from April to September. Prayer reception (inside the prayer hall) is 8:30–15:50 (the official prayer guide says the same). Reception for goshuin, weddings and naming ceremonies is 8:30–16:30.
sengen.parking: Official: cars are ¥200 per hour or ¥1,500 per day (free for worshippers leaving within 30 minutes); buses are ¥1,000 per hour (overnight stays only: ¥2,000). People receiving a prayer ritual get 2 hours free. Parking hours are 5:00–19:00 (leaving is possible 24 hours).
sengen.goshuin: Official top page: goshuin are received 8:30–16:30. The fee is not confirmed in the official text.

sumiyoshi.name: Sumiyoshi Taisha
sumiyoshi.summary: The head shrine of the roughly 2,300 Sumiyoshi shrines across Japan, in Sumiyoshi Ward, Osaka. It enshrines the Sumiyoshi Ōkami — Sokotsutsu-no-O, Nakatsutsu-no-O and Uwatsutsu-no-O — and Empress Jingū (Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto).
sumiyoshi.deity_note: The Sumiyoshi Ōkami are the three deities Sokotsutsu-no-O, Nakatsutsu-no-O and Uwatsutsu-no-O. The Kojiki, Part 1, writes them as Sokotsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto, Nakatsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto and Uwatsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto and calls them the "Suminoe-no-Mimae-no-Ōkami"; in the Nihon Shoki, Book 1 (the first part of the Age of the Gods), Sokotsutsu-no-O, Nakatsutsu-no-O and Uwatsutsu-no-O are called the "Sumiyoshi-no-Ōkami". In the Kojiki, Part 2, in the Emperor Chūai section, Empress Jingū (Okinagatarashi-hime) is possessed by a deity, and the three great deities speak. The assignment of deities to the four main sanctuaries (first to third = the three deities, fourth = Empress Jingū) was confirmed on tourist sites and could not be confirmed on the relevant official page (to confirm).
history: The official account says that in the 11th year of Empress Jingū's regency (211) the Sumiyoshi Ōkami was enshrined at the present site. It is said that, after returning from the expedition to Silla with the deities' protection, she enshrined them on the way back in triumph.

The official site records that it was ranked as a Myōjin Taisha of the Engishiki, with the highest divine rank of Shō-ichi-i, one of the Twenty-Two Shrines, Ichinomiya of Settsu Province and a former Kanpei Taisha.
The official site records that repainting was carried out at the 49th Shikinen Sengū in 2011 (Heisei 23).
highlights: The four main sanctuaries, designated National Treasures (mentioned on the official top page). Details of the arrangement of the main shrines and the Sumiyoshi-zukuri style are not confirmed on the relevant official page.

On the official page about the deities, there is a description of the deity of the fourth main shrine: Empress Jingū called a woman rice-planter (uneme) from Nagato Province, made the sacred rice field, and prayed for abundant harvests.
sumiyoshi.access: About a 3-minute walk east of Sumiyoshitaisha Station on the Nankai Main Line; about a 5-minute walk west of Sumiyoshi-higashi Station; right by Sumiyoshi-torimae Station on the Hankai Tramway (official).
sumiyoshi.hours: The gates open at 6:00 from April to September and at 6:30 from October to March. They close at 16:00 for the outer gate and 17:00 for the inner enclosure (as written on the official site).
sumiyoshi.parking: The official access page has parking information, but the number of spaces and the fees are not confirmed on the official site. Hours differ during the New Year period and the Sumiyoshi Festival.
sumiyoshi.goshuin: The official site has a goshuin page, but the fee and reception hours are not confirmed on the official site.

usa.name: Usa Jingū
usa.summary: The official site describes it as the head shrine of the more than 40,000 Hachiman shrines across Japan. Located in Usa, Oita, it enshrines three deities: Hachiman-no-Ōkami, Hime-no-Ōkami and Empress Jingū.
usa.deity_note: The official site explains that Hachiman-no-Ōkami is the divine spirit of Emperor Ōjin; that Hime-no-Ōkami is the three goddesses Tagitsu-hime-no-Mikoto, Ichikishima-hime-no-Mikoto and Tagiri-hime-no-Mikoto; and that Empress Jingū is Emperor Ōjin's mother (us1 us2). Emperor Ōjin appears in the Kojiki, Part 2, and the Nihon Shoki, Book 10, and Empress Jingū in the Nihon Shoki, Book 9 and elsewhere; the three goddesses of Hime-no-Ōkami have the same names as the three Munakata goddesses of the oath scene. The official site explains Hime-no-Ōkami as the deity said in the Nihon Shoki to have descended to Usa-jima, and there is a corresponding passage in a variant account of Book 1, Section 6 of the Nihon Shoki. The title Hachiman-no-Kami itself does not appear in the text of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki that were consulted.
history: The official site explains that Hachiman-no-Ōkami is said to have first appeared in Usa in 571, in the reign of Emperor Kinmei.
The official site regards the founding of Usa Jingū as 725 (Jinki 2), when, by imperial order, a hall was built at the present site and the deity Hachiman was enshrined.

According to the official site, in 733 (Tenpyō 5) the Second Hall was built following an oracle and Hime-no-Ōkami was enshrined, and in 823 (Kōnin 14) the Third Hall was built and Empress Jingū was enshrined.

The official site says the shrine is especially famous for helping with the building of the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji and for giving Wake no Kiyomaro an oracle to set the nation right. It adds that the imperial family revered it as the ancestral shrine second only to the Grand Shrines of Ise, and that it is one of the 16 Chokusai-sha.
highlights: The official site says the main sanctuary (the three halls of the Upper Shrine) is designated a National Treasure. Visitors normally cannot approach it closely.

The official site explains that the grounds cover about 140,000 tsubo, most of which is a national historic site, and that the shrine forest, where ichii-gashi oaks grow in clusters, is designated a natural monument.

There is a saying, "If you do not visit the Lower Shrine, your visit is only half done": after the Upper Shrine, visitors also pay their respects at the Lower Shrine. Worship follows the ancient form: two bows, four claps and one bow.
The Meoto-ishi (Married Couple Stones) are said to bring blessings for a good match, and the official site says they are among the paving stones on the steps leading to Wakamiya Shrine.
For people with difficulty walking and elderly visitors, a monorail runs up to the Upper Shrine (it stops on some days for cleaning and other reasons).
usa.access: By car, about 6 km (about 15 minutes) from Usa IC on the Higashi-Kyūshū Expressway via National Route 10. From Usa Station on the JR Nippō Main Line, take a bus (Usa Hachiman stop) or a taxi (about 4 km, about 10 minutes). The official site says it takes about 1 hour by limited express from Kokura Station and about 40 minutes from Ōita Station.
usa.hours: The official top page shows visiting hours of 5:30–19:00 from April to September and 6:00–18:00 from October to March. The FAQ of the same official site says the gate opens at 6:00 and closes at 18:00, so the two do not agree.
usa.parking: There is no parking near the main sanctuary. The official site lists Times Usa Jingū Omotesandō Parking (180 standard cars, ¥500), Gaien Parking (150 standard cars, ¥500 for 12 hours), Hachiman Parking (400 standard cars, ¥500) and others. Fees change during the New Year period.
usa.goshuin: The FAQ on the official site explains the meaning of goshuin, but whether they are given, where, and the fee are not confirmed on the official site.

munakata.name: Munakata Taisha
munakata.summary: A shrine that collectively refers to three shrines: Hetsu-miya in Munakata, Fukuoka, Nakatsu-miya on Ōshima, and Okitsu-miya on Okinoshima. It enshrines the three Munakata goddesses. The official site describes it as one of the oldest shrines in Japan.
munakata.deity_note: The deities named on the official site are Tagori-hime-no-Kami (Okitsu-miya), Tagitsu-hime-no-Kami (Nakatsu-miya) and Ichikishima-hime-no-Kami (Hetsu-miya), explained as three goddesses born in the oath between Amaterasu-Ōmikami and Susanoo-no-Mikoto (mu2 mu3 mu4 mu5). They appear in the oath scene of the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki (Kojiki, Part 1; Nihon Shoki, Book 1, Section 6). The Kojiki gives Okitsu-miya = Takiri-bime, Nakatsu-miya = Ichikishima-hime and Hetsu-miya = Tagitsu-hime; the Nakatsu-miya and Hetsu-miya assignments differ from the present ones.
history: The official site explains that the Nihon Shoki preserves words in which Amaterasu-Ōmikami told the three Munakata goddesses that if they helped the successive emperors, the emperors would enshrine them. The site interprets this as reflecting that Munakata was Japan's first international port and took on the roles of diplomacy, trade and defense.

Many of the objects excavated on Okinoshima date from the 4th to the 9th century, and about 80,000 items are designated National Treasures. The official site explains these as traces of state rituals.

The official account lists records of imperial envoys being sent: 465 (Emperor Yūryaku; Nihon Shoki), 838 and 842 (Emperor Ninmyō; Shoku Nihon Kōki), 870 (Emperor Seiwa; Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku) and 1017 (Emperor Go-Ichijō; Nihon Kiryaku).
The main sanctuary of Hetsu-miya was built in 1578 (Tenshō 6) and the worship hall in 1590 (Tenshō 18); both are designated Important Cultural Properties.
highlights: Takamiya Saijō is said to be the place where Ichikishima-hime descended, an ancient-style ritual ground with no buildings. The official site says that on October 3 a night kagura (Yūkyū-no-mai) is performed.
The Treasure Hall stores and displays the treasures of Okinoshima (80,000 National Treasures) at its center, together with Important Cultural Properties handed down at Munakata Taisha.
The Second Shrine and the Third Shrine were received from the old buildings of Ise Jingū; Tagori-hime-no-Kami is enshrined in the Second Shrine and Tagitsu-hime-no-Kami in the Third Shrine.

In 2017 it was inscribed as a World Heritage Site as part of "Sacred Island of Okinoshima and Associated Sites in the Munakata Region", and the World Heritage official site says the three shrines of Munakata Taisha and others are included among the component parts.
munakata.access: The text of the official access page could not be retrieved, and the routes by train, bus and car are not confirmed on the official site.
munakata.hours: Only two points are confirmed on the official site: the prayer hall (Kigan-den) reception is open 9:00–17:00, and the Treasure Hall (Shinpōkan) is open 9:00–16:30 (last entry 16:00), every day of the year. The hours when the grounds can be visited are not confirmed on the official site.
munakata.parking: The number of spaces, fees and hours of the parking lots are not confirmed on the official site.
munakata.goshuin: The official site says that amulets, charms and goshuin are given out at the prayer hall (reception 9:00–17:00).

omiwa.name: Ōmiwa Jinja
omiwa.summary: Ichinomiya of Yamato Province, which takes Mt. Miwa as its sacred mountain and has no main sanctuary, worshipping the mountain from the worship hall through the Mitsu-torii. The official site presents it as the oldest shrine in Japan, enshrining Ōmononushi-no-Ōkami.
omiwa.deity_note: The official site names Ōmononushi-no-Ōkami as the enshrined deity. The Kojiki records that the cooperating deity in the building of the land asked to be enshrined "on the mountain to the east of the green fence of Yamato", but in Part 1 it calls this deity "the deity who dwells on Mt. Mimoro" and does not write the name Ōmononushi. In Part 2, the Jinmu section writes "Miwa-no-Ōmononushi-no-Kami" and the Sujin section writes "Ōmononushi-no-Ōkami". One variant account in Section 8 of the Nihon Shoki gives Ōmononushi-no-Kami as another name of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami and says that the Sakimitama and Kushimitama became the deity of Ōmiwa who dwells on Mt. Mimoro. The relationship with Ōkuninushi-no-Kami differs by source. The shrine's official engi account says that Ōmononushi-no-Ōkami rests at the rock seat on the summit of Mt. Miwa, Ōanamuchi-no-Kami midway up the slope, and Sukunabikona-no-Kami at the foot.
history: The official site says that the founding tradition is recorded in the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki: Ōmononushi-no-Ōkami appeared before Ōkuninushi-no-Kami and wished to be enshrined on Mt. Miwa. The official site explains it as an ancient shrine that began in the age of the gods.

The official site explains that in the reign of Emperor Sujin, Ōmononushi-no-Ōkami calmed a great epidemic, and the sake brewer Takahashi Ikuhi-no-Mikoto brewed fine sake with the deity's help. The Sujin section of the Kojiki also tells of the epidemic and Ōmononushi-no-Ōkami's message in a dream.

The official site explains that in the Heian period the Ōmiwa Festival, the Chinkasai and the Saegusa Festival continued as court festivals, and that the shrine's divine rank reached the highest, Shō-ichi-i, in 859 (Jōgan 1).

The official site explains that its shrine rank in the Engishiki was Kanpei Taisha, and that it later became Ichinomiya of Yamato Province and one of the Twenty-Two Shrines. It was also a Kanpei Taisha in the Meiji period.
highlights: The worship hall is a national Important Cultural Property. Rebuilt in 1664 (Kanbun 4) by Tokugawa Ietsuna, it has no main sanctuary because it is a form for worshipping Mt. Miwa (official).

The Mitsu-torii (Miwa-torii) divides the sacred mountain from the worship hall, behind the hall, and is a national Important Cultural Property. The official grounds map notes that visits are suspended (confirm the current situation).
Mt. Miwa is 467 m high and 16 km around. Its cedars are called the "divine cedars of Miwa", and rock seats are scattered across the mountain (official).
The Mi-no-Kamisugi is a sacred tree named for the white snake, thought to be an incarnation of Ōmononushi-no-Ōkami, that lives in it; it is said to be about 500 years old (official).
omiwa.access: A 5-minute walk from Miwa Station on the JR Sakurai Line (Manyō Mahoroba Line) (official). The shuttle bus from the north exit of Sakurai Station carries a note on the official page that it is suspended, so confirmation is needed.
omiwa.hours: The visiting hours of the worship hall are not confirmed on the retrieved official page. The amulet office is open 9:00–17:00 (until 16:30 from December to February), the Sanshūden hall 7:00–17:30, and prayer reception 9:00–16:00 (until 15:30 from December to February) (official). Climbing Mt. Miwa is noted as suspended at times because of landslide damage; check the current situation on the official top page.
omiwa.parking: There are four free parking lots for worshippers, about 320 spaces in total (official; west of the JR level crossing). They can be used all day, but the Ni-no-Torii parking lot is closed to parking during the New Year period and on the 1st of every month (official).
omiwa.goshuin: The giving of goshuin is not confirmed on the retrieved official page. To confirm.

makata.name: Makata Jinja
makata.summary: Of the many Makata shrines of the same name around Lake Inba, this is the one in Kaburagi-machi, Sakura City. It is known as the chief guardian shrine of the Sakura Domain.
makata.deity_note: The enshrined deity is Wakumusubi-no-Mikoto (the official spelling). The official site explains it as "Wakumusubi-no-Kami of the Kojiki, Wakumusubi-no-Mikoto of the Nihon Shoki". The deity's place in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki is set out on the deity page. There are also Makata shrines of a separate corporation in Narita City (Daikata and Funakata), whose descriptions of the deity differ (encyclopedia only; to be confirmed).
history: The founding is "said to be around the time the Sakura area was first opened, and is not certain" (official).

The official site explains that, by oral tradition, the shrine's name can be read as "the shrine of the deity that the Ō clan honours in the land of hemp". The official site records that the appointment of Itsukori-no-Mikoto of the Ō clan as kuni-no-miyatsuko (governor) of Inba is found in the Sendai Kuji Hongi.

In the Edo period it was the guardian shrine of the Sakura Castle grounds and the chief guardian shrine of the Sakura Domain. The present shrine buildings were rebuilt in 1843 (Tenpō 14) by the domain lord Hotta Masayoshi, and underwent major repairs in 2003 (Heisei 15) (official).

The official site records that the shrine's name appears in the Engishiki (Book 9, Shimōsa Province). The official site does not explicitly state its rank as a shrine listed in the Engishiki (shikinaisha). Its former rank of Gōsha is from the encyclopedia only and is to be confirmed.
highlights: Within the grounds are the auxiliary shrines Mitsumine Jinja (Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto) and Inari Jinja (Toyouke-hime-no-Mikoto), and the subsidiary shrine Hōsō Jinja (Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto).
makata.access: About a 15-minute walk from JR Sakura Station or Keisei Sakura Station. By car, about 10 minutes from Sakura IC or Yotsukaidō IC (official).
makata.hours: No information found on the official site.
makata.parking: Free; 20 spaces for cars; large buses not allowed (information from a tourist site).

katori.name: Katori Jingū
katori.summary: Ichinomiya of Shimōsa Province. It enshrines Futsunushi-no-Ōkami. Before the Meiji era, only Ise, Katori and Kashima are said to have borne the title "Jingū" (official).
katori.deity_note: Futsunushi-no-Kami appears in the Nihon Shoki and the Kogo Shūi, and is not found in the Kojiki (confirmed by search; to be confirmed). The official Katori Jingū site gives "Iwainushi-no-Mikoto" as another name.
history: Said to have been founded in the 18th year of Emperor Jinmu (the official site records this as "the tradition of the elders").
A former Kanpei Taisha. It became a Chokusai-sha in 1942 (Shōwa 17) (official).
The ranks of Myōjin Taisha listed in the Engishiki and Beppyō shrine are from the encyclopedia only.
katori.access: About a 30-minute walk (about 2 km) from JR Katori Station. About 10 minutes by taxi from JR Sawara Station. By highway bus from Tokyo Station, get off at "Katori Jingū-mae", then a 5-minute walk. About 1.5 km from Sawara-Katori IC (official).
katori.hours: Amulet office and goshuin 8:30–17:00; prayer reception until 16:30; treasure hall reception until 16:00 (official). The opening and closing hours of the grounds themselves are not confirmed on the official site.
katori.parking: Free No. 1 lot (about 100 spaces) and No. 3 lot (about 100 spaces). Notices of restrictions on event days (official).

ikisu.name: Ikisu Jinja
ikisu.summary: One of the Three Shrines of the East, together with Katori and Kashima. Its chief deity is Kunado-no-Kami, with Ame-no-Torifune-no-Kami and the Three Sumiyoshi Deities enshrined alongside in the same hall.
ikisu.deity_note: Kunado-no-Kami is said to correspond to "Tsukitatsu-Funado-no-Kami" of the Kojiki and "Funado-no-Kami" of the Nihon Shoki (an understanding from the encyclopedia and shrine tradition; to be confirmed). In the Kojiki, Ame-no-Torifune-no-Kami accompanies Takemikazuchi-no-Kami as deputy envoy in the transfer of the land.
history: Said to have been first enshrined in the reign of Emperor Ōjin, and tradition holds that in 807 (Daidō 2) Fujiwara no Uchimaro moved it to the present site by order of Emperor Heizei (official).
The present shrine buildings were completed in 1963 (Shōwa 38) (official).
Its ranks (Kokushi Genzaisha, former Kensha) are from the encyclopedia only. It is said not to be listed in the Engishiki register of shrines.
highlights: Beside the first torii are two wells called Oshioi (official).
ikisu.access: Not directly connected to a railway station. About 15 minutes by taxi from Omigawa Station, or about 20 minutes by taxi from Kashima-jingū Station or Itako Station. Community bus from Kashima-jingū Station, or the "Kashima-gō" bus from the Yaesu South Exit of Tokyo Station (official).
ikisu.hours: Shrine office 8:30–16:00; goshuin 9:00–16:00; last reception for prayers 15:30 (official). Opening and closing of the grounds to be confirmed.
ikisu.parking: Kamisu City lists the "Ikisu-no-Mori Parking Lot" as free, with 82 spaces for cars and 4 for large buses.

awa.name: Awa Jinja
awa.summary: Ichinomiya of Awa Province. It enshrines Ame-no-Futodama-no-Mikoto, ancestral deity of the Inbe clan, and the Lower Shrine enshrines Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto, said to be his grandson deity.
awa.deity_note: Ame-no-Futodama-no-Mikoto appears in the Kojiki in the Heavenly Rock Cave and the descent of the heavenly grandson. Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki and is found only in the Kogo Shūi. Ame-no-Hiritome-no-Mikoto is said to be his consort, but does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki.
history: The official site records that the founding is said to date from the first year of the Kōki imperial era (660 BC).

The origin is said to be when Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto led the Inbe clan of Awa in Shikoku on the Kuroshio current, landed at the southern tip of Bōsō, and enshrined the ancestral deity on Mt. Ogami and Mt. Megami at Mera Beach; it is said to have been moved to the present site in 717 (Yōrō 1). Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto's opening of Bōsō is recorded in the Kogo Shūi, but historical confirmation requires separate study.
A Myōjin Taisha of the Engishiki. A Kanpei Taisha in the Meiji period, and a Beppyō shrine from 1946 (Shōwa 21) (official).
highlights: There are the Upper Shrine (main shrine) and the Lower Shrine (auxiliary shrine), and the subsidiary shrines Itsukushima-sha and Kotohira-sha (official).
awa.access: The nearest station and travel time are not confirmed in the official text.
awa.hours: Amulets and goshuin 8:30–16:30; prayers 9:00–16:00 (official). Visiting hours for the grounds to be confirmed.

susaki.name: Susaki Jinja
susaki.summary: A shrine enshrining Ame-no-Hirinome-no-Mikoto, said to be the consort of Ame-no-Futodama-no-Mikoto, the deity of Awa Jinja. It is a candidate shrine (ronsha) for a listing in the Engishiki, and in the Edo period was regarded as Ichinomiya of Awa Province.
susaki.deity_note: The deity is not found in the portions of the Kojiki, Nihon Shoki and Kogo Shūi obtained, so rather than stating "not in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki" we mark it "to be confirmed". The entries in the Engishiki register of shrines and the Six National Histories are as described in the encyclopedia; the original texts have not been confirmed.
history: According to the shrine record "Susaki Daimyōjin Yuisho Kyūki" (1753, Hōreki 3), it began in the reign of Emperor Jinmu when Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto enshrined on Mt. Mitarai a mirror of his grandmother deity Ame-no-Hirinome-no-Mikoto as the sacred object.

The encyclopedia records that the Azuma Kagami says Minamoto no Yoritomo visited after the Battle of Ishibashiyama and donated shrine lands (the original text of the Azuma Kagami has not been confirmed).
The main sanctuary is a Tangible Cultural Property designated by Tateyama City (said to have been built in the Enpō era, 1673–81; designated in 1967).
One of the candidate shrines (ronsha) for the shrine listed in the Engishiki as "Kisaki-gami Ame-no-Hirinome-no-Mikoto Jinja". The other candidate is Sunomiya Jinja. This has not been settled.
highlights: There are 148 stone steps up to the worship hall (quoted by the encyclopedia from Chiba Prefecture's guide).
susaki.address: 1344 Susaki, Tateyama, Chiba (Tateyama City and the encyclopedia). The introduction on the official Awa Jinja site gives 1334, which does not match.

tamasaki.name: Tamasaki Jinja
tamasaki.summary: An old shrine listed as a Myōjin Taisha in the Engishiki register of shrines as Ichinomiya of Kazusa Province; its deity is Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto. It is known for the annual festival in September and the Kazusa Jūnisha Festival (a hamaori rite of going down to the beach).
tamasaki.deity_note: The deity on the official site is Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto (in the Engishiki it has been taken to be Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto alone). The official site notes that old shrine records also list the name Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto alongside, and that study of the enshrined deity continues today. Tamayori-hime appears in the Umisachi-Yamasachi section of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (as the younger sister of Toyotama-hime, entrusted with raising the child). The official top page also says "Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto and the deities of her family", but the specific names are not confirmed on the official pages.
history: It is listed as a Myōjin Taisha of Kazusa Province in the Engishiki register of shrines, compiled in the Heian period (official history page).

The official top page says it "is said to have been founded in 807 (Daidō 2), in the reign of Emperor Heizei". However, this statement was confirmed only once, and the encyclopedia (Wikipedia) gives the founding year as unknown.

Many shrine buildings and documents were lost in the fires of war in the Eiroku era. Even so, the official site states that the annual festival held every year from 10 to 13 September has a history of at least 1,200 years.
highlights: The Kazusa Jūnisha Festival, an Intangible Folk Cultural Property. The official site explains that it has the oldest history and tradition among the many hamaori beach rites of the Bōsō Peninsula.
The official site has guides to the "Ley Line of the Path of the Rising Sun" and a "Precinct Walking Course" (details not confirmed).
tamasaki.access: Official: an 8-minute walk from Kazusa-Ichinomiya Station on the JR Sotobō Line, along National Route 128. Right by the Ichinomiya interchange of the Kujūkuri Naminori Road.
tamasaki.hours: Not confirmed on the official site (a search-result summary gave prayer reception as 9:00–15:30, but this is not confirmed in the text of the official pages).
tamasaki.parking: Parking available. Large buses should enquire in advance (official). The number of spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official site.
tamasaki.goshuin: Not confirmed on the official site.

hikawa.name: Hikawa Jinja (Ōmiya)
hikawa.summary: An old shrine in Ōmiya regarded as Ichinomiya of Musashi Province. It enshrines three deities, Susanoo-no-Mikoto, Inada-hime-no-Mikoto and Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto, and was designated a shrine of imperial festivals in 1868 (Meiji 1). It is known for its approach, about 2 km of zelkova-lined avenue leading from the Nakasendō.
hikawa.deity_note: The official deities are Susanoo-no-Mikoto, Inada-hime-no-Mikoto and Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto. Susanoo-no-Mikoto and Inada-hime-no-Mikoto (Kushinada-hime in the Kojiki) are married in the Yamata-no-Orochi section. In the Kojiki, Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto is one of the other names of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami and is a descendant of Susanoo-no-Mikoto. All three appear in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. The relation between the shrine name "Hikawa" and the Hi River (Hikawa) of Izumo is not confirmed on the official site, so we do not assert it.
history: The official site tells that it was founded on the day of the Sheep in the fourth month of the third year of the reign of Emperor Kōshō, the fifth emperor.
It is said that in the reign of Emperor Seimu, Etamohi-no-Mikoto of the Izumo clan became kuni-no-miyatsuko (governor) of Musashi by order of the court and revered this shrine, raising its standing.

On 17 October 1868 (Meiji 1) it received the "Edict for the Emperor's Personal Worship at Hikawa Jinja" and was designated a shrine of imperial festivals, and in 1871 (Meiji 4) it was ranked a Kanpei Taisha.
highlights: The approach, about 2 km of zelkova-lined avenue running from the first torii on the Nakasendō (official site).

Within the grounds are the Rōmon gate (which the official site explains was modelled on the Rōmon of the Kamo shrines in Kyoto), the spring-fed Hebi-no-Ike (Snake Pond), a sazare-ishi stone, chikara-ishi strength stones and more.
The present main sanctuary was built in 1940 (Shōwa 15) (official precinct guide).
hikawa.access: Official: about 15 minutes from the East Exit of JR Ōmiya Station. About 10 minutes from Kita-Ōmiya Station on the Tōbu Urban Park Line to the west parking lot.
hikawa.hours: According to a search summary of the official site, the Rōmon gate is open 5:30–17:30 in March, April, September and October, 5:00–18:00 from May to August, and 6:00–17:00 in January, February, November and December. This has not been directly confirmed in the page text.
hikawa.parking: Official: No. 1 lot 40–100 spaces (24 hours; paid after 40 minutes), No. 2 lot about 20 spaces (8:00–17:00), west lot about 120 spaces (7:00–18:00; for group buses). Fully closed during the Daitōsai Tōkamachi fair (10 December) and the New Year period (1–3 January).
hikawa.goshuin: According to a search summary of the official site, the fee for a handwritten goshuin is ¥500, pre-written sheets are ¥500 for the regular version and ¥1,000 for the special version, and amulets are given 8:30–16:30. This has not been directly confirmed in the page text.

suwa.name: Suwa Taisha Kamisha Honmiya
suwa.summary: The Kamisha Honmiya (Upper Shrine, Main Shrine) of the head shrine of the Suwa shrines, said to number about 10,000 across Japan, and Ichinomiya of Shinano Province. The official site explains that it has no main sanctuary and preserves an old form of worship in which the sacred mountain itself is venerated.
suwa.deity_note: The official site gives the deity of the Kamisha Honmiya as Takeminakata-no-Kami (the Maemiya enshrines Yasakatome-no-Kami; the Shimosha Harumiya and Akimiya enshrine Takeminakata-no-Kami, Yasakatome-no-Kami and Yaekotoshironushi-no-Kami). In the transfer of the land in the Kojiki, Part 1, Takeminakata-no-Kami is a child of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami who contests strength with Takemikazuchi-no-Kami, loses, is pursued to the Suwa Sea in Shinano Province, and surrenders, saying he will go nowhere but this place. The name Takeminakata-no-Kami does not appear in the Nihon Shoki (Books 1–3 and 14, which have been obtained, were searched). The name Yasakatome-no-Kami does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki (Part 3 of the Kojiki not checked). Yaekotoshironushi-no-Kami corresponds to Kotoshironushi-no-Kami of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (identification of the name to be confirmed).
history: The official site explains that the founding goes back to the myth of the transfer of the land in the Kojiki, and that Takeminakata-no-Kami is the deity who moved from Izumo to Suwa and governed Shinano Province. It records that the date of enshrinement is not known in detail, and that, estimated from the Kojiki and other sources, it is said to be at least 1,500–2,000 years ago.

The official site explains that it is recorded in the Engishiki register of shrines as "Minakatatomi Jinja", first among the 48 seats of Shinano Province, and was already worshipped at that time as Ichinomiya of Shinano Province.

The official site records that in 691 (the fifth year of Empress Jitō) an imperial envoy was sent to pray for the peace of the nation and abundant harvests. Confirmation in the Nihon Shoki has not been completed.

According to the official site, it was ranked a Kokuhei Chūsha in 1871 (Meiji 4), raised to Kanpei Chūsha in 1896 (Meiji 29) and to Kanpei Taisha in 1916 (Taishō 5). After the war, in 1948 (Shōwa 23), the shrine ranks were abolished and the head shrine was renamed "Suwa Taisha".
highlights: The Shikinen Zōei Onbashira Taisai is the greatest rite, held every seventh year in the years of the Tiger and the Monkey, when great fir trunks are hauled and raised at the four corners of the grounds of each of the four shrines (official).

The Shikyakumon (four-legged gate) is the oldest building of the Honmiya; in 1608 (Keichō 13) Tokugawa Ieyasu ordered his retainer Ōkubo Nagayasu to build and donate it. An Important Cultural Property (official).

The East and West Hōden (treasure halls) in the centre of the grounds are thatched and are rebuilt alternately in the years of the Tiger and the Monkey. The "heavenly drops of the Hōden", drops of water said to fall from the roof, is one of the Seven Wonders of Suwa (official).

The Heihaiden and the left and right Kata-haiden stand in a row, in a distinctive layout with no main sanctuary. The present buildings are Tatekawa-school architecture built over the years from 1831 (Tenpō 2) to 1837 (Tenpō 8) (official).
The Nunobashi of the entrance gate (Iriguchi Gomon) was built in 1829 (Bunsei 12), and its long corridor is about 70 m. An Important Cultural Property (official).
suwa.access: The official site gives it as about 6 km south-east of Kami-Suwa Station on the Chūō Line. Kami-Suwa, Shimo-Suwa and Chino stations are listed as the nearest stations; by car, use Okaya IC or Suwa IC on the Chūō Expressway. Bus and walking times from the stations are not confirmed on the official site.
suwa.hours: The shrines do not close their gates and can be visited freely (official). The amulet office is open 8:30–17:00; the treasure hall is open 9:00–16:00, with admission ¥500 for adults and ¥300 for children (official).
suwa.parking: The number of parking spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official pages obtained. To be confirmed.
suwa.goshuin: Each of the four shrines has its own goshuin (official FAQ). The amulet office is open 8:30–17:00, but the hours and place for goshuin are not confirmed on the official site.

takachiho.name: Takachiho Jinja
takachiho.summary: An old shrine in Takachiho, Miyazaki, enshrining the deities of the three generations of Hyūga and their consorts (Takachiho Sumegami), and the Jissha Daimyōjin. It is regarded as the head shrine (sōja) of the 88 shrines of the Takachiho district.
takachiho.deity_note: The deities are given as Takachiho Sumegami (the collective name for Ninigi-no-Mikoto, Konohanasakuya-hime, Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto, Toyotama-hime, Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto and Tamayori-hime) and the Jissha Daimyōjin (Mikeirino-no-Mikoto, his wife Unome-hime-no-Mikoto and their eight child deities) (tk1 tk4 tk5). The three generations of Hyūga and Mikeirino-no-Mikoto appear in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, but the names of Unome-hime-no-Mikoto and the child deities are not found in the texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki obtained. The shrine's official site could not be reached, so the deities were confirmed only on sites run by the town, the tourist association and the Miyazaki Prefecture Shinto Youth Association. The list of the child deities' names is from a private site (tk4) only.
history: Said to have been founded about 1,900 years ago, in the reign of Emperor Suinin.
A Kokushi Genzaisha, recorded in the Six National Histories, and said to have been granted the highest divine rank in Hyūga Province (details of when the rank was granted are not confirmed).
The present main sanctuary is said to have been built in 1778 (An'ei 7). It is a nagare-zukuri building with a copper-plate roof, and a National Important Cultural Property.
The encyclopedia records that in 1971 it was listed as a Beppyō shrine of the Association of Shinto Shrines (not confirmed officially).
highlights: The main sanctuary and a pair of iron komainu (guardian lion-dogs) are designated National Important Cultural Properties.
The Chichibu cedar is said to be about 800 years old, and is said to have been planted by Hatakeyama Shigetada when he visited on behalf of Minamoto no Yoritomo.
The Meoto-sugi (married couple cedar) is a cedar whose two trunks have joined into one; it is said that a couple who walk around it three times will be happy.

Tourist kagura is performed in the kagura hall every day from 8 to 9 p.m.; the pieces are the Tajikarao dance, the Uzume dance, the Totori dance and the Goshintai dance. Fees: ¥1,000 for individuals, among others (subject to change).
takachiho.address: 1037 Ōaza Mitai, Takachiho, Nishiusuki District, Miyazaki (882-1101). Tel. 0982-72-2413 (as listed by the tourist association).
takachiho.access: The tourist association gives it as about a 15-minute walk from Takachiho Bus Center. Not confirmed on the shrine's official site.
takachiho.hours: Visiting and amulet hours are not confirmed on the official site (the tourist association's page does not list them either, and advises enquiring by telephone).
takachiho.parking: The tourist association says there is free parking for about 100 cars. Not confirmed on the official site.
takachiho.goshuin: Whether goshuin are available, where they are given and the fee are not confirmed on the official site.

hokkaido.name: Hokkaidō Jingū
hokkaido.summary: Located at Maruyama in Sapporo, it enshrines four deities: Ōkunitama-no-Kami, Ōnamuchi-no-Kami and Sukunahikona-no-Kami (the three deities of pioneering), and Emperor Meiji. Its founding in 1869 (Meiji 2) began with a rite enshrining the guardian deities of the pioneering of Hokkaidō.
hokkaido.deity_note: The official site gives four deities and explains them as: Ōkunitama-no-Kami, the deity of the land of Hokkaidō; Ōnamuchi-no-Kami, the deity of land management and pioneering, the same deity as Ōkuninushi-no-Kami; Sukunahikona-no-Kami, the deity of land management, medicine and sake brewing; and Emperor Meiji, the 122nd emperor, who laid the foundations of modern Japan. Emperor Meiji was added in 1964 (Shōwa 39) and is not a deity of the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki. Ōnamuchi-no-Kami corresponds to Ōnamuji-no-Kami of the Kojiki (later Ōkuninushi-no-Kami), and Sukunahikona-no-Kami, as Sukunabikona-no-Kami of the Kojiki and Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto of the Nihon Shoki, appears in the scene where he joins forces with Ōnamuji-no-Kami (Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto) to build and firm up the land. As for Ōkunitama-no-Kami, in the classical texts obtained the name "Ōkunitama-no-Kami" does not appear in the Kojiki; a variant account in the Nihon Shoki gives "Ōkunitama-no-Kami" (written 大国玉神) as one of the other names of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, and a note in the Kogo Shūi gives "Ōkunitama-no-Kami" (大国魂神) as another name of Ōnamuchi-no-Kami. However, the official site counts Ōkunitama-no-Kami as a separate deity from Ōnamuchi-no-Kami and does not say they are the same. A direct connection between the pioneering of Hokkaidō and the myths of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki is not written in those texts.
history: The official site records that on 1 September 1869 (Meiji 2), by the will of Emperor Meiji, the "Hokkaidō Chinza Shinsai", a rite enshrining Ōkunitama-no-Kami, Ōnamuchi-no-Kami and Sukunahikona-no-Kami as guardian deities of pioneering, was held at the Jingikan in Tokyo, and this is regarded as the founding of Hokkaidō Jingū.

In May 1871 (Meiji 4) the shrine's name was fixed as "Sapporo Jinja", and in September of the same year the shrine buildings were completed at the present site in Maruyama and the rite of relocation was held (official).
In 1964 (Shōwa 39) Emperor Meiji was added to the enshrined deities and the name was changed to "Hokkaidō Jingū" (official).

In November 1974 (Shōwa 49) the shrine buildings were destroyed by arson, and they were restored in 1978 (Shōwa 53). In 1988 (Shōwa 63) the worship hall was renovated, giving the present appearance (official).
highlights: Kaitaku Jinja, a shrine within the grounds, was founded in 1938 (Shōwa 13) to enshrine forebears who devoted themselves to the pioneering of Hokkaidō, and now enshrines 37 of them. Its annual festival is on 15 August every year (official).
hokkaido.address: 474 Miyagaoka, Chūō Ward, Sapporo (the official English page writes it as 474 Miyagaoka, Chuo-ku, Sapporo-city). The postal code is not confirmed on the official pages.
hokkaido.access: Official: about a 15-minute walk from Maruyama-Kōen Station on the Tōzai subway line. About a 1-minute walk from the JR Bus stop "Hokkaidō Jingū". About 15 minutes by taxi from JR Sapporo Station.
hokkaido.hours: The official opening and closing hours of the grounds are: 8–31 January 7:00–16:00; February 7:00–16:00; March 7:00–17:00; 1 April–31 October 6:00–17:00; 1 November–30 December 7:00–16:00 (different hours on New Year's Eve, the first three days of January and so on). Amulets and goshuin are given from 9:00 a.m. until closing on ordinary days. The date of the official page is unknown, so check the official site again before visiting.
hokkaido.parking: The official site has information on the Kita-Ichijō and Minami-Ichijō parking lots. Those who receive a prayer service park free for 2 hours from entry (official prayer page). The number of spaces and regular fees are not confirmed on the official site.
hokkaido.goshuin: Hours for goshuin are as above (from 9:00 a.m. on ordinary days). The fee is not confirmed on the official pages. A notice on the official top page announces a "suspension of writing in goshuin books (1 Dec–15 Feb)", so in some years handwritten goshuin are suspended in winter.

shiogama.name: Shiogama Jinja
shiogama.summary: Standing on Mt. Ichimori overlooking Shiogama Bay, it enshrines Shiotsuchi-no-Oji-no-Kami in the Betsugū, Takemikazuchi-no-Kami in the Left Shrine and Futsunushi-no-Kami in the Right Shrine. Shiwahiko Jinja stands in the same grounds. The shrine buildings were completed by the Sendai Domain in 1704 (Hōei 1) and are National Important Cultural Properties.
shiogama.deity_note: According to the official site, Shiotsuchi-no-Oji-no-Kami is enshrined in the Betsugū, Takemikazuchi-no-Kami in the Left Shrine and Futsunushi-no-Kami in the Right Shrine, and the present buildings also have three main sanctuaries, one for each deity: the Betsugū, the Left Shrine and the Right Shrine (with two worship halls, one for the Betsugū and one for the Left and Right Shrines). The tradition the official site tells is that, with Shiotsuchi-no-Oji-no-Kami as their guide, Takemikazuchi-no-Kami and Futsunushi-no-Kami came down to Shiogama, pacified Mutsu Province, returned in triumph and were enshrined here; the two deities then moved to Hitachi Province (Kashima Jingū) and Shimōsa Province (Katori Jingū), and further to Mt. Mikasa in Nara (Kasuga Taisha). Shiotsuchi-no-Oji-no-Kami is said to have stayed in Shiogama and taught the people how to make salt. In the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, Takemikazuchi-no-Kami and Futsunushi-no-Kami appear side by side in the Nihon Shoki (Book 2, section 9) as the deities who pacify Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni. Shiotsuchi-no-Oji appears in the Umisachi-Yamasachi section of the Nihon Shoki (section 10) and in the book of Emperor Jinmu, and in the Kojiki Shiotsuchi-no-Kami appears in the same section (regarding the two as the same deity is the generally accepted understanding; the texts obtained do not say so). A search of the classical texts obtained found no occurrence of the words "Shiogama" or "Mutsu", and no passage in which Shiotsuchi-no-Oji guides Takemikazuchi-no-Kami and Futsunushi-no-Kami could be confirmed. The official tradition is not a story written in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki.
history: The official site records, "according to tradition", that with Shiotsuchi-no-Oji-no-Kami as their guide, Takemikazuchi-no-Kami and Futsunushi-no-Kami came down to Shiogama, pacified Mutsu Province, and were later enshrined here. The place name Shiogama is also said to derive from the shrine's name.

The official site records that the oldest official record is the entry "ten thousand sheaves for the worship of the Shiogama deity" in the Shuzei-shiki of the Kōnin-shiki, from the early Heian period.

In the Edo period, successive lords of the Date family of the Sendai Domain built the shrine buildings and presided over the rites themselves as "Ōkannushi" (chief priest). The present buildings were begun in the Genroku era and completed in 1704 (Hōei 1); 14 buildings, including the three main sanctuaries of the Betsugū, Left Shrine and Right Shrine, and the stone torii are designated National Important Cultural Properties (official).

Since the Hōei era the buildings have been repaired at roughly 20-year intervals; according to the ridge tablets, eight sengū (rites of relocation) were carried out between 1727 (Kyōhō 12) and 1862 (Bunkyū 2). The 19th Shikinen Sengū is scheduled for 2031 (Reiwa 13) (official).
highlights: The grounds cover about 30 hectares, with about 500 species of plants including the Shiogama cherry and the tarayō, and the official site records that they are valued academically as a boundary between northern and southern plants.

At Okama Jinja, a subsidiary shrine outside the grounds, four flat iron cauldrons called the "Shinkama" (sacred cauldrons), said to have been used by Shiotsuchi-no-Oji-no-Kami when he taught salt-making, are enshrined; they are counted among the "Three Wonders of Japan" (official).
Shiwahiko Jinja, in the same grounds, is listed in the Engishiki register of shrines and enshrines Shiwahiko-no-Kami (official).
shiogama.access: Official: about a 15-minute walk (about 3 minutes by taxi) from Hon-Shiogama Station on the JR Senseki Line. About a 25-minute walk (about 5 minutes by taxi) from Shiogama Station on the JR Tōhoku Main Line. About 10 minutes from Rifu-Naka IC or Rifu-Shiogama IC on the Sanriku Expressway, or about 15 minutes from Sendai-Kōhoku IC.
shiogama.hours: Official gate hours (Shiogama Jinja): January–February 5:00–17:00; March–October 5:00–18:00; November–December 5:00–17:00 (separate notice for the first three days of January). Even when the gates are closed, the grounds outside the gate can be visited freely. Shiwahiko Jinja's hours differ by month (see the official access guide).
shiogama.parking: Official: four free parking lots for worshippers (No. 1, No. 2, No. 3 and a bus-only lot) from the east to the north side of the grounds, about 350 spaces in total.
shiogama.goshuin: Official: the goshuin of both Shiwahiko Jinja and Shiogama Jinja are stamped across a two-page spread, and the fee is ¥500 for both. The reception counter is on the left after entering the main gate of Shiogama Jinja, and follows the prayer reception hours. At other times, only pre-written sheets are available at the amulet office on the right after entering the gate (while the gates are open).

dewa.name: Dewa Sanzan Jinja
dewa.summary: A shrine that enshrines the three mountains of Dewa: Mt. Haguro, Mt. Gassan and Mt. Yudono. Of its three shrines, Gassan Jinja (Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto), Ideha Jinja (Ideha-no-Kami and Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto) and Yudonosan Jinja (Ōyamatsumi-no-Mikoto, Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto and Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto), Gassan and Yudono cannot be visited in winter, so the deities of the three mountains are enshrined together in the Sanjin Gōsaiden on the summit of Mt. Haguro.
dewa.deity_note: The official history records that Gassan Jinja enshrines Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto, that Ideha Jinja enshrines Ideha-no-Kami, the land spirit (kunitama) of Dewa Province, and Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto, and that Yudonosan Jinja enshrines Ōyamatsumi-no-Mikoto, Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto and Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto. In the inner sanctuary of the Sanjin Gōsaiden, Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto is in the centre at the front, Ideha-no-Kami (Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto) on the right, and Ōyamatsumi-no-Mikoto, Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto and Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto on the left. Until the Edo period it was a mountain of Shugendō in which Shinto and Buddhism were fused; since the Meiji era it has been served according to Shinto. Relation to the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki: Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto appears in both (in the Kojiki he is one of the Three Noble Children, born when Izanagi-no-Mikoto washed his right eye). Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto (稲倉魂命) corresponds to Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto (倉稲魂命) of the Nihon Shoki and to Ukanomitama-no-Kami (宇迦之御魂神) of the Kojiki (treating them as the same deity is the generally accepted understanding). Ōyamatsumi-no-Mikoto, Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto (Ōkuninushi-no-Mikoto) and Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto also appear in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. Ideha-no-Kami, on the other hand, does not appear in either (confirmed by searching the classical texts obtained). The relation between the Dewa Sanzan mountains themselves, Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto and the myths of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki is not confirmed in the texts obtained.
history: According to the official history, in 593 (the first year of Empress Suiko) Prince Hachiko, a son of Emperor Sushun, came to Dewa, was led by a three-legged sacred crow into Mt. Haguro, witnessed the appearance of Ideha-no-Kami, the great deity of Haguro, and established Ideha Jinja on the summit. He is said to have later opened Mt. Gassan and Mt. Yudono as well.

The official top page records that until the Edo period the Dewa Sanzan were mountains of Shugendō enshrining gongen in the fusion of Shinto and Buddhism, and that they became Shinto sacred mountains from the Meiji era on; but the old Haguro-school Shugendō practised since the mountains were opened has been carried on, and faith in the Dewa Sanzan remains unchanged today.

According to the official guide to the grounds, the present Sanjin Gōsaiden was completed in 1818 (Bunsei 1) and has a thatched roof about 28 m high. It was designated a National Important Cultural Property in 2000 (Heisei 12).
highlights: The Sanjin Gōsaiden stands on the summit of Mt. Haguro and holds the worship hall and main sanctuary within a single building, a distinctive style called "gōsaiden-zukuri". The interior is entirely lacquered in vermilion, and it enshrines the three deities of Gassan, Haguro and Yudono. Because Gassan and Yudono cannot be visited in winter, all festivals of the three mountains are held in this building (official guide to the grounds).

On the main approach to Mt. Haguro, it is about 10 minutes from the Zuishinmon gate up the stone steps to the National Treasure five-storey pagoda, and about 1 to 1.5 hours to climb the stone steps to the summit (official access page).

At the foot of Mt. Haguro stands the five-storey pagoda that the official site calls the "National Treasure Haguro-san Five-Storey Pagoda", about 10 minutes from the Zuishinmon gate by the stone steps (official access page).
dewa.address: 7 Tōge Aza Tōge, Haguro-machi, Tsuruoka, Yamagata 997-0292. Tel. 0235-62-2355 (footer of the official top page). The location is taken as the Sanjin Gōsaiden on the summit of Mt. Haguro.
dewa.access: Official: from Tsuruoka City, about 50 minutes by Shōnai Kōtsū bus bound for "Haguro-sanchō" (Haguro summit), to the last stop. To climb the stone steps of the main approach or to see the National Treasure five-storey pagoda, take the same bus and get off at "Zuishinmon". By car, the road to the summit is the Haguro-san toll road: about 10 km from Tsuruoka IC on the Yamagata Expressway, about 15 km from Shōnai-Asahi IC, and about 30 km from Shōnai Airport.
dewa.hours: Official FAQ: prayer services are held every hour from 9:00 to 16:00, and prayer reception is about 8:40–15:50 (apply at least 15 minutes before the start). Telephone reception on the official top page is 8:30–17:00. Visiting hours for the grounds and the hours of the amulet offices (a search-result summary gives the summit amulet office as about 8:30–16:30 and the Zuishinmon amulet office as about 9:00–16:30) are not confirmed directly in the official text.
dewa.parking: Official: by car you can reach the summit on the Haguro-san toll road (there is a summit parking lot; visitors are told to check fees and operating hours with the operator, Shōnai Kōtsū). The toll road is open all year, but it is not cleared of snow early in the morning or at night in winter. From the parking lot at the foot, it is about 15 minutes from the Zuishinmon gate up the stone steps of the main approach to the National Treasure five-storey pagoda.
dewa.goshuin: Official: the amulet and goshuin offices are open about 8:30–16:30 at the Sanshūden on the summit of Mt. Haguro and about 9:00–16:30 at the Zuishinmon amulet office at the foot. Goshuin cannot be sent by post. The fee is not confirmed in the official text.

hakusan.name: Shirayamahime Jinja
hakusan.summary: Ichinomiya of Kaga Province, with the sacred Mt. Hakusan as its divine mountain; the official site records it as the head shrine of the more than 3,000 Hakusan shrines across Japan. It enshrines three deities: Shirayama-hime-no-Ōkami (Kukuri-hime-no-Mikoto), Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto.
hakusan.deity_note: The official site gives the deities as Shirayama-hime-no-Ōkami (Kukuri-hime-no-Mikoto), Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto. Izanagi and Izanami are the deities of the birth of the land and of Yomi in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. Kukuri-hime-no-Kami does not appear in the Kojiki; she appears only once, in a variant account of the fifth section of Book 1 of the Nihon Shoki (the passage at Yomotsu Hirasaka), where, after the exchange between Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Yomotsu-chimoribito, "Kukuri-hime-no-Kami had something to say, and Izanagi-no-Mikoto heard it and approved". What she said is not written. The official site links "kukuri" to "kukuru" (to bind together) and records that she is also revered as a deity of harmony and matchmaking.
history: The official site records that the shrine "is said to have been founded in 91 BC (the 7th year of Emperor Sujin) on Funaoka-yama (now Yahoro-machi (八幌町; reading to be confirmed), Hakusan City)". It then says the shrine was moved to the Tedori River in 297 (the 28th year of Emperor Ōjin) and to the "Akudo-no-mori" grove in 716 (Reiki 2).
The official chronology lists "Taichō's ascent of Hakusan (Taichō Oshō-den)" on 18 June 717 (Yōrō 1). Taichō's opening of Mt. Hakusan is handed down as tradition.

The official site positions the shrine as "the great shrine protecting Hokuriku, Hakusan Hongū and Ichinomiya of Kaga", and records it as the head shrine of the more than 3,000 Hakusan shrines across Japan.
highlights: The official top page introduces the main sanctuary, the main approach, the treasure hall and a map of the grounds (the contents of each are not confirmed).
hakusan.access: Official: by car, about 20 minutes from Mikawa IC or about 35 minutes from Hakusan IC. By train, from Kanazawa Station take the IR Ishikawa Railway to Shin-Nishi-Kanazawa, change to the Hokuriku Railway to Tsurugi Station (about 28 minutes), then about 5 minutes by taxi from the station.
hakusan.hours: Visiting hours are not confirmed on the official site.
hakusan.parking: Official: free. Main approach lot about 30 spaces, north approach lot about 300 spaces, south approach lot about 130 spaces.
hakusan.goshuin: The official top page says "Goshuin: available", but the hours and fee are not confirmed on the official site.

keta.name: Keta Taisha
keta.summary: Located in Hakui City on the Noto Peninsula, it enshrines Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto in the main sanctuary. Many of its buildings are National Important Cultural Properties, and the shrine grove behind it, the "Irazu-no-mori", is a National Natural Monument.
keta.deity_note: The official site gives the deity of the main sanctuary as Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto. In the Kojiki, Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto is another name of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami (Ōnamuji-no-Kami and others); in the Nihon Shoki and the Kogo Shūi he appears as Ōnamuchi-no-Kami, and he is the same deity as in the existing entry for Ōkuninushi. The official site records the auxiliary shrines Okumiya (Susanoo-no-Mikoto and Kushinadahime-no-Mikoto), Hakusan Jinja (Kukuri-hime-no-Kami) and Wakamiya Jinja (Kotoshironushi-no-Kami).
history: The oldest documentary record the official site cites is the Man'yōshū: in 748 (Tenpyō 20, in the reign of Emperor Shōmu), Ōtomo no Yakamochi, governor of Etchū, visited the shrine.

The official explanation records that the shrine's divine rank rose in the early Heian period (a passage that reads as Junior Third Rank in 784 and First Order of Merit in 896) and that it became the great shrine representative of Noto.

Tourist sites say that the shrine "is said to have been founded in the reign of Emperor Sujin" and that "Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto opened up Noto and settled there as its guardian deity", but the founding tradition could not be confirmed on the official history page. Its position as Ichinomiya of Noto Province is also not confirmed on the official site.
highlights: Official: the main sanctuary (1982, Shōwa 57), the worship hall (1961, Shōwa 36), the shrine gate (1961, Shōwa 36), Hakusan Jinja (1982, Shōwa 57) and Wakamiya Jinja (1950, Shōwa 25) are National Important Cultural Properties.
Official: the shrine grove "Irazu-no-mori" is a National Natural Monument (designated 1967, Shōwa 42).
keta.access: Official: about 10 minutes by car from Hakui Station, about a 7-minute walk from the "Ichinomiya" bus stop, or about 5 minutes from Yanagida IC on the Noto Satoyama Kaidō.
keta.hours: Visiting hours are not confirmed on the official site.
keta.parking: The number of spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official site.
keta.goshuin: Hours and fee are not confirmed on the official site.

yahiko.name: Yahiko Jinja
yahiko.summary: Located at the foot of Mt. Yahiko, it enshrines Ame-no-Kaguyama-no-Mikoto (Iyahiko-no-Ōkami) and is Ichinomiya of Echigo Province. The official site records that it has been revered as a Myōjin Taisha, Ichinomiya of Echigo and Kokuhei Chūsha, and it is affectionately called "Oyahiko-sama".
yahiko.deity_note: The official site gives the deity as Iyahiko-no-Ōkami (Ame-no-Kaguyama-no-Mikoto). Ame-no-Kaguyama-no-Mikoto does not appear as a person in the Kojiki; "Ame-no-Kaguyama" appears there as the name of the mountain in the Ama-no-Iwayato episode (confirmed by search). A variant account in the ninth section of Book 2 (Age of the Gods, Part 2) of the Nihon Shoki says "Ame-no-Kaguyama, child of Ame-no-Hoakari-no-Mikoto, is the distant ancestor of the Owari no Muraji and others", which is the closest passage, but regarding this as the same deity as the one enshrined at Yahiko is an identification made by the shrine and later generations and cannot be confirmed from the text itself. Ame-no-Kaguyama-no-Mikoto as a person could not be confirmed in the Kogo Shūi either. The spelling "Ame-no-Kagoyama-no-Mikoto" and the story of presenting a sacred sword to Emperor Jinmu appear in the Kojiki as the story of Takakuraji of Kumano. Identifying Takakuraji with Ame-no-Kagoyama-no-Mikoto is the view of the Sendai Kuji Hongi, which is not among the texts obtained this time.
history: The official site records that roughly 2,400 years have passed since the founding. The date is shrine tradition and cannot be confirmed as historical fact.
The official site records that, as a Myōjin Taisha, Ichinomiya of Echigo and Kokuhei Chūsha, the shrine received the deep reverence of the imperial court, the shogunate and warlords.

A third-party site introduces the shrine tradition that in the first year of Emperor Kōan Ame-no-Kaguyama-no-Mikoto passed away and was buried on Mt. Yahiko, and that his child Ame-no-Itane-no-Mikoto built a mausoleum shrine, which was the beginning. This is not confirmed on the official site.
highlights: The official top page introduces the treasure hall and the Chrysanthemum Festival held from 1 to 24 November.
yahiko.access: Official: about 1 km (about a 15-minute walk) from Yahiko Station, the terminus of the Yahiko Line. By car, about 13 km (about 30 minutes) from Sanjō-Tsubame IC on the Hokuriku Expressway, or about 15 km (about 30 minutes) from Makikatahigashi IC.
yahiko.hours: Visiting hours are not confirmed on the official site (a third-party site gives 9:00–17:00, with the amulet office 8:30–16:00, but this is not confirmed).
yahiko.parking: Official: free. The lot beside the shrine (20 large buses, 50 cars) and the village-run No. 1 lot (345 cars and others). Both are about a 5-minute walk to the worship hall. Partly paid during the Chrysanthemum Festival.
yahiko.goshuin: The official top page has a section for "ofuda, omamori and goshuin". Hours and fee are not confirmed on the official site.

togakushi.name: Togakushi Jinja Okusha
togakushi.summary: Of Togakushi Jinja, whose five shrines (Okusha, Chūsha, Hōkōsha, Hinomikosha and Kuzuryūsha) stand at the foot of Mt. Togakushi, this is the Okusha (inner shrine), which enshrines Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Mikoto, the deity who opened the Ama-no-Iwato.
togakushi.deity_note: The official deities are: Okusha, Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Mikoto; Chūsha, Ame-no-Yagokoro-omoikane-no-Mikoto; Hōkōsha, Ame-no-Uwaharu-no-Mikoto; Hinomikosha, Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto and others; Kuzuryūsha, Kuzuryū-no-Ōkami. In the Kojiki, Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Kami stands hidden beside the door at the Ama-no-Iwayato, takes Amaterasu-Ōmikami by the hand and draws her out; in the Nihon Shoki too, Tajikarao-no-Kami stands beside the rock door. The place name and shrine name "Togakushi" do not appear in the texts of the Kojiki, Nihon Shoki and Kogo Shūi obtained (confirmed by search). The official site introduces the legend that the rock door fell to the earth and became Mt. Togakushi.
history: The official site records that Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Mikoto is the deity who opened the Ama-no-Iwato, and that his enshrinement at the foot of Mt. Togakushi was the beginning. It also introduces the legend that "the rock door fell and became Mt. Togakushi".
The official site records that the Kuzuryūsha is an older faith, enshrined as the local land deity before Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Mikoto.

The official site records that the spread of Tendai esoteric Buddhism led to the founding of Kenkōji, a temple of fused Shinto and Buddhism, and that the ordinance separating Shinto and Buddhism in the early Meiji years forced a choice between Shinto and Buddhism. It gives the founding of the Hinomikosha as around 1098 (Jōtoku 2).

The official site explains that the deity of the Chūsha, Ame-no-Yagokoro-omoikane-no-Mikoto, is the deity who devised the Iwato kagura (Daidai kagura) and created the occasion for opening the rock door, and that Ame-no-Uwaharu-no-Mikoto of the Hōkōsha is his child.
highlights: Official: the approach to the Okusha is about 2 km and closed to general vehicles; the Okusha and Kuzuryūsha are reached on foot. About 15 minutes from the entrance of the approach to the Zuishinmon gate, and about 20–25 minutes from the Zuishinmon gate to the Okusha.
The official site has a guide page for visiting the five shrines.
togakushi.address: 3506 Togakushi, Nagano, Nagano (third-party information found by search; an address could not be confirmed on the official pages).
togakushi.access: Official: from Nagano Station by local bus or taxi. By car, Nagano IC or Shinano-machi IC on the Jōshin-etsu Expressway.
togakushi.hours: Visiting hours are not confirmed on the official site (third-party information says it is open from late April to early January; not confirmed).
togakushi.parking: Official: about 200 spaces in several lots near the entrance of the Okusha approach (large buses allowed). Large vehicles use the paid parking lot.
togakushi.goshuin: Hours and fee are not confirmed on the official site.

kashihara.name: Kashihara Jingū
kashihara.summary: A jingū founded in 1890 (Meiji 23) on the site southeast of Mt. Unebi that is held to be where Emperor Jinmu's Kashihara Palace stood when he took the throne. It enshrines Emperor Jinmu and his empress, Himetatara-isuzu-hime-no-Mikoto.
kashihara.deity_note: The official site gives the deities as Emperor Jinmu and Empress Himetataraisuzu-hime. Emperor Jinmu is Kamu-yamato-iwarebiko-no-Mikoto in the Kojiki and Kamuyamato-iwarebiko-no-Sumeramikoto in the Nihon Shoki, and the Nihon Shoki records that he took the throne at Kashihara Palace. The empress is, in the Nihon Shoki, the child of Tamakushi-hime, daughter of Kotoshironushi-no-Kami, and in the Kojiki corresponds to Hototatara-isusuki-hime-no-Mikoto, daughter of Ōmononushi-no-Kami; the official site also notes that "Kotoshironushi-no-Kami corresponds to Ōmononushi-no-Kami in the Kojiki". The founding was not in the age of myth but in 1890 (Meiji 23); the place of the deities in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki and the founding year of the shrine should be read as separate things.
history: The official site records that on 2 April 1890 (Meiji 23) Kashihara Jingū, a Kanpei Taisha, was enshrined and founded.

The official site records that in the Meiji era a petition from private citizens arose to found a jingū on the site of Kashihara Palace, and that Emperor Meiji granted the Naishidokoro (Kashikodokoro) of the Kyoto Imperial Palace as the main sanctuary and the Shinkaden as the worship hall.

The official site records that Emperor Jinmu travelled east from Hyūga in Kyushu and took the throne as the first emperor at Kashihara Palace southeast of Mt. Unebi, which it dates as "the first year of the imperial era, some 2,680-odd years ago". The Nihon Shoki also records the accession at Kashihara Palace.
highlights: The main sanctuary is the Naishidokoro (Kashikodokoro) of the Kyoto Imperial Palace and the worship hall is the Shinkaden, both granted by Emperor Meiji (official history).

The official site records that the subsidiary shrine Nagayama Inari-sha was enshrined on this site before Kashihara Jingū was established. Its deities are Ukanomitama-no-Kami, Toyouke-no-Kami and Ōmiyanome-no-Kami.
11 February is the annual festival, the Kigensai, and a special goshuin is given on this day and from 1 to 7 January (official goshuin guide).
kashihara.address: 934 Kume-chō, Kashihara, Nara 634-8550 (official: Access; checked 12 Oct 2026)
kashihara.access: About a 10-minute walk from the central exit of Kashiharajingū-mae Station (official: Access).
kashihara.hours: Opening and closing times differ by month (official: Access). October and November 6:30–17:30; December and January 6:30–17:00; February and March 6:30–17:30; April and May 6:00–18:00; June and July 5:30–18:00; August and September 6:00–18:00. Subject to change for festivals and other events; 31 Dec to 7 Jan is set separately.
kashihara.parking: About 800 spaces. Fees: cars ¥500 per day, medium vehicles ¥1,000 per day, large vehicles ¥2,000 per day. Additional charges after 24 hours; fees differ during festivals such as the New Year period (official: Access; checked 12 Oct 2026).
kashihara.goshuin: The Kashihara Jingū goshuin is ¥500 (goshuin office inside the shrine gate), the Nagayama Inari-sha goshuin is ¥500 (at the prayer hall; at Nagayama Inari-sha from 1 to 7 Jan), and the special goshuin is ¥500 (limited to 1–7 Jan and 11 Feb) (official goshuin guide; checked 12 Oct 2026).

oomishima.name: Ōyamazumi Jinja
oomishima.summary: Located on Ōmishima island in the Seto Inland Sea, it is Ichinomiya of Iyo Province and a former Kokuhei Taisha. Honoured since ancient times as "the guardian shrine of all Japan", it enshrines Ōyamazumi-no-Ōkami, a deity of the mountains who is also regarded as a deity of the sea and of sea voyages. The official site records it as the head shrine of Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami (大山祇神) and Ōyamazumi-no-Kami (大山積神) enshrined across Japan.
oomishima.deity_note: The deity Ōyamazumi-no-Kami is "Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami" (大山津見神) in the Kojiki, where he appears in the descent of the heavenly grandchild in Part 1 as the father of Konohanasakuya-hime (Kamuatatsu-hime) and Iwanaga-hime. In the Nihon Shoki he is "Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami" (大山祇神), appearing in a variant account in Book 1 as a deity who came into being when Izanagi-no-Mikoto cut down Kagutsuchi, and in Book 2 as the father of Kamuatakashitsu-hime (Konohanasakuya-hime). The faith in him as a guardian deity of safety at sea is the shrine's own explanation (said to be based on the Iyo no Kuni Fudoki), not a description in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki.
history: It is said that Ochi-no-Mikoto, a descendant of Ōyamazumi-no-Ōkami who crossed to Shikoku ahead of Emperor Jinmu's eastern expedition, invited the deity to Ōmishima and enshrined him there. The sacred camphor tree in front of the main sanctuary is said to have been planted by Ochi-no-Mikoto himself.

On 22 April 719 (Yōrō 3) the shrine was moved to its present site (Miyaura, Ōmishima-chō), and for this reason the annual festival is held on 22 April of the old calendar. Before that it is said to have been enshrined at Seto in the southeast of Ōmishima (Seto, Kamiura-chō).

Honoured since ancient times as "the guardian shrine of all Japan", in the Taishō era it was ranked as the only Kokuhei Taisha in Shikoku. The main sanctuary and worship hall were rebuilt in the early Muromachi period and are both National Important Cultural Properties.
