highlights: The official site introduces the treasure hall as preserving and displaying about 80% of the arms and armour designated National Treasures or Important Cultural Properties across Japan. It holds items such as the National Treasure great sword (unsigned, attributed to Bungo Tomoyuki); its collection of armour is said to be the finest in Japan, and Ōmishima is called "the island of National Treasures".
oomishima.access: By car, 7 km from Ōmishima IC on the Nishiseto Expressway (Shimanami Kaidō). By bus from the Honshu side, take the Shimanami Liner from JR Fukuyama Station to Ōmishima BS, then Setonaikai Kōtsū (bound for Miyaura Port) for about 12 minutes and get off at "Ōyamazumi Jinja-mae". From the Shikoku side, about 65 minutes from JR Imabari Station by Setouchi Bus (limited express) or Setonaikai Kōtsū (express), getting off at "Ōyamazumi Jinja-mae" (official guide).
oomishima.hours: The gates are open from around sunrise to 17:00. The amulet office (ofuda, omamori and goshuin) is open 9:00–17:00, and prayer reception is 9:30–16:00. The treasure hall is open 9:00–16:30 (last entry 16:00) according to an official notice dated 1 March 2024.
oomishima.parking: 13 spaces beside the torii. The official site also says that the Ōmishima Fuji Park parking lot and others can be used (details of fees and number of spaces are not confirmed on the official site).
oomishima.goshuin: Goshuin are given at the amulet office (which also serves as the prayer reception) together with ofuda and omamori; hours are 9:00–17:00. The fee is not confirmed on the official site.

miho.name: Miho Jinja
miho.summary: Located in Mihonoseki-chō, Matsue City, Shimane, it enshrines Kotoshironushi-no-Kami (Ebisu-sama) and Mihotsu-hime-no-Mikoto. It is regarded as the head shrine of the 3,385 "Ebisu shrines" across Japan that enshrine Kotoshironushi-no-Kami. The main sanctuary, in the Miho-zukuri (Hiyoku Taisha-zukuri) style with two halls joined by a shōzoku-no-ma, is a National Important Cultural Property.
miho.deity_note: In the Kojiki, Kotoshironushi-no-Kami appears in the transfer of the land as "Yaekotoshironushi-no-Kami", a child of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami. Book 2 of the Nihon Shoki (a variant account of the ninth section) records that "Kotoshironushi-no-Kami" was fishing at the cape of "Miho" in Izumo Province (an original note gives the reading Miho), which links to the shrine's place name. Mihotsu-hime-no-Mikoto appears in the same variant account of the Nihon Shoki as "Mihotsu-hime", a daughter of Takamimusubi-no-Mikoto, and is made the wife of Ōmononushi-no-Kami. She does not appear in the Kojiki (confirmed by search). The right hall is said to be Kotoshironushi-no-Kami and the left hall Mihotsu-hime-no-Mikoto (as given in an encyclopaedia).
history: The shrine's name appears in the Izumo no Kuni Fudoki (compiled in 733, Tenpyō 5) and the Engishiki (completed in 927, Enchō 5), so the official site explains that a "shrine" existed by that time at the latest. Fragments of magatama beads from around the 4th century and a clay horse from around the late 6th century have been excavated from the grounds, which is said to suggest that rituals were held here even before the Kofun period.
An encyclopaedia records that from the medieval period the Yokoyama family held the priesthood by heredity.

The present main sanctuary was rebuilt in 1813 (Bunka 10) and is in the Miho-zukuri (Hiyoku Taisha-zukuri) style, with two halls in Taisha-zukuri joined by a shōzoku-no-ma. It is a National Important Cultural Property. The worship hall, shrine gate and corridors were built in 1928 (Shōwa 3) under the design and supervision of Itō Chūta.
highlights: The official site records that two rites that re-enact and ritualise the myth of the transfer of the land are held: the Aofushigaki Shinji on 7 April and the Morotabune Shinji on 3 December.
miho.access: The official site says that by public transport the only way, from either Matsue Station or Sakaiminato Station, is by bus (Ichibata Bus or the Mihonoseki community bus). There is also a notice of a seasonal direct bus, the "Ebisu Liner" (from Sakaiminato Station and Yonago Kitaro Airport), but the operating period shown is for 2020. Times and whether it runs are to be confirmed on the official transport page.
miho.hours: The official top page says "Worship: free / Amulet office: from 8:30 / Prayers: from 8:30" (there may be a wait during festivals or busy times). Closing times for the amulet office and prayers are not confirmed on the official site.
miho.parking: Not confirmed on the official site.
miho.goshuin: The official annual festivals page says that only on the 7th of each month (Nanoka Ebisu Festival) a "kirie goshuin" (cut-paper goshuin) is given to those who wish (the paper comes in six colours in all, including pale blue, pale pink, yamabuki, futaai and vermilion, changing by month). Whether goshuin are given on days other than the 7th, and the fee, are not confirmed on the official site.

kirishima.name: Kirishima Jingū
kirishima.summary: An ancient shrine representative of southern Kyushu, located at the foot of Takachiho-no-mine, the peak known from the myth of the descent of the heavenly grandchild. Its deity is the heavenly grandchild Ninigi-no-Mikoto; the present buildings were rebuilt in 1715 in the Edo period and became National Treasures in the Reiwa era.
kirishima.deity_note: The official site writes the deity as "Ninigi-no-Mikoto". The Kojiki, Part 1 (the descent of the heavenly grandchild), records that at the command of the heavenly deities he descended to "Kujifurutake of Takachiho in Hyūga of Tsukushi", and Book 2 of the Nihon Shoki (Age of the Gods, Part 2; the ninth section, including variant accounts) also has the descent to "Takachiho in Hyūga". However, the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki only say "Takachiho in Hyūga"; it is not settled that this means Takachiho-no-mine in Kirishima (there are other proposed sites, such as Takachiho Town in Miyazaki Prefecture, and views differ). Kirishima Jingū is positioned as the shrine that has worshipped Takachiho-no-mine as the mountain of the descent. The long formal name given in the request (Ame-nigishi-kuni-nigishi-amatsu-hiko-hiko-ho-no-Ninigi-no-Mikoto) is one of the names found in Book 2 of the Nihon Shoki (Age of the Gods, Part 2); the same form is not confirmed on the official site.
history: The official site explains that the shrine has stood on the sacred peak Takachiho-no-mine since the age of the gods, and that the Engishiki also lists it as Kirishima Jinja in Morokata District, Hyūga Province.

The official site relates that the shrine was originally enshrined on Semonoka hill, between Takachiho-no-mine and the Ohachi crater, but was destroyed by an eruption, and that in the Tenryaku era of Emperor Murakami the Tendai monk Shōkū Shōnin restored it and moved it to Takachiho-gawara.

The official site records that in 1484 (Bunmei 16) Kenkei Shōnin restored the shrine, and that after a later fire burned it down completely, it was rebuilt in 1715 (Shōtoku 5) with a donation from Shimazu Yoshitaka; these are the present buildings.

The buildings became Important Cultural Properties in 1989 (Heisei 1), and on 9 February 2022 (Reiwa 4) the main sanctuary, offering hall and worship hall were designated National Treasures (as recorded on the official site; the Agency for Cultural Affairs press release is dated 19 November 2021 (Reiwa 3) and may treat this differently, so this is to be confirmed).
highlights: The main sanctuary, offering hall and worship hall are National Treasures. The official site explains that the main sanctuary is five bays wide and four bays deep, in the irimoya style with a copper-plate roof, and that the carved dragon pillars at the front show a regional character unique to the Satsuma domain.
The official guide to the grounds says that the "Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety" are painted on the outer walls of the main sanctuary (normally not open to the public).
The official guide to the grounds says that from the viewpoint on the main approach, Kagoshima Bay and Sakurajima can be seen in good weather.
kirishima.access: By car, from Ebino JCT (outbound) via Takaharu IC, or via Mizobe-Kagoshima-Kūkō IC, to Kirishima Jingū. By rail, the official site says buses are available from JR Kirishima-Jingū Station (from Kagoshima Airport, change at Maruo). Bus times and fares are not individually confirmed on the official site.
kirishima.hours: Worship in the grounds is free. Reception for prayers and the amulet office is 8:00–17:00 (official). Admission is free. Checked 12 Oct 2026.
kirishima.parking: Visitor parking: 500 spaces, free; bus parking: 10 spaces (official). Groups of 10 or more vehicles are asked to contact the shrine, as a separate parking area is used.
kirishima.goshuin: Not confirmed on the official site (no mention of goshuin on the pages obtained).

udo.name: Udo Jingū
udo.summary: A shrine whose vermilion-lacquered main sanctuary stands inside a sea cave facing the Hyūga-nada sea. Its chief deity is Hiko-nagisatake-Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto, the father of Emperor Jinmu, and the cave is said to be the site of the birthing hut where he was born.
udo.deity_note: The official chief deity is "Hiko-nagisatake-Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto" (the Nihon Shoki-style spelling). In the Kojiki, Part 1, he is "Amatsu-hiko-hiko-nagisatake-Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto"; it records that Toyotama-bime began to thatch a birthing hut with cormorant feathers at the water's edge (nagisa), but the child was born before the thatching was finished, which is why he received this name. The same birth story is found in Book 2 of the Nihon Shoki (Age of the Gods, Part 2; the tenth section). The official page on the chief deity also carries this birth myth. The point that the Udo cave is the site of that birthing hut is a tradition that the official site calls a "sacred place handed down", and the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki themselves do not name the place as Udo. The official site also mentions Toyotama-hime-no-Mikoto, who appears in the same myth, but the full list of associated deities (names and number) is not confirmed on the official site, so this is to be confirmed.
history: The official site describes the cave as a sacred place said to be the site of the chief deity's birthing hut, and explains that the vermilion-lacquered shrine buildings stand inside the cave.
The explanation for the prefectural cultural property says that the date of founding is unknown, with various theories such as the reigns of Emperor Keikō, Emperor Sujin or Empress Suiko.

In 1711 (Shōtoku 1) Itō Sukezane, fifth lord of the Obi domain, rebuilt the shrine. It is in the gongen-zukuri style and stands inside a rock cave facing the Hyūga-nada sea. It was also repaired in 1889 (Meiji 22), 1968 (Shōwa 43) and fiscal 1996 (Heisei 8).

The main sanctuary was designated a prefectural structure on 23 March 1995 (Heisei 7), and "Udo", the whole area of the grounds, was designated a National Place of Scenic Beauty on 13 October 2017 (Heisei 29).
highlights: On the rocky shore in front of the main sanctuary is the sacred stone "Kameishi" (about 8 m); it is said that if you throw an undama (lucky ball) into the square hollow, 60 cm on a side, on its back and it goes in, your wish will come true (men throw with the left hand, women with the right).

The "Ochichi-iwa" in the rock cave of the main sanctuary is the rock to which Toyotama-hime-no-Mikoto is said to have attached both her breasts before leaving, and is a focus of faith for those praying for safe childbirth and child-rearing. There is a legend that the chief deity was raised on "ochichi-ame", a sweet made from the dripping spring water, in place of mother's milk.

The scenery of wave-cut benches and sea caves formed by wave erosion of the Miyazaki Group strata, laid down about 12 million to 1.5 million years ago, is given as the reason for designating "Udo" a National Place of Scenic Beauty.
udo.access: From JR Miyazaki Station take the JR Nichinan Line to Ibii Station or Aburatsu Station, then about 20 minutes by local bus from either station, followed by about a 10-minute walk. From the Miyazaki Airport bus stop, about 60–70 minutes by local bus. By car, about 50 minutes from Miyazaki IC on National Route 220 (official).
udo.parking: Not confirmed on the official site (the access page gives no number of spaces or fees).
udo.goshuin: Not confirmed on the official site (no mention of goshuin reception hours or fee).

iwakiyama.name: Iwakiyama Jinja
iwakiyama.summary: Located at the foot of Mt. Iwaki, the sacred mountain of Tsugaru, and known locally as "O-Iwaki-sama" or "O-yama", it is a former Kokuhei-sha. It consists of the Okumiya on the summit and the Oriinomiya at the foot, and enshrines five deities.
iwakiyama.deity_note: The five deities the official site lists are Utsushikunitama-no-Kami, Tatsuhi-hime-no-Kami, Ukanome-no-Kami, Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami and Sakanoue-no-Karitamaro-no-Mikoto. Utsushikunitama-no-Kami (顕國魂神) has the same sound as "Utsushikunitama-no-Kami" (宇都志国玉神), which the Kojiki gives as another name of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, and "Utsushikunitama-no-Kami" (顕国玉神), listed in a variant account of the Nihon Shoki, but it is not confirmed whether the official site explains them as the same deity. Tatsuhi-hime-no-Kami and Ukanome-no-Kami were not found in the range searched of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki texts obtained, and Sakanoue-no-Karitamaro-no-Mikoto appears to be the name of a person rather than a deity (the official site records that Sakanoue no Tamuramaro rebuilt the shrine). Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami appears in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.
history: The official site records that the shrine began in 780 (Hōki 11), when a shrine building was built on the summit of Mt. Iwaki, and that in 800 (Enryaku 19) Sakanoue no Tamuramaro rebuilt it, built the Oriinomiya at the foot of the mountain and called the summit shrine the Okumiya.
The official site records that in 1091 (Kanji 5), following a divine oracle, the Oriinomiya was moved to its present site.

The main sanctuary, inner gate, mizugaki fence and middle gate were built by Nobumasa, fourth lord of the Hirosaki domain, between 1686 (Jōkyō 3) and 1694 (Genroku 7). This is according to Aomori Prefecture's cultural property commentary. The main sanctuary and other buildings were designated National Important Cultural Properties on 22 June 1971 (Shōwa 46).
The Oyama Sankei (the pilgrimage climb of Mt. Iwaki) was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property on 21 January 1984 (Shōwa 59).
highlights: The Oyama Sankei is an event held with the annual festival on the 1st day of the 8th month of the old calendar (Tsuitachi-yama), in which groups from each village across Tsugaru climb to the Okumiya on the summit and worship the sunrise. It refers to the three days including Mukai-yama two days before and Yoi-yama the day before, and the official site records it as the largest autumn festival in the Tsugaru region.

The two-storey gate (rōmon) was originally built in 1628 (Kan'ei 5) as the gate of Hyakutakuji, the temple attached to the Oriinomiya. It is 17.85 m in total height and painted red. Together with the worship hall it was designated an Important Cultural Property on 23 April 1908 (Meiji 41) (Aomori Prefecture's commentary; the period heading on the same page says "Kanbun 7", but the text says Kan'ei 5 (1628)).
iwakiyama.address: 27 Aza Terasawa, Ōaza Hyakuzawa, Hirosaki, Aomori 036-1343 (Tel. 0172-83-2135)
iwakiyama.access: The official access page gives only the address and telephone number; there is no description of how to get there by rail, bus or car.
iwakiyama.hours: Worship is possible 24 hours a day (official). Prayer reception is 9:00–16:00 in summer (April–October) and 9:00–15:00 in winter (November–March); the amulet office is open 9:00–17:00 in summer and 9:00–16:00 in winter (access page). The prayers and amulets page gives winter prayer reception until 15:30, which conflicts with the 15:00 on the access page, so winter prayer reception is to be confirmed.
iwakiyama.parking: No parking information is confirmed on the official site.
iwakiyama.goshuin: On the official prayers and amulets page, the goshuin section showed "In preparation" (checked 12 Oct 2026).

nukisaki.name: Ichinomiya Nukisaki Jinja
nukisaki.summary: Ichinomiya of Kōzuke Province. It stands in a valley on the north slope of a hill and is known for its "descending approach": the shrine buildings lie below the Sōmon gate, down a flight of stone steps. It enshrines Futsunushi-no-Kami and Himegami (the Princess Deity).
nukisaki.deity_note: The official site explains that the name Futsunushi-no-Kami appears in the transfer of the land in the Nihon Shoki and elsewhere, and that he is a deity who appears only in the Nihon Shoki and not in the Kojiki (the term is not found in the Kojiki text we obtained either). As for Himegami (the Princess Deity), the official site writes that "neither the exact name of the deity nor the origin of its enshrinement has been handed down", and only introduces one theory that immigrants from the continent brought sericulture and weaving. We do not identify her here with any particular deity of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.
history: According to shrine tradition, the Isobe clan, of Mononobe lineage, enshrined their clan deity Futsunushi-no-Kami at Saginomiya (present-day Annaka City) and then fixed the shrine on the present site in the first year of Emperor Ankan (531).

The official site records that the first imperial offerings were made in the reign of Emperor Tenmu, that the shrine is listed in the Engishiki register of shrines, and that it has been revered as Ichinomiya of Kōzuke Province.

The present main sanctuary was built in 1635 (Kan'ei 12) by order of the third shogun, Tokugawa Iemitsu. Major repairs were carried out by Tokugawa Tsunayoshi in 1698 (Genroku 11), and the "Great Heisei Restoration" was carried out in fiscal years 2009–2013 (Heisei 21–25).
The shrine rank assigned in the Meiji era was Kokuhei Chūsha, the highest in Gunma Prefecture. After the war it came under the Association of Shinto Shrines (Jinja Honchō).
highlights: The "descending approach" layout: the southern approach climbs to the Sōmon gate, and the shrine buildings lie below it, down a flight of stone steps (official).

The main sanctuary, worship hall and Rōmon gate are nationally designated Important Cultural Properties. The main sanctuary became a National Treasure under the old system (now an Important Cultural Property) on 8 February 1912 (Meiji 45), and the worship hall and Rōmon gate were designated Important Cultural Properties in 1976 (Shōwa 51). The wooden walls inside the Rōmon gate bear the names of the 647 people involved in the repairs of 1698 (Genroku 11), among other inscriptions (official).
nukisaki.access: About a 15-minute walk from Jōshū-Ichinomiya Station on the Jōshin Dentetsu line. By car, about 20 minutes from Tomioka IC or Shimonita IC on the Jōshin-etsu Expressway (official).
nukisaki.hours: The Sōmon gate is open all year round (worship possible 24 hours); the Rōmon gate is open 6:00–17:00. The shrine office is open 8:00–17:00 (prayer reception until 15:00; amulets and goshuin until 16:30) (official).
nukisaki.parking: The shrine has no parking lot of its own, but parking is not prohibited near the Sōmon gate. West of the Sōmon gate there is a free municipal parking lot; large buses should use it (official).
nukisaki.goshuin: The official access guide says goshuin are received at the shrine office until 16:30. The types and fees are not confirmed on the official site.

kehi.name: Kehi Jingū
kehi.summary: Known as the chief guardian shrine of the Hokurikudō and Ichinomiya of Echizen Province, and called "Kei-san" locally. It enshrines the main deity Izasawake-no-Mikoto and six others, and the Engishiki register of shrines lists it as "Kehi Jinja, seven seats, all Myōjin Taisha".
kehi.deity_note: The main deity, Izasawake-no-Mikoto, is the deity whom the Kojiki writes as "Izasawake-no-Ōkami" and "Kehi-no-Ōkami" and a variant account in the Nihon Shoki writes as "Izasawake-no-Kami". The Kojiki tells that Emperor Ōjin (as the imperial prince) exchanged names at Tsunuga with the great deity who appeared to him in a dream. Emperor Chūai, Empress Jingū, Emperor Ōjin, Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto and Takenouchi no Sukune appear in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. The official site writes that Tamahime-no-Mikoto is the younger sister of Empress Jingū, but she is not found in the range of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki we searched.
history: The official site records a tradition that more than 2,000 years ago Izasawake-no-Mikoto left a sacred trace on the peak of Tezutsu and descended on the sacred ground within the precincts (the present Dokō).

The official site records that in 702 (Taihō 2) Emperor Monmu ordered the construction of this shrine, and Emperor Chūai and Empress Jingū were enshrined together with the main deity to form the main shrine. Later, four deities were enshrined in the Tōden-gū, Sōsha-gū, Hiraden-gū and Saiden-gū, called the "Shisha-no-miya".

In 1614 (Keichō 19) Yūki Hideyasu, founder of the Fukui domain, built the shrine buildings. This main sanctuary was designated a National Treasure in 1906 (Meiji 39), but it burned down in the Tsuruga air raid of 12 July 1945 (Shōwa 20) and was rebuilt in 1950 (Shōwa 25).
On 26 March 1895 (Meiji 28) the shrine was renamed "Kehi Jingū" by imperial grant of the title Jingū, and in the same year it was ranked as a Kanpei Taisha.
highlights: The great torii is about 10.9 m high, a wooden torii of the ryōbu type, built in 1645 (Shōhō 2). It is a national Important Cultural Property, and the official site counts it among the three great torii of Japan. It escaped the fire of the Tsuruga air raid of 1945 (Shōwa 20).

The Minakae-sai on 8 March is a rite based on the story that in the 13th year of Empress Jingū's regency Emperor Ōjin visited Kehi-no-Ōkami at Tsunuga, and the great deity appeared in a dream and exchanged names with him (official).
kehi.access: About a 15-minute walk from Tsuruga Station on the JR Hokuriku Line, or about 5 minutes by bus from in front of the station (Tsuruga City community bus, get off at "Kehi Jingū-mae"; some routes excepted). By car, about 10 minutes from Tsuruga IC on the Hokuriku Expressway (official).
kehi.hours: The gates are open 5:00–17:00 from April to September and 6:00–17:00 from October to March. Amulets and goshuin are given 8:45–16:45 (official).
kehi.parking: Free (100 spaces). Beside the great torii and on the east side of the precincts (official).
kehi.goshuin: Given 8:45–16:45 (official). The official top page notes that a new goshuin book with an acrylic cover has gone on offer. The types and fees are not confirmed on the official site.

nangu.name: Nangū Taisha
nangu.summary: Ichinomiya of Mino Province. Its main deity is Kanayamahiko-no-Ōkami, deity of mines and iron, and the official site records that, as the "head shrine of metals", it draws the faith of people in the metal trades and smithing across Japan.
nangu.deity_note: The official site explains Kanayamahiko-no-Ōkami as the deity born when Izanami-no-Mikoto gave birth to Hinokagutsuchi-no-Kami. The Kojiki records that Kanayamabiko-no-Kami and Kanayamabime-no-Kami were born from the vomit of Izanami-no-Mikoto, and a variant account in the Nihon Shoki also records that Kanayamahiko was born from vomit. The co-enshrined deity Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto appears in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. Mino-no-Mikoto is not found in the range of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki texts we obtained and searched.
history: According to the shrine's own tradition, during the eastern expedition of Emperor Jinmu, the first emperor, Kanayamahiko-no-Ōkami showed his power by aiding Yatagarasu and came to be enshrined at Fuchū in Fuwa District.

The official site relates that the shrine settled on its present site in the reign of Emperor Sujin, the tenth emperor. It relates that the shrine was anciently called "Nakayama Kanayamahiko Jinja" and came to be called Nangū Taisha because it lies south of the provincial capital.
All the shrine buildings burned down in the fires of the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 (Keichō 5).
In 1642 (Kan'ei 19), at the request of Kasuga no Tsubone, the third shogun, Tokugawa Iemitsu, rebuilt the present buildings.
highlights: The vermilion-painted shrine buildings are in a distinctive style mixing Japanese and Chinese modes, called "Nangū-zukuri", and the buildings from the Rōmon gate to the main sanctuary stand in a straight line (official). The precinct guide shows the offering hall, corridor, Chokushi-den, Takamai-den, Rōmon gate, Ishiwa Bridge, Gekō Bridge, stone torii, Juge-sha and others as Important Cultural Properties.

The tachi sword in its collection, signed "Sanjō" (made by Sanjō Munechika), is a nationally designated Important Cultural Property. The treasure hall is open to the public every year on 3 November (official).
nangu.access: A 20-minute walk from Tarui Station on the JR Tōkaidō Line. By car, use the Yōrō SA (smart IC) on the Meishin Expressway (official). The bus from in front of Ōgaki Station runs only on the first three days of the New Year.
nangu.hours: The gates are open 6:00–17:30 in winter (15 October to 15 April) and 5:00–18:00 in summer (16 April to 14 October). Prayer reception is 9:00–16:00 (official).
nangu.parking: There is a large free parking lot on the Nangū Taisha grounds just before the precincts. Traffic restrictions apply over the New Year period (official).
nangu.goshuin: Within the range of the official site we checked, no mention of goshuin hours or fees was found.

izanagijingu.name: Izanagi Jingū
izanagijingu.summary: Ichinomiya of Awaji Province, at Taga on Awaji Island, held to be the island of the birth of the land. The shrine traces its origin to the account in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki that Izanagi-no-Mikoto, having finished the birth of the land and of the deities, built a hidden palace (kakuri-no-miya) on Awaji, the first island he had made, and settled there.
izanagijingu.deity_note: The deities are Izanagi-no-Ōkami (main deity) and Izanami-no-Ōkami (co-enshrined). The prefectural shrine association (Jinjachō) records that the origin lies in the account of the Nihon Shoki and Kojiki that Izanagi-no-Mikoto, having finished the birth of the land and of the deities, built a hidden palace at Taga on Awaji Island and settled there. In the original texts we obtained, the Nihon Shoki, Book 1, says "so he built a hidden palace on the island of Awaji and quietly withdrew there for good" (是以構幽宮於淡路之洲，寂然長隱者矣), which confirms that the hidden palace was built on Awaji. The Kojiki, Part 1, on the other hand, says of Izanagi-no-Ōkami that he "dwells at Taga in Ōmi" (坐淡海之多賀也); if 淡海 is read as Ōmi Province (近江), this matches the location of Taga Taisha in Shiga Prefecture (there are several views on the reading). The two texts give different places where the same deity settled, which may be the background to this shrine and Taga Taisha standing side by side; but this is our own arrangement in this survey, not the shrine's view. There is a statement that Izanami-no-Mikoto was co-enshrined in 1932 (Shōwa 7), but this is confirmed only in an encyclopedia and is to be confirmed.
history: The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki record that Izanagi-no-Mikoto, having finished the birth of the land and of the deities, built a hidden palace at Taga on Awaji, the first island he had made, and settled there; that hidden palace is said to be the origin of this shrine (description by the Jinjachō).
The Engishiki register of shrines lists it as "Awaji Izanagi Jinja" and it was ranked as a Myōjin Taisha. From the end of the Heian period it was regarded as Ichinomiya of Awaji Province.

It became a Kokuhei Chūsha in 1871 (Meiji 4) and was later promoted to Kanpei Taisha (an encyclopedia gives the year of promotion as 1885 (Meiji 18), but the Jinjachō text gives no year, so this is to be confirmed).

In 1954 (Shōwa 29) the name was changed from "Izanagi Jinja" to the present "Izanagi Jingū". An encyclopedia states that his consort Izanami-no-Mikoto was co-enshrined in 1932 (Shōwa 7), but this is not confirmed on the official site.
highlights: The Meoto Ōkusu, a great camphor tree in the precincts, is estimated to be 800–900 years old and is a natural monument designated by Hyōgo Prefecture. An encyclopedia gives the designation date as 9 March 1973 (Shōwa 48).
izanagijingu.address: 740 Taga, Awaji, Hyōgo 656-1521. Tel. 0799-80-5001 (as listed by the Hyōgo Prefectural Jinjachō).
izanagijingu.access: An encyclopedia says the shrine is a short walk from the "Izanagi Jingū-mae" bus stop of Awaji Kōtsū and Shinki Bus. A guide for the souvenir shop in the precincts says "about 5 minutes by car from Tsuna-Ichinomiya IC", but this is not the shrine's official information. Not confirmed on the official site.
izanagijingu.hours: Visiting hours are not confirmed on the official site (tourist sites say only "free to visit, no charge").
izanagijingu.parking: The number of parking spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official site (tourist sites disagree, giving 30 or 60 spaces).
izanagijingu.goshuin: Whether goshuin are offered, and the hours and fees, are not confirmed on the official site.

tagataisha.name: Taga Taisha
tagataisha.summary: An old shrine in Shiga Prefecture enshrining the two deities Izanagi-no-Ōkami and Izanami-no-Ōkami. Affectionately called "Otaga-san", it has been worshipped as a deity of long life, matchmaking and protection from misfortune.
tagataisha.deity_note: The official site gives the deities as the two Izanagi-no-Ōkami and Izanami-no-Ōkami, and explains that according to the Kojiki these two first began the way of husband and wife and gave birth to the land of Japan and to the myriad deities, beginning with Amaterasu-Ōmikami. The Kojiki, Part 1, in the passage after Izanagi-no-Ōkami divided the realm among the three noble children, says "that Izanagi-no-Ōkami dwells at Taga in Ōmi" (其伊耶那岐大神者，坐淡海之多賀也). 淡海 (Ōmi) is generally taken to mean Ōmi Province, which matches the location of this shrine, but some take it as Taga on Awaji (Izanagi Jingū), and the wording of the Kojiki alone cannot decide it (a point to be confirmed). The official site conveys the deities' virtues as the parents of divine life: long life, matchmaking and protection from misfortune.
history: The official site relates that Izanagi-no-Ōkami, having finished the great work of the birth of the land, descended from heaven at Sugisaka Pass, ate the millet rice offered by an old man, and when he thrust the cedar chopsticks into the ground they grew into a great tree.
The Kojiki, Part 1, records that Izanagi-no-Ōkami dwells at "Taga in Ōmi" (淡海之多賀). There are several views on whether 淡海 is to be read as Ōmi or as Awaji.

The official site records that the faith spread from the Kamakura period to the Edo period and branch shrines came to extend across Japan (the official site gives 239 branch shrines, but the figure was checked via a summary and is to be confirmed).
An encyclopedia records that it became a Kanpei Taisha in 1914 (Taishō 3) and was renamed "Taga Taisha" in 1947 (Shōwa 22). Not confirmed on the official site.
highlights: The official site has a "Guide to the Precincts" introducing the shrines within the precincts, such as Hyūga Jinja, Koyasu Jinja and Kanasaki Inari Jinja, and the virtues of each.
The official site has a page with visiting information for the "Oku-shoin Garden" (the admission fee and hours are not confirmed in the summary of the official top page).
tagataisha.address: 604 Taga, Taga, Inukami District, Shiga 522-0341. Tel. 0749-48-1101.
tagataisha.access: The official site gives directions: 10 minutes by car from Hikone IC on the Meishin Expressway, or 15 minutes from Kotō-Sanzan Smart IC; or change at JR Hikone Station to the Ōmi Railway, get off at "Taga-Taisha-mae" Station, then a 10-minute walk.
tagataisha.hours: Visiting hours are not confirmed on the official site (no mention could be confirmed in the summaries of the official top page and prayer guide).
tagataisha.parking: The number of parking spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official site (tourist sites mention a large parking lot near the town hall, but without official backing).
tagataisha.goshuin: Whether goshuin are offered, and the hours and fees, are not confirmed on the official site.

kibitsu.name: Kibitsu Jinja
kibitsu.summary: Ichinomiya of Bitchū Province, with Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Ōkami as its main deity. The main sanctuary and worship hall, National Treasures, were rebuilt in 1425 (Ōei 32). The shrine is known for the legend of the subjugation of Ura and for the Narukama rite, which reads good or ill fortune from the sound of a cauldron.
kibitsu.deity_note: The official site gives Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Ōkami as the main deity. The Kojiki, Part 2, records among the children of Emperor Kōrei "Hikoisaseribiko-no-Mikoto, also named Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto", who together with his younger brother Wakatake-Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto subdued and pacified Kibi. The subjugation of Ura is a story the official site relates as the shrine's history; the name Ura is not found in the original texts of the Kojiki, Part 2, and the Nihon Shoki that we obtained (a tradition not in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki). "Kibitsuhiko" is said to appear in the passage on the generals of the four roads in the Nihon Shoki, Book 5 (Emperor Sujin), but word-by-word checking against the original has not been done, so this is to be confirmed. Co-enshrined deities other than the main deity are not confirmed in the summary of the official site.
history: The official site relates the story of Kibitsuhiko's subjugation of Ura as the shrine's history. In it, Ura, said to be a prince of Baekje, builds a castle and torments the people, and is subdued by Kibitsuhiko; it is a tradition not found in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.

The main sanctuary and worship hall, National Treasures, were rebuilt in 1425 (Ōei 32). Their style, called "hiyoku irimoya-zukuri", is the only one of its kind in Japan and is also called "Kibitsu-zukuri". The official site records that they were rebuilt over about 25 years in the time of Ashikaga Yoshimitsu.

The official top page records that this shrine accounts for 8 of the 27 cultural properties making up a Japan Heritage designation. The corridor is a prefecturally designated Important Cultural Property.

An encyclopedia records that it is a shrine listed in the Engishiki (shikinaisha; Myōjin Taisha), Ichinomiya of Bitchū Province, and that its former rank was Kanpei Chūsha. Not confirmed on the official site.
highlights: The main sanctuary and worship hall are National Treasures. The official site explains the hiyoku irimoya-zukuri style as bringing the buildings under one large cypress-bark roof.
The official FAQ introduces the Narukama rite in the Okama-den as a rite that reads good or ill fortune from the sound the cauldron makes, under the tradition that Ura's head is buried there.
The official top page lists the corridor and a 600-year-old great ginkgo tree as highlights.
kibitsu.access: The official site gives directions: about 17 minutes by train from JR Okayama Station to JR Kibitsu Station (the top page says about 30 minutes, which does not agree), then about a 10-minute walk from the station. By car, about 15 minutes from Okayama IC or Okayama-Sōja IC.
kibitsu.hours: The official FAQ says the gates open at 5:00 and close at 18:00, worship is free between those hours, the reception desk is open from about 8:30 to 16:00, and goshuin are received until 16:00 (the top page gives prayer reception as 9:00 to about 14:30 and goshuin as 9:00 to about 16:00). Checked 12 Oct 2026.
kibitsu.parking: The number of parking spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official site (the official FAQ says only that there is parking for wheelchair users on the upper level of the car purification area).
kibitsu.goshuin: Received until 16:00 (official FAQ). The fee is not confirmed on the official site.

ube.name: Ube Jinja
ube.summary: Ichinomiya of Inaba Province, enshrining Takenouchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto. It is said to have been founded in 648 (Taika 4), and in the Engishiki it is the only Myōjin Taisha in Tottori Prefecture.
ube.deity_note: The official site gives the deity as Takenouchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto and explains that he served five reigns from Emperor Keikō to Emperor Nintoku, was the first in Japan to be granted the title of "Great Minister" (Ōomi), and passed away at more than 360 years of age. The Kojiki, Part 2, in the Emperor Seimu section, says "Takenouchi no Sukune was made Great Minister" (建内宿禰爲大臣), and Takenouchi no Sukune also appears in the Chūai, Jingū and Ōjin sections. In the Nihon Shoki, Book 9, Takenouchi no Sukune is also seen accompanying Empress Jingū. On the other hand, the age of more than 360 years and the story that he died in Inaba cannot be confirmed in the original texts of the Kojiki, Part 2, and the Nihon Shoki, Book 9, that we obtained, and we treat them as traditions related by the official site. The official site names the Sōriseki stone in Inaba Province as the sacred trace of this.
history: The official site gives the founding as 648 (Taika 4), in the reign of Emperor Kōtoku. An encyclopedia records that the origin is thought to be the enshrinement of the ancestral deity of the Ifukibe clan, but this is not confirmed in the summary of the official site.
In the Engishiki it is the only Myōjin Taisha in Tottori Prefecture, and in 1871 (Meiji 4) it was ranked as a Kokuhei Chūsha.

The present shrine buildings were completed in 1898 (Meiji 31). The official site records that it was the first shrine in Japan to appear on a five-yen banknote (the year of issue is not in the summary of the official site, and the date of the banknote is to be confirmed).

An encyclopedia records that the shrine burned down in the siege of Tottori Castle in 1581 (Tenshō 9) and was restored in 1633 (Kan'ei 10) through a donation of shrine lands by Ikeda Mitsunaka. Not confirmed on the official site.
highlights: The official visiting page describes the Sōriseki stone on the hill behind the shrine as the stone where Takenouchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto passed away.

The official site notes that the precincts contain the shrine office, the Chōkokan hall and Kokufu Jinja, and that the surrounding area has Mt. Inaba, the site of the Inaba provincial government office, and the graves of the Ikeda family, lords of the Tottori domain (a nationally designated historic site), among others.
ube.access: The official site gives directions: from Tottori Station, take a local bus and get off at "Miyanoshita", or take a taxi. Routes by car, motorcycle, highway bus and air are also on the official page.
ube.hours: The official site gives visiting hours as 9:00–17:00 (prayers until 16:00). Checked 12 Oct 2026.
ube.parking: The number of parking spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official site (the official site posts a parking map and says there is a lot opened for groups that contact the shrine in advance).
ube.goshuin: Received at the amulet office 9:00–17:00. The fee is not confirmed on the official site.

aso.name: Aso Jinja
aso.summary: Ichinomiya of Higo Province, at Ichinomiya-machi in Aso City on the north side of Mt. Aso. It enshrines Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto, whom the official site describes as a grandson of Emperor Jinmu, and his family deities, 12 deities in all. It is the head shrine of the roughly 500 Aso shrines across Japan; the Rōmon gate, which collapsed in the 2016 (Heisei 28) Kumamoto earthquake, had its restoration work completed in December 2023 (Reiwa 5).
aso.deity_note: The official site writes that the main deity is Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto, grandson of Emperor Jinmu, who opened up Aso, and that 12 deities including his family are enshrined. The name "Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto" is not found in the Kojiki (the relevant parts of Parts 1, 2 and 3), the Nihon Shoki (Books 1–3, 7, 9, 10 and 14) or the Kogo Shūi that we obtained, so he cannot be confirmed as a deity appearing in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (a deity of shrine tradition and later legend). In the Emperor Jinmu section of the Kojiki, an interlinear note lists "Aso no Kimi" among the clans descended from Kamuyaimimi-no-Mikoto, but Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto is not named. The Nihon Shoki, in the entry for the 18th year of Emperor Keikō, has a story in which the two deities "Asotsuhiko and Asotsuhime" appeared in the land of Aso and gave the land its name, but these too are names other than Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. The names of each of the 12 deities are not given on the official pages we checked and are to be confirmed.
history: The official top page writes that, according to the shrine records, the founding is traditionally dated to the 9th year of Emperor Kōrei (282 BC), and that the shrine, with about 2,300 years of history, is the head shrine of the roughly 500 Aso shrines across Japan. The date is what the shrine records relate, not a confirmed historical fact.

The official site explains that the Aso clan, which held the office of chief priest by heredity, became warriors in the medieval period and grew into one of the leading powerful families of Higo Province, and that the roughly 500 branch shrines are thought to stem from this historical background (the "are thought to" part is the official site's own conjecture).

The present group of shrine buildings was rebuilt between 1835 (Tenpō 6) and 1850 (Kaei 3) with donations from the Kumamoto domain. Six buildings — the First, Second and Third Sanctuaries, the Rōmon gate, the Shinkō-mon gate and the Kangyo-mon gate — were designated national Important Cultural Properties in 2007 (Heisei 19).

In the 2016 (Heisei 28) Kumamoto earthquake most of the shrine buildings suffered heavy damage, including the collapse of the Rōmon gate, an Important Cultural Property, and the worship hall; restoration work was completed in December 2023 (Reiwa 5).
highlights: The Rōmon gate is a two-story gate about 18 meters high, said to be the largest in Kyushu, and is also called one of the "three great rōmon gates of Japan" (official description). Built in 1850 (Kaei 3), it is a national Important Cultural Property.

The series of agricultural festivals held at Aso Jinja and elsewhere (such as the Tatsukuri-sai, Onda-sai and Tanomi-sai) was designated a national Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property in 1982 (Shōwa 57) as the "Agricultural Rites of Aso". The Onda-sai (Otaue Shinkō-shiki) is on 28 July.
aso.access: About a 15-minute walk from Miyaji Station on the JR Hōhi Line. By bus, get off at "Aso Jinja-mae". By car, about 1 hour from Kumamoto IC on the Kyushu Expressway via National Route 57 toward Aso (official wording: about 60 minutes).
aso.hours: Visiting hours (opening of the parking lot) are 6:00–18:00, and the amulet office (talismans, amulets and goshuin) is open 9:00–17:00. Open every day. Prayer reception is 9:00–16:30. There are times when prayers cannot be received because of festivals and events, so check the official calendar. Checked 12 Oct 2026.
aso.parking: According to the official site, the parking lot in the precincts holds 115 cars and 4 buses (cars free for the first 30 minutes, then paid), and next to it is a municipal lot with 70 spaces (paid). The official page also shows the current availability. This may change, so check the official site before use.
aso.goshuin: Given at the amulet office (9:00–17:00). Goshuin are handed over on paper sheets "for pasting in (to take home)"; if you buy a new goshuin book of this shrine, it is written on the first page. The fee is not confirmed on the official site.

ooasahiko.name: Ōasahiko Jinja
ooasahiko.summary: Ichinomiya of Awa Province, at Ōasa-chō in Naruto City. The official site relates that it began in the reign of Emperor Jinmu, when Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto of the Inbe clan came to Awa, sowed seeds of hemp and paper mulberry to open up the land, and enshrined the ancestral deity Ame-no-Futodama-no-Mikoto as its guardian. Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami is enshrined together with him, and the shrine has been revered as the chief tutelary deity of both Awa and Awaji Provinces.
ooasahiko.deity_note: The official site gives the deities as the two Ōasahiko-no-Ōkami and Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami, and explains Ōasahiko-no-Ōkami as the great ancestral deity of the Inbe clan of Awa. The official Q&A and history state that in the reign of Emperor Jinmu, Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto, grandson of Ame-no-Futodama-no-Mikoto, came to Awa and enshrined his great ancestor Ame-no-Futodama-no-Mikoto as guardian deity, and that this deity is called Ōasahiko Jinja. In the official explanation, then, Ōasahiko-no-Ōkami corresponds to Ame-no-Futodama-no-Mikoto (in the Kojiki, Ame-no-Futodama-no-Mikoto is written "Futodama-no-Mikoto"). The name "Ōasahiko" itself is not found in the Kojiki, Nihon Shoki or Kogo Shūi at hand, and is not a deity name appearing in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. The Kogo Shūi records "Ame-no-Hiwashi-no-Mikoto", a deity led by Ame-no-Futodama-no-Mikoto, as the ancestor of the Inbe of Awa Province, and a variant account in the Nihon Shoki, Book 1, also shows Ame-no-Hiwashi, distant ancestor of the Inbe of the land of Awa (粟国), making yū (bark-fiber cloth). The official Q&A, however, explains that Ame-no-Hiwashi-no-Mikoto is the deity of a different shrine (Inbe Jinja in Tokushima City) and that Ame-no-Futodama-no-Mikoto is its great ancestor. Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami is the deity who guided the descent of the heavenly grandson; the official site relates that he once rested on the peak of Mt. Ōasa and, at a time now unknown, came to be enshrined together at this shrine (official). Some encyclopedias make Ōasahiko-no-Kami a child of Ame-no-Hiwashi-no-Mikoto, but this differs from the official explanation.
history: The official site relates that in the reign of Emperor Jinmu, Ame-no-Tomi-no-Mikoto, grandson of Ame-no-Futodama-no-Mikoto, following an imperial command, sought fertile land and came to Awa Province, where he sowed seeds of hemp and paper mulberry, laid the foundations of the industries making hemp cloth and yū cloth, and enshrined his great ancestor Ame-no-Futodama-no-Mikoto on this spot as their guardian deity. The official Q&A also writes that the date of founding is not clear.

It is listed in the Engishiki register of shrines (completed in 927, Enchō 5) as one of the major shrines (taisha) of Awa Province. The official history writes "Myōjin Taisha under the Engi system" and says it was honored as Ichinomiya of Awa Province.

According to the official history, it was granted the Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade, in 859 (Jōgan 1) under Emperor Seiwa and rose step by step to the Senior First Rank in 1719 (Kyōhō 4) under Emperor Nakamikado. It was also deeply revered by successive provincial governors and lords, and the shrine buildings were built at the domain's expense.

In 1873 (Meiji 6) it was ranked as a Kokuhei Chūsha, and in 1880 (Meiji 13) the main sanctuary and other buildings were built at state expense. In October 2022 (Reiwa 4), re-roofing and repair work on the main sanctuary and other buildings was completed as a project commemorating the Reiwa enthronement ceremonies.
highlights: The great camphor tree in the precincts is the sacred tree, more than 1,000 years old, with a trunk girth of 8.3 meters and a height of 22 meters. It is a natural monument designated by Naruto City (official).

A bridge remains in Maruyama Park within the precincts, built with the civil engineering techniques of their homeland by German soldiers held at the nearby Bandō prisoner-of-war camp during the First World War. It is introduced as a bridge of friendship between Japan and Germany (official guide to the surroundings).

From the great torii at the entrance of the approach (rebuilt in steel pipe in 2002 (Heisei 14), 14.6 meters high), the approach continues for about 800 meters. On the summit of Mt. Ōasa (538 meters above sea level) behind the shrine is the inner shrine, Mine Jinja.
ooasahiko.address: 13 Hirotsuka, Bandō, Ōasa-chō, Naruto, Tokushima. Tel. 088-689-1212 (main line). Telephone and fax are answered 8:00–17:00. The postal code is not given on the official page we checked.
ooasahiko.access: By car, about 15 minutes from Aizumi IC, about 10 minutes from Itano IC, or about 20 minutes from Naruto IC (official). Public transport directions are not given on the official page we checked and are to be confirmed.
ooasahiko.hours: The amulet office and the giving of talismans and amulets are 7:30–16:30, and prayer reception is 9:00–16:00 (at 30-minute intervals). Prayers are not available 9:00–11:30 on 1 November, the day of the annual festival, or from 13:00 on 31 December. The opening hours of the precincts themselves are not stated on the official page we checked. Checked 12 Oct 2026.
ooasahiko.parking: Free parking for 1,000 cars (official). During the New Year visiting period (22:00 on 31 December to 18:00 on 5 January) the roads around the shrine are subject to traffic restrictions, and the official top page asks visitors to follow the directions of the security staff.
ooasahiko.goshuin: On the official pages we checked (amulets, Q&A and location), no mention was found of whether goshuin are offered, the fee or the reception hours. The amulet office is open 7:30–16:30. Not confirmed on the official site.

tosa.name: Tosa Jinja
tosa.summary: Ichinomiya of Tosa Province, at Ikku in Kōchi City, affectionately called "Shinane-sama". The official site relates that it was founded in the reign of Emperor Yūryaku in the late 5th century, and it enshrines Ajisukitakahikone-no-Kami and Hitokotonushi-no-Kami. The Shinane Festival on 24 and 25 August each year is one of the three great festivals of Tosa.
tosa.deity_note: The official page on the deities says the shrine enshrines the two deities Ajisukitakahikone-no-Kami and Hitokotonushi-no-Kami, and explains Ajisukitakahikone-no-Kami as a child of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami and deity of opening up the land and of prosperity in industry, and Hitokotonushi-no-Kami as the deity of harmony and cooperation. The official prospectus for donations writes differently, "the main deity is Ajisukitakahikone-no-Kami (味鉏高彦根神), child of Ōkuninushi-no-Mikoto (by one view, Hitokotonushi-no-Kami)", so the treatment of the main deity varies between official documents. The official site explains that because the Nihon Shoki, in the entry for the 4th year of Emperor Tenmu (675), says that "Tosa-no-Ōkami" presented a sacred sword, the deity was originally Tosa-no-Ōkami; and because a surviving fragment of the Tosa-no-Kuni Fudoki gives "Hitokotonushi-no-Mikoto" and also "by one view, Ajisukitakahikone-no-Mikoto, child of Ōanamuchi-no-Mikoto", the deities became the two Hitokotonushi-no-Mikoto and Ajisukitakahikone-no-Mikoto (we have not been able to check the original text of this Nihon Shoki entry or the Fudoki fragment). Ajisukitakahikone-no-Kami is written 阿遅鉏高日子根神 in the Kojiki and 味耜高彦根神 in the Nihon Shoki, and is a deity appearing in both. Hitokotonushi-no-Kami appears in the Emperor Yūryaku section of the Kojiki, Part 3, as "Katsuragi-no-Hitokotonushi-no-Ōkami" and in the Nihon Shoki, Book 14, in the entry for the 4th year of Emperor Yūryaku, as "Hitokotonushi-no-Kami" (一事主神), but in both the setting is Mt. Katsuragi in Yamato, and no reference to Tosa can be read in the original texts we obtained. The official site explains that the link with Tosa rests on the Fudoki fragment and the tradition of the Kamo clan.
history: The official site writes that Tosa Jinja is said to have been founded in the reign of Emperor Yūryaku in the late 5th century. At the same time it says the founding is not clear: the beginning is thought to have been worship of a natural rock called the Tsubute-ishi, northeast of the precincts, as a sacred rock seat (iwakura), and it is also said to go back to antiquity.

In the Heian period, under the Engi system in the reign of Emperor Daigo, it was ranked as a major shrine listed in the Engishiki and was called Tosa-ni-imasu Jinja. In 940 (Tengyō 3), in the reign of Emperor Suzaku, its divine rank rose to the Senior First Rank (official). The official site writes that by the beginning of the Kamakura period it was regarded as Ichinomiya, chief guardian shrine of Tosa Province.

According to the official site, in 1570 (Genki 1) Chōsokabe Motochika rebuilt the main sanctuary, offering hall and worship hall. In 1601 (Keichō 6) Yamauchi Kazutoyo entered Tosa and confirmed the former shrine lands, and the second lord, Yamauchi Tadayoshi, added auxiliary and subsidiary shrines, the torii, the Rōmon gate and the drum tower.

The era of the fusion of Shinto and Buddhism ended with the separation order of 1868 (Meiji 1), and in 1871 (Meiji 4) the shrine was renamed Tosa Jinja and ranked as a Kokuhei Chūsha. After the war, in 1946 (Shōwa 21), the system of state and national shrines was abolished, and today it is a Beppyō shrine of the Association of Shinto Shrines (official).
highlights: The official site writes that the drum tower and the Rōmon gate are designated national Important Cultural Properties. The Rōmon gate was built by Yamauchi Tadayoshi, and partial-dismantling conservation repairs have been under way since April 2022 (Reiwa 4), scheduled to take about 4 years (as stated in the prospectus for donations dated November 2019 (Reiwa 1); the schedule may since have changed and is to be confirmed).

The Shinane Festival on 24 and 25 August each year is the shrine's most important festival and one of the three great festivals of Tosa. The sacred fire received at the Imibi-sai on the morning of the 24th is transferred to a bonfire and kept burning until the evening of the 25th; the "Otaimatsu", a torch lit from that fire and taken home, is a special item offered to worshippers (official).
tosa.access: Official directions: about a 4-minute walk from the "Ikku Higashimon" bus stop of Tosaden Kōtsū, about a 5-minute walk from the "Ikku Jinja-mae" bus stop, about a 19-minute walk from JR Tosa-Ikku Station, about 15 minutes by car from JR Kōchi Station, about 5 minutes by car from Kōchi IC, and about 25 minutes by car from Kōchi Ryōma Airport.
tosa.hours: Prayer reception is 9:00–16:00 (held every 30 minutes). The hours during which the precincts themselves can be visited are not stated on the official page we checked (tourist sites give 8:30–17:00, but this is not confirmed on the official site). During the Imigomori-sai on 11–13 March, the official site asks visitors to refrain from entering the precincts (worship during this period is from the torii). Checked 12 Oct 2026.
tosa.parking: The number of parking spaces, fees and hours are not stated on the official page we checked (tourist sites give 80 spaces, but this is not confirmed on the official site).
tosa.goshuin: Whether goshuin are offered, the fee and the reception hours are not stated on the official page we checked, and are not confirmed on the official site.

chichibu.name: Chichibu Jinja
chichibu.summary: The chief guardian shrine of Chichibu Province and one of the foremost ancient shrines of the Kantō region, listed in the Engishiki. It is a Beppyō shrine of the Association of Shinto Shrines, and its annual festival on 3 December is known as the "Chichibu Night Festival" (Chichibu Yomatsuri).
chichibu.deity_note: The official site gives four deities: Yagokoro-omoikane-no-Mikoto, Chichibuhiko-no-Mikoto, Ame-no-Minakanushi-no-Kami and Prince Chichibu Yasuhito. Yagokoro-omoikane-no-Mikoto corresponds to Omoikane-no-Kami of the Kojiki (written 思金神) and Omoikane-no-Kami of the Nihon Shoki (written 思兼神), the deity who supplies the wisdom at the Heavenly Rock Cave and elsewhere. Chichibuhiko-no-Mikoto does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki; the official site, citing the Kokuzō Hongi of the Sendai Kuji Hongi, makes him a tenth-generation descendant of Yagokoro-omoikane-no-Mikoto and the first kuni no miyatsuko (provincial governor) of Chichibu (the original text is not confirmed). Ame-no-Minakanushi-no-Kami is the deity who appears at the opening of the Kojiki; the official site records that at Chichibu he was enshrined together with the others in the Kamakura period as Hokushin Myōken. Prince Chichibu Yasuhito was added to the shrine in 1953 (Shōwa 28) and is not a deity of the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki.
history: The official site says the shrine began when Chichibuhiko-no-Mikoto (a tenth-generation descendant of Yagokoro-omoikane-no-Mikoto), who became the first kuni no miyatsuko of Chichibu Province in the reign of Emperor Sujin, enshrined his ancestral deity (according to the Kokuzō Hongi of the Sendai Kuji Hongi).
In 878 (Gangyō 2) the shrine's divine rank was raised to Senior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade, and it is also listed in the Engishiki, compiled in 927 (Enchō 5).
The present shrine buildings were donated by Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1592 (Tenshō 20) and are designated a Tangible Cultural Property of Saitama Prefecture.
In 1928 (Shōwa 3) it was ranked a Kokuhei Shōsha, and it is now a Beppyō shrine of the Association of Shinto Shrines. In 2014 (Heisei 26) it marked the 2,100th anniversary of its founding.
highlights: The annual festival, the Chichibu Night Festival (3 December), is a national Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property and Important Tangible Folk Cultural Property, and in 2016 (Heisei 28) it was inscribed on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list as one of the "Yama, Hoko, Yatai float festivals".
Among the carvings on the main sanctuary, the "Tiger of Children and Child-rearing" and the "Linked Dragon" are said to be the work of the master craftsman Hidari Jingorō, the official site records.
chichibu.access: A 3-minute walk from Chichibu Station on the Chichibu Railway. A 15-minute walk from Seibu-Chichibu Station on the Seibu Chichibu Line. By car, about 30 km from Hanazono IC on the Kan-etsu Expressway.
chichibu.hours: Applications for worship and prayers of all kinds are accepted at any time between 9:00 and 16:30 daily at the amulet office in front of the main sanctuary. The opening and closing times of the amulet office itself are not clearly stated on the official site.
chichibu.parking: The number of parking spaces and fees are not confirmed in the official access information.
chichibu.goshuin: The regular goshuin costs ¥500 and is available written directly in your book or as a pre-written sheet (one design). From 1 to 6 December a special goshuin limited to the annual grand festival is given as pre-written sheets only. The reception hours for goshuin are not clearly stated on the official site.

mishima.name: Mishima Taisha
mishima.summary: It enshrines Ōyamatsumi-no-Mikoto and Tsumiha-yae-kotoshironushi-no-Kami, known together as Mishima Daimyōjin. A Myōjin Taisha of the Engishiki, it is known as a shrine revered by Minamoto no Yoritomo, and its main sanctuary, offering hall and worship hall are national Important Cultural Properties. Its standing as Ichinomiya of Izu Province is not confirmed on the official pages.
mishima.deity_note: The official site gives the deities as Ōyamatsumi-no-Mikoto and Tsumiha-yae-kotoshironushi-no-Kami, and calls the two together Mishima Daimyōjin. The official site records that Ōyamatsumi-no-Mikoto is the guardian deity of mountains, forests and farm produce, and that Kotoshironushi-no-Kami, also called Ebisu-sama, is revered by merchants, craftsmen and fishermen as a deity of good fortune. Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami appears in the Nihon Shoki, and Kotoshironushi-no-Kami in the transfer of the land in the Kojiki (see the existing deity entries). The form with the prefix "Tsumiha-yae" could not be confirmed in the texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki we have obtained (the Nihon Shoki has the form "Yaekotoshironushi-no-Kami"); to be confirmed.
history: The official site says the date of founding is unknown, and records that the shrine arose against a background of faith in the volcanic island-building of the Izu Peninsula and islands and in sea travel, and that records of it remain in old books of the Nara and Heian periods.
Under the "Engi system" of the mid-Heian period it was ranked a Myōjin Taisha.

At the end of the Heian period Minamoto no Yoritomo, exiled to Izu, revered the shrine deeply and prayed there for the revival of the Minamoto clan. The shrine holds the National Treasure "Ume Maki-e Tebako" (a maki-e lacquer box with plum design), said to have been donated by Hōjō Masako.
Under the modern shrine ranking system of 1871 (Meiji 4) it was ranked a Kanpei Taisha.
highlights: The main sanctuary, offering hall and worship hall were designated national Important Cultural Properties in 2000 (Heisei 12). The main sanctuary was completed in 1866 (Keiō 2) and bears carvings by the school of the Izu master craftsmen Ozawa Hanbei and his son Kidō.

The national Natural Monument "Kinmokusei (Fragrant Olive) of Mishima Taisha" is estimated to be 1,200 years old, and the official site records that it comes into full bloom twice each year, in early and late September.
mishima.access: About a 15-minute walk from JR Mishima Station. About a 7-minute walk from Mishima-Tamachi Station on the Izuhakone Railway. 10 minutes by bus from Mishima Station. By car, about 20 minutes from Numazu IC on the Tōmei Expressway.
mishima.hours: Prayer requests are accepted at the prayer reception in the guest hall (kyakuden) from about 8:30 to 16:00, with no closing days (no advance reservations). The hours of the amulet office (talismans, amulets, lucky charms and omikuji) are not clearly stated on the official site.
mishima.parking: The parking area on the grounds holds about 55 cars and 13 large buses. For small cars, from 1 April 2026 (Reiwa 8) the fee is ¥300 per hour. Those receiving prayers get a 2-hour free ticket. Closed from 31 December to 3 January and during the annual festival (15–17 August).
mishima.goshuin: The official grounds guide says goshuin are received at the guest hall (kyakuden) on the grounds. Reception hours and the fee are not clearly stated on the official site (they need to be confirmed separately from the prayer reception hours).

oyama.name: Oyama Jinja
oyama.summary: The sacred peak Tateyama is its object of worship, and the shrine consists of three sites: the Mine Honsha on the summit, the Chūgū Kiganden at Ashikuraji and the Maedate Shadan at Iwakuraji. A shrine listed in the Engishiki (shikinaisha) and a former Kokuhei Shōsha, it has also been called Ichinomiya of Etchū Province. The coordinates and amulet hours are those of the Maedate Shadan.
oyama.deity_note: The official site gives the deities as Izanagi-no-Kami (Tateyama Daigongen, Oyama-no-Kami; whose honji, or Buddhist original form, is Amida Nyorai) and Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Kami (Tachio Tenjin, Tsurugidake-no-Kami; whose honji is Fudō Myōō). Izanagi-no-Kami is the deity of the birth of the land in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, and Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Kami (written 天手力男神 or 天手力雄神) appears in both as the deity who pulls open the door of the Heavenly Rock Cave (see the existing deity entries). The legend of the white hawk of Saeki no Ariyori, who opened Tateyama, and the explanation of honji under the fusion of Shinto and Buddhism are not in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki; they are traditions unique to this mountain.
history: According to shrine tradition, in 701 (Taihō 1) Ariyori, eldest son of Saeki no Ariwaka, governor of Etchū Province, was led by a white hawk to a rock cave on Tateyama, received a divine command from Oyama-no-Ōkami, and opened the mountain.

The official site records that the Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku and Nihon Kiryaku show the shrine being granted Senior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade, in 863 (Jōgan 5) under Emperor Seiwa and Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade, in 889 (Kanpyō 1) under Emperor Uda; it is also a noted shrine listed in the Engishiki.

It is said that Minamoto no Yoritomo rebuilt the main sanctuary in the Kenkyū era (1190–1198), and that later Ashikaga Yoshitane in 1492 (Meiō 1) and Sassa Narimasa in 1583 (Tenshō 11) carried out construction and repairs (Maedate Shadan).

In 1940 (Shōwa 15), as a project marking the 2,600th year of the imperial era, the worship hall and other buildings were put in order and the shrine was ranked a Kokuhei Shōsha. In 1873 (Meiji 6) it had become a prefectural shrine.
highlights: The main sanctuary of the Maedate Shadan is a national Important Cultural Property, in the nagare-zukuri style with a five-bay frontage. The official site records that it is the largest shrine main sanctuary in the Hokuriku region. The stone komainu and the cauldron for the yudate rite are cultural properties designated by Tateyama Town.
The Mine Honsha stands on the summit of Oyama, 3,003 m above sea level, and the mountain is open from 1 July to 30 September. The Chūgū Kiganden stands in a grove of cedars about 500 years old.
oyama.address: 1 Iwakuraji, Tateyama, Nakaniikawa District, Toyama (Maedate Shadan). The Chūgū Kiganden is at 2 Ashikuraji in the same town, and the Mine Honsha at 1 Ashikuraji Tateyama-mine in the same town.
oyama.access: The Maedate Shadan is a 10-minute walk from Iwakuraji Station on the Toyama Chihō Railway. 15 minutes by car from Tateyama IC or Toyama IC.
oyama.hours: The Maedate Shadan can be visited daily from 6:00 to 18:00; for prayers, arrive by 16:00 (no reservation system, but you may have to wait during ceremonies, so checking by phone is recommended). The shrine office is open 8:30–16:30. The hours of the Chūgū Kiganden and Mine Honsha were not confirmed on the official site in this survey.
oyama.parking: The number of parking spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official pages.
oyama.goshuin: At the Maedate Shadan, goshuin and amulets are available 8:30–16:30. Amulets are given and prayer requests received at the first-floor window of the shrine office.

isonokami.name: Isonokami Jingū
isonokami.summary: The chief clan shrine of the Mononobe clan, standing at the north-western foot of Mt. Furu in the eastern part of the Yamato Basin. The official site explains that it is one of the oldest shrines in Japan, and it reveres three deities, including the sacred sword "Futsu-no-Mitama", as Isonokami-no-Ōkami. The worship hall is a National Treasure as the oldest surviving worship hall.
isonokami.deity_note: The official site gives the main deities as the three Futsunomitama-no-Ōkami, Furunomitama-no-Ōkami and Futsushimitama-no-Ōkami (together called Isonokami-no-Ōkami), and lists Umashimaji-no-Mikoto, Inishiki-no-Mikoto, Emperor Shirakawa and Ichikawa-no-Omi-no-Mikoto as associated deities. Futsunomitama-no-Ōkami is the spiritual power dwelling in the sacred sword "Futsu-no-Mitama", which the official site explains as the sword held by Takemikazuchi-no-Kami in the myth of the transfer of the land. The Kojiki, Part 2 (the Emperor Jinmu section), gives the name of the sword that Takemikazuchi-no-Kami sent down to Takakuraji in a gloss as "Sajifutsu-no-Kami, Mikafutsu-no-Kami, Futsu-no-Mitama", and records that this sword resides at Isonokami Jingū. The Nihon Shoki, Book 3 (the record before Emperor Jinmu's accession), gives the name of the sword that Takemikazuchi-no-Kami announced to Takakuraji as Futsu-no-Mitama. "Futsu-no-Mitama" is therefore the name of a sword (and its spiritual power), and is treated separately from the deity name Futsunushi-no-Ōkami (existing ID futsunushi; not in the Kojiki). Furunomitama-no-Ōkami is the deity the official site describes as the spiritual power dwelling in the Amatsu-shirushi Tokusa-no-Mizutakara (the ten sacred treasures received by Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto); the term "Tokusa-no-Kandakara" could not be confirmed in the text of the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki (the Kojiki records that Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto presented the "Amatsu-shirushi"), so we write it as the official tradition. Futsushimitama-no-Ōkami is the deity the official site describes as the spiritual power dwelling in the Ame-no-Totsuka-no-Tsurugi with which Susanoo-no-Mikoto slew the Yamata-no-Orochi; the name "Futsushi-mitama" itself does not appear in the parts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki we checked. However, the main text of Section 8 of the Nihon Shoki says the sword that cut the great serpent is called "Orochi-no-Aramasa" and is now at Isonokami.
history: The official site explains that the shrine began when its deities were enshrined in the high court of Isonokami Furu in the 7th year of the 10th emperor, Sujin. The chronology says that Ikagashikoo-no-Mikoto, ancestor of the Mononobe clan, moved Futsu-no-Mitama and the ten sacred treasures to the land of Isonokami by imperial command and founded this shrine.

The official site explains that Emperor Shirakawa especially revered this shrine, and that the Shinkaden hall of the imperial palace, which he donated, is said to be the present worship hall (National Treasure). By its architectural style it is thought to have been built in the early Kamakura period, and it is said to be the oldest surviving worship hall.
The official site explains that in 1871 (Meiji 4) the shrine was ranked a Kanpei Taisha, and in 1883 (Meiji 16) it was permitted to resume the title Jingū.

The official site explains that the shrine formerly had no main sanctuary and called its forbidden ground the Go-honchi, but in 1874 (Meiji 7) the chief priest Kan Masatomo obtained official permission to excavate the forbidden ground, and the sacred sword "Futsu-no-Mitama" was revealed. The main sanctuary was built in 1913 (Taishō 2).
highlights: The worship hall is a National Treasure. Emperor Shirakawa is said to have donated the Shinkaden hall of the imperial palace in 1081 (Eihō 1), and it is regarded as the oldest surviving worship hall (official).
The Rōmon gate is an Important Cultural Property. An ink inscription on the ridge beam shows it was built in 1318 (Bunpō 2) (official).

Behind the worship hall is the forbidden ground (about 1,300 square metres), enclosed by a stone fence with sword-point-shaped posts carved "Furu-sha"; it is regarded as the most sacred area of the shrine precincts (official).

The azekura-style storehouse (hokura) standing at the south-western corner of the forbidden ground was rebuilt in 1851 (Kaei 4), and the Hokura Festival is held there every year on 31 December (official).
isonokami.access: About a 30-minute walk from Tenri Station on the Kintetsu Tenri Line and JR Sakurai Line, or under 10 minutes by taxi for about ¥1,500 (official). By car, about 5 minutes from Tenri-Higashi IC on the Meihan National Route, or about 15 minutes from Tenri IC on the Nishi-Meihan Expressway (official).
isonokami.hours: Worship at the worship hall is possible roughly from 5:30 to 17:30, as the Rōmon gate is opened and closed according to the season (the gate times change with the season). Amulets are available from 9:00 to 17:00 (16:30 in winter), and prayer requests are accepted 8:30–16:00 from March to October and 8:30–15:30 from November to February (all official).
isonokami.parking: There are four free parking areas: No. 1 holds 23 cars, No. 2 50, No. 3 36 and No. 4 50 (official). No. 3 can also take 3 large buses (official).
isonokami.goshuin: Goshuin are received at the "prayer reception and amulet office" on the left after entering the Rōmon gate (official visitor guide). The amulet office hours are as above; the official pages we obtained give no separate hours or fee for goshuin alone.

hiyoshi.name: Hiyoshi Taisha
hiyoshi.summary: Standing at the foot of Mt. Hiei, it is explained by the official site as the head shrine of the roughly 3,800 Hiyoshi, Hie and Sannō shrines across Japan. The West Main Shrine enshrines Ōnamuchi-no-Kami and the East Main Shrine Ōyamakui-no-Kami; both main shrines are National Treasures.
hiyoshi.deity_note: The official site calls the deities of the roughly 40 shrines on the grounds collectively Hiyoshi-no-Ōkami, and gives the deities of the Seven Sannō Shrines as: West Main Shrine = Ōnamuchi-no-Kami, East Main Shrine = Ōyamakui-no-Kami, Usa-gū = Tagori-hime-no-Kami, Ushio-gū = the aramitama (rough spirit) of Ōyamakui-no-Kami, Shirayama-gū = Kukuri-hime-no-Kami, Juge-gū = Kamo-tamayori-hime-no-Kami, and Sannomiya = the aramitama of Kamo-tamayori-hime-no-Kami. The genealogy of Ōtoshi-no-Kami in the Kojiki, Part 1, records Ōyamakui-no-Kami (also named Yamasue-no-Ōnushi-no-Kami) as the deity residing on "Mt. Hie in the province of Chikatsu-Ōmi", and the name matches the deity of the East Main Shrine of Hiyoshi Taisha. However, the official pages we obtained do not cite the Kojiki. Ōnamuchi-no-Kami is another name of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami in the Nihon Shoki, and we reuse the existing ID ookuninushi. The official site of Karasaki Jinja says Emperor Tenji transferred Ōnamuchi-no-Kami from Mt. Miwa in Nara to Ōtsu. Because sources differ on the relationship between the deity of Mt. Miwa and Ōkuninushi-no-Kami (see the note on Ōmiwa Jinja), here we go no further than linking the official name "Ōnamuchi-no-Kami" to the existing entry for Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami (confidence: medium). Tagori-hime-no-Kami corresponds to munakata3 as one of the Three Munakata Goddesses, and Kukuri-hime-no-Kami to kukurihime. No deity IDs have been created this time for Kamo-tamayori-hime-no-Kami or the aramitama.
history: The official site explains that Hiyoshi Taisha was founded about 2,100 years ago, in the 7th year of Emperor Sujin.

The official site of the auxiliary shrine Karasaki Jinja explains that when Emperor Tenji transferred Ōnamuchi-no-Kami from Mt. Miwa in Nara to Ōtsu, the deity is said to have crossed Lake Biwa and alighted at Karasaki, a place closely tied to the enshrinement of the West Main Shrine.

The official site explains that when the capital moved to Heian-kyō, this place lay in the capital's front demon gate (north-east), so the shrine was revered as a place to pray for protecting the capital from evil and disaster, and later, after Dengyō Daishi founded Enryakuji on Mt. Hiei, it was also revered as a guardian deity of the Tendai school.

The official site explains that it was a Kanpei Taisha until the shrine ranking system was abolished after the war. The change from "Jinja" to "Taisha" and the adoption of the reading "Hiyoshi" are also said to date from after the war.
highlights: The shrine has many cultural properties, including 2 National Treasure buildings (the main sanctuaries of the West and East Main Shrines) and 17 Important Cultural Property buildings (official).

The "Hiyoshi-zukuri" style used for the three shrines of the East and West Main Shrines and Usa-gū is a distinctive architecture that looks like irimoya-zukuri with the rear cut off. The "geden" beneath the floor is said to be the room where the Buddhist honji images were kept until the separation of Shinto and Buddhism in the Meiji period (official).
The Sannō torii has a triangular gable set on top of a Myōjin-style torii, and is regarded as a symbol of the Sannō faith that fused Shinto and Buddhism (official).

The messenger of the deity is the monkey, called "masaru" (sacred monkey). It is held to be auspicious because the word sounds like "evil departs" and "to excel", and there are many masaru amulets (official).
hiyoshi.access: A 20-minute walk from Hieizan-Sakamoto Station on the JR Kosei Line, or a 10-minute walk from Sakamoto-Hieizanguchi Station on the Keihan Ishiyama-Sakamoto Line (official).
hiyoshi.hours: Visiting hours are 9:00–16:00; the gates of the West and East Main Shrines are open 6:00–16:00 from April to September and 7:00–16:00 from October to March (official top page). Prayer requests are accepted 9:00–15:30, and the amulet office (amulets, goshuin, etc.) is open 9:00–16:00. The garden entry donation is ¥500 for adults, ¥300 for junior and senior high school students, and free for elementary school children and younger (all official).
hiyoshi.parking: The parking area on the grounds holds about 50 cars only. It is normally free, but fees apply in busy periods such as the autumn leaves festival; in November it is ¥1,000 every day (official). Large buses cannot enter the grounds and are directed to the Ōmiyagawa tourist parking area and elsewhere (official).
hiyoshi.goshuin: Goshuin are received at the amulet office of the West Main Shrine. The official amulet page lists "goshuin ¥500", and there are also goshuin for each of the Seven Sannō Shrines (the East Main Shrine goshuin alone is also available at the East amulet office). Reception follows the amulet office hours (9:00–16:00).

niutsuhime.name: Niutsuhime Jinja
niutsuhime.summary: Ichinomiya of Kii Province, standing in the village of Amano at the foot of Mt. Kōya. It enshrines Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami and three other deities, and the official site explains that it is the chief guardian shrine of Mt. Kōya and the head shrine of the more than 180 Niu shrines across Japan. It is a component of the World Heritage Site "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range".
niutsuhime.deity_note: The official site explains that the First Hall enshrines Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami, the Second Hall Kōya-miko-no-Ōkami, the Third Hall Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami and the Fourth Hall Ichikishima-hime-no-Ōkami, and that they are also called the Shisha Myōjin (Four Shrine Deities). The name Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami does not appear in the parts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki we checked (it is absent from both). The place name "Niu-kawakami" appears in the Jinmu chronicle, but it is not a deity name. The official site explains this deity as the younger sister of Amaterasu-Ōmikami, also called Wakahirume-no-Mikoto, citing the Niu Daimyōjin Norito, said to have been written by Emperor Ōjin himself. Wakahirume-no-Mikoto appears in the first variant account of Section 7 in Book 1 of the Nihon Shoki and in Book 9 (the record before Empress Jingū's regency), but the name Niu is not there, so we treat the official identification as a shrine tradition (to be confirmed). Kōya-miko-no-Ōkami is also absent from the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki; it is a deity of the traditions of the founding of Mt. Kōya (such as the Konjaku Monogatari). The official site describes Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami as the goddess of the five grains and food, but it does not state that she is identical with Ōgetsuhime-no-Kami of the Kojiki, so we treat her under a separate ID (to be confirmed). Ichikishima-hime-no-Ōkami corresponds to the existing ID munakata3 as one of the Three Munakata Goddesses (the official site explains she was transferred from Itsukushima Jinja).
history: The official site explains that the shrine was founded more than 1,700 years ago. According to the Niu Daimyōjin Norito, said to have been written by Emperor Ōjin himself, Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami travelled through the Kinokawa river basin in the age of the gods, spreading farming and weaving, and settled in this place.

The official site explains that 1,200 years ago, Kōya-miko-no-Ōkami appeared in the form of a hunter with a white dog and a black dog before Kōbō Daishi, who was searching for a place to practise Shingon esoteric Buddhism, and that under this guidance he was granted Mt. Kōya by Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami at Amano. The Daishi built a shrine to the deity in the Danjō Garan as chief guardian of Mt. Kōya.
