The official site explains that during the Kōan invasion of the Kamakura period, just as Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami had foretold, the Mongol army withdrew in a storm on the 1st day of the intercalary 7th month; the shogunate offered treasured swords, including the National Treasure silver-and-copper hirumaki tachi mounting, and designated this shrine Ichinomiya of Kii Province.

The official site explains that in 1924 (Taishō 13) the shrine was ranked a Kanpei Taisha, the highest rank at the time. In 2004 (Heisei 16) it was inscribed as part of the World Heritage Site "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range".
highlights: The National Treasure "Gindō Hirumaki Tachi Koshirae" (silver-and-copper hirumaki tachi mounting) dates from the late Heian period and is regarded as one of the swords dedicated by the Kamakura shogunate at the time of the Mongol invasions. It is currently on deposit at the Tokyo National Museum (official).

The sight of the four red main sanctuaries in a row is likened to "kakkaku" (brilliant achievement), and there are "Kakkaku Hisshō" (certain victory) prayers and amulets. The official site explains that the shrine is counted as one of the "Three Great Yakujin (deities against misfortune) of Japan".
The messengers of the deity are the white and black "sacred dogs". The 16th of each month is sacred dog viewing day, from 10:00 to 11:30 and 13:00 to 14:30 (official).

In 2004 (Heisei 16) it was inscribed as part of the World Heritage Site "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range", and it is said to preserve a religious landscape of prayer in which kami and buddhas exist together (official).
niutsuhime.address: 230 Kami-Amano, Katsuragi, Ito District, Wakayama 649-7141 (official). Telephone 0736-26-0102 (daily 8:45–16:30, official).
niutsuhime.access: About 30 minutes by Katsuragi Town community bus from Kaseda Station on the JR Wakayama Line, alighting at "Niutsuhime Jinja-mae" (official). By car, about 20 minutes from Katsuragi-Nishi IC on the Keinawa Expressway, or about 30 minutes from the Daimon gate of Mt. Kōya (official).
niutsuhime.hours: The grounds can basically be visited at any time. Prayer requests are accepted 9:00–15:00, and goshuin and amulets 8:45–16:30 (official). Hours may change for festivals and other events; check the official notices (there is also a separate notice for October).
niutsuhime.parking: The free No. 1 and No. 2 lots together hold about 60 cars. Large buses use the No. 1 lot and must contact the shrine in advance. At New Year a temporary lot (about 27 spaces) is also opened (official).
niutsuhime.goshuin: Goshuin are given. Both direct writing in your goshuin book and pre-written sheets are available, 8:45–16:30. During festivals and other events only pre-written sheets may be available (official). The fee is not confirmed on the official pages we obtained.

miyazaki.name: Miyazaki Jingū
miyazaki.summary: Standing in Miyazaki City, it enshrines the first emperor, Jinmu. Shrine tradition says it was founded by Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto, grandson of Emperor Jinmu, and in 1885 (Meiji 18) it became a Kanpei Taisha.
miyazaki.deity_note: The official site gives the deity as Kamuyamato-iwarebiko-no-Sumeramikoto (the first emperor, Jinmu), with his father Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto and his mother Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto enshrined alongside. The Nihon Shoki, Book 3, records that the emperor's mother was Tamayori-hime (the younger daughter of the sea deity Watatsumi), that he became crown prince at 15 and set out eastward at 45; the Kojiki, Part 2, records that he departed from Hyūga for Tsukushi. The official site gives the emperor's birthplace as Sano in Takaharu Town (Sano Jinja) and explains, citing the Shokugenshō and other works, that the site of this shrine is the "Miyazaki Palace in Hyūga". However, the place name "Miyazaki" cannot be confirmed in the original texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (checked by search). The founder Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto is a figure of shrine tradition and is not an enshrined deity.
history: The official site records, as shrine tradition, that the shrine began when Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto, grandson of Emperor Jinmu, on taking up the post of governor of Kyushu, enshrined his grandfather in his memory.

The official site records that according to old records, shrine buildings were constructed in the reigns of Emperor Sujin and Emperor Keikō, and in the reign of Emperor Ōjin the kuni no miyatsuko of Hyūga repaired them and held rites of enshrinement.
The official site records that in the Kenkyū era (1190–1199) the land steward Tsuchimochi Nobutsuna built the shrine buildings and transferred the deity there.

The official site records that in 1885 (Meiji 18) the shrine was promoted to Kanpei Taisha, in 1913 (Taishō 2) it was renamed Miyazaki Jingū, and with the reform of the shrine system in 1946 (Shōwa 21) the shrine ranks were abolished.
highlights: The official site records that the present shrine buildings were completed in 1907 (Meiji 40), using local Sano cedar more than 100 years old, and were designed by Itō Chūta.
The official site records that the annual festival is on 26 October, and that the Goshinkōsai procession that follows ("Jinmu-sama") commemorates Emperor Jinmu's eastward migration.
miyazaki.address: 2-4-1 Jingū, Miyazaki, Miyazaki 880-0053 (as written on the official site). Telephone 0985-27-4004.
miyazaki.access: The official site gives a 10-minute walk from JR Miyazaki-Jingū Station, a 5-minute walk from the "Miyazaki Jingū" bus stop, or about 30 minutes by taxi from Miyazaki Airport.
miyazaki.hours: The official site records that the shrine gate is open 5:30–17:30, the offering hall (main buildings) 6:00–17:30, and the talisman and amulet office 8:00–17:00 (all year round). Prayer requests are accepted 9:00–16:30 (at the amulet office).
miyazaki.parking: The official site directs visitors to the "Miyazaki Jingū West Garden parking area". The number of spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official site.
miyazaki.goshuin: The official site records two kinds, "Miyazaki Jingū" and "Kōgū Jinja (the original shrine)", each ¥300, given at the talisman and amulet office.

naminoue.name: Naminoue-gū
naminoue.summary: The chief guardian shrine of Okinawa, standing on a cliff facing the sea at Naha, revered since the days of the Ryūkyū royal government as "the first shrine of this country". Its deities are Izanami-no-Mikoto, Hayatama-no-O-no-Mikoto and Kotosaka-no-O-no-Mikoto, and even the official site gives the year of founding as "unknown".
naminoue.deity_note: The official deities are the three Izanami-no-Mikoto, Hayatama-no-O-no-Mikoto and Kotosaka-no-O-no-Mikoto; separately enshrined are the fire deity (Hinukan), the ubusuna (local tutelary) deity and Sukunahikona-no-Kami (deity of medicine). Izanami-no-Mikoto appears in the Kojiki, Part 1 (the birth of the deities and the land of Yomi), and in the Nihon Shoki, Book 1. "Hayatama-no-O" and "Yomotsu-kotosaka-no-O", corresponding to Hayatama-no-O-no-Mikoto and Kotosaka-no-O-no-Mikoto, appear in a variant account of Section 5 of the Age of the Gods, Part 1, in Book 1 of the Nihon Shoki, as deities who came into being from the spittle and the purification when Izanagi-no-Mikoto parted from his wife in the land of Yomi (they do not appear in the Kojiki; checked by search). However, whether the official deity names and the deity names in the Nihon Shoki refer to the same deities is not confirmed in any official statement (to be confirmed). The fire deity (Hinukan) belongs to the Ryūkyūan faith in the god of fire and does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki. Sukunahikona-no-Kami appears in the Kojiki, Part 1, and in the Nihon Shoki. The official site records "an oracle of Kumano Gongen" as the legend of the shrine's founding, but no official explanation of its relationship to the deities has been confirmed.
history: The official site gives the year of founding as unknown and records that the shrine began with prayers offered on the cliff edge, a sacred place for worshipping the land of the gods beyond the sea (Nirai Kanai). As the legend of the shrine's founding, it further relates that a village headman of Sakiyama who was fishing obtained a "speaking stone", and when he reached Naminoue-yama there was an oracle: "I am Kumano Gongen; build a shrine in this place", and the royal government built the shrine buildings.

The official site records that ships entering and leaving Naha port looked up to the cliff and shrine hall of Naminoue-gū and prayed for safe voyages, that the Ryūkyū royal government also held deep faith in it, and that when the system of the Eight Ryūkyū Shrines (official shrines) was established, this shrine was placed first and revered as "the first shrine of this country".
The official site records that in 1890 (Meiji 23) the shrine was ranked a Kanpei Shōsha and became the chief guardian shrine of Okinawa.

The official site records that after being damaged in the last war, the main sanctuary and shrine office were rebuilt in 1953 (Shōwa 28) and the worship hall in 1961 (Shōwa 36), and that in the reconstruction of 1993 (Heisei 5) the main sanctuary and other buildings were completed.
highlights: The official site records that, centred on the annual grand festival on 17 May, the "Nanmin Festival" is held with a procession of the portable shrine (mikoshi), an all-island sumo tournament, Ryūkyūan dance and more (check the dates each year in the official annual events).
naminoue.address: 1-25-11 Wakasa, Naha, Okinawa (as written on the official site).
naminoue.access: The official site gives about a 15-minute walk from Asahibashi Station on the monorail, or about 10 minutes by taxi from Naha Airport.
naminoue.hours: The official site gives the amulet office (talismans, amulets, etc.) as "9:00–16:30" (map and contact page), while a notice of January 2026 (Reiwa 8) also gives "9:00 to 16:45", so the statements do not agree. Prayer requests are accepted 10:00–15:30. Visiting hours for the grounds themselves are not confirmed on the official site.
naminoue.parking: The official site records a free parking area for 20 cars (nearby paid parking when crowded). There is an official notice that the parking area cannot be used during the New Year period (a notice from a past year).
naminoue.goshuin: Goshuin information (fee and reception hours) is not confirmed on the official site. Only the amulet office hours are given officially.

isasumi.name: Isasumi Jinja
isasumi.summary: Ichinomiya of Iwashiro Province, standing in Aizumisato Town in the south of the Aizu Basin. The official site records that Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto, together with the father and son Ōbiko-no-Mikoto and Takenunakawawake-no-Mikoto, are revered as the four deities called Isasumi-no-Ōkami, and that the shrine is said to have been founded in the 10th year of Emperor Sujin.
isasumi.deity_note: The official site records that Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto are the deities, with the father and son Ōbiko-no-Mikoto and Takenunakawawake-no-Mikoto enshrined together, and that the four are revered as Isasumi-no-Ōkami. Izanagi and Izanami are the deities of the birth of the land and the birth of the deities in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. Ōbiko-no-Mikoto and Takenunakawawake-no-Mikoto appear in the Kojiki, Part 2; Ōbiko-no-Mikoto is a son of Emperor Kōgen, and Takenunakawawake-no-Mikoto is his son. The Emperor Sujin section tells the origin of the place name: Ōbiko was sent along the Koshi road and Takenunakawawake along the twelve eastern roads, and because father and son met at "Aizu" the place is called Aizu; the official site also cites this passage to link the origin of the name Aizu with the founding of the shrine. In the Nihon Shoki, in the 10th year of Emperor Sujin, Ōhiko-no-Mikoto was sent to Hokuriku and Takenunakawawake to Tōkai as generals of the four roads, and the names are written differently. The word "Aizu" (相津) was not found in the same book of the Nihon Shoki obtained this time (the place-name origin is the Kojiki account).
history: The official site records, as shrine tradition, that in the 10th year of Emperor Sujin, Ōbiko-no-Mikoto and his son Takenunakawawake-no-Mikoto, sent out to pacify the provinces, met at Aizu and held rites to Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto on Amatsu-dake, which was the beginning of the shrine.

The official site records that the shrine is said to have then moved by way of Mt. Hakase and Mt. Hasama (now Myōjin-dake) to Takada Minamihara (now the Takamagahara on the grounds) in 552 (the 13th year of Emperor Kinmei), and to have settled at the present site in 560 (the 21st year).

The official site records that the Jōgan Kyakushiki contains a record of the shrine being granted the divine rank of Senior First Rank, that it is listed as a Myōjin Taisha in the Engishiki register of shrines, that from the Meiji period it was a Kokuhei Chūsha, and that since the war it has been a Beppyō shrine of the Association of Shinto Shrines.
The official site records that in 1799 (Kansei 11) the shrine received from Emperor Kōkaku the grant of the title Daijingū and was styled "Isasumi Daijingū".
highlights: The official site records that the Usuzumi cherry (Aizu Usuzumi) on the grounds is the foremost sacred tree, designated a Fukushima Prefecture Green Cultural Property and an Aizumisato Town Natural Monument, and that the Hanaiwai Festival is held every year on 29 April.

The official site records that because entry to the shrine grove has been forbidden since ancient times, its natural forest has been preserved, and it is designated a Fukushima Prefecture Green Cultural Property and an Aizumisato Town Natural Monument.

The official site records that the Ayame Festival is held in the iris garden of the outer precinct from early to late June every year, when more than 200 varieties of Japanese iris and other flowers bloom.
isasumi.address: 4377 Miyabayashi-kō, Aizumisato, Ōnuma District, Fukushima 969-6263 (as written on the official site).
isasumi.access: The official site gives about 30 minutes from Aizu-Wakamatsu IC on the Ban-etsu Expressway, about 15 minutes from Niitsuru PA Smart IC, or about a 25-minute walk from Aizu-Takada Station on the JR Tadami Line. From Aizu-Wakamatsu Station, take the bus bound for Nagaino to the Yokomachi bus stop (about 40 minutes), then walk 3 minutes.
isasumi.hours: The official site records goshuin reception 9:00–16:00 and prayer (purification) reception 9:00–15:00 (no reservation needed). The amulet office hours are not confirmed on the official pages.
isasumi.parking: The official site records 120 cars and 5 large buses. Fees are not confirmed on the official site.
isasumi.goshuin: The official goshuin guide gives reception hours of 9:00–16:00. It lists the goshuin at ¥1,000 (a pre-written sheet when the chief priest is absent), a block-script version at ¥500, the Aizu Seven Lucky Gods goshuin at ¥500, and goshuin of the subsidiary shrines at ¥500 each (on goshuin paper), among others.

kitaguchi.name: Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Jinja
kitaguchi.summary: A Sengen shrine at the northern foot of Mt. Fuji, at the start of the Yoshida (north) trail. The official site records that it enshrines Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto as the main deity, together with her husband Ninigi-no-Mikoto and her father Ōyamatsumi-no-Mikoto, and notes that the main sanctuary (Honden), the Tōgū Honden and the Saigū Honden are national Important Cultural Properties.
kitaguchi.deity_note: The official site records that Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto is enshrined as Asama-no-Ōkami, together with her husband Hikoho-no-Ninigi-no-Mikoto and her father Ōyamatsumi-no-Mikoto (father of Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto and deity of all mountains). All are deities of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki tell how Konohanasakuya-hime was joined with Ninigi-no-Mikoto and gave birth to her children amid fire, and the official site explains that her virtues of safe childbirth and protection from fire derive from this story. The official site names Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto in the tradition of the shrine's founding, and also records that Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto is enshrined at Ōtsuka-oka, the place of the shrine's origin (Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto is a figure in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, with an existing entry). The official site says the shrine began as a place for worshipping Mt. Fuji itself from afar as the object of worship.
history: The official site records that in the 40th year of Emperor Keikō (110), Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto, during his eastern expedition, worshipped the spirit of Mt. Fuji from Ōtsuka-oka, and that the shrine was founded later, in the 50th year of Emperor Keikō, when a small shrine was built to enshrine Asama-no-Ōkami and Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto.

The official site records that after the eruption of Mt. Fuji in 781 (Ten'ō 1), Ki no Toyoniwa no Ason, governor of Kai Province, performed divination and in 788 (Enryaku 7) built shrine buildings to the north of Ōtsuka-oka. This is the present site, and Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto was enshrined at Ōtsuka-oka.

The official site records that after construction by Hōjō Yoshitoki, the shrine building rebuilt by Takeda Shingen in 1561 (Eiroku 4) is the oldest surviving one and is a national Important Cultural Property as the Tōgū Honden. For the construction year Jōō 2, the same official page gives two different Western years, 1223 and 1233.

The official site records that Murakami Kōsei of the Fuji-kō confraternity carried out a great reconstruction of the shrine buildings from 1733 to 1738 (Kyōhō 18 to Genbun 3), and that most of the surviving buildings and the layout of the grounds were fixed at this time.
highlights: The official site records that the main sanctuary (built in 1615 (Genna 1) by Torii Tosa-no-kami Narutsugu), the Tōgū Honden and the Saigū Honden are all national Important Cultural Properties.

The official site records that the "Yoshida Fire Festival" is the annual festival of Suwa Jinja, now held under the name Chinkasai over two days, 26 and 27 August, and explains that it is said to be based on the story of the deity giving birth safely amid raging fire.
The official site presents "Ōtsuka-oka" as the place of the shrine's origin, and records that goshuin are available for it as well as for Suwa Jinja on the grounds (said to be the deity of the land).
kitaguchi.address: 5558 Kami-Yoshida, Fujiyoshida, Yamanashi 403-0005 (as written on the official site).
kitaguchi.access: The official site gives about 3 km from Kawaguchiko IC on the Chūō Expressway via National Route 139, or about 3 km from Fujiyoshida IC on the Higashi-Fuji-Goko Road. For trains, it says to check the Fujikyū Railway pages.
kitaguchi.hours: The reception hours of the shrine office and amulet office (goshuin) are not confirmed on the official site. The official site records telephone reception for prayers and weddings as 9:00–17:00. Tourist information sites give the amulet office as 8:30–17:00, but this is not confirmed on the official site.
kitaguchi.parking: The official site says there are normally eight parking areas, starting with the No. 1 lot (about 50 cars; large buses accepted), with temporary parking during festivals. Fees are not confirmed on the official site.
kitaguchi.goshuin: The official site records that, in addition to the shrine's own goshuin, goshuin for Suwa Jinja on the grounds and for Ōtsuka-oka, the place of origin, are also available, and that there is a goshuin book, "Sakura", made with Gunnai textiles. Reception hours and fees are not confirmed on the official site.

tsubaki.name: Tsubaki Ōkamiyashiro
tsubaki.summary: A shrine at the foot of the Suzuka mountains whose chief deity is Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami. The official site records that it is the head shrine of the more than 2,000 shrines across Japan that enshrine Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami, and that he is worshipped as the "ancestral deity of guidance".
tsubaki.deity_note: The official site records that Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami is the chief deity, with Ninigi-no-Mikoto and Takuhatachijihime-no-Mikoto in the joint sanctuary and Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto and Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto as associated deities. Sarutahiko is an earthly deity (kunitsukami) who, in the descent of the heavenly grandson in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, appeared at the eight crossroads of heaven and guided the heavenly grandson; the official site follows the same line and calls him the "Chiwaki-no-Ōkami" (existing entry). Ame-no-Uzume (spelled with different characters in the Nihon Shoki) danced before the heavenly rock cave, asked Sarutahiko his name at the descent of the heavenly grandson, and is later regarded as the ancestor of the Sarume no Kimi. Takuhata-chijihime appears in the Nihon Shoki (Section 9) as a daughter of Takamimusubi-no-Mikoto and the mother of Ninigi-no-Mikoto, but the Kojiki writes the mother as Yorozuhata-toyoakitsushi-hime-no-Mikoto and the name Takuhata-chijihime does not appear. The main sanctuary also enshrines Gyōman Daimyōjin, said to be a descendant of Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami, and 32 other merged deities, but Gyōman Daimyōjin is not found in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki.
history: The official site records that in autumn of the 27th year of Emperor Suinin (3 BC), by an oracle of Yamatohime-no-Mikoto, a sanctuary was established at this site as the "shrine of Chiwaki-no-Ōkami", and calls it the oldest shrine in Japan.
The official site records that in the reign of Emperor Nintoku, following a divine dream, the character "tsubaki" (camellia) was adopted for the shrine's name, which continues to this day.
The official site records that the name of the Shishidō hall in the grounds derives from a lion's head dedicated by imperial wish of Emperor Shōmu.

The encyclopedia (Wikipedia) gives the former rank as a prefectural shrine (kensha), and states that it is now a Beppyō shrine of the Association of Shinto Shrines, Ichinomiya of Ise Province and a shrine listed in the Engishiki (shikinaisha, minor). The rank is not confirmed on the official site. Since there may be more than one theory on which shrine the Engishiki listing refers to, this is to be confirmed.
highlights: The official site describes the keyhole-shaped tumulus "Takayama Dokō Shinryō" halfway along the approach as the tomb of Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami, and records that the Yamamoto family of priests has guarded this tomb since the age of the gods.
The official site describes the "Mifune Iwakura" as the place where, by tradition, the boat of the heavenly grandson Ninigi-no-Mikoto and his party arrived.

The official site records that the auxiliary shrine Tsubakikishi Jinja has as its chief deity Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto, the wife of Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami, who is revered as the ancestral deity of the performing arts and a deity of matchmaking, and that Shinto weddings are held there.
tsubaki.address: 1871 Yamamoto-chō, Suzuka, Mie 519-0315 (as written on the official site).
tsubaki.access: The official site gives 10 minutes from Suzuka IC on the Higashi-Meihan Expressway, or 2 minutes from Shin-Meishin Suzuka PA Smart IC (ETC vehicles only). About 55 minutes from Kintetsu Yokkaichi Station by Mie Kotsu bus bound for Tsubaki Ōkamiyashiro, or about 1 hour from JR Yokkaichi Station.
tsubaki.hours: The official site gives visiting hours as 5:00–18:00 from November to April and 5:00–19:00 from May to October, prayer reception 8:00–16:00 (prayers start at 8:30; no reservation needed), and the amulet office (amulets and goshuin) 8:00–16:30.
tsubaki.parking: The official site records that the free parking area holds about 500 cars.
tsubaki.goshuin: The official site gives the amulet office (amulets and goshuin) hours as 8:00–16:30, and its page of items lists goshuin books of Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami, Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto and others. The fee and types of goshuin are not confirmed on the official site.

ikuta.name: Ikuta Jinja
ikuta.summary: Its chief deity is Wakahirume-no-Mikoto; in the Empress Jingū section of the Nihon Shoki there is an oracle in which she says she wishes to dwell in "Ikuta Nagao no Kuni". The official site also says that the place name Kobe derives from this shrine's kanbe (shrine households).
ikuta.deity_note: Wakahirume-no-Mikoto appears in the Nihon Shoki and does not appear in the Kojiki (confirmed by search). In the Nihon Shoki, she appears in a variant account of Section 7 of Book 1 (the first part of the Age of the Gods) as the deity who was weaving the deities' garments in the sacred weaving hall, and in the Empress Jingū section of Book 9 she says "I wish to dwell in Ikuta Nagao no Kuni" and has Unakami no Isachi enshrine her. The official site explains Wakahirume-no-Mikoto as "said to be the gentle spirit (nigimitama) of Amaterasu-Ōmikami or her younger sister", but this is the official site's tradition, and no passage in the text of the Nihon Shoki describing her as the nigimitama of Amaterasu-Ōmikami has been confirmed.
history: The official site says that in the first year of Empress Jingū (which the official site gives as AD 201), on the way back from the expedition to the three Korean kingdoms, the ship would not move in what is now Kobe port; when divination was performed, Wakahirume-no-Mikoto appeared and said "I wish to dwell in Ikuta Nagao no Kuni", so Unakami no Isachi was made priest and enshrined her.

The official site says that the shrine originally stood on Sunayama, but when the buildings were tilted by a flood in 799 (Enryaku 18), Tone Shichidayū carried the sacred object on his back in search of a site and installed it at the spot in the Ikuta forest where he could go no further. It is also said that in 806 (Daidō 1) the court granted 44 kanbe households, which became the place name "Kōbe".

The official site records that the shrine is a "shrine of revival" that recovered from the Great Kobe Flood of 1938 (Shōwa 13), the Kobe air raids of 1945 (Shōwa 20), and the Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake of 1995 (Heisei 7).

Ranks such as a shrine listed in the Engishiki (shikinaisha), Myōjin Taisha and former Kanpei Chūsha were not found on the official pages checked this time, and come only from encyclopedias and tourist sites.
highlights: The official site records a tradition that sacred sake brewed at the shrine was served to guests from Silla, and that it is called the "shrine that brews sacred sake".

The official site records that at weddings the "Musubi no Shinkyoku", composed by Miyagi Michio, is played during the san-san-kudo exchange of cups (the lyrics are based on the song at the marriage of Izanagi and Izanami, among others).
ikuta.access: About a 10-minute walk north from JR Sannomiya Station or the private-railway Sannomiya stations. About a 20-minute walk south from JR Shin-Kobe Station (about 5 minutes by taxi). By car, about 5 minutes from Ikutagawa IC or Kyōbashi IC on Hanshin Expressway Route 3 (Kobe Line) (official).
ikuta.hours: The gates open at 7:00 and close around 17:00 (around 18:00 in summer). The amulet office is open 9:00–16:30, goshuin reception 9:00–16:30, and prayer reception 9:30–16:00 (official).
ikuta.parking: The parking area is open 24 hours (the gate is closed from 23:00 to 6:00). ¥200 per 15 minutes; on weekdays (Monday to Friday) from 7:00 to 18:00 the maximum is ¥2,000. Those receiving prayers should take their parking ticket to the prayer reception (official).
ikuta.goshuin: Available. Reception is 9:00–16:30 (official). There are seasonal limited goshuin (the official site announces a limited goshuin for October 2026). The official site states that distribution by post has ended.

kumanoizumo.name: Kumano Taisha (Ichinomiya of Izumo Province)
kumanoizumo.summary: Ichinomiya of Izumo Province. It enshrines Kaburogi Kumano-no-Ōkami Kushimikenu-no-Mikoto, whom the official site honors as Susanoo-no-Mikoto. The official site records a custom by which the chief priest of Izumo Taisha, on succeeding to the office, receives the fire-drill board and drill (hikiri-usu and hikiri-gine) from this shrine. It is a different shrine from Kumano Hongū Taisha in Kii.
kumanoizumo.deity_note: The official site gives the chief deity as "Susanoo-no-Mikoto, honored as Kaburogi Kumano-no-Ōkami Kushimikenu-no-Mikoto". The names "Kumano-no-Ōkami" and "Kushimikenu-no-Mikoto" are not found in the texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki examined this time (Part 3 of the Kojiki and Book 26 onward of the Nihon Shoki are not yet checked). Whether this is the same deity as Susanoo-no-Mikoto of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (existing susanoo) is left as the official site's way of honoring him, and is not asserted here. The official site's list of sources says that Kumano-no-Ōkami or Kumano Taisha appear in the Nihon Shoki, the Izumo no Kuni Fudoki, the Ryō no Gige, the Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku and the Engishiki, but the original texts have not been checked.
history: The official site records that the shrine appears as Kumano Taisha in the Izumo no Kuni Fudoki (733) and as Kumano-ni-imasu Jinja in the Engishiki register of shrines (927), that it was also called Nihon Hidezome Jinja, and that it was treated as a great shrine of Izumo Province alongside Kizuki Taisha (Izumo Taisha). The original texts have not been checked.
The official site records that the shrine was granted the divine rank of Junior Third Rank in 851 (Ninju 1) and Senior Second Rank in 867 (Jōgan 9).
The official site records that it was raised to Kokuhei Chūsha in 1871 (Meiji 4) and to Kokuhei Taisha in 1916 (Taishō 5) (former ranks).

The official site records that, by a custom from ancient times which continues today, the succession of the chief priest of Izumo Taisha begins with receiving the sacred fire-drill board and drill (hikiri-usu and hikiri-gine) from this shrine.
highlights: The official site gives the alternative name "Nihon Hidezome-sha", lists the Setsubun-sai, Mikushi-sai, Sanka-sai and Mikari-sai as the main festivals, and gives the annual festival date as 14 October.
The official top page records that the Kamiari-sai was revived in 2013 (Heisei 25).
kumanoizumo.access: By car, go south from Matsue on National Route 432 and take Prefectural Route 53 (Daitō–Higashi-Izumo Line) toward Daitō, or leave the San-in Expressway at Higashi-Izumo IC and take Prefectural Route 53. By train and bus, take an Ichibata bus from Matsue to the Yakumo-chō bus terminal, then the reservation-only AI demand bus to Kumano Taisha (official).
kumanoizumo.hours: The amulet office is open 8:30–16:30, prayer reception 9:00–15:30, and the grounds can be visited freely (official top page).
kumanoizumo.parking: The number of parking spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official pages.
kumanoizumo.goshuin: Information on goshuin and their reception hours is not confirmed on the official website (only the amulet office hours are given).

iminomiya.name: Iminomiya Jinja
iminomiya.summary: An old shrine in Chōfu, Shimonoseki City, Yamaguchi, the Ninomiya of Nagato Province and a former Kokuhei-sha. It is said to be the old site where Emperor Chūai governed from the Toyura Palace in Anato (Nagato), and enshrines Emperor Chūai, Empress Jingū and Emperor Ōjin.
iminomiya.deity_note: The official site gives the deities as Emperor Chūai, Empress Jingū and Emperor Ōjin, and explains that they are also recorded in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. The Emperor Chūai section of the Kojiki, Part 2, says that he ruled the realm from the "Toyura Palace in Anato", and the name "Anato Toyura Palace" also appears in the Emperor Chūai chronicle of the Nihon Shoki (checked against the original texts). All three are emperors and an empress who appear in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, not deities of myth. The origin of the shrine (that Empress Jingū, returning in triumph from Silla, enshrined the spirit of the emperor at the Toyura Palace) is shrine tradition. The Empress Jingū chronicle of the Nihon Shoki also has a passage in which the empress moved to the Anato Toyura Palace and held the emperor's funeral, so the story is consistent, but the founding of the shrine itself is not written in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki.
history: The official site records that this is the old site where Emperor Chūai, who went west to subdue the Kumaso, built the Toyura Palace in Anato (Nagato) and governed for 7 years (the guide to the grounds also writes "stayed until the first month of the 8th year"). After the emperor's death, Empress Jingū returned in triumph from Silla and enshrined the emperor's spirit at the Toyura Palace, which is regarded as the origin of the shrine.

The official site says that in 728 (Jinki 5, in the reign of Emperor Shōmu) there was an oracle, and the spirit of Empress Jingū was invited from Kashii-gū in Chikuzen and enshrined in the central hall, with Emperor Chūai and Emperor Ōjin enshrined in the joint sanctuary.

Shrine tradition says that it was a shrine with three separate halls, the Toyura-gū, Iminomiya and Toyoake-gū, but the Toyura-gū and Toyoake-gū burned down in a medieval fire and were merged into the Iminomiya.
The official site gives the rank as "Ninomiya of Nagato Province, former Kokuhei-sha", and the top page shows it as a shrine listed in the Engishiki (shikinaisha).
highlights: Suhōtei-sai: every night from 7 to 13 August, people dance holding tall banners (nobori) and lanterns (kirikō) around the "Oni-ishi" stone, where the Silla general Jinrin, who attacked the Toyura Palace, is said to have been shot down and his head buried. The largest banners exceed 30 m (official).

Treasure hall: it holds more than 400 items including old documents, swords and armor; the hōraku waka poems by four members of the Ashikaga family, Takauji among them, the documents of the Takeuchi chief-priest family and the painted map of the grounds, and the tachi swords (attributed to Norimune, and by Osafune Morimitsu) are National Important Cultural Properties (official).

Manju and Kanju: these two islands off Chōfu are detached precincts of the shrine and a National Natural Monument (official). It is said that when Empress Jingū returned to the sea the tide-raising jewel and tide-ebbing jewel she had received from the Sumiyoshi Ōkami, they became the two islands.
iminomiya.access: 6 minutes by bus from Chōfu Station on the San'yō Main Line, or 20 minutes by bus from Shimonoseki Station; get off at the "Jōkamachi Chōfu" bus stop and walk 3 minutes. 10 minutes by taxi from Shin-Shimonoseki Shinkansen Station (official).
iminomiya.hours: Kagura and amulet reception is 8:30–16:30. Prayers are also received daily 8:30–16:30 (no closing days; not available during festival ceremonies). During the "Oimi-sai" from the evening of 7 December to the early morning of 15 December, general worship is prohibited and there are no amulets, goshuin or prayers (official).
iminomiya.parking: Free parking in the grounds (about 20 cars; a temporary lot is opened when crowded). Bus parking requires advance notice: ¥500 for a minibus, ¥1,000 for a large bus (official).
iminomiya.goshuin: The official FAQ mentions that goshuin are given (not during the Oimi-sai), and the page of items has the shrine's original goshuin book (main sanctuary on the front, Suhōtei on the back). The goshuin fee and dedicated reception hours are not confirmed on the official site (amulet reception is 8:30–16:30).

sumiyoshihakata.name: Sumiyoshi Jinja (Hakata)
sumiyoshihakata.summary: Ichinomiya of Chikuzen Province, in Hakata Ward, Fukuoka. It enshrines the Three Sumiyoshi Deities, Sokotsutsu-no-O, Nakatsutsu-no-O and Uwatsutsu-no-O, and the official site records that it is said to be the first of all the Sumiyoshi shrines in Japan (a different shrine from Sumiyoshi Taisha in Osaka and Sumiyoshi Jinja in Shimonoseki).
sumiyoshihakata.deity_note: The official site says that the Kojiki records the Three Sumiyoshi Deities (Sokotsutsu-no-O-no-Kami, Nakatsutsu-no-O-no-Kami and Uwatsutsu-no-O-no-Kami) as born when Izanagi-no-Ōkami performed purification at Awakihara in Odo of Tachibana in Himuka of Tsukushi, and that with Amaterasu-Ōmikami and Empress Jingū enshrined in the joint sanctuary they are also called the "Sumiyoshi Gosho Ōkami". In the Kojiki, Part 1 (the purification of Izanagi), Sokotsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto, Nakatsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto and Uwatsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto appear as the "Suminoe-no-Mimae-no-Ōkami", and in a variant account in the Nihon Shoki, Book 1, Sokotsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto, Nakatsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto and Uwatsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto are called the "Sumiyoshi-no-Ōkami" (checked against the original texts). In the Emperor Chūai section of the Kojiki, Part 2, the deity who possesses Empress Jingū names itself as the three great deities "Sokotsutsu-no-O, Nakatsutsu-no-O and Uwatsutsu-no-O". The expedition to the three Korean kingdoms is a story recorded in the Empress Jingū chronicle of the Nihon Shoki (treated separately from shrine tradition and legend), and the same chronicle also has a passage in which the Sumiyoshi deity instructed that his rough spirit (aramitama) be enshrined at Yamada village in Anato (taken to correspond to Sumiyoshi Jinja in Shimonoseki). However, the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki only give the place of purification as "Awakihara in Odo of Tachibana in Himuka of Tsukushi"; identifying it with the present site of Sumiyoshi in Hakata is this shrine's tradition, and the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki do not say that it refers to this place.
history: The official site states that the shrine's history goes back roughly 1,800 years or more, that it is said to be the first of the 2,129 Sumiyoshi shrines across Japan, and that old books also record it as "Sumiyoshi Honsha" and "Nihon Daiichi Sumiyoshi-gū".

The present main sanctuary was rebuilt in 1623 (Genna 9) with a donation of 2,000 ryō of silver and timber from Kuroda Nagamasa, and is a National Important Cultural Property. The official site records that the building is in the "Sumiyoshi-zukuri" style and that a sengū (rebuilding and repair) is carried out every 25 years.

The official site gives its rank as "Ichinomiya of Chikuzen Province". The encyclopedia records that the Engishiki register of shrines (compiled in 927) is said to list "Sumiyoshi Jinja, three deities" in Naka District, Chikuzen Province, as a Myōjin Taisha, and that the shrine became a Kanpei Shōsha in 1925 (Taishō 14) and a Beppyō shrine after the war. (The parts confirmed only in the encyclopedia are to be confirmed.)
highlights: The main sanctuary in Sumiyoshi-zukuri style: the official site describes it as the oldest special style in the history of shrine architecture, with a straight-lined gabled roof, vermilion-painted pillars and walls painted with white gofun. A National Important Cultural Property (official).

Annual grand festival (Sumō-e Taisai): on 13 October each year, there is a children's procession, yabusame horseback archery, and boys' sumo by local elementary schools (festival section of the official top page).

The sacred tree "Ichiya-matsu" (one-night pine): it stands to the left of the shrine buildings, and it is said that when a pine leaning over the buildings was about to be cut down as an obstacle to construction, it straightened itself in a single night (official).
sumiyoshihakata.access: About an 8-minute walk from JR Hakata Station or Hakata subway station. About a 2-minute walk from the Nishitetsu bus stop "Sumiyoshi" (official).
sumiyoshihakata.hours: Reception hours are 9:00–17:00 (official top page and footer). Goshuin reception is the same, 9:00–17:00 (grounds guide page). Prayer reception hours are announced month by month in the official notices (for example, the notice of prayer reception hours for October).
sumiyoshihakata.parking: Parking is available, with about 30 spaces (official). Those coming for off-site ceremonies park in a different place.
sumiyoshihakata.goshuin: Goshuin are received at the shrine office (9:00–17:00); you hand over your goshuin book. Goshuin books are not sold on their own but are distributed with an entry written in them. It is crowded at New Year and during the grand festival. There is also a notice (dated 14 September 2026) of an autumn-only "Yabusame clear goshuin". The fee could not be read in this check.

suwanagasaki.name: Suwa Jinja (Nagasaki)
suwanagasaki.summary: The "Chinzei Taisha", the tutelary shrine of all Nagasaki, in Kaminishiyama-machi, Nagasaki City. It enshrines the three shrines of Suwa (Takeminakata-no-Kami and Yasakatome-no-Kami), Morisaki and Sumiyoshi, and its annual grand festival on 7, 8 and 9 October is known as Nagasaki Kunchi.
suwanagasaki.deity_note: The official deities are the chief deity Suwa-no-Ōkami (Takeminakata-no-Kami and Yasakatome-no-Kami), Morisaki-no-Ōkami in the joint sanctuary (Izanagi-no-Kami and Izanami-no-Kami), and Sumiyoshi-no-Ōkami in the joint sanctuary (Sokotsutsu-no-O-no-Kami, Nakatsutsu-no-O-no-Kami and Uwatsutsu-no-O-no-Kami). Their treatment in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki differs from deity to deity. Takeminakata-no-Kami appears in the transfer of the land in the Kojiki, Part 1, as a child of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, is pursued by Takemikazuchi-no-Kami, flees as far as the "sea of Suwa in Shinano Province" and surrenders (not found in the Nihon Shoki texts obtained). Yasakatome-no-Kami does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki texts obtained; she is a deity regarded in Suwa tradition as the consort of Takeminakata-no-Kami and is absent from the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (to be confirmed). Kotoshironushi-no-Kami of the same transfer-of-the-land section appears in the Kojiki as a brother of Takeminakata-no-Kami, but is not included among the shrine's official deities. Izanagi, Izanami and the Three Sumiyoshi Deities (born at the purification) are deities of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. The shrine itself was re-established in the early modern period (17th century), and the official site has no description indicating a founding in the age of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.
history: The official site records that in Nagasaki, which in the Sengoku period had become church land of the Jesuits, the three shrines of Suwa, Morisaki and Sumiyoshi, formerly enshrined in the town, were re-established in 1625 (Kan'ei 2) by the first chief priest, Aoki Kensei, at Maruyama in Nishiyama-gō (the present site of Matsunomori Jinja) as the ubusunagami (local tutelary deity) of Nagasaki, and that this was the beginning.
The official site records that in 1648 (Keian 1) the shrine received land under a vermilion seal from the Tokugawa shogunate, and the shrine buildings were built at the present site.

Most of the shrine buildings were lost in a fire in 1857 (Ansei 4), and by the wish of Emperor Kōmei they were rebuilt over about ten years, completed in 1869 (Meiji 2). The official site records that two further constructions, commemorating 1984 (Shōwa 59) and 1994 (Heisei 6), produced the present buildings.

The encyclopedia records that it was ranked as a Kokuhei Chūsha in 1921 (Taishō 10) and became a Beppyō shrine after the war. The rank could not be confirmed on the official site. (Confirmed only in the encyclopedia.)
highlights: Nagasaki Kunchi: the grand festival on 7, 8 and 9 October. Counted as one of the three great festivals of Japan as a splendid festival with an exotic flavor, it is designated a National Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property (official).
English fortune slips: the first English-language omikuji in Japan, created in 1914 (Taishō 3) by Kugimoto Kohachirō, an English teacher at the former Nagasaki Middle School (official).
400th anniversary of enshrinement: 2025 (Reiwa 7) marks 400 years since the enshrinement, and commemorative projects such as the renovation of the main sanctuary are being carried out (official).
suwanagasaki.access: Get off at the "Suwa Jinja" tram stop and take the underpass to the shrine approach. By car, about 10 minutes from the Nagasaki Susukizuka and Dejima interchanges (as written on the official site).
suwanagasaki.hours: Prayer reception is 8:00–16:00 (at any time). Outside these hours is also possible, but from 7:30 to 8:00 and from 16:30 to 17:30 only one priest is on duty. The hours of the amulet office and goshuin reception are not confirmed on the official site.
suwanagasaki.parking: 100 cars and 5 large buses. Large buses require advance notice. At busy times for purifications and prayers, such as New Year and the holidays in November, parking may not be possible (official).
suwanagasaki.goshuin: The goshuin fee is ¥500. The Kunchi-only goshuin book (¥2,000) and limited goshuin (the single character "kami", ¥1,000) are limited in number, and the distribution period is posted in the notices on the official top page (official). Reception hours are not confirmed.

komagata.name: Komagata Jinja
komagata.summary: The "Ichinomiya of Rikuchū", in Mizusawa, Ōshū City, Iwate. It enshrines Komagata-no-Ōkami, the mountain deity of Mt. Komagatake in the Yakeishi range, and the official site reveres as its deities the six deities (Amaterasu-Ōmikami and others) recorded on the ridgepole tablet of the inner shrine (okumiya).
komagata.deity_note: The official site states that "the deities are unknown" and then records that it reveres as its deities the six deities recorded on the ridgepole tablet of the inner shrine (Amaterasu-Ōmikami, Ame-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto, Kuni-no-Satsuchi-no-Mikoto, Akatsu-no-Mikoto, Okise-no-Mikoto and Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto). The shrine history says the mountain deity was called "Komagata-no-Ōkami" and enshrined, but this deity name "Komagata-no-Ōkami" is not found in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki (a separate tradition). Of the six, Amaterasu-Ōmikami is the chief deity of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. Ame-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto appears in the Kojiki as "Ame-no-Tokotachi-no-Kami" (one of the Kotoamatsukami) and in the Nihon Shoki as "Ame-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto" in a variant account of Section 1. Kuni-no-Satsuchi-no-Mikoto is in the Nihon Shoki only (Section 1, with the alternative name "Kuni-no-Satachi-no-Mikoto" in a variant account) and does not appear in the Kojiki. Akatsu-no-Mikoto is written "Amatsu-oya Akatsu-no-Mikoto" in the Kogo Shūi and is thought to correspond to "Masakatsu-akatsu-kachihayahi-ame-no-oshihomimi-no-Mikoto" of the Nihon Shoki, but the official site does not state the identification explicitly (to be confirmed). The official site treats Okise-no-Mikoto as the same as the heavenly grandson Ninigi, but this name is not in the texts of the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki; a variant account of Section 9 of the Nihon Shoki has the name "Ame-no-Kihohookise-no-Mikoto" (whether the official site relies on this is unknown; to be confirmed). Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto is Yamasachihiko and appears in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.
history: The official site says that the shrine began in the reign of Emperor Yūryaku (around 456), when Kamitsukeno no Isawa no Kimi invited Komagata-no-Ōkami to the summit of Mt. Komagatake, which is seen from the Isawa plain.

The official site records that, of all the Komagata shrines in Japan, only two are listed in the Engishiki register of shrines: Komagatane Jinja in Miyagi Prefecture and this shrine. It is also said that through the devotion of Sakanoue no Tamuramaro its divine rank rose to Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade.

In 1903 (Meiji 36) the shrine was moved from the summit of Mt. Komagatake to the present site (in Mizusawa Park). The inner shrine (okumiya) is on Mt. Komagatake in Kanegasaki Town, and village shrines (satomiya) are at Nishine Hinakozawa in Kanegasaki Town and elsewhere.
highlights: The blessings listed on the official site are industrial development (business prosperity), traffic safety, victory, success in examinations, protection against unlucky directions, household safety, good matches, warding off misfortune, and fulfillment of wishes.

The annual festival is on 19 September (eve festival on 18 September), and the grand festival commemorating the relocation is on 3 May (children's mounted-warrior procession). The official site records that the doors of the main sanctuary are opened only twice a year, at the annual festival and the relocation commemoration festival.
Within the grounds are Shiogama Jinja, Yama Jinja and Mizusawa Shōkonsha (official "shrines in the grounds").
komagata.address: 1-83 Mizusawa Nakauwano-chō, Ōshū, Iwate 023-0857 (in Mizusawa Park). The inner shrine is on Mt. Komagatake in Nishine, Kanegasaki Town, Isawa District.
komagata.access: A 10-minute walk from JR Mizusawa Station. 15 minutes by car from JR Mizusawa-Esashi Station. 12 minutes by car from Mizusawa IC on the Tōhoku Expressway, or 7 minutes by car from Ōshū Smart IC (official).
komagata.hours: Reception for talismans, amulets and goshuin is 9:00 to around 17:00 (except New Year). Prayer reception is 9:30 to around 16:30 (outside these hours, on request). The gates open at 5:30 and close at 18:00 from April to October and 17:30 from November to March (on New Year's Day they open at 0:00). Confirmed on the official site on 12 Oct 2026.
komagata.parking: The shrine lot has 30 free spaces (entrance on the uphill road on the north side of Mizusawa Park; not available on New Year's Day). There are also the Z Plaza Aterui lot (free) and the Mizusawa Park south lot (paid; ¥300 for up to 24 hours) (official).
komagata.goshuin: Goshuin are received at the shrine office during the hours above (official). The official site also mentions distributing Komagata Jinja's own goshuin book and the nationwide Ichinomiya goshuin book. The types of goshuin, fees and whether pre-written sheets are available are not confirmed on the official pages.

tsushima.name: Tsushima Jinja
tsushima.summary: The head shrine of the roughly 3,000 Tsushima and Tennō shrines across Japan, in Tsushima City, Aichi. Its chief deity is Takehaya-Susanoo-no-Mikoto, with Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto (Ōkuninushi-no-Mikoto) in the joint sanctuary. It was formerly called Tsushima Gozu Tennō-sha and is affectionately known as "Otennō-sama".
tsushima.deity_note: The chief deity Takehaya-Susanoo-no-Mikoto is written as in the Kojiki (Susanoo-no-Mikoto in the Nihon Shoki); Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto of the joint sanctuary is recorded in the Kojiki as another name of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami and is written Ōnamuchi-no-Kami (with different characters) in the Nihon Shoki. The official site records that, after the myth in which he married Inada-hime-no-Mikoto, he is also worshipped as a deity of marital harmony and good matches. The former name "Gozu Tennō" does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki and is thought to be a name deriving from the syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism, but the official site does not explain the background (to be confirmed).
history: According to shrine tradition, the shrine was established in the first year of Emperor Kinmei (540), and will mark 1,500 years since its founding in 2040 (Reiwa 22).

The official site records that in 810 (Kōnin 1) the shrine was granted the divine rank of Senior First Rank and the title Nihon Sōsha, and in the Shōryaku era (990–995) under Emperor Ichijō it was granted the title Tennō-sha.

The present main sanctuary (Important Cultural Property) is in the "Owari-zukuri" style, built in 1605 (Keichō 10) with a donation from the wife of Matsudaira Tadayoshi, lord of Kiyosu Castle. The Rōmon gate (Important Cultural Property) was donated by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in 1591 (Tenshō 19).
It was ranked as a prefectural shrine (kensha) in 1873 (Meiji 6) and as a Kokuhei Shōsha in 1926 (Taishō 15) (official).
highlights: The "Owari Tsushima Tennō Festival" in July is inscribed on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list (official).
The main sanctuary and Rōmon gate, National Important Cultural Properties, and the South Gate, an Aichi Prefecture cultural property (1598, Keichō 3; donated by Toyotomi Hideyori), survive.
tsushima.access: Leave the ticket gates of Tsushima Station, turn right and go straight along Prefectural Route 68 (toward Tennōgawa Park) for about 10–12 minutes (official directions). By car, go south on National Route 155, turn right at the "Tsushima Jinja Kita" intersection, and the entrance to the parking area on the west side of the grounds is about 200 m ahead.
tsushima.hours: Prayer and amulet office reception is 9:00–12:00 and 13:00–16:00 on weekdays (until 15:30 from July to September), and 9:00–16:00 on weekends and holidays. Confirmed on the official top page on 12 Oct 2026. The opening and closing times of the grounds are not confirmed on the official site.
tsushima.parking: There is a parking area on the west side of the grounds (official directions). The number of spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official site.
tsushima.goshuin: The list of items includes a "goshuin book", distributed at the amulet office. The official Instagram announces a limited goshuin for the "Tsuitachi-mairi" visit on the 1st of each month. The reception hours and fee for regular goshuin are not confirmed on the official pages (whether they follow the amulet office hours is to be confirmed).

hirota.name: Hirota Jinja
hirota.summary: A shrine at the foot of Mt. Hirota in Nishinomiya City, Hyōgo. It enshrines the aramitama (rough spirit) of Amaterasu-Ōmikami as its chief deity, and the official site, citing the Nihon Shoki, explains that Empress Jingū enshrined it on her way back from Silla. The official site records that in 1871 (Meiji 4) it became the only Kanpei Taisha in Hyōgo Prefecture.
hirota.deity_note: The chief deity is the one the official site writes as "the aramitama of Amaterasu-Ōmikami", explaining that her name is Tsukisakaki-itsu-no-mitama-amasakaru-mukatsuhime-no-Mikoto and that she corresponds to the aramitama of Amaterashimasu-Ōkami of the Inner Shrine of the Grand Shrine of Ise. Whether she is regarded as the same as the existing Amaterasu-Ōmikami (amaterasu) or as a separate divine personality follows the official site's explanation, and this note does not assert either. In the Empress Jingū section of the Nihon Shoki, Book 9, there is a scene in which a deity naming itself "Tsukisakaki-itsu-no-mitama-amasakaru-mukatsuhime-no-Mikoto" appears to the empress after she entered the sacred hall, and a scene in which, on the way back from Silla, Amaterasu-Ōmikami declares "My aramitama must not come near the imperial residence; it should dwell in Hirota Province" and has it enshrined by Hayama-hime, daughter of Yamashiro no Neko; these were checked in the original text. However, the text of the Nihon Shoki does not explain any link between "Hirota Province" and the present site of Nishinomiya, nor does it name the shrine (that link is the official site's explanation). The official site explains that the auxiliary shrine Saiden Jinja enshrines Hayama-hime-no-Mikoto, the first saigū (consecrated priestess). Part 2 of the Kojiki (obtained) contains neither the word Hirota nor a scene of enshrining the aramitama, so this origin rests on the Nihon Shoki. In the side halls, the first holds the Sumiyoshi Mimae-no-Ōkami (the three Tsutsu-no-O deities), the second the Hachiman Sansho-no-Ōkami (Emperor Ōjin, Empress Jingū and Nakatsuhime-no-Mikoto), the third Suwa Takeminakata-no-Ōkami (whom the official site explains as a child of Ōkuni-sama), and the fourth Takamimusubi-no-Ōkami (whom the official site explains as the chief deity of the Hasshinden of the imperial palace); the official site records that in old times these were together called the Hirota Gosha (five shrines). Empress Jingū is named as the founder, and the existing Empress Jingū (jingu) and Emperor Ōjin (ojin) have been linked. Nakatsuhime-no-Mikoto is not among the existing deities and so has not been linked.
history: The official site explains that Empress Jingū, in the first year of her regency (201), received the divine instruction of Amaterasu-Ōmikami and sent troops overseas, and on her triumphant return enshrined the aramitama of the great deity in Hirota Province in Muko (from Ashiya and Nishinomiya to western Amagasaki) as a guardian of the land and protection against foreign peril; this was the founding, and it is recorded in the Nihon Shoki.

The official site records that the shrine received 41 fuko households in 806 (Daidō 1), the Junior First Rank in 868 (Jōgan 10), and in the Engi era (901–923) was listed as a Kanpei Myōjin Taisha and among the shrines receiving the Ainame and rain-prayer offerings, and in 991 (Shōryaku 2) was added as one of the Nineteen Shrines.

The official site records that in the time of Emperor Shirakawa (late 11th century) it was the only shrine in the prefecture chosen as one of the Twenty-Two Shrines receiving imperial offerings, and that in 1871 (Meiji 4) it was the only shrine in Hyōgo Prefecture ranked at the highest level, Kanpei Taisha (29 shrines nationwide at the time).

The official site records that the present shinmei-zukuri buildings were built in 1956–63 (Shōwa 31–38), having received the old buildings of the Aramatsuri-no-miya at the first postwar Shikinen Sengū of the Grand Shrine of Ise. It states that in 2001 (Heisei 13) the shrine marked 1,800 years since its enshrinement.
highlights: The colony of Kobano-mitsuba-tsutsuji azaleas spreading through the outer garden of the grounds is estimated, according to the official site, at about 20,000 plants, and became a Hyōgo Prefecture Natural Monument on 25 March 1969 (Shōwa 44) (Nishinomiya City also records the prefectural designation in 1969). The official site also announces a goshuin limited to the flowering season (usually late March to mid-April).

The official site records that the Hanshin Tigers' prayer for victory has continued for more than 80 years since the team's formation in 1936 (Shōwa 11), and reports on the prayer ceremony of 24 March 2026.

The official site records that the shrines of Muko District, Hyōgo, listed in the Engishiki are four: the main Hirota Jinja and the auxiliary shrines Nasuki Jinja, Okada Jinja and Iwashizu Jinja, all under the administration of Hirota Jinja.
hirota.address: 7-7 Taisha-chō, Nishinomiya, Hyōgo 662-0867 (as written at the foot of the official site)
hirota.access: By train and bus: Hankyu bus (bound for Kōtōen) from the south exit of Hankyu Nishinomiya-kitaguchi Station, Hanshin bus (Yamate higashi-mawari route) from the north exit of Hanshin Nishinomiya Station, or Hankyu bus from the northwest of JR Nishinomiya Station; in each case get off at "Hirota Jinja-mae" (official). By car, go north from the Murokawa-chō intersection on National Route 171; the visitors' parking area is just north of the large torii on the left.
hirota.hours: Amulet and goshuin reception is 8:30–16:30 (may change for the shrine's convenience). Prayers are received daily 9:30–15:00, but as the hours vary by day, check the official notices (no reservation needed; about 20–30 minutes). The opening and closing times of the grounds themselves are not confirmed on the official site.
hirota.parking: There is a visitors' parking area (north of the large torii). The number of spaces and fees are not found in the official access information. Large buses must be reserved in advance (Hirota Jinja shrine office, tel 0798-74-3489).
hirota.goshuin: Information is on the official site. The fee is ¥500. Besides the regular goshuin of the main shrine (Hirota Jinja, the aramitama of Amaterasu-Ōmikami), there are goshuin for the auxiliary shrine Iwashizu Jinja within the grounds (available at any time), the auxiliary shrines outside the grounds, Nangū Jinja, Nasuki Jinja and Okada Jinja (available only to those who have visited them), and a limited goshuin for the flowering season (Kobano-mitsuba-tsutsuji). Reception is 8:30–16:30.

otori.name: Ōtori Taisha
otori.summary: Ichinomiya of Izumi Province. It enshrines Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto and Ōtori-no-Muraji-no-Mioya-no-Kami, and both the official site and Sakai City record that it is the only Myōjin Taisha of Izumi Province listed in the Engishiki register of shrines. Shrine tradition says that it began when a shrine was built at the place where the spirit of Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto, having become a white bird, alighted.
otori.deity_note: The deity Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto is the one the official site explains as the second prince of Emperor Keikō, who appears in the Nihon Shoki and Kojiki, and the existing Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto (yamatotakeru) has been linked. For the white-bird tradition, the Kojiki records that Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto, who died in Ise, became a "yahiro shirochidori" (a great white bird), soared into the sky, headed for the shore, settled at Shiki in Kawachi Province, where the White Bird Mausoleum was made, and from there flew into the sky again; the Nihon Shoki, Book 7, records that the white bird settled at Kotohiki-no-hara in Yamato, then at Furuichi village in Kawachi, and finally rose high into the sky (both checked in the original texts). Up to Kotohiki-no-hara and Furuichi in Kawachi these overlap, but the part in which the white bird finally alighted at Ōtori is shrine tradition and cannot be confirmed in the texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (the word "Ōtori" is not found in the texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki obtained). The other deity, Ōtori-no-Muraji-no-Mioya-no-Kami, is explained by the official site as the enshrined ancestor of the Ōtori clan, which flourished in Izumi Province, and as said in the Shinsen Shōjiroku to have Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto as its ancestor. He is a clan ancestral deity; no basis for his appearing as an independent deity in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki was confirmed, and the text of the Shinsen Shōjiroku was not checked this time, so the new deity page notes that he is absent from the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. In the official explanation of the auxiliary shrines, Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto's consorts are enshrined as follows: Kibi-no-Anato-no-Takehime-no-Mikoto at Ōtori Kitahama Jinja, Futaji-no-Irihime-no-Mikoto at Ōtori Hagoromohama Jinja and Ototachibana-hime-no-Mikoto at Ōtori Ise Jinja, while Mihahi Jinja enshrines Amaterasu-Ōmikami. Book 7 of the Nihon Shoki has Kibi-no-Anato-no-Takehime and Princess Futaji-no-Irihime as consorts of Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto, and the Kojiki has Ototachibana-hime-no-Mikoto, but the matching to each shrine follows the official explanation.
history: The official site records that shrine tradition tells how the spirit of Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto became a white bird, passed through Kotohiki-no-hara in Yamato and Furuichi in Kawachi Province, and alighted at this place, where a shrine was built to enshrine it; this was the origin of the shrine, about 1,900 years ago. The inner shrine (the Yōgō-seki stone) of the auxiliary shrine Ōtori Mihahi Jinja is held to be the place where, in the 43rd year of Emperor Keikō, the spirit descended as a great white bird.

The official site records that in the reign of Emperor Shōmu the monk Gyōki built the shrine temple Jinpōji by imperial wish, but it was abolished under the order separating Shinto and Buddhism at the Meiji Restoration.

The official site records that it is a Myōjin Taisha listed in the Engishiki register of shrines completed in 927 (Enchō 5), and the Ichinomiya of Izumi Province. Sakai City's cultural property page also explains that it is a shrine listed in the Engishiki (shikinaisha), the only Myōjin Taisha of Izumi Province, and the Ichinomiya of Izumi Province. The official site also records that it was one of the 85 shrines designated by the Jingikan for prayers against disaster and for rain in times of national calamity, and that it rose to Junior Third Rank in the 7th month of 861 (Jōgan 3) and later to Senior First Rank.

The official site records that the shrine buildings burned in the wars of the Tenshō era (1573–92), were restored by Toyotomi Hideyori in 1602 (Keichō 7) and rebuilt by order of Tokugawa Ietsuna in 1662 (Kanbun 2), but were lost to fire from lightning in 1905 (Meiji 38) and rebuilt in the traditional form in 1909 (Meiji 42).
highlights: The official site explains that the main sanctuary is called "Ōtori-zukuri": gabled with the entrance on the gable end, resembling the taisha-zukuri of Izumo, but differing in that the entrance is at the center of the front, there is no central pillar, and there is no shin-no-mihashira. Sakai City designates the main sanctuary, the shrine gate and mizugaki fence, the worship hall, and the offering hall and tamagaki fence as municipal tangible cultural properties, and records that according to the ridgepole tablet the main sanctuary was rebuilt in 1907 (Meiji 40), designed by Andō Tokizō, an engineer of the Home Ministry.

The grounds are called the "Chigusa no Mori" from the tradition that trees grew thick in a single night when the white bird alighted, and the official site records that the grounds of about 15,000 tsubo contain three ponds and a great camphor tree with raised roots. There are also a monument (in the hand of Tomioka Tessai) to the poem Taira no Kiyomori composed when he prayed here on his way to Kumano, and a statue of a sacred horse modeled on the beloved horse Kiyomori dedicated.

The day after the first Friday of October is the annual festival of the auxiliary shrine Ōtori Mihahi Jinja, and the official site announces that 10 danjiri floats enter the shrine as the Ōtori Danjiri Festival (check the official site for the 2026 dates).
otori.address: 1-chōme 1-2, Ōtori-kitamachi, Nishi Ward, Sakai, Osaka (Sakai City's cultural property page; the official supporters' association page gives the shrine office as "1-1-2 Ōtori-kitamachi, Nishi Ward, Sakai"). The postal code is not confirmed on the official site.
otori.access: About a 5-minute walk from the west exit of Ōtori Station on the JR Hanwa Line (about 30 minutes from Kansai-Airport Station by Kanku Rapid, about 15 minutes from Tennōji Station). By car, go straight from the Hamadera exit of the Hanshin Expressway Sakai Line, turn left at the Hamadera-minamimachi 3-chōme intersection on National Route 26, and continue to the end of the road. By bus, a 3-minute walk from "Ōtori Kitaguchi" or a 1-minute walk from "Ōtori Jinja-mae" (official).
otori.hours: The gates open at 5:30 and close at 18:00. The amulet office is open 9:00–16:30, and prayers are received until 16:00 (no reservation needed; apply in person). The official access page also has a separate note giving prayer reception as 9:00–16:30, so check the details on the official site.
otori.parking: Free parking is available (go straight through the large torii on the west). Parking may be refused when the lot is full or crowded. Large buses require advance application, and on some days cannot park (official; in 2026 (Reiwa 8), not available all day on 16, 23 and 30 August, 20 September, and 2–5 October).
otori.goshuin: Information is on the official site. Besides the goshuin of the main shrine and Mihahi Jinja, which can be written in your goshuin book, there are the monthly limited goshuin "Ōtori no Shiki", limited goshuin themed on festivals and events, and seasonal goshuin books (no writing in goshuin books during January). The fee is not found on the official pages obtained.

kibitsuhiko.name: Kibitsuhiko Jinja
kibitsuhiko.summary: Ichinomiya of Bizen Province. It stands at the eastern foot of Kibi-no-Nakayama, the sacred mountain, and its chief deity is Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto, a son of Emperor Kōrei and said to be one of the Four Generals (Shidō Shōgun). The official site records that it is said to be the birthplace of the Momotarō legend. It is a separate shrine from Kibitsu Jinja in Bitchū.
kibitsuhiko.deity_note: The official site explains that the chief deity is Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto (also Hikoisaseribiko-no-Mikoto and Isaseribiko-no-Mikoto), the third prince of the 7th emperor, Emperor Kōrei, and one of the Four Generals (the General of the Western Route). In the joint sanctuary it enshrines Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto (a son of Emperor Kōrei, Wakatake-Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto), Emperors Kōrei, Kōgen, Kaika and Sujin, Hikosashikatawake-no-Mikoto, Ame-no-Tarashihiko-kuni-oshihito-no-Mikoto, Ōyamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-Mikoto, Ōyamato-totohiwakaya-hime-no-Mikoto, Kanayamahiko-no-Ōkami and Ōyamakui-no-Ōkami. Because the chief deity is explained as Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto of the Kojiki, like Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto (ookibitsuhiko) of Kibitsu Jinja in Bitchū, an existing ID was reused. Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto (Wakatake-Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto) of the joint sanctuary is a different deity, and a new ID was made for him. The Emperor Kōrei section of the Kojiki treats Hikoisaseribiko-no-Mikoto (also called Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto) and Wakahiko-Takekibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto as separate princes, and records that the two subdued and pacified the land of Kibi, using Harima as the entrance of the road. The Nihon Shoki, in the 2nd year of Emperor Kōrei in Book 4, writes Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto as another name of Hikoisaseribiko-no-Mikoto and also lists Wakatakehiko-no-Mikoto as a prince, and in the 10th year of Emperor Sujin in Book 5 says that Kibitsuhiko was sent to the western route (confirmed against the original text). The official site's distinction of the joint-sanctuary Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto as Wakatake-Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto is the shrine's own arrangement; the person the Nihon Shoki calls Kibitsuhiko is Isaseribiko-no-Mikoto (corresponding to Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto). The battle with Ura-no-Mikoto and the Momotarō story are recorded by the official site as a tradition; the name Ura is not found in the Kojiki Part 2 and the Nihon Shoki Books 4 and 5 that were obtained, so this is a tradition not found in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. Kanayamahiko and Ōyamakui were linked to existing deities. The treatment of the auxiliary shrine Koyasu Jinja (Izanagi-no-Mikoto, Izanami-no-Mikoto, Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto, Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto), the minor shrines Ise-gū (Amaterasu-Ōmikami) and Sachi Jinja (Sarutahiko-no-Kami), Inari Jinja (Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto) and others is given in the section on the grounds and they are not included in deity_ids.
history: The official site records that Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto was sent by order of the Yamato court, in the reign of the 10th emperor, Emperor Sujin, as one of the Four Generals to subdue the land of Kibi, and that the shrine buildings were built on the site of the residence from which he ruled Kibi; this is said to be the beginning of the shrine.

The Okayama Prefectural Association of Shrines records that in the 10th month, 24th day of 843 (Jōwa 10), in the reign of Emperor Ninmyō, the shrine was granted the divine rank of Ippon (First Rank), and that Emperor Ichijō built the shrine buildings. Its former rank was Kokuhei Shōsha.

The official site records that the existing main hall was begun in 1668 (Kanbun 8) by Ikeda Mitsumasa, lord of Okayama domain, and completed in 1697 (Genroku 10) under his son Tsunamasa. The main hall, the connecting corridor, the Saimon-den and the worship hall stand in a straight line. The Association of Shrines records that in a fire in 1930 (Shōwa 5) everything except the main hall and the Zuishin-mon gate burned down, and that it was rebuilt in 1936 (Shōwa 11).

The official site records that in May 2018 (Heisei 30) the shrine was certified as one of the component cultural properties of the Japan Heritage story "Okayama, the Town Where the Momotarō Legend Was Born".
highlights: The official site records that, because at sunrise on the summer solstice the sun rises directly in front of the front torii and enters the sacred mirror in the sanctuary, the shrine is also called the "Asahi no Miya" (Shrine of the Morning Sun). On the summit there is an Okumiya iwakura (sacred rock seat), and beside it Ryū Jinja enshrines Hachidai-ryūō-no-Kami.

The official site records that the sacred sword "Momotarō Sukesada" (made in 1666, Kanbun 6) was designated an Important Cultural Property of Okayama Prefecture in 2019 (Heisei 31). Together with the tachi sword (by Inoue Shinkai), an Important Cultural Property designated by the state, the swords are managed by the Okayama Prefectural Museum.

The official site records that the Otaue Festival (rice-planting festival) is an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Okayama Prefecture. According to the Association of Shrines, the Otaue Festival is held on 2 and 3 August, and the autumn grand festival on the 3rd Saturday and Sunday of October.
kibitsuhiko.access: From JR Okayama Station take the JR Momotarō Line to Bizen-Ichinomiya Station, then a 3-minute walk to the front torii. By car, about 3.5 km toward Sōja from the smart IC (ETC only, 6:00–22:00) at Kibi SA on the Sanyō Expressway, or via national roads from Okayama IC or Sōja IC (official).
kibitsuhiko.hours: The gate opens at 6:00 and closes at 18:00 (no worship is possible while the gate is closed, for crime and disaster prevention). The amulet office is open 8:30–17:00 (talismans, amulets, goshuin and so on). Prayers are held 9:00–16:00 (no reservation needed; about every 30 minutes). Because there are times when reception is not possible during festivals and weddings, confirm in advance (official).
kibitsuhiko.parking: There is a parking lot (open 6:00–18:00). The number of spaces and fees are not found on the official access page. The Okayama Prefectural Association of Shrines records "yes, 200 spaces".
kibitsuhiko.goshuin: The official site gives the reception hours of the amulet office (talismans, amulets, goshuin and so on) as 8:30–17:00, so it can be confirmed that goshuin are given. Details such as the fee and whether they are pre-written sheets are not found on the official pages that could be obtained.

nichizen.name: Hinokuma Jingū and Kunikakasu Jingū
nichizen.summary: Ichinomiya of Kii Province, where two shrines, Hinokuma Jingū and Kunikakasu Jingū, stand side by side in the same grounds. The deity of Hinokuma has the Higata mirror as its sacred object and the deity of Kunikakasu has the Hiboko mirror, and together they are called "Nichizen-gū". The official site records that both shrines were ranked as Myōjin Taisha under the Engi regulations.
nichizen.deity_note: The official site gives the deity of Hinokuma Jingū as Hinokuma-no-Ōkami (joint sanctuary: Omoikane-no-Mikoto and Ishikoridome-no-Mikoto) and the deity of Kunikakasu Jingū as Kunikakasu-no-Ōkami (joint sanctuary: Tamanooya-no-Mikoto, Akarutatsu-ame-no-Mikage-no-Mikoto and Uzume-no-Mikoto). It explains that at the time of the heavenly rock cave, following the counsel of Omoikane-no-Mikoto, Ishikoridome-no-Mikoto served as the smith and cast the sacred mirrors from the copper of Ame-no-Kaguyama. It further says that the Nihon Shoki records that the two sacred mirrors of Amaterasu-Ōmikami cast at the same time were enshrined as the sacred objects of the two shrines; checked against the original texts obtained, the position is as follows. A variant account in Nihon Shoki Book 1, Section 7, says that Ishikoridome was made the smith and had the "Hiboko" made from the metal of Ame-no-Kaguyama, and records the deity who made it as the deity Hinokuma who dwells in Kii Province (it ties the Hiboko to the deity of Hinokuma). The Kogo Shūi has Ishikoridome cast a mirror of the sun image; the first casting did not satisfy him, and a note identifies that one as the deity of Hinokuma of Kii Province and the next casting as the Great Deity of Ise. The Kojiki, in the rock-cave section, only records that Ishikoridome was made to make a mirror, and has no names Hinokuma or Kunikakasu. The name Kunikakasu is not found in the texts of the Kojiki, Nihon Shoki and Kogo Shūi that were obtained. The shrine gives the sacred object of Nichizen-gū as the Higata mirror and that of Kunikakasu-gū as the Hiboko mirror, but in the variant account of the Nihon Shoki the "Hiboko" is tied to the deity of Hinokuma, so this does not match the shrine's assignment, which is to be confirmed (the official explanation and the Nihon Shoki account are shown side by side). The official site also explains Hinokuma-no-Ōkami and Kunikakasu-no-Ōkami as other names of Amaterasu-Ōmikami, and writes that Nichizen-gū enshrines Amaterasu-Ōmikami. Following the official wording, the relationship to the existing Amaterasu-Ōmikami (amaterasu) is not included in deity_ids. Ame-no-Michine-no-Mikoto (deity of an auxiliary shrine) is explained by the official site as a deity who followed the descent of the heavenly grandson and was the ancestor of the Ki clan, appointed Kii no Kuni no Miyatsuko in the 2nd year of Emperor Jinmu; he is not found in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki texts obtained. Akarutatsu-ame-no-Mikage-no-Mikoto is likewise not found.
history: The official site records that at the descent of the heavenly grandson the sacred objects of both shrines were sent along with the three sacred treasures, and that after the eastern expedition of Emperor Jinmu, Ame-no-Michine-no-Mikoto, ancestor of the Kii no Kuni no Miyatsuko family, was appointed Kii no Kuni no Miyatsuko and enshrined the two sacred mirrors in Kemi village (gō), Nagusa District, Kii Province; this is said to be the origin of the shrine. It says the founding goes back more than 2,600 years.

The official site records that the shrine moved to Hama-no-miya in Nagusa District in the 51st year of Emperor Sujin, and to Yorozuyo-no-miya in Nagusa District (the present site) in the 16th year of Emperor Suinin.

The official site records that under the Engi regulations both shrines were ranked as Myōjin Taisha, received offerings (heihaku) from the emperor at the Toshigoi, Tsukinami, Ainame and Niiname rites, and have been revered since ancient times as Ichinomiya of Kii Province.

The official site records that the grounds fell into ruin in the Tenshō wars of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, that the shrine buildings were restored when Tokugawa Yorinobu entered the province, and that in 1871 (Meiji 4) a proclamation of the Council of State ranked the shrine as a Kanpei Taisha. It says that the improvement work on the buildings in the grounds, paid for by the state in Taishō 8, was completed in March 1926 (Taishō 15), giving the shrine its present appearance.
highlights: The official site says that at the auxiliary shrine Ichiebisu Jinja (Hiruko-no-Kami), Ebisu worship is held on the evening before Ebisu on 9 January, Hon-Ebisu on the 10th and the "remaining fortune" day on the 11th, and that the approach is decorated with Ichiebisu banners and the grounds are kept open until late at night.

The official site records that the auxiliary shrine Matsuo Jinja (Ōyamakui-no-Kami and Nakatsushima-hime-no-Mikoto) was branched from Matsuo Taisha in Kyoto, is revered as the ancestral deity of brewing, and holds the Matsuo Festival every November.
nichizen.access: A 1-minute walk from Nichizengū Station on the Wakayama Electric Railway Kishigawa Line (change to the Kishigawa Line at platform 9 of JR Wakayama Station). By Wakayama Bus, get off at "Nichizengū Station" from the East Exit bus terminal and walk 1 minute. About a 20-minute walk from the East Exit ticket gate of Wakayama Station. By car, take national route 24 from Wakayama IC toward the city and enter by the East Gate (official).
nichizen.hours: The descriptions differ between pages of the official site. The access page gives the reception of the Nichizen-gū shrine office as 8:00–17:00 (prayer reception until 16:00), while the top page and the foot of each page give 9:00–16:40 (gate closing) (prayers 9:00–16:00, last reception 15:50). Which one is the current practice must be confirmed with the official site.
nichizen.parking: Parking is free for worshippers' vehicles. Enter by the East Gate and follow the staff's instructions. Up to 100 vehicles, and large buses can also park (travel agencies and others using large buses should inquire in advance).
