Vehicles may not enter by the West Gate or the Taikobashi bridge (official).
nichizen.goshuin: The official top page says "goshuin are handed over as pre-written sheets". The fee is not found on the official pages that could be obtained.

ishizuchi.name: Ishizuchi Jinja
ishizuchi.summary: A shrine whose sacred mountain is Mt. Ishizuchi (1,982 m), the highest peak of western Japan, in Saijō City, Ehime. Four shrines, the Kuchinomiya head shrine at the foot, Jōju-sha halfway up, Chōjō-sha on the summit and the Tsuchigoya worship hall, together make up "Ishizuchi Jinja", and it enshrines Ishizuchibiko-no-Mikoto. The official site explains it as a Beppyō shrine.
ishizuchi.deity_note: The official site says that the deity Ishizuchibiko-no-Mikoto is also called Ishitsuchibiko-no-Mikoto and Ishizuchi-no-Ōkami, and is the second child of Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto. In the section on the birth of the land and the deities in the Kojiki, Part 1, "Ishitsuchibiko-no-Kami" is born after Ōkotooshio-no-O-no-Kami (checked against the original text), which also matches the official "second" in order. However, the name "Ishitsuchibiko" is not found in the main text of the Nihon Shoki or in the variant accounts within the range obtained (a variant account in Book 1, Section 5, has a deity name "Iwatsuchi-no-Mikoto", but it cannot be confirmed from the text that this is the same deity, so he is treated as a different deity). The link between the mountain name "Ishizuchi" and the name "Ishitsuchi" in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki is based on the official explanation.
history: The official site says that Mt. Ishizuchi is said to have been opened in the Asuka period (685) by En no Gyōja (En no Ozunu), and that afterwards Jakusen Bosatsu revered it as Ishizuchi Zaō Daigongen, opened the mountain paths and founded Jōjū-sha (now Jōju-sha).

The official site records that Jōju-sha was built in 1610 (Keichō 15) by Toyotomi Hideyori. It explains that this building was lost in a fire in Meiji 22, and that the present Jōju-sha was restored in 1982 (Shōwa 57) after a fire in Shōwa 55.

The official site records that in the early Meiji years the mixing of Shinto and Buddhism was banned, the temples serving as administrators (Yokomine-ji and Maegami-ji) were abolished, the shrine was established as Ishizuchi Jinja, and at that time it was ranked as a prefectural shrine (kensha).

The official site explains that after the war Ishizuchi Jinja received the treatment of a Beppyō shrine, equal in standing to the former Kankokuhei shrines, and founded Ishizuchi Honkyō as a religious body under it.
highlights: Four-shrine structure: Kuchinomiya Honsha (priests resident), Chūgū Jōju-sha (staff resident all year), Okumiya Chōjō-sha (staff resident 1 May–3 November) and Tsuchigoya Yōhaiden (staff resident 1 April–end of November; closed in winter). The official site explains that these four places together make up one Ishizuchi Jinja.

Receiving the sacred images (Goshinzō Haitai): a rite in which the three sacred images, Tamamochi, Kagamimochi and Tsurugimochi (the jewel-bearer, mirror-bearer and sword-bearer), are received directly on the body to receive the deity's virtue. The official site explains that among the 80,000 shrines across Japan it is performed only at this shrine (available for groups with a sendatsu guide).

The approach to Chōjō-sha has the "chain training places", the Tameshi no Kusari, Ichi-no-Kusari, Ni-no-Kusari and San-no-Kusari, and the official site records that the total distance of the chains is about 230 m.
ishizuchi.address: 797 Nishida-kō, Saijō, Ehime 793-8555 (Ishizuchi Jinja head shrine, TEL 0897-55-4044). Jōju-sha: 422 Komatsu-chō Ishizuchi, Saijō 799-1112 (TEL 0897-59-0106). Tsuchigoya Yōhaiden: at the end of the Ishizuchi Skyline in Kumakōgen Town (TEL 0897-53-0008; closed in winter). Chōjō-sha is on the summit of Mt. Ishizuchi (Misen). The coordinates are based on the address of the head shrine (Geospatial Information Authority of Japan address search).
ishizuchi.access: The head shrine is 15 minutes by car from Saijō IC or Komatsu IC, and 10 minutes by car from JR Saijō Station. The red great torii on national route 11 is the entrance to the head shrine. To reach Chōjō-sha, visitors climb either via Jōju-sha (about 7 minutes from Shimotani Station of the Ishizuchi Ropeway plus 20–30 minutes on foot to Jōju-sha, then about 2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours on foot from there) or via the Tsuchigoya Yōhaiden (about 2 hours 30 minutes on foot) (official).
ishizuchi.hours: Prayer requests are received at the talisman office beside the main hall of the head shrine, 8:30–16:00 on weekdays, Saturdays, Sundays and festival days (there may be a wait during festivals and weddings). The individual reception hours of the amulet offices and the gate opening and closing times are not confirmed on the official site. Chōjō-sha and the Tsuchigoya Yōhaiden have staff resident only for limited periods (the periods in the highlights above).
ishizuchi.parking: The head shrine has a parking lot in its grounds (official). The number of spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official site. The official site records that the parking lot of the adjacent Ishizuchi Jinja Kaikan holds 50 cars and 20 large buses (it is not confirmed whether this is the same as the lot in the head shrine's grounds).
ishizuchi.goshuin: The official site announced on 6 September 2024 that goshuin of Ishizuchi Jinja (the head shrine, Jōju-sha, Tsuchigoya Yōhaiden and Chōjō-sha) are accepted only as pre-written sheets (kakioki), and are not written in visitors' own books, because a unified response across the four shrines is difficult. The fee and the reception hours for giving them are not confirmed on the official site.

tamura.name: Tamura Jinja
tamura.summary: Ichinomiya of Sanuki Province, in Ichinomiya-chō, Takamatsu City, Kagawa. Five deities, beginning with Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime-no-Mikoto, are enshrined under the collective name "Tamura-no-Ōkami", and the official site explains that it became an official shrine in 861 (Jōgan 3) and was ranked as a Myōjin Taisha. The sacred object is said to be the pool under the floor of the inner hall.
tamura.deity_note: The official site gives the deities as five: Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime-no-Mikoto, Isaseribiko-no-Mikoto (Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto), Sarutahiko-no-Kami, Ame-no-Kagoyama-no-Mikoto (Takakuraji-no-Mikoto) and Ame-no-Itane-no-Mikoto (Ame-no-Murakumo-no-Mikoto), and calls them collectively Tamura-no-Ōkami. Yamato-totohi-momoso-hime-no-Mikoto is counted among the children of Emperor Kōrei in the Emperor Kōrei section of the Kojiki as Yamatototomomosobime-no-Mikoto, and also appears in the Kōrei and Sujin chapters of the Nihon Shoki (checked against the original text). The official statement that she "foresaw the rebellion of Takehaniyasuhiko" corresponds to an item in the Sujin chapter, and also matches the Hashihaka item (the official "Hashi no Misasagi"). On the other hand, the official statement that she "went down to Sanuki Province with Isaseribiko-no-Mikoto under an order to pacify the western seas, and became the founding deity of agriculture and productive industry" is shrine tradition and is not written in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. Isaseribiko-no-Mikoto has a note "also called Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto" in the Kōrei chapter, and in the Kojiki is Hikoisaseribiko-no-Mikoto (also called Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto); he is treated as the same deity as the existing Ōkibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto. Sarutahiko-no-Kami appears in the descent of the heavenly grandson in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. Identifying Ame-no-Kagoyama-no-Mikoto with Takakuraji-no-Mikoto is the official explanation; the Takakuraji of Kumano who appears in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki is noted in the Kojiki with a personal-name gloss ("this is a person's name"). The names Ame-no-Kagoyama-no-Mikoto and Ame-no-Itane-no-Mikoto (Ame-no-Murakumo-no-Mikoto) are not found in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki texts obtained and rest on other traditions (to be confirmed).
history: The official site records that, according to the shrine records, the shrine buildings were founded in 709 (Wadō 2), and that from ancient times the shrine was also called "Tamura Taisha", "Jōsui Daimyōjin" and "Ichinomiya Daimyōjin".

The official site records that the shrine was granted the Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade, in 849 (Kashō 2), became an official shrine in 861 (Jōgan 3), was ranked as a Myōjin Taisha and fixed as Ichinomiya of Sanuki Province, and was then granted the highest rank, Senior First Rank, in 1201 (Kennin 1).

The official site explains that the present inner hall and main hall are in the Kasuga-zukuri style and were built by the Matsudaira clan in 1710 (Hōei 7), and that the heiden and the worship hall are in the irimoya-zukuri style and were rebuilt in Meiji 10.
highlights: The official site records that the sacred object is a pool deep in the inner hall, that according to shrine tradition a dragon lives in that pool, and that the pool under the floor of the inner hall has never been opened.

Tamotoi (the sleeve well): the official site explains that it is said to be the well where, when Momosohime-no-Mikoto came down to the place, a maidservant dipped her sleeve and offered water, and that it is still a source of irrigation water for rice fields.

The grounds have auxiliary shrines such as Ichinomiya Tenmangū, which enshrines Sugawara no Michizane, Subakura-sha, which enshrines Sukunabikona-no-Kami, and Itsukushima-sha (Miyajima-sha), which enshrines Ichikishima-hime-no-Mikoto (official).
tamura.address: 286 Ichinomiya-chō, Takamatsu, Kagawa 761-8084 (TEL 087-885-1541). The access page also writes "Ichinomiya-chō 286-1". The coordinates are from the address search of the Geospatial Information Authority of Japan.
tamura.access: About a 10-minute walk from Ichinomiya Station on the Kotoden Kotohira Line, or about a 1-minute walk from the Ichinomiya bus stop of Kotoden Bus. By car, about 10 minutes from Takamatsu-nishi IC, about 15 minutes from Takamatsu-chūō IC and about 15 minutes from Takamatsu Airport (official).
tamura.hours: Prayer reception is open every day of the year, 9:00–17:00, with no reservation needed, at the amulet office (it may be suspended on festival days and the like). The opening and closing times of the grounds and the individual reception hours of the amulet office are not confirmed on the official site.
tamura.parking: The official site asks those who come for traffic-safety prayers or car purification to enter from the entrance near the Tamura Jinja Kaikan (north of national route 172) and park there. The number of spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official site.
tamura.goshuin: Goshuin are accepted at the amulet office. The fee for a handwritten goshuin is ¥500 (from 23 December to 3 February of the next year, only pre-written sheets). The Ryūtai Jigen goshuin is ¥500 (large ¥1,000), the paper-cut goshuin is ¥1,000, and the double-page paper-cut goshuin is ¥1,500 (official). The reception hours for goshuin are not confirmed on the official site.

oosaki.name: Ōsaki Hachimangū
oosaki.summary: A Hachimangū that Date Masamune enshrined northwest of Sendai Castle and which continues as the guardian shrine of all Sendai. Its Momoyama-period shrine buildings are designated National Treasures.
oosaki.deity_note: The deities are three: Emperor Ōjin, Empress Jingū and Emperor Chūai (official). In the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, Emperor Ōjin is Hondawake-no-Mikoto in the Kojiki and Homutawake-no-Mikoto in the Nihon Shoki, Empress Jingū is Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto (Kojiki) and Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto (Nihon Shoki), and Emperor Chūai is Tarashinakahiko-no-Sumeramikoto (Kojiki) and Tarashinakahiko-no-Sumeramikoto (Nihon Shoki); the three are recorded as the family of Emperor Chūai, Empress Jingū and Emperor Ōjin. The official site says that it performs the rite of the shaken bells of the "Okinaga bell", named after Empress Jingū (Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto), and gives out safe-childbirth amulets, since Empress Jingū is known as a deity of safe childbirth. The divine title "Hachiman" itself is not found in the texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki confirmed in the research so far (the same range of confirmation as the existing Emperor Ōjin page). The official site tells its origin as beginning when Sakanoue no Tamuramaro invited the deity of Usa Hachimangū.
history: The official site says that in the Heian period Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, praying for lasting good fortune in arms for the subjugation of the eastern tribes, invited the deity of Usa Hachimangū to what is now Mizusawa City, Iwate Prefecture, and founded Chinjufu Hachimangū. In the Muromachi period the Ōsaki clan, the Ōshū Tandai, moved it within their domain (now Taijiri Town, Tōda District), and it is said that it came to be called "Ōsaki Hachimangū" from this.

After the fall of the Ōsaki clan, Date Masamune moved the sacred object to a small shrine inside Iwadeyama Castle, and after the founding of Sendai he enshrined it at the present site, which lies to the northwest (inui) of Sendai Castle. The shrine buildings were built from 1604 (Keichō 9) to 1607 (Keichō 12) at Masamune's order (official).

The shrine buildings (main hall, Ishi-no-ma and worship hall) were designated Specially Protected Buildings in Meiji 36 and National Treasures in 1952 (Shōwa 27). The official site records that they are the only surviving buildings of the Azuchi-Momoyama period of their kind in Japan. The Nagatoko in front of the shrine buildings is an Important Cultural Property of the state (official).

After the Meiji period it was called "Ōsaki Hachiman Jinja", but ahead of the 400th anniversary of the enshrinement, the shrine name was restored to "Ōsaki Hachimangū" in June 1997 (Heisei 9) (official).
highlights: The National Treasure shrine buildings are in the Ishi-no-ma style (gongen-zukuri), lacquered black with brilliantly coloured carvings and bracket sets. Inside the worship hall are wall paintings of karajishi (Chinese lions) by Sakuma Sakyō, a painter of the Kanō school, and 53 kinds of flowers and plants are painted on the coffered ceiling (official).

The grounds have auxiliary shrines such as Taigen-sha (Taigen Myōō), a shrine enshrining Takeminakata-no-Kami, Kashima-sha (Takemikazuchi-no-Ōkami), Hokushin-sha (Ame-no-Minakanushi-no-Kami) and Kotohira-sha (Ōmononushi-no-Kami) (official). The correspondence of the names of each shrine has not been examined closely.
oosaki.access: From the Sendai Station West Exit bus terminal by Sendai City Bus (the official site gives destination guidance). From Kita-yonbanchō Station on the subway, take a city bus at the "Futsukamachi Kita-yonbanchō" stop and get off at "Ōsaki Hachimangū-mae". A 15-minute walk from Kunimi Station or Tōhoku Fukushi Daigaku-mae Station on the JR Senzan Line (official).
oosaki.hours: Prayer reception is 9:00–16:00 (no reservation needed; there are days when it is not available because of festivals and the like). Only the prayer reception could be confirmed on the official site; the opening and closing times of the amulet office and the visiting hours of the grounds are not confirmed on the official site.
oosaki.parking: Not confirmed on the official site (no parking information was found on the access map page).
oosaki.goshuin: Goshuin are explained by the official site (Hachiman-sama Dayori No. 48). The fee is not fixed and is "as you feel". When the writer is away at prayers, and during the period from the New Year to the Matsutaki festival or during festivals, there may be a wait or only paper goshuin may be available. The original goshuin book with a picture of the shrine buildings is ¥3,000 (given out at the amulet office). The reception hours are not confirmed on the official site.

kasamainari.name: Kasama Inari Jinja
kasamainari.summary: An Inari shrine that enshrines Ukanomitama-no-Kami and describes itself as one of the Three Great Inari shrines of Japan. The main hall is an Important Cultural Property of the state.
kasamainari.deity_note: The deity is Ukanomitama-no-Kami (the official spelling). The official site says that in the Kojiki he is a child of Susanoo-no-Mikoto and Kamuōichi-hime-no-Kami, and that his elder brother is Ōtoshi-no-Kami. Kojiki Part 1 also says that the children born were Ōtoshi-no-Kami and then Ukanomitama (-no-Kami), which matches the original text on this point. The official site treats Ukanomitama-no-Kami as the same deity as Ōgetsuhime-no-Kami of the Kojiki and Ukemochi-no-Kami of the Nihon Shoki, but this is the shrine's view, and the texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki do not write it so (to be confirmed). The Nihon Shoki gives a separate account under the name Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto. See the existing deity page (Ukanomitama-no-Kami).
history: The official site says that, by shrine tradition, the shrine was founded in 651 (Hakuchi 2), in the reign of the 36th emperor, Emperor Kōtoku. In ancient times the great deity Inari was enshrined in a dense grove of walnut trees, and for this reason it is also said to have been called "Kurumi-shita Inari".

The official site cites the Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki, which records "to the east of Niihari District, at fifty ri, there is the village of Kasama", and says that by that time (the order to compile it was given in 713, Wadō 6) faith in Ukanomitama-no-Kami had probably taken root in this place. This is the official site's estimate.

In 1743 (Kanpō 3) Inoue Masakata, lord of Kasama Castle, enlarged the shrine grounds and buildings, and in 1747 (Enkyō 4) Makino Sadamichi, who became lord of the castle, made it a place of prayer for the domain and donated grounds and ritual implements. Since then it has received the veneration of successive domain lords (official).

The present main hall was rebuilt in the Ansei and Man'en years (1854–1860) at the end of the Edo period, and is in the gongen-zukuri style with a copper-tile roof, built entirely of zelkova. It was designated an Important Cultural Property of the state in 1988 (Shōwa 63) (official).
highlights: The Rōmon gate (Bansei Taihei-mon) is a two-storied irimoya-zukuri structure completed in Shōwa 36. The two wisteria vines in the grounds are said to be 400 years old, and the double-flowered wisteria among them was designated a Natural Monument of the prefecture in Shōwa 42 (official).
The official site has a page introducing the Kasama Inari Museum of Art.
kasamainari.access: From JR Joban Line Tomobe Station take the JR Mito Line to Kasama Station, then about a 20-minute walk or about 5 minutes by taxi. By car, about 15 minutes from Tomobe IC on the Kita-Kantō Expressway via national route 355. By bus, "Kasama Sightseeing Circular Bus (not running on Mondays), Kasama Inari Jinja-mae" and "Express bus, Kasama Inari Jinja entrance" (official).
kasamainari.hours: Prayers are held every hour on the hour from 8:00 to 16:00 (including noon), and reception is at the prayer reception office next to the shrine office up to 15 minutes before the start. Times may differ during festivals. During the New Year visit period: 1 January 0:00–5:00 and 7:00–17:00, and 2–3 January 8:00–17:00 (official). The reception hours of the shrine office for amulets and goshuin and the visiting hours of the grounds are not confirmed on the official site.
kasamainari.parking: The parking lot in the grounds is free, with 25 spaces (no large vehicles). Large vehicles use the Jizō-mae parking lot, a 5-minute walk from the shrine (90 ordinary cars). The Jizō-mae lot is paid on weekends and holidays during the Chrysanthemum Festival period, at the New Year and in Golden Week, is not available on 2–4 November, and cannot be reserved (official).
kasamainari.goshuin: The official site describes the shrine office as the "reception for prayers and goshuin". The fee and the reception hours are not confirmed in the main text of the official site (the official site for viewing offerings has categories for goshuin books and goshuin).

wakasahiko.name: Wakasahiko Jinja (Kamisha)
wakasahiko.summary: Ichinomiya of Wakasa Province. The Upper Shrine, which enshrines Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto, said to be Yamasachihiko, and a pair with the Lower Shrine (Wakasahime Jinja), which enshrines Toyotama-hime-no-Mikoto.
wakasahiko.deity_note: The official site explains that Wakasahiko Jinja consists of the Upper Shrine (Wakasahiko Jinja, Ryūzen, Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto) and the Lower Shrine (Wakasahime Jinja, Onyū, Toyotama-hime-no-Mikoto). The deity of the Upper Shrine is Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto (Yamasachihiko), who is Hoori-no-Mikoto (also called Amatsuhiko-Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto) in the Kojiki and Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto in the Nihon Shoki. Toyotama-hime-no-Mikoto, the deity of the Lower Shrine, is Toyotama-bime-no-Mikoto in the Kojiki, recorded as the wife of Hoori-no-Mikoto and the mother of Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto. Wakamiya Jinja in the grounds enshrines Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto, whom the official site explains as "the father of Emperor Jinmu, and child of Wakasahiko-no-Kami and Wakasahime-no-Kami". Regarding Tamamori Jinja of the Lower Shrine, the official site mentions the tide-flowing jewel and tide-ebbing jewel, saying that "a text in which the sea god spoke to Wakasahiko-no-Kami remains in the Kojiki", but the relevant passage in Kojiki Part 1 is the scene in which the sea god gives Hoori-no-Mikoto the jewels, saying that if he brings out the tide-flowing jewel the other will drown, and if he laments and begs, he is to bring out the tide-ebbing jewel to save him. Identifying Wakasahiko-no-Kami with Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto is the shrine's explanation; neither the place name "Wakasa" nor the name Wakasahiko is confirmed in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (to be confirmed).
history: The official site says that first Wakasahiko-no-Kami and then Wakasahime-no-Kami descended onto a huge rock at Unose in Shimo-negoro Shiraishi, Obama City. They then travelled in search of permanent seats, and Wakasahiko Jinja was enshrined at Ryūzen on 10 September 715 (Reiki 1), and Wakasahime Jinja at Onyū six years later, on 10 February 721 (Yōrō 5).

The official site lists, as a shrine recorded in the Engishiki (Heian period), "Wakasahiko Jinja, two seats (Myōjin Taisha)". Comparison with the original text of the Engishiki register of shrines has not been completed.

The Lower Shrine was called "Wakasahime Jinja" and "Onyū Jinja (Onyū Myōjin)" from ancient times, and after it was ranked as a Kokuhei Chūsha and became a state-officiated shrine in 1871 (Meiji 4), it was officially called "the Lower Shrine of Wakasahiko Jinja" (official). Until before the war it was the only Kokuhei Chūsha in the Wakasa region.

The official site announces that the main hall, Shinmon gate and Zuishin-mon gate of the Upper Shrine have been damaged by age and by heavy snow and rain, and that repair work is planned from the autumn of fiscal 2024 (Reiwa 6) under the guidance of Fukui Prefecture and Obama City (both the Upper and Lower Shrines are cultural properties of Fukui Prefecture).
highlights: In front of the Rōmon gate of the Upper Shrine there is a Meoto-sugi (a pair of cedars whose roots are joined). The Lower Shrine has the Sennen-sugi (thousand-year cedar), the Chi-no-ki (ginkgo) and the Ogatama-no-ki (a Natural Monument of Obama City) (official).

As Important Cultural Properties of the state, the official introduction lists a tachi sword inscribed "Mune-[one character]" (attributed to Munechika; Heian period; held by the Tokyo National Museum) and the Norito Shidai (1303, Kengen 2).
wakasahiko.address: 28-7 Ryūzen, Obama, Fukui (Upper Shrine, official). The Lower Shrine (Wakasahime Jinja) is at 65-41 Onyū, Obama
wakasahiko.access: The official site gives only the address and a link to Google Maps, and access guidance is not confirmed.
wakasahiko.hours: Neither the Upper nor the Lower Shrine has a closing time, and visitors may worship freely (official). Only the Lower Shrine has a shrine office, and its reception hours are 10:00–15:00 (it may be absent on days of local rites). The Upper Shrine has no shrine office.
wakasahiko.parking: Not confirmed on the official site
wakasahiko.goshuin: There are handwritten goshuin for each of the Upper and Lower Shrines, and they are received at the shrine office of the Lower Shrine (Wakasahime Jinja). The fee is ¥300 for one shrine and ¥600 for two shrines, and the goshuin book is ¥2,000. Applications for prayers are also made at the shrine office of the Lower Shrine (telephone possible, 0770-56-1116) (official).

toga.name: Toga Jinja
toga.summary: Ichinomiya of Mikawa Province, in Ichinomiya-chō, Toyokawa City, Aichi. It enshrines Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto (Ōkuninushi-no-Mikoto), and is revered as "two places, one body": the Okumiya, which stands on the summit of Mt. Hongū (789 m above sea level), and the Satomiya in the village below. This data covers the Satomiya (the shrine buildings in the village); the Okumiya is at a different location.
toga.deity_note: The official site writes the deity as "Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto (Ōkuninushi-no-Mikoto)" and explains that he is the chief deity of the earthly deities (kunitsukami) in Japanese mythology, revered as a deity of good fortune, land development and matchmaking. Kojiki Part 1 lists Ōanamuchi-no-Kami among the other names of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, and a variant account in Nihon Shoki Book 1, Section 8, gives "Kunitsukuri-Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto" as another name of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami. So the official "Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto" can be treated as the same deity as the existing Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami (ookuninushi). The official site explains how the deity came to remain on Mt. Hongū on the basis of the Tajima Zoku Fudoki and shrine tradition, and this is a local tradition not found in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.
history: The official site explains that Mt. Hongū has been a sacred mountain since the age of the gods where the spirit of Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto dwells, and that huge rocks and trees on the summit and in the mountain have been revered as iwakura and iwasaka. It says that the Okumiya shrine building was called the "Okumiya" when a shrine building was made in the village in the Taihō years.

The official site tells the origin of the Satomiya as follows, based on the "Mikawa no Kuni Ichinomiya Toga Daibosatsu Goengi" of Tenshō 2. In the Taihō years of Emperor Monmu, an imperial envoy was guided by an old man in the mountains of Mikawa, and, at the old man's wish, a shrine was set up at the foot of the mountain. The official site gives the enshrinement of the Satomiya as 701–704.

The official site explains that in the Heian period it was ranked as a shrine listed in the Engishiki, and became the "Ichinomiya", the foremost shrine at which the governor of Mikawa Province made rounds of worship and offerings to the shrines of the province. It also records that it held the Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade, in Kashō 3, and reached the Junior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade, in Jōgan 18.
The official site records that the Senior First Rank was granted in Bunsei 10 in the Edo period, and that in 1871 (Meiji 4) it was ranked as the foremost of the Kokuhei Shōsha.
highlights: The "sazare-ishi" of the Satomiya: the official site explains that it is the largest sazare-ishi in Japan, 2.6 m high and 3.4 m wide (it is also called the good-fortune stone and the childbirth stone).

The great torii: erected in 1842 (Tenpō 13) at Ichida Village in the former Hoi District, damaged in the air raid on the Toyokawa Naval Arsenal in Shōwa 20, and moved in Shōwa 31 to the side of national route 151. The official site explains that marks of bomb hits remain and that it was designated a tangible cultural property of Toyokawa City in Heisei 25.

The auxiliary shrine "Mikawa Ebisu-sha": it enshrines Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto and Takeminakata-no-Mikoto. The official site announces that the Hatsu-Ebisu Festival is held on 10 January each year and the Ebisu Grand Festival on 20 November.
toga.address: 2 Nishigaito, Ichinomiya-chō, Toyokawa, Aichi 441-1231 (Satomiya, TEL 0533-93-2001). The Okumiya is at 4 Hongūshita, Kaminagayama-chō, Toyokawa 441-1202 (TEL 0533-93-2057), on the summit of Mt. Hongū. The coordinates are based on the address of the Satomiya (Geospatial Information Authority of Japan address search).
toga.access: The Satomiya is about a 5-minute walk from Mikawa-Ichinomiya Station on the JR Iida Line (the 4th station from Toyohashi Station on the Iida Line). By car, about 5 minutes from Toyokawa IC on the Tōmei Expressway to the Satomiya and about 50 minutes to the Okumiya (official).
toga.hours: The official site gives "Reception 8:30–16:30" (Monday to Sunday, open all year, free to visit; reception for amulets, goshuin and so on). The opening and closing times of the grounds and the reception hours of the Okumiya are not confirmed on the official site.
toga.parking: The Satomiya has free parking lots: about 30 spaces at the front gate and about 170 at the West Gate (official). Temporary parking lots are prepared nearby for the New Year visit. The Okumiya also has a free parking lot, but the number of spaces is not confirmed on the official site.
toga.goshuin: Goshuin are given at the shrine office or the guest hall (bring your own goshuin book; a Toga Jinja goshuin book is also available). At the New Year there are limited pre-written goshuin (silver for the Satomiya and gold for the Okumiya; limited numbers) (official). The fee is not confirmed on the relevant official page. The place and hours for receiving goshuin at the Okumiya are also not confirmed on the official site.

takebe.name: Takebe Taisha
takebe.summary: Ichinomiya of Ōmi Province, in Seta, Ōtsu City, Shiga. It enshrines Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto in the main hall and Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto in the subsidiary sanctuary (gonden). The official site explains that it is a shrine listed in the Engishiki and has been revered as Ichinomiya of Ōmi Province.
takebe.deity_note: The official site explains that the deity Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto was a prince of Emperor Keikō, defeated the Kumaso brothers, pacified the eastern tribes and died at the age of 30. He is written Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto in the Kojiki and Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto in the Nihon Shoki, and the Keikō chapter of the Nihon Shoki records, after his death at Nobono, that "to record his merits, the Takebe were then fixed". The official statement that "Emperor Keikō fixed the Takebe" can be read as an explanation that follows this item. The Keikō section of the Kojiki also notes of Prince Inayorivake, a child of Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto, that he was "the ancestor of the Takebe no Kimi", and the Nihon Shoki likewise makes him ancestor of the "Takebe no Kimi". The official site gives the origin as Prince Inayorivake and his consort Futaji-hime enshrining Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto. Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto, on the other hand, is explained by the official site as the enshrinement of "Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto of Ōmiwa Jinja, Ichinomiya of Yamato Province". In the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, Ōnamuchi is another name of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, but the deity of Ōmiwa Jinja is Ōmononushi-no-Kami, and the degree to which the two deities are identified differs between sources (see the note on the existing Ōmononushi-no-Kami, omonushi). The official site also records that Emperor Keikō and the empress are enshrined in auxiliary shrines.
history: The official site explains that the origin is that, by a divine command in the 46th year of Emperor Keikō (AD 116), shrine buildings were founded at Takebe in Kanzaki District and at the village of Nobono and Chigusa-dake in Suzuka District, where his consort Futaji-hime and his child Prince Inayorivake lived, and Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto was enshrined. However, the official top page also writes that the place of origin was Inobe-chō, Gokashō, Higashiōmi City, so the explanation of the place of origin is not consistent within the official site.

The official site explains that in the 4th year of Hakuhō (AD 675), in the reign of Emperor Tenmu, about 1,300 years ago, the shrine was moved and enshrined in this place, Seta (the top page also writes "about 1,350 years ago").

The official site explains that Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto was enshrined in the gonden in 755 (Tenpyō-shōhō 7), that at that time the Sanbon-sugi (three cedars) is said to have grown in a single night, and that the two deities, Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto and Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto, were fixed as Ichinomiya of Ōmi Province. However, in the same sentence the official site writes "the reign of Emperor Kōtoku", so the era name and the emperor do not agree.

The official site explains that the Heiji Monogatari records that Minamoto no Yoritomo, defeated in the Heiji Rebellion, worshipped at this shrine and prayed for the revival of the Minamoto clan, and that when his wish was later fulfilled he prayed again before the shrine and donated many sacred treasures and shrine lands.
highlights: Takebe's sacred water: called Lord Yoritomo's "success-in-life water", and visitors may drink it when they worship (official).
Sanbon-sugi: a sacred tree said to have grown in a single night when Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto was enshrined in the gonden (official).

Important Cultural Properties: the official site introduces as Important Cultural Properties the oldest stone lantern in the prefecture, inscribed with the year Bun'ei 7, and a statue of a goddess from the Heian period (the centre is said to be the consort of Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto and the two sides his children). Viewing the goddess statue requires a reservation and a ¥300 fee.

The old 1,000-yen note: the official site explains that Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto and Takebe Taisha were depicted on Japan's first 1,000-yen note of 1945 (Shōwa 20) (it was in circulation for only about 7 months and is called a "phantom note").
takebe.address: 1-16-1 Jinryō, Ōtsu, Shiga 520-2132 (TEL 077-545-0038). The coordinates are based on the address (Geospatial Information Authority of Japan address search).
takebe.access: A 25-minute walk from Ishiyama Station on the JR Biwako Line, or a 10-minute walk from Karahashi-mae Station on the Keihan Ishiyama-Sakamoto Line. From Ishiyama Station by Ōmi Railway Bus or Teisan Bus, get off at "Takebe Taisha-mae". By car, 5 minutes from Seta-nishi IC (from the Osaka direction) or Seta-higashi IC (from the Nagoya direction) on the Meishin Expressway (official).
takebe.hours: The gate opens at 5:00 and closes at 17:00 (may change during festivals and the like). Amulet office 8:00–17:00, prayer reception 9:00–16:00 (no reservation needed), treasure hall 9:00–16:00 (reservation required; ¥300 admission) (official).
takebe.parking: There are free parking lots for worshippers only. The first lot takes only passenger cars, up to 45 (with a barrier-free toilet), and the second lot has 27 passenger cars and about 5 to 6 large buses, with a third and fourth lot besides (official). Large vehicles cannot park in the first lot.
takebe.goshuin: Goshuin and amulets are given 8:00–17:00 (extended depending on the period). The official site announces limited-period items, such as an autumn-only goshuin and the distribution of the "Ōkuni goshuin" on 17 October only. The fee for the regular goshuin is not confirmed on the relevant official page.

heian.name: Heian Jingū
heian.summary: A shrine in Okazaki, Sakyō Ward, Kyoto, founded in 1895 (Meiji 28). It was built to enshrine Emperor Kanmu in commemoration of the 1,100th anniversary of the move of the capital to Heian-kyō, and Emperor Kōmei was enshrined with him in 1940 (Shōwa 15). Its vermilion shrine buildings, modelled on the Chōdōin of Heian-kyō, are designated Important Cultural Properties.
heian.deity_note: Emperor Kanmu (50th emperor, 737–806) and Emperor Kōmei (121st emperor, 1831–1866), the deities, are both emperors of history from a time later than the period recorded in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, and do not appear in them. They are not deities of myth, and the official site explains that Emperor Kanmu is enshrined as the "founder of Kyoto" and Emperor Kōmei as the "last emperor of Heian-kyō". For this reason the listing criterion 3, a link to the deities of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, is not met.
history: The official site records that on 15 March 1895 (Meiji 28), the 1,100th anniversary of the move of the capital to Heian, "Kanpei Taisha Heian Jingū" was founded with Emperor Kanmu as its deity. It explains that this was timed with the holding of the 4th National Industrial Exhibition and the commemoration of the 1,100th anniversary of the move of the capital to Heian.
The official site records that in 1940 (Shōwa 15), the 2,600th year of the imperial era, Emperor Kōmei was enshrined together with Emperor Kanmu at the wish of the citizens.
The official site explains that the shrine garden was designated a Place of Scenic Beauty of the state in 1975 (Shōwa 50).

The official site records that in 1976 (Shōwa 51) the east and west main halls and other buildings were destroyed by fire in a terrorist attack by extremists, and that the present main hall, combining the two buildings into one, was built in 1979 (Shōwa 54).
highlights: The vermilion shrine buildings: the Daigokuden, Ōtenmon, Sōryūrō, Byakkoro and Hon-ryūbidan are Important Cultural Properties (official). Modelled on the Chōdōin of Heian-kyō, they were built in Meiji 28 to designs by Kigo Kiyoyoshi and Itō Chūta. The official site explains that the Sōryūrō, Byakkoro and others were reduced to 5/8 of the scale of the Heian-kyō original.

The shrine garden (Shinen): a pond-strolling garden made up of four gardens, east, middle, west and south, with a total area of about 33,000 m² (about 10,000 tsubo). The official site explains that it was laid out by Ogawa Jihei VII (the 7th Ogawa Jihei) and draws its water from the Lake Biwa Canal.

Jidai Matsuri: the shrine's grand festival, held on 22 October each year (postponed in case of rain). The official site explains that it continues the procession of the ages that was held as an entertainment at the commemoration of Meiji 28, and has been kept up since the following year.
heian.address: 97 Okazaki Nishitennō-chō, Sakyō Ward, Kyoto 606-8341 (TEL 075-761-0221; telephone 9:00–16:00). The coordinates are based on the address (Geospatial Information Authority of Japan address search).
heian.access: About 30 minutes from JR Kyoto Station. By Kyoto City Bus route 5 or 100, get off at "Okazaki Kōen Bijutsukan-Heian Jingū-mae" and walk 5 minutes north. By car, about 20 minutes from Kyoto-higashi IC on the Meishin Expressway (official).
heian.hours: Visiting hours are 6:00–18:00 from 1 March to 30 September, 6:00–17:30 from 1 October to 31 October, and 6:00–17:00 from 1 November to the end of February (official). Prayer reception is 9:00–16:00 (no reservation needed), at the left side of the Daigokuden. On 22 October the gate hours change because of the Jidai Matsuri. The individual reception hours of the amulet offices are not confirmed on the official site.
heian.parking: There is no parking lot (official). Use a nearby paid parking lot (such as the Kyoto City Okazaki Kōen parking lot, 075-761-9617). It becomes very crowded at certain times of year.
heian.goshuin: Goshuin are given for ¥500 (paper sheets are also available). Amulets, talismans and goshuin are received at the amulet offices of the Daigokuden and the Ōtenmon (the official FAQ). Limited-period items, such as a goshuin only for the Jidai Matsuri, are also announced.

hakozaki.name: Hakozaki-gū
hakozaki.summary: An old shrine in Fukuoka that enshrines Emperor Ōjin (Hachiman Ōkami), Empress Jingū and Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto. The official site says it is counted, with Usa and Iwashimizu, as one of the Three Great Hachiman Shrines of Japan. There are several theories about when it was founded; old records say the shrine buildings were built and the deity moved here in the first half of the 10th century. The surviving main sanctuary, worship hall and Rōmon gate are nationally designated Important Cultural Properties.
hakozaki.deity_note: The official deities are Emperor Ōjin (Hachiman Ōkami) as the main deity, with Empress Jingū (mother of Emperor Ōjin) and Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto (a sea deity and mother of Emperor Jinmu). Emperor Ōjin and Empress Jingū are recorded in the Kojiki, Part 2, and in the Nihon Shoki; the Nihon Shoki, Book 10, says Emperor Ōjin was born at Kada in Tsukushi. Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto is, in both the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki, the younger sister of Toyotama-hime, who appears in the Umisachi–Yamasachi story, and the mother of Emperor Jinmu. However, calling Emperor Ōjin "Hachiman Ōkami" is the official site's explanation; the word Hachiman does not appear in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki texts obtained.
history: The official site says that, according to old records, Emperor Daigo granted a calligraphy in his own hand reading "Tekikoku Kōfuku" ("enemy nations shall submit") in 921 (Engi 21) and the shrine buildings were built, and that the deity was moved from Daibu-gū (Honami-gū) in Chikuzen in 923 (Enchō 1). It also notes that there are several theories about the time of founding and that it is hard to say for certain.

The official site says the shrine records tell that the buildings burned in the Mongol invasion of 1274 (Bun'ei 11), in the mid-Kamakura period, and that for the rebuilding Retired Emperor Kameyama dedicated a calligraphy in his own hand reading "Tekikoku Kōfuku". Because the divine wind (kamikaze) blew, the deity is also said to be known as a deity of warding off misfortune and of victory.

The official site says the surviving main sanctuary and worship hall were built in 1546 (Tenbun 15) by Ōuchi Yoshitaka, Dazai no Daini; the main sanctuary and worship hall are nationally designated Important Cultural Properties.
According to the official site, the shrine's rank was raised to Kanpei Chūsha in 1885 (Meiji 18) and to Kanpei Taisha in 1914 (Taishō 3).
highlights: The Rōmon gate was built in 1594 (Bunroku 3) by Kobayakawa Takakage, lord of Chikuzen, and is a nationally designated Important Cultural Property. The official site says it is also called Fukuteki-mon because it bears a plaque reading "Tekikoku Kōfuku".

The sacred tree "Hakomatsu" beside the Rōmon gate: the official site says tradition holds that the name "Hakozaki" arose because Emperor Ōjin's placenta was placed in a box (hako) and buried, and a pine (matsu) was planted as a marker.

The Ichi-no-Torii bears an inscription saying it was built in 1609 (Keichō 14) by Kuroda Nagamasa, and is a nationally designated Important Cultural Property. The official site says it is called the "Hakozaki torii", with pillars divided into three sections.
hakozaki.address: 1-22-1 Hakozaki, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka 812-0053 (as written on the official site).
hakozaki.access: The official site says it is about a 3-minute walk to the Rōmon gate from Hakozakimiya-mae Station on the Fukuoka City Subway Hakozaki Line, and also about a 3-minute walk from the Nishitetsu bus stop "Hakozaki". The official FAQ says that passing through the Rōmon gate to worship inside is possible during the New Year period and the Hōjō-e festival period in September, but how to worship at ordinary times is not confirmed on the official site.
hakozaki.hours: The shrine office (amulets, talismans, lucky charms and goshuin) is open 8:30–17:30 (cash only). The official FAQ says it is open until about 18:30 from June to August, and that the hours are a guide and change with conditions in the grounds. Checked 12 Oct 2026.
hakozaki.parking: The official site lists a paid lot closest to the Rōmon gate (about 100 spaces) and a paid lot entered from National Route 3 (about 230 spaces). For wedding reception, prayers and similar, parking is free for up to 3 hours. It says parking on surrounding roads is prohibited, and the lot on the Oshioi-hama side is open only on 1–3 January.
hakozaki.goshuin: Received at the amulet office of the shrine office. The official FAQ says both direct writing in your book and pre-written sheets on hōsho paper are available. Postal requests are not accepted, since the goshuin is proof of a visit. Reception is 8:30–17:30.

yutoku.name: Yūtoku Inari Jinja
yutoku.summary: It enshrines Ukanomitama-no-Ōkami (Inari-ōkami), Ōmiyanome-no-Ōkami and Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami. The official site says that in 1687 (Jōkyō 4) Manko-hime, wife of the lord of the Hizen Kashima domain, invited a divided spirit of Inari-ōkami from an imperial prayer shrine of the court. It is regarded as one of the Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan, and the Myōbu-sha, a shrine within the grounds, is a Saga Prefecture Important Cultural Property.
yutoku.deity_note: The official deities are Ukanomitama-no-Ōkami (generally Inari-ōkami), Ōmiyanome-no-Ōkami and Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami. Ukanomitama is the Uka-no-Mitama of the Kojiki (a child of Susanoo) and the Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto of a variant account in the Nihon Shoki (existing ID ukanomitama). The official site says Ōmiyanome-no-Ōkami is also called Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto (written in two ways) and treats her as the deity who danced before the heavenly rock cave (existing ID amenouzume). However, the "Ōmiyanome-no-Kami" of the Kogo Shūi is a different deity, born from the mysterious power (kushibi) of Futodama-no-Mikoto; "Ōmiyanome" is not found in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki texts obtained, and the official identification cannot be confirmed in the Kojiki, Nihon Shoki or Kogo Shūi (to be confirmed). Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami, as the official site says he led the descent of the heavenly grandson, also appears in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki as a guide deity (existing ID sarutahiko). The official site only says that a divided spirit of Inari-ōkami was invited from an imperial prayer shrine of the court; no description of a relationship with Fushimi Inari Taisha is confirmed.
history: The official site says that in 1687 (Jōkyō 4) Kazan'in Manko-hime, wife of Nabeshima Naotomo, lord of the Hizen Kashima domain, invited a divided spirit of Inari-ōkami from what had been an imperial prayer shrine of the court. A Saga Prefecture document also records the building of the shrine in the Jōkyō era (1684–1688).

According to the prefectural document, the present building of the Myōbu-sha is known from its ridge tag to have been built in 1804 (Kyōwa 4); when Yūtoku Inari Jinja was rebuilt in 1926 (Taishō 15), this building, the former main sanctuary, was moved to its present site.
The Myōbu-sha within the grounds was designated a Saga Prefecture Important Cultural Property (building) on 11 March 1977 (Shōwa 52).
highlights: The official site says the main sanctuary, kagura hall, Rōmon gate and other buildings are fully lacquered in rich colors, and that for their splendor the shrine is called the "Nikkō of Chinzei".
yutoku.address: Furueda, Kashima, Saga 849-1321 (as written in the official contact section; the office in the outer garden is listed as Furueda Otsu 1686). The street number of the main shrine is not confirmed on the official site.
yutoku.access: The official site says it is 30–40 minutes toward Kashima from Takeo-Kitagata IC or Ureshino IC on the Nagasaki Expressway, and about 10 minutes by taxi (or bus) from Hizen-Kashima Station on the JR Nagasaki Main Line.
yutoku.hours: Official inquiries are received 8:30–16:30, telephone reception for daily prayers is also 8:30–16:30, and the office in the outer garden is open 9:00–16:30 (open every day). Dedicated hours for the amulet office and visiting hours for the grounds are not confirmed on the official site. Checked 12 Oct 2026.
yutoku.parking: The official site lists the Outer Garden No. 1 lot: the first 30 minutes are free, then ¥300 for 24 hours after parking. Those receiving prayers get a parking service ticket at the shrine office. The number of spaces is not confirmed on the official site.
yutoku.goshuin: The official site describes the procedure: leave your goshuin book at the reception to the left of the shrine office at the back left of the grounds, worship, then collect it in exchange for a numbered tag. Goshuin books are available in navy and pink, and it takes time when crowded. Dedicated reception hours for goshuin are not confirmed on the official site.

kagoshimajingu.name: Kagoshima Jingū
kagoshimajingu.summary: Its main deities are Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto (Yamasachihiko), known from the Umisachi–Yamasachi myth, and Toyotama-hime-no-Mikoto. The official site describes it as a former Kanpei Taisha, a shrine listed in the Engishiki (shikinaisha), and Ichinomiya of Ōsumi Province. Its founding is said to date to the Age of the Gods or the reign of Emperor Jinmu, and the main sanctuary, worship hall, imperial envoy hall and other buildings are nationally designated Important Cultural Properties.
kagoshimajingu.deity_note: The official main deities are Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto (Yamasachihiko) and Toyotama-hime-no-Mikoto, with Tarashinakatsuhiko-no-Mikoto (Emperor Chūai), Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto (Empress Jingū), Homudawake-no-Mikoto (Emperor Ōjin, Hachiman Ōkami) and Nakatsuhime-no-Mikoto (empress of Emperor Ōjin) enshrined alongside. Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto is the Hoori-no-Mikoto of the Kojiki (also named Amatsuhiko-Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto) and the Hohodemi-no-Mikoto of the Nihon Shoki; his father is Ninigi-no-Mikoto (existing ID ninigi) and his wife is Toyotama-hime (existing ID toyotama). The official site says Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto set up the Takachiho Palace (his residence) at this place, but the Kojiki only writes "dwelt at the Takachiho Palace", and no passage in the texts of the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki identifies its location with the site of Kagoshima Jingū. As for the Hayato, the Kojiki notes that Hoderi-no-Mikoto was "the ancestor of the Hayato Ata no Kimi", and the Nihon Shoki records that the Hayato, descendants of the elder brother Hosuseri-no-Mikoto, served beside the palace fence of the emperor; but whether the official site links this to the place name Hayato Town or to the traditions of Ōsumi is not confirmed (to be confirmed). Nakatsuhime-no-Mikoto is recorded as a new deity.
history: The official site says the deity Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto set up the Takachiho Palace (his residence) at this place, and that the founding lies far back in the Age of the Gods, or by another tradition in the reign of Emperor Jinmu, the imperial grandson.
The official site says it was ranked a Taisha in the Engishiki of the Heian period and, as Ichinomiya of Ōsumi Province, drew the reverence of court and people alike.
According to the official site, it was ranked Kokuhei Chūsha in 1871 (Meiji 4), Kanpei Chūsha in Meiji 7 when the title Jingū was granted by imperial decree, and Kanpei Taisha in 1895 (Meiji 28).

The official site says the present buildings were built in 1756 (Hōreki 6) by the Shimazu lords of the Satsuma domain, and that the main sanctuary, worship hall, imperial envoy hall and the auxiliary Shisho Jinja are nationally designated Important Cultural Properties. Because the official pages differ on the name of the lord who built them ("Shigetoshi" and "Shigehide"), we write the Shimazu family here.
highlights: The official site says the Hatsuuma Festival is held on the first Sunday after the 18th day of the first month of the old calendar; its highlight is the "Suzukake-uma", horses hung with bells that visit the shrine with dance troupes, and about 100,000 people come each year.
The official site says the auxiliary Shakutai Jinja is worshipped as a deity of safe childbirth, and there is a custom of taking home a round stone from its grounds as an amulet.
The official site says the sacred horse Seiran was dedicated on 10 March 2018 (Heisei 30).
kagoshimajingu.address: 2496 Hayato-chō Uchi, Kirishima, Kagoshima 899-5116 (official top page and history page). The official FAQ writes 2496-1, so the sub-number is written inconsistently.
kagoshimajingu.access: The official site says it is a 15-minute walk from Hayato Station on the JR Nippō Main Line, or a 5-minute walk from the Kagoshima Kōtsū bus stop "Kagoshima Jingū-mae" (few services). By car, Hayato-Nishi IC and Hayato-Higashi IC on the Higashi-Kyūshū Expressway and Kūkō IC on the Kyūshū Expressway can be used, but the travel times do not agree between official pages (the transport guide and the FAQ differ).
kagoshimajingu.hours: The official top page gives visiting hours as 8:30–17:00, and the FAQ gives the shrine office and amulet office hours as 8:30–17:00. The FAQ also writes that worship in the grounds is from sunrise to sunset. Prayer reception is given as 8:30–16:30 (FAQ) and 9:00–16:30 (prayer guide), so the descriptions differ. Checked 12 Oct 2026.
kagoshimajingu.parking: Free parking for 200 cars in total across the approach, bus and large lots (official). Temporary parking may be provided during major festivals such as the Hatsuuma Festival.
kagoshimajingu.goshuin: Received at the shrine office. Reception hours are 8:30–17:00 (official FAQ). An original goshuin book is also available.

hayatani.name: Hayatani Jinja
hayatani.summary: It enshrines Akihayatamao-no-Mikoto, regarded as the founding ancestral deity of Aki. The official site describes it as an old shrine ranked Kanpei Taisha and Myōjin Taisha in the Engishiki, and now a Beppyō shrine of the Association of Shinto Shrines (Jinja Honchō). The date of its founding is not clear, but the official site states it is more than 1,800 years old. It is known as a shrine of traffic safety, with the saying "When you buy a car, go to Hayatani-san".
hayatani.deity_note: The official deity is a single one, Akihayatamao-no-Mikoto (Akihayatama-no-Mikoto); the official site says he was granted the post of Kuni no Miyatsuko of Aki in the time of Emperor Seimu and opened up the land, and is the founding ancestral deity of Aki. The name Akihayatama-no-Mikoto is not found in the Kojiki (Parts 1 and 2) or the Nihon Shoki (Books 1–5, 7, 9, 10 and 14) obtained (Part 3 of the Kojiki and the other books of the Nihon Shoki are not checked). The name appears in the Kokuzō Hongi in Book 10 of the Sendai Kuji Hongi, which records that in the reign at Shiga no Takaanaho, Akihayatama-no-Mikoto, a fifth-generation descendant of Ame-no-Yutsuhiko-no-Mikoto, was appointed Kuni no Miyatsuko of Aki. This is a book separate from the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki; in the Kojiki, the emperor who dwelt at the Shiga no Takaanaho Palace is Emperor Seimu. He is treated as a different deity from Hayatama-no-O-no-Kami of Kumano Hayatama Taisha (existing ID hayatamano).
history: According to the official site, Hayatani Jinja first appears in the official histories in 811 (Kōnin 2), under Emperor Saga, when the Nihon Kōki records that Hayatani-no-Kami and Itsukishima-no-Kami of Aki Province were ranked as Myōjin.

The official site says that in the Engishiki register of shrines, Hayatani Jinja, Itsukishima Jinja and Take Jinja of Aki Province are all Myōjin Taisha, and that only Hayatani Jinja is marked "Tsukinami, Niiname", which shows it was a Kanpei Taisha.

According to the official site, the shrine fell into ruin after the Fukushima family confiscated its lands; in 1646 (Shōhō 3) Asano Mitsuakira, who had become lord of the Hiroshima domain, confirmed its location and history, and two years later built the shrine buildings at the domain's expense.

The official site says the new shrine buildings were completed in October 1924 (Taishō 13), the shrine was ranked Kokuhei Chūsha in November, and after the war it became a Beppyō shrine belonging to the Association of Shinto Shrines (Jinja Honchō).
highlights: The official site says two items, a pair of wooden komainu (mid-Muromachi period) and one scroll of Sonkai documents (late Muromachi period), are designated Important Cultural Properties of Hiroshima Prefecture.

For traffic safety prayers, the official site says the driver receives a prayer in the shrine hall and each car is purified one by one at the car purification site in the grounds (offering ¥5,000 or more per car).
The official site says the four great pillars supporting the Rōmon gate were made by dividing a single giant cypress into four.
hayatani.address: 308-1 Kamihera, Hatsukaichi, Hiroshima 738-0026 (as written on the official site).
hayatani.access: The official site says it is 8 minutes by taxi from Miyauchi-Kushido Station or Hatsukaichi Station on the JR San'yō Line, a 1-minute walk from the "Hayatani Jinja" stop on the Hara route of the Hatsukaichi Sakura Bus, and by car just off the Miyajima SA Smart IC (ETC vehicles) on the San'yō Expressway.
hayatani.hours: The official site gives the shrine office hours as 8:00–17:00 and prayer hours as 8:00–17:00 (no reservation needed). Amulets are given at the amulet office from 8:00 until about 18:00 (FAQ). Checked 12 Oct 2026.
hayatani.parking: The number of parking spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official site.
hayatani.goshuin: Received at the prayer reception desk, by 17:00 (official FAQ). A Hayatani Jinja goshuin book is also available.

samukawa.name: Samukawa Jinja
samukawa.summary: Known as Ichinomiya of Sagami Province, it enshrines two deities, Samukawahiko-no-Mikoto and Samukawahime-no-Mikoto, as Samukawa Daimyōjin. The official site says it has been worshipped as the only guardian deity of happō-yoke (protection from misfortune from all directions) in Japan.
samukawa.deity_note: The word "Samukawa" does not appear in the Kojiki (Parts 1 and 2), the Nihon Shoki (Books 1–3 and 14) or the Kogo Shūi obtained, so the deities Samukawahiko-no-Mikoto and Samukawahime-no-Mikoto cannot be confirmed as deities recorded in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (Part 3 and the other books are not checked). The official site explains that the two are revered as Samukawa Daimyōjin, deities who opened up the Kantō region centered on Sagami Province and developed and taught the foundations of human life such as clothing, food and shelter, and that they have been honored as the parent deities of Kantō culture. No relation to the deities of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki is shown on the official site, and this note cannot confirm a connection to them.
history: The official site, after noting that the date of founding is not recorded in surviving materials, writes that there is a record saying offerings were presented in the reign of Emperor Yūryaku (456–479). The official site cites the "Sōkoku Fudoki" as its basis, but the title and content of this book are not confirmed in this note.
The official site says there is a record stating that the shrine buildings were built in 727 (Jinki 4), and explains that the shrine has at least about 1,600 years of history.

The official site writes that the first public record is in the Shoku Nihon Kōki, which says the shrine was granted the divine rank of Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade, in 846 (Jōwa 13). It then advanced to Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade, in 854 (Saikō 1), Senior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade, in 884 (Gangyō 8), and Senior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade, in 916 (Engi 16).
According to the official site, in the Engishiki register of shrines (compiled in 927) it is the only Myōjin Taisha among the thirteen shrines of Sagami Province.
highlights: The main prayer is happō-yoke (protection against directional misfortune); the official site says directional protection for travel, renovation, new construction, moving house and so on is also accepted.
Two cedars beside the main sanctuary are the sacred trees, and Samukawahiko-no-Mikoto and Samukawahime-no-Mikoto are said to dwell in them.
The shrine buildings, completed in October 1997 (Heisei 9), are built entirely of cypress. The worship hall has seating for 216 people to sit and worship at once.

The Kantakeyama Shin'en garden may be entered only by those who have received prayers. In the October notice it is closed on Mondays (open on Mondays that are national holidays), and kagura dances and gagaku are performed on the stone stage.
samukawa.access: According to the official site, the nearest station is Miyayama on the JR Sagami Line, a 5-minute walk (not Samukawa Station). By car, about 5 minutes from the Ken-Ō Expressway Samukawa-Kita Interchange to the shrine parking lot. By bus, about 20 minutes from Ebina Station East Exit stop 2 on the service bound for Samukawa Station, getting off at "Samukawa Jinja Sandō" and walking 5 minutes. Heavy crowds are expected on weekends and holidays, so visitors are urged to use public transport; waiting on the road to enter the lot and parking on nearby streets are prohibited. In July 2026 a tree fell on the approach, and the official site urges visitors to watch overhead and the surrounding trees.
samukawa.hours: Prayer reception is 8:00–17:00 (arrive by 17:00), open every day. The amulet office is open 8:00–16:30, every day. Both have different opening times during the New Year period. The official site does not give opening and closing times for the grounds themselves (not confirmed on the official site).
samukawa.parking: The official site says that in addition to lots No. 1 to No. 3 there is a No. 4 lot opened only at busy times, and all lots are entered by left turn only. The number of spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official site.
samukawa.goshuin: Given at two places, the shrine office and the prayer reception desk; the offering is at your discretion (no set amount). Both writing in your book and pre-written sheets are available, and goshuin books are sold at the shop in the grounds. At New Year only pre-written sheets are given, and the contents and place change. No postal service. Hours are not given under the goshuin heading and are not confirmed on the official site (the amulet office is open 8:00–16:30).

kanda.name: Kanda Jinja (Kanda Myōjin)
kanda.summary: Its formal name is Kanda Jinja. Familiarly known as the "guardian shrine of all Edo", it enshrines Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto as Ichinomiya, Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto as Ni-no-miya and Taira no Masakado-no-Mikoto as San-no-miya. The shrine buildings are a nationally Registered Tangible Cultural Property, and the shrine is known for the Kanda Festival held every two years.
kanda.deity_note: Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto corresponds to Ōnamuji-no-Kami (Ōkuninushi-no-Kami) of the Kojiki and is written Ōnamuchi-no-Kami in the Nihon Shoki. The official site also explains that he is the same deity as Ōkuninushi-no-Mikoto, the deity of Izumo Taisha. For Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto, the official site calls him "the child of Takamimusubi-no-Kami", but the Kojiki obtained writes "the child of Kamimusubi-no-Kami"; it is a variant account in the Nihon Shoki (Book 1) that makes him the child of Takamimusubi-no-Mikoto, so the sources differ. Taira no Masakado-no-Mikoto of the San-no-miya was a real person of the Heian period (the Masakado of the Jōhei–Tengyō rebellion) and does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki. The official site writes that he was enshrined in 1309 (Enkyō 2), moved temporarily to an auxiliary shrine in 1874 (Meiji 7), and enshrined again in the main sanctuary in 1984 (Shōwa 59). Therefore the deities who meet criterion 3 (deities of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki) are Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto and Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto; Masakado is a deity from a separate tradition.
history: Shrine tradition says it was founded in 730 (Tenpyō 2) by Makanda no Omi of the Izumo clan at Shibasaki Village, Toshima District, Musashi Province (around present-day Ōtemachi, Chiyoda Ward, and the Masakado-zuka mound).

Because natural disasters continued around the Masakado-zuka mound, the itinerant monk Shinkyō Shōnin is said to have appeased the spirit, and Taira no Masakado-no-Mikoto was enshrined at this shrine in 1309 (Enkyō 2).

In 1616 (Genna 2) the shrine was moved to its present site, which lies in the direction of the "front demon gate" (northeast) of Edo Castle, and the shogunate built the shrine buildings. The official site writes that from then on, throughout the Edo period, it was revered as the "guardian shrine of all Edo".

According to the official site, in the Meiji period the name was changed from Kanda Myōjin to Kanda Jinja, and it was designated a "Jun-Chokusai-sha" (quasi-imperial festival shrine) and a "Tokyo Prefectural Shrine". Whether it is a Chokusai-sha itself or a Beppyō shrine is not confirmed on the official site.
highlights: The shrine buildings, completed in 1934 (Shōwa 9), are in the gongen-zukuri style, built of steel-framed reinforced concrete and fully coated in vermilion lacquer. They were registered as a national Registered Tangible Cultural Property in September 2003 (Heisei 15). The official site writes that they withstood the Great Tokyo Air Raid of Shōwa 20.
The Kanda Festival is held once every two years; the official site explains that it is counted as one of the Three Great Festivals of Edo and of Japan.

The water basin in the grounds (dedicated in 1805, Bunka 2) is a Tangible Folk Cultural Property designated by Chiyoda Ward (designated in Heisei 14), and the chikara-ishi strength stone (1822, Bunsei 5) is also a ward-designated cultural property. The hōren and mikoshi palanquins in which Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto and Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto ride during the Kanda Festival are kept in the Hōren Mikoshi Hōanden hall.
kanda.access: According to the official site: a 5-minute walk from JR Ochanomizu Station (Hijiribashi Exit), a 7-minute walk from JR Akihabara Station (Electric Town Exit), a 5-minute walk from Ochanomizu and Shin-Ochanomizu Stations on the Tokyo Metro Marunouchi and Chiyoda Lines, a 5-minute walk from Suehirochō Station on the Ginza Line, and a 7-minute walk from Akihabara Station on the Hibiya Line. A 1-minute walk from the Kanda Myōjin stop of Toei bus route "Cha 51".
kanda.hours: Talismans and amulets are given 9:00–18:00 until 31 December 2026 (Reiwa 8). At the start of Reiwa 9 the hours change day by day (for example 0:00–21:40 on 1 January), and from 18 January they are 9:00–18:00 (official notice, 28 September, Reiwa 8). For formal worship in the hall (prayers), individuals go on the day to the worship reception in the Cultural Exchange Hall (no reservation; received at any time, with groups led in roughly every 20 minutes). The reception hours and the opening and closing times of the grounds are not confirmed on the official site.
kanda.parking: The official site says "visitor parking: a small number of spaces", entered by passing through the torii at the front of the shrine and the side gate to the right of the Zuishin-mon gate, then parking in the visitor lot on the north side. The number is given only as "a small number", and fees are not confirmed on the official site. Nearby lots such as Akihabara UDX Parking (800 spaces) are said to be about a 5-minute walk away.
kanda.goshuin: An official notice, in a note to the New Year hours table, says "from 12 January the goshuin will include the date", which confirms that goshuin are given. However, a dedicated goshuin page, the offering and the place are not confirmed on the official site. The hours can be read as included in the same 9:00–18:00 table as talismans and amulets (until the end of Reiwa 8), but they are not stated explicitly as goshuin hours.

suwashimosha.name: Suwa Taisha Shimosha (Harumiya and Akimiya)
suwashimosha.summary: The Shimosha (Lower Shrine) of Suwa Taisha, Ichinomiya of Shinano Province, consisting of two shrines, Harumiya and Akimiya. The official site gives the deities of both as Takeminakata-no-Kami, Yasakatome-no-Kami and Yaekotoshironushi-no-Kami, and explains that the sacred object is a cedar at Harumiya and a yew at Akimiya.
suwashimosha.deity_note: The official site gives the deities of the Shimosha Harumiya and Akimiya as Takeminakata-no-Kami, Yasakatome-no-Kami and Yaekotoshironushi-no-Kami (the Kamisha Honmiya enshrines Takeminakata-no-Kami and the Maemiya Yasakatome-no-Kami). Takeminakata-no-Kami appears in the transfer of the land in the Kojiki: pursued by Takemikazuchi-no-Kami, he reaches the sea of Suwa in Shinano Province and swears, "I will go nowhere but this land". The official site treats this as the origin of the deity who moved to Suwa and ruled Shinano Province. The name Takeminakata-no-Kami is not confirmed in the Nihon Shoki (Books 1–5, 7–10 and 14 obtained). Yaekotoshironushi-no-Kami corresponds to the written form of Kotoshironushi-no-Kami, who is summoned by Ame-no-Torifune-no-Kami and answers in the transfer of the land in the Kojiki. Yasakatome-no-Kami does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki; she is a deity of Suwa tradition whom the official site calls his consort.
history: The official site writes that the founding goes back to the myth of the transfer of the land in the Kojiki, and that Takeminakata-no-Kami, who opposed the transfer, is said to have moved from Izumo to Suwa. The date of enshrinement is not known in detail, but it is said, judging from the Kojiki and other sources, to be at least 1,500–2,000 years ago.

The official site writes that in the 5th year of Empress Jitō (691) an imperial envoy was sent and prayers were offered for the peace of the nation and abundant harvests. Checking the corresponding passage in the Nihon Shoki has not been done in this note.

According to the official site, the Engishiki register of shrines records it as Minakatatomi Jinja, listed first among the forty-eight seats of Shinano Province. This is an explanation of Suwa Taisha as a whole, including the Kamisha and Shimosha; whether the entry refers to the Shimosha alone is not shown on the official site.

According to the official site, it became Kokuhei Chūsha in 1871 (Meiji 4), Kanpei Chūsha in Meiji 29 and Kanpei Taisha in Taishō 5, and after the shrine ranking system was abolished in Shōwa 23 it was renamed Suwa Taisha as the head shrine.
highlights: At Akimiya, the heihaiden offering and worship hall with its left and right side halls (1781, An'ei 10) and the kagura hall (1835, Tenpō 6) are national Important Cultural Properties. The official site writes that they were the work of the first and second Tatekawa Washirō.
The heihaiden and left and right side halls of Harumiya are also Important Cultural Properties; it is said the same drawings as for Akimiya were given, and the carvers competed in their craft.

Suwa Taisha has no main sanctuary; at the Shimosha, the sacred object is a cedar at Harumiya and a yew at Akimiya. The Shikinen Zōei Onbashira Taisai is held every seven years, in the years of the Tiger and the Monkey, and is the greatest rite, served by 200,000 parishioners of the Suwa region.
The water pavilion in the grounds of Akimiya has the "Goshin'yu", where natural hot spring water of Shimosuwa flows.
suwashimosha.address: Shimosha Akimiya: 5828 Shimosuwa, Suwa District, Nagano (tel. 0266-27-8035) / Shimosha Harumiya: 193 Shimosuwa, Suwa District, Nagano (tel. 0266-27-8316) (official; postal codes are not confirmed on the official site)
suwashimosha.access: According to the official site, Harumiya is about 1 km northwest of Shimo-Suwa Station on the JR Chūō Main Line, and about 1 km west of Akimiya. Akimiya stands at the fork of the old Nakasendō and the Kōshū Dōchū roads. The distance and walking time from the station to Akimiya, and where to park when coming by bus or car, are not confirmed on the official site. By car, Okaya IC or Suwa IC on the Chūō Expressway is given.
suwashimosha.hours: According to the official site, none of the shrines close their gates, and they can be visited freely. The amulet office is open 8:30–17:00 at Akimiya and 8:30–16:30 at Harumiya, and the treasure hall (Akimiya) 9:30–15:00 (closed 1–3 January at Akimiya). For prayers, individuals need no reservation and apply at the reception window on the day between 9:00 and 16:00 (reception is listed for Honmiya and Akimiya). Groups are by reservation. Prayer reception at Harumiya is not confirmed on the official site.
suwashimosha.parking: The number of spaces, fees and hours of the Shimosha parking lots are not confirmed on the official site.
suwashimosha.goshuin: The official FAQ says each of the four shrines has its own goshuin, all different (those who receive the goshuin of all four are given a commemorative gift). Reception hours, offering and place for goshuin are not individually confirmed on the official site (the amulet office is open 8:30–17:00 at Akimiya and 8:30–16:30 at Harumiya).

minashijinja.name: Minashi Jinja
minashijinja.summary: Formally "Hida Ichinomiya Minashi Jinja". The Ichinomiya of Hida Province; the official site describes it as the head of the shrines listed in the Engishiki (shikinaisha), a Kokuhei Shōsha in the Meiji period, and after the war a Beppyō shrine of the Association of Shinto Shrines (Jinja Honchō). Its sacred mountain is Mt. Kurai, the source of the Miya and Hida rivers, and it enshrines Minashi-no-Ōkami, the "master of water".
minashijinja.deity_note: The official site gives the main deity as Mitoshi-no-Ōkami (other names: Mitoshi-no-Ōkami and Toshigami, each also written with different characters) and lists alongside him Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto, Emperor Jinmu, Emperor Ōjin, Ame-no-Hoakari-no-Mikoto, Mihotsu-hime-no-Mikoto, Takateruhime-no-Mikoto, Takaorihime-no-Mikoto, Sunumahime-no-Mikoto, Ōtoshi-no-Ōkami, Amaterasu-sume-Ōkami, Toyouke-hime-no-Ōkami, Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto, Ame-no-Kumaushi-no-Mikoto and Ōyahashi-no-Mikoto. It also says the shrine enshrines the deities of all Hida Province. The official site writes that there are two views of Minashi-no-Ōkami: that it refers to Mitoshi-no-Ōkami, and that it is a collective name for the fifteen deities, main and alongside, together. Minashi-no-Ōkami (Minashi-no-Kami, Minushi-no-Kami, Sakugami-sama) is a deity whose name does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki, and a search of the texts obtained does not find the word "Minashi". The official site does not state whether Mitoshi-no-Ōkami is the same deity as "Mitoshi-no-Kami", the child of Ōtoshi-no-Kami in the Kojiki (to be confirmed). Of the deities enshrined alongside, Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto is the Ōkuninushi-no-Kami of the Kojiki, and Mihotsu-hime-no-Mikoto, Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto, Amaterasu-sume-Ōkami, Toyouke-hime-no-Ōkami, Emperor Jinmu and Emperor Ōjin are also deities and emperors who appear in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, so existing IDs were used. No deity data has been made this time for Ame-no-Hoakari-no-Mikoto, Takateruhime-no-Mikoto, Takaorihime-no-Mikoto, Sunumahime-no-Mikoto, Ame-no-Kumaushi-no-Mikoto or Ōyahashi-no-Mikoto.
history: The official site writes that the founding is said to date to the Age of the Gods, but old records have been scattered and lost, so details are unknown.

It appears in history in the early Heian period; the first record is the granting of the divine rank of Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade, in 867 (Jōgan 9). The official site writes that in 881 (Gangyō 5) it advanced to Junior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade.

The official site writes that Kanamori Nagachika, having become lord of the Takayama domain, carried out the building of the shrine in 1607 (Keichō 12), and that during the Edo period it received the reverence of successive lords and magistrates.
The official site writes that it was ranked Kokuhei Shōsha in 1871 (Meiji 4), and after the war it joined the Association of Shinto Shrines (Jinja Honchō) and became a Beppyō shrine.
highlights: The official site says there is an old precedent of presenting to the court a shaku scepter made from the yew (ichii) of Mt. Kurai, the inner shrine, and that one is still presented at the enthronement of an emperor and at the Shikinen Sengū of Ise Jingū.

The official site introduces the great cedar in the grounds, about 800 years old and a prefectural Natural Monument. The grounds also have a sacred horse stable (the "rice-eating horses", two wooden horses) and an ema hall (its ridge tag is dated Keichō 12).
minashijinja.access: The official guidance is to take a local train from JR Takayama Station to JR Hida-Ichinomiya Station (limited express trains do not stop at Hida-Ichinomiya, and local trains are few, so the official site advises checking the timetable), or the Nōhi Bus from JR Takayama Station to the Hida-Ichinomiya bus stop (the official site gives the one-way fare from Takayama Station as ¥250). The walking time from the station or bus stop to the shrine is not confirmed on the relevant official page. The official site writes that in winter car navigation may direct you onto Prefectural Route 98 (Miya-Hagiwara Line), which is closed in winter, and that care is needed for snow and ice at the Miya Pass on National Route 41.
minashijinja.hours: The official top page gives reception for talismans, amulets, goshuin and so on as 8:30–16:30, and prayer reception as 9:00–16:00 (0:00–16:00 on 1 January only). No reservation is needed for individual prayers, but the official site writes that there are times when prayers cannot be held because of festivals, weddings and so on, so please contact the shrine. The opening and closing times of the grounds themselves are not confirmed on the official site (the parking guide says "24 hours" and "grounds open freely").
minashijinja.parking: The official site says parking is free, 100 spaces, available 24 hours. Parking for anything other than worship is not allowed.
minashijinja.goshuin: The official top page says goshuin can be received at the same reception as talismans and amulets (8:30–16:30). The types of goshuin, the offering, and whether they are pre-written sheets or written directly in your book are not confirmed on the official pages obtained.

ooyamato.name: Ōyamato Jinja
ooyamato.summary: An old shrine of Yamato Province standing west of the Yamanobe-no-Michi road. It enshrines Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Ōkami, Yachihoko-no-Ōkami and Mitoshi-no-Ōkami. The official chronology says it is a Myōjin Taisha listed in the Engishiki (shikinaisha), heading the entries for Yamabe District of Yamato Province in the Engishiki register of shrines, and that it became a Kanpei Taisha in Meiji 5.
ooyamato.deity_note: The official deities are Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Ōkami (center), Yachihoko-no-Ōkami (right, facing the shrine) and Mitoshi-no-Ōkami (left, facing the shrine). Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Ōkami is the land deity of Yamato, whom the official site explains as "Ōtokonushi-no-Ōkami" (the great landowner deity). The Nihon Shoki, Book 5 (6th year of Emperor Sujin), says that the two deities Amaterasu-Ōmikami and Yamato-Ōkunitama were enshrined side by side within the emperor's great hall, but in awe of their divine power he moved Amaterasu-Ōmikami to Kasanui Village in Yamato and entrusted Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Kami to Nunakiirihime-no-Mikoto to worship. The founding the official site describes corresponds to this passage (the official site writes "is said to"). Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Kami does not appear in the Kojiki. The "Ōkunimitama-no-Kami" of the Kojiki, Part 1, is a child of Ōtoshi-no-Kami and a different deity. Whether "Ōkunitama-no-Kami" (existing ID okunitama), which a variant account in the Nihon Shoki gives as another name of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, is the same deity as the Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Kami of the Sujin chronicle cannot be determined from the texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (the Kogo Shūi lists Ōkunitama-no-Kami as one name of Ōnamuchi-no-Kami and notes "the present Ōmiwa-no-Kami of Shikinokami District, Yamato Province"). Yachihoko-no-Ōkami corresponds to Yachihoko-no-Kami (written in two ways), which the Kojiki and a variant account in the Nihon Shoki give as another name of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, so the existing ID ookuninushi is used; but whether this shrine's official site states this identification is not confirmed (to be confirmed).
