Mitoshi-no-Ōkami is generally held to be the same deity as Mitoshi-no-Kami, the child of Ōtoshi-no-Kami in the Kojiki (the collated text reads "Toshimi-no-Kami"), but whether the official site states this is not confirmed (to be confirmed).
history: The official site writes that in the 6th year of Emperor Sujin, the tenth emperor, when the emperor in awe of the divine power moved Amaterasu-Ōmikami to Kasanui Village in Yamato, he entrusted Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Ōkami to Nunakiirihime-no-Mikoto and moved the deity to Ichishi Village (Ōyamato-gō), and this is said to be the founding of the shrine (more than 2,000 years ago).

The Engishiki register of shrines, which the official chronology places under 905 (Engi 5), records "Ōyamato-ni-imasu Ōkunitama Jinja, three seats" at the head of Yamabe District, Yamato Province; the official chronology writes that as a Myōjin Taisha listed in the Engishiki it received imperial offerings at the Kinensai, Tsukinamisai, Niinamesai and other festivals.
The official chronology records that it became a Kanpei Taisha in 1872 (Meiji 5), and the building of new shrine buildings was completed in May of the following year.

The official site writes that it is regarded as the guardian deity of the battleship Yamato, and that the 2,736 souls, including the commander of the Second Fleet, who went down in the Okinawa special attack mission of 7 April 1945 (Shōwa 20), are enshrined together in the Soreisha ancestral shrine in the grounds.
highlights: The "Chan-chan Matsuri" on 1 April is the annual festival and procession festival of Yamato-Ōkunitama-no-Ōkami, in which more than two hundred parishioners, including the tōya households and children, go to and from the otabisho resting place about 2 km away. The official site writes that its designation as a Nara Prefecture Intangible Folk Cultural Property was decided by the Nara Prefectural Board of Education on 17 January 2018 (Heisei 30).
The official top page says a Man'yōshū poem monument, the "Kōkyo Kōrai" poem stone, was erected on 5 August 2015 (Heisei 27).
ooyamato.access: The official site says: from Kintetsu Tenri Station, about 10 minutes by Nara Kōtsū bus (bound for Sakurai Station) to "Ōyamato Jinja-mae", then a 5-minute walk. About a 7-minute walk from Nagara Station on the JR Man'yō Mahoroba Line. By car, about 15 minutes from Tenri IC on the Nishi-Meihan Expressway.
ooyamato.hours: The official site writes that prayer reception is 9:00–16:00 (prayers cannot be held during festivals and the like, so please inquire in advance). Telephone and fax are answered 9:00–16:00. The hours of the amulet office and the opening and closing of the grounds are not confirmed on the official pages obtained.
ooyamato.parking: The official site says there is a parking lot immediately to the left after passing through the Ichi-no-Torii, and tour buses can also park. The number of spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official site. On the day of the Chan-chan Matsuri parking is limited, so the official site urges the use of public transport.
ooyamato.goshuin: The official Q&A writes that goshuin are received at the "amulet office" where talismans and amulets are given. The types, offering and amulet office hours are not confirmed on the official pages obtained.

tsurugijinja.name: Tsurugi Jinja
tsurugijinja.summary: An old shrine in Ota, Echizen Town, Fukui, which the official site describes as "Ninomiya of Echizen Province". It enshrines Susanoo-no-Ōkami, Kehi-no-Ōkami and Prince Oshikuma (Oshikuma-no-Ō); tradition says the ancestors of Oda Nobunaga served as its priests and Nobunaga revered it as his clan deity. Its temple bell, with an inscription from the Nara period, is a National Treasure.
tsurugijinja.deity_note: The official deities are Susanoo-no-Ōkami, Kehi-no-Ōkami and Prince Oshikuma (Oshikuma-no-Ō). Susanoo-no-Ōkami is a deity of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki; the official site writes that the founding was the enshrinement of Susanoo-no-Ōkami on the peak of Zagatake to the north under the name "Tsurugi-no-Ōkami". This story of "Tsurugi-no-Ōkami" is shrine tradition and is not in the texts of the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki. Kehi-no-Ōkami appears by name in the Kojiki, Part 2, as Izasawake-no-Ōkami (later Kehi-no-Ōkami), and the existing ID izasawake was used. How Kehi-no-Ōkami came to be enshrined at this shrine is not confirmed on the official pages obtained (to be confirmed). The official site explains Prince Oshikuma as the second son of Emperor Chūai, and says the shrine records tell that he built the shrine in gratitude for having governed this region through the divine power of Tsurugi-no-Ōkami. The Prince Oshikuma of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki is a prince who is defeated by Empress Jingū's army and drowns himself at Ōmi (Seta); the story of his pacifying Koshi is not in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki (a separate tradition). The connection with Oda Nobunaga (that Nobunaga revered the shrine as his clan deity and his ancestors were its priests) is a matter of history and not in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki.
history: The official site writes that the shrine records tell that around the time of Empress Jingū's regency, Prince Oshikuma, second son of Emperor Chūai, in gratitude for having been able to govern this region by the divine power of Tsurugi-no-Ōkami, built a shrine on the present site and revered the deity as "Tsurugi Daimyōjin".

The temple bell in the shrine's collection bears an inscription dated 770 (Jingo-keiun 4) and is a National Treasure (designated in Meiji 35). The official site writes that it is the third oldest surviving inscribed bell in Japan. It is said to have been dedicated by Emperor Kōnin. It is currently on deposit at the Echizen Town Ota Culture and History Museum.

The official site writes that Tsunemasa, son of a priest, had his talent recognized by the Shiba family, shugo of Echizen, in the Ōei era (1394–1427), was sent to Owari, and took the name Oda from his home place; it explains that the Oda family was of the line of this shrine's priests. Scholarly assessments may vary (to be confirmed).

The official site explains that a 1575 (Tenshō 3) exemption document from Shibata Katsuie states "this shrine is the lord's clan deity", which shows that Nobunaga revered it as his clan deity. After the Honnōji Incident of 1582 (Tenshō 10), the people of Oda enshrined Nobunaga's spirit together at Komatsu Takeisao Jinja in the grounds.
highlights: From the official cultural properties page it can be read that the National Treasure bell (Nara period) is currently on deposit at the Ota Culture and History Museum and cannot be seen in the shrine grounds. The Kamakura-period "Shaka Hassō Nehan-zu" (painting of the eight phases and nirvana of Shakyamuni) and "Nehan Kōshiki Dankan" (fragment of a nirvana liturgy) are Important Cultural Properties (designated in Shōwa 25), on deposit at the Nara National Museum.

The official site explains that the shrine crest is the Oda mokkō crest (five-mokkō crest), the same as the family crest of the Oda clan. The shrine also holds a confirmation letter from Oda Nobunaga (1573, Tenshō 1), but it is on deposit at the Ota Culture and History Museum.
tsurugijinja.address: 113-1 Ota (Kin'eizan), Echizen, Nyū District, Fukui 916-0215 (tel. 0778-36-0404, fax 0778-36-0902).
tsurugijinja.access: The official site says by car it is about 40 minutes from Fukui IC and about 20 minutes from Takefu or Sabae IC. By JR, from Takefu Station on the Hokuriku Main Line, about 35 minutes by bus via Ota toward the Echizen coast.
tsurugijinja.hours: Prayers are received every day without reservation: the morning session is 9:00–12:00 (last reception 11:50) and the afternoon session 13:00–16:00 (last reception 15:50). The official site writes that as a rule they are held twice an hour, on the hour and at 30 minutes past. The official site cautions that prayers may not be available because of festivals, events, weddings and so on, so please inquire about availability. At New Year: 0:00–17:00 on 1 January, 8:30–17:00 on 2 and 3 January, and 9:00–16:00 from 4 January (official notice dated 24 December 2025). The hours of the amulet office and shrine office and the opening and closing times of the grounds are not confirmed on the official pages obtained.
tsurugijinja.parking: The official site asks visitors to use the large parking lot of the Ota Culture and History Museum, and those receiving prayers to park in the shrine grounds. The number of spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official site.
tsurugijinja.goshuin: The official grounds map says the shrine office handles prayer reception, the giving of talismans and amulets, and goshuin reception. The types of goshuin, offering and reception hours are not confirmed on the official pages obtained.

hiraoka.name: Hiraoka Jinja
hiraoka.summary: Ichinomiya of Kawachi Province. Four deities — Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto, Himegami (the Princess Deity), Takemikazuchi-no-Ōkami and Futsunushi-no-Ōkami — are enshrined in the First to Fourth Sanctuaries. It is also called "Moto-Kasuga" (the original Kasuga) as the source of Kasuga Taisha in Nara (official). The official site explains that it is a Myōjin Taisha of the Engishiki and a former Kanpei Taisha.
hiraoka.deity_note: Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto is a deity whom the official site explains is described in the Age of the Gods volume of the Nihon Shoki as the "senior ancestor of the Nakatomi"; we also confirmed the wording "Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto, distant ancestor of the Nakatomi no Muraji" in the text of the Nihon Shoki at hand. The Kojiki notes him as an ancestor of the Nakatomi no Muraji and others (see the existing entry for Ame-no-Koyane). Himegami (the Princess Deity) is a deity whom the official site calls Ame-no-Mitsutamateruhime-no-Mikoto as well, while saying "there are various theories and the details are unclear", and regards as the consort of Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto; she does not appear as a specific deity in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki. Because the official site says that the two deities were enshrined at Kasuga Shrine (the present Kasuga Taisha) in 768 (Jingo-keiun 2), the existing entry for Himegami (himegami) is reused here as the same deity as the Himegami of the Fourth Sanctuary of Kasuga Taisha; however, the official site does not state that they are identical. The official site explains Takemikazuchi-no-Ōkami as the deity of Kashima Jingū and Futsunushi-no-Ōkami as the deity of Katori Jingū, both sent for the transfer of the land (Futsunushi appears in the Nihon Shoki but is not found in the Kojiki). Emperor Jinmu's eastern expedition and the founding by Ame-no-Taneko-no-Mikoto are Hiraoka Jinja's own tradition, and no account of Hiraoka's founding is confirmed in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki. In addition, Nihon Shoki Book 3 has a passage that calls Ame-no-Taneko-no-Mikoto the "distant ancestor of the Nakatomi clan", and the battle with Nagasunehiko during Jinmu's eastern expedition also appears in the same book.
history: The official site records a tradition that the shrine was founded three years before Emperor Jinmu took the throne in Yamato. During Jinmu's eastern expedition, Ame-no-Taneko-no-Mikoto, acting on an imperial command, prayed for the pacification of the land, and is said to have enshrined the two deities Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto and Himegami (the Princess Deity) at the sacred site Kamitsudake; this is regarded as the beginning.

The official site records a tradition that the shrine, which had been enshrined at Kamitsudake, was moved to the present site at the foot of the mountain by Hiraoka no Muraji and others in 650 (Hakuchi 1), in the reign of Emperor Kōtoku, on the 16th day of the 9th month.

The official site records that in 768 (Jingo-keiun 2) the two deities Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto and Himegami (the Princess Deity) appeared on the peak of the Kasugayama Hongū and were enshrined at Kasuga Shrine (the present Kasuga Taisha), and that this is why this shrine is called "Moto-Kasuga". In 778 (Hōki 9), it says, Takemikazuchi-no-Ōkami and Iwainushi-no-Mikoto (Futsunushi-no-Ōkami) were welcomed from Kasuga Shrine and enshrined alongside, making four sanctuaries.

The official site records that in 856 (Jōgan 1) Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto received the divine rank of Shō-ichi-i (Senior First Rank) and that the shrine was ranked as a Myōjin Taisha in the Engishiki register of shrines. It says that in the medieval period it was revered as Ichinomiya of Kawachi Province, and that on the 14th day of the 5th month of 1871 (Meiji 4) it was ranked as a Kanpei Taisha (the official site's own description; checking against a third party such as the prefectural shrine association (Jinjachō) is not yet done).
highlights: The official site records that the present main sanctuary was built in 1826 (Bunsei 9) with offerings from parishioners of the neighboring districts, and was renewed in the Great Heisei-Reiwa Reconstruction, completed in September 2020 (Reiwa 2). The four sanctuaries, the First to the Fourth, stand side by side.

The official site records that the shrine grove was chosen in 2001 (Heisei 13) as one of the "100 Scented Landscapes of Japan" by the Environment Agency (as it was then). The plum grove along the approach was entirely cut down in 2016 (Heisei 28) because of plum pox virus, but the site explains that it came back in 2021 (Reiwa 3) as a new plum grove where flowers of the four seasons can be enjoyed.

The autumn harvest thanksgiving festival, the "Shūgōsai", has had different dates since fiscal 2024 (Reiwa 6): the Saturday two days before Sports Day and the Sunday the day before are the pre-festival (zensai), and 15 October is the Shūgōsai (official top page). In 2026 the pre-festival is on 10 and 11 October, and the parking lot cannot be used all day from 6 to 12 October.
hiraoka.access: Right next to Hiraoka Station on the Kintetsu Nara Line (only local trains stop; at some times of day section semi-express trains also stop). About 30 minutes from Osaka Namba (official). By car, about 10 minutes from the Mizuhaya exit (toward Nara) of the Hanshin Expressway Route 13 Higashiōsaka Line (official).
hiraoka.hours: [Items confirmed on the official site] Prayer reception is from 9:00 to 15:30. No reservation is needed and requests are taken at any time (official "Prayers" page; there are times of waiting during events). Offering fees: ¥10,000 for the first shrine visit of a newborn (hatsumiyamairi) and for safe-childbirth prayers; ¥6,000 per person for Shichi-Go-San; ¥8,000 for others such as yakuyoke (warding off misfortune) and car purification; from ¥30,000 for groups. The shrine office reception hours are 9:00–16:00 (official "Guide to the grounds", in the section on how to use the misogi place). [Items not confirmed on the official site] The opening hours of the amulet office (where ofuda, omamori and so on are given; the official site records that the office exists). The opening and closing times of the grounds.
hiraoka.parking: The official site says there is a Times parking lot of about 40 spaces (fees and opening hours are not confirmed on the official site). Those receiving a prayer should tell the staff at the prayer reception that they have parked. The parking lot cannot be used from 6 October through the whole of 12 October 2026 (because of the pre-festival of the Shūgōsai).
hiraoka.goshuin: The announcements on the official top page give guidance on goshuin from 10 to 12 October 2026 (on the 10th and 11th only limited-edition goshuin; on the 12th only pre-written goshuin; from the 13th, written directly in the goshuin book). Regular reception hours and the offering fee are not confirmed on the official site.

taiheizanmiyoshi.name: Taiheizan Miyoshi Jinja
taiheizanmiyoshi.summary: Consisting of the Satomiya (village shrine) at Hiroomote in Akita City and the Okumiya (inner shrine) at the summit of the sacred Mt. Taihei (1,170 m), it is the head shrine of the Miyoshi shrines and the Taiheizan confraternities (Taiheizan-kō) across Japan. It enshrines Ōnamuchi-no-Ōkami, Sukunahikona-no-Ōkami and Miyoshi Reishin, regarded as a guardian deity born in Akita. The Akita prefectural shrine association (Jinjachō) records it as a prefectural shrine (kensha) from 1879 (Meiji 12) and as a Beppyō shrine.
taiheizanmiyoshi.deity_note: Ōnamuchi-no-Ōkami (also called Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami and Daikoku-sama) corresponds to Ōkuninushi-no-Kami (Ōanamuji-no-Kami) in the Kojiki and Ōnamuchi-no-Kami in the Nihon Shoki (see the existing entry for Ōkuninushi). Sukunahikona-no-Ōkami corresponds to Sukunabikona-no-Kami in the Kojiki and Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto in the Nihon Shoki; in both works he is told of as the deity who joined forces with Ōkuninushi to make and firm up the land. Miyoshi Reishin is a deity whom the official site explains as "a guardian deity born in Akita" and "a deity of strength and of winning contests". The tradition is that Fujiwara no Tsurujumaru Miyoshi, lord of the castle at Taihei, gave up the world and shut himself away on Mt. Taihei, trained in the faith of Ōnamuchi-no-Ōkami and Sukunahikona-no-Kami, and was enshrined as a deity: a local deity. He does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki; he is a deity of Akita tradition.
history: The official site records a tradition that En no Gyōja Ozunu founded the shrine in the 5th month of 673 (Hakuhō 2), in the reign of Emperor Tenmu. The text of the Akita prefectural shrine association (Jinjachō) on the same history writes "the 2nd year of Hakuhō (646 in the Western calendar)", so the Western-calendar years disagree. Here we follow the wording of the official site.

The official site records that in 801 (Enryaku 20), in the reign of Emperor Kanmu, the Seii Taishōgun Sakanoue no Tamuramaro prayed for victory during his campaign against the eastern Emishi and built a hall, and that the whistling arrows (kaburaya) dedicated then are handed down to this day as sacred treasures.

The official site records that Lord Satake, the lord of the Akita domain, grateful for the divine favor in the Boshin War of the first year of Meiji (1868), dedicated as a thanks-offering the site of the Yukimi Goten (a lodge from which Mt. Taihei was worshipped from afar), which is the site of the present Satomiya.

The shrine search of the Akita prefectural shrine association (Jinjachō) records it as a prefectural shrine (kensha) and a Beppyō shrine in 1879 (Meiji 12) (the history on the official site gives no shrine rank).
highlights: The Miyoshi Bonten Festival on 17 January each year is a special rite unique to Akita Prefecture that began around the Edo period (the year it began is unknown); a yorishiro (an object a deity enters) called a bonten is dedicated to the shrine (official).

The buildings of the Satomiya were completed in 1977 (Shōwa 52); the roof is in a modified nagare-zukuri style modeled on the shape of Mt. Taihei. A prayer hall, amulet office, shrine office and others are attached (official).

The Okumiya stands at the summit of Mt. Taihei (1,170 m) and is open only in summer (June to September). At the Mountain-Opening Festival on 17 July the sacred object (goshintai) is moved from the Satomiya to the Okumiya, and priests stay there to perform festivals and prayers until the Mountain-Closing Festival on 17 September (official).
taiheizanmiyoshi.address: 3-2 Akanuma, Hiroomote, Akita, Akita 010-0041 (Satomiya). Tel. 018-834-3443. The Okumiya is at the summit of Mt. Taihei, Akita City (the Akita prefectural shrine association (Jinjachō) gives "21 Aza-Taniyama (谷山), Taiheizandani, Akita City" (reading of the place name to be confirmed)).
taiheizanmiyoshi.access: About 6 minutes by taxi from the east exit of Akita Station (tell the driver "to the Miyoshi Jinja at Akanuma"). From the front (west) exit of Akita Station, about 10 minutes by a bus bound for "Taihei" (Akita Chūō Kōtsū); get off at "Miyoshi Jinja Iriguchi" and walk 2 minutes. By car, about 8 minutes from Akita Chūō IC on the Akita Expressway (official).
taiheizanmiyoshi.hours: [Items confirmed on the official site] Prayer reception is from 8:30 in the morning to 5:00 in the evening (served at any time; no days off). Prayers start at 9:00, 9:40, 10:20, 11:00, 11:40, 12:20, (13:20 or 13:30), 14:00, 14:40, 15:20, with 16:00 the last; go to the reception on the left as you face the main hall by 10 minutes before. No reservation is needed for individuals; reservations are taken for companies and large groups. The official top page says "13:20 after 12:20" and the prayer page says "13:30", so the times written conflict (we do not decide either). The prayer page says "basically every 40 minutes" and the top page says "roughly every 30 minutes on busy days". The news page and the yakudoshi (unlucky age) page say "prayers start from 9:00 to 16:00". The official site says the Satomiya is open all year without days off. [Items not confirmed on the official site] The hours of the amulet office (ofuda and omamori). The opening and closing times of the grounds.
taiheizanmiyoshi.parking: There are two parking lots. The east side (Hiroomote Kodōri) has the large lot, and there is also a lot on the main approach side (official). The number of spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official site.
taiheizanmiyoshi.goshuin: No guidance on goshuin could be found on the official site (top page, shrine introduction, various prayers, amulets, FAQ, and shrine bulletin No. 192). Whether goshuin are given, the reception hours and the offering fee are not confirmed on the official site (for inquiries, the telephone number given on the official site, 018-834-3443).

hinomisaki.name: Hinomisaki Jinja
hinomisaki.summary: It stands at Hinomisaki, Taisha-chō, Izumo City, at the westernmost tip of the Shimane Peninsula. It consists of two shrines: the Lower Shrine, "Hishizumi-no-Miya", which enshrines Amaterasu-Ōmikami, and the Upper Shrine, "Kami-no-Miya", which enshrines Susanoo-no-Mikoto. The 14 buildings and two torii in the precinct are Important Cultural Properties of Japan (official).
hinomisaki.deity_note: The official site explains that Susanoo-no-Mikoto is enshrined at the Kami-no-Miya and Amaterasu-Ōmikami at the Hishizumi-no-Miya. In the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, Amaterasu-Ōmikami and Susanoo-no-Mikoto are two of the three noble children born from the misogi of Izanagi-no-Mikoto (Kojiki, Part 1, commonly called "Misogi-harae"); see the existing entries. The feature of Hinomisaki Jinja is that these two deities are enshrined separately in an upper and a lower shrine. According to the shrine tradition, in the Age of the Gods, when Ame-no-Fukine-no-Mikoto was at Kiyoe Beach, Amaterasu-Ōmikami descended and gave the divine command "I am the deity of the sun", and enshrining her on Fumishima is said to be the beginning of the Hishizumi-no-Miya. Also, after building the land of Izumo, Susanoo-no-Mikoto divined with kashiwa (oak) leaves at Kumanari-no-Mine to find a place to settle, and at Kakurega-oka, where a leaf came to rest, his child Ame-no-Fukine-no-Mikoto built a shrine building and enshrined him; this is said to be the beginning of the Kami-no-Miya. These are shrine traditions; the place name and shrine name Hinomisaki and the founding of the Hishizumi-no-Miya do not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki. The name of Ame-no-Fukine-no-Mikoto could not be confirmed in the text of Kojiki Parts 1 and 2 and the Nihon Shoki at hand (to be confirmed).
history: The official site records, as the shrine tradition, that the Kami-no-Miya had been enshrined at Kakurega-oka (the hill behind the present shrine building) and was moved to the present site in the 13th year of Emperor Annei.

The official site records a tradition that the Hishizumi-no-Miya, enshrining Amaterasu-Ōmikami, moved to the present shrine site around 948 (Tenryaku 2); until then it had stood on Fumishima, about 200 m west of the present site. The official site explains that this move was by imperial command, and that the joint name of the two shrines became "Hinomisaki Daijingū (Hinomisaki Jinja)".

The official site records that the present buildings of the precinct were built in the Kan'ei era, in the early Edo period. The shrine's documents show that Tokugawa Iemitsu ordered Kyōgoku Tadataka, lord of the Matsue domain, to begin construction in 1635 (Kan'ei 12), that it was completed in 1643 (Kan'ei 20), and that the transfer ceremony (sengū) was held the following year (Kan'ei 21).

The official site records that in 1953 (Shōwa 28) the 14 buildings and two torii in the precinct were designated Important Cultural Properties of Japan, and that five stone lanterns and the documents related to the construction were designated as accompanying items.
highlights: The annual festival (Shinkō Shinji, the divine procession rite) on 7 August each year is the most important festival of the year. In the evening the portable shrine (mikoshi) is carried from the Hishizumi-no-Miya to the resting place (otabisho) on the shore opposite Fumishima, and priests land by small boat on Fumishima, the sacred ground, to perform the rite. It is often held against the setting sun and so is also called the "Sunset Festival" (official).

The official site records that the shrine's treasures include the National Treasure Shiraito-odoshi armor (white-laced armor), and that many other items, such as armor and swords, are Important Cultural Properties of Japan or cultural properties designated by Shimane Prefecture (the National Treasure designation comes only from the official description and has not yet been checked against the database of the Agency for Cultural Affairs).

The official site explains that the buildings such as the Hishizumi-no-Miya, the Kami-no-Miya and the Rōmon gate have over 100 carvings, and that no two designs are the same (in brilliant colors). Hinomisaki is a component of the Japan Heritage story "Izumo, the Sacred Land Where the Sun Sets" of the Agency for Cultural Affairs.
hinomisaki.address: 455 Hinomisaki, Taisha-chō, Izumo, Shimane 699-0763. Hinomisaki Jinja shrine office, tel. 0853-54-5261.
hinomisaki.access: The official "Access" page has guidance pages for plane, car, train and bus, but the routes and travel times are mainly in diagrams and are not confirmed as text. The parking lots shown are: one for worshippers of Hinomisaki Jinja (no large vehicles), the Hinomisaki Public Parking Lot (large vehicles allowed) and the Hinomisaki Prefectural Parking Lot (large vehicles allowed). Buses use the public parking lot in front of the torii because the road beside the shrine is narrow. When Prefectural Road 29 (Taisha–Hinomisaki Line) is expected to be completely closed, the amulet office is closed (official).
hinomisaki.hours: Prayer reception is from 8:30 to 16:00, at any time (reception is at the amulet office). No reservation is needed, it takes about 20 minutes, and the offering fee starts from ¥3,000. Reception is paused from 12:00 to 13:00 (except in busy seasons). Prayers cannot be received during the annual festival period (5 to 7 August) and so on, and the hours may change because of festivals (official). Amulets are given out at the amulet office. Goshuin reception is at the amulet office from 8:30 to 16:50 (official). The opening and closing times of the grounds are not confirmed on the official site.
hinomisaki.parking: There is a lot for worshippers of Hinomisaki Jinja (no large vehicles). Large vehicles use the Hinomisaki Public Parking Lot in front of the torii, or the Hinomisaki Prefectural Parking Lot about 1 minute from the shrine. The number of spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official site (official).
hinomisaki.goshuin: Reception is at the amulet office from 8:30 to 16:50, with an offering of ¥500 or more. For one person with three or more goshuin books, all are given as pre-written sheets. Pre-written sheets are also given from New Year's Day to the last day of the Coming-of-Age Day three-day weekend, at Setsubun, Golden Week, the Marine Day holiday weekend, the whole of August and November, Silver Week, the Sports Day holiday weekend, and from 27 December to New Year's Eve, and so on. In Kamiarizuki (the 10th month of the old calendar), limited Kamiarizuki goshuin are given. Changes may be made without notice (official, added 27 September 2026).

tsuno.name: Tsuno Jinja
tsuno.summary: Ichinomiya of Hyūga Province, standing at Kawakita, Tsuno, Koyu District, Miyazaki. It enshrines Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto (Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami), and the official site displays "a shrine listed in the Engishiki (shikinaisha) and former Kokuhei Shōsha".
tsuno.deity_note: The enshrined deity is Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto (another name Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami) (official). He corresponds to Ōkuninushi-no-Kami (another name Ōanamuji-no-Kami) in the Kojiki and Ōnamuchi-no-Kami in the Nihon Shoki (see the existing entry for Ōkuninushi). The official site explains him as a deity of matchmaking and prosperity of descendants because he had many children with many consorts, as a deity of healing because he set down the methods of medicine, and as a deity of pioneering enterprise (business prosperity) because he made the land together with Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto. About the subsidiary shrine Susanoo Jinja in the precinct, the official site notes that "he is also said to be the father of Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto". The main text of the Nihon Shoki makes Ōnamuchi-no-Kami a child of Susanoo-no-Mikoto, and the Kojiki describes him as a sixth-generation descendant (existing entry), so the official note is close to the main text of the Nihon Shoki. The shrine tradition that Emperor Jinmu stopped here and held a rite on his eastward move is not confirmed in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki (the Kojiki records that Jinmu set out from Hyūga, but Tsuno does not appear).
history: The official site records a tradition that the shrine was founded when Emperor Jinmu, six years before his enthronement, left the Miyazaki Palace on his eastward move, stopped at this place, prayed for peace of the land, calm seas and lasting good fortune in battle, and performed a rite enshrining the deity.

The official "Compilation History" records that in 837 (Jōwa 4) the shrine was ranked as an official shrine and received a divine rank (Shoku Nihon Kōki), in 858 (Tennan 2) it was given the Junior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade (Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku), and in 927 (Enchō 5) it was listed as a shrine in the Engishiki (the Engishiki register of shrines).

The official site records that it was the foremost great shrine of Hyūga Province, but in 1578 (Tenshō 6), in the strife between the Shimazu and the Ōtomo, the shrine buildings, treasures and old documents were all lost to fire by Ōtomo troops (the sacred object was evacuated to the foot of Mt. Osuzu). For a long time only a small shrine remained, and in 1692 (Genroku 5) Akizuki Tanemasa, lord of the Takanabe domain, rebuilt the shrine buildings.
The official site records that it was ranked as a Kokuhei-sha in 1871 (Meiji 4), and the top of the official site displays "a shrine listed in the Engishiki (shikinaisha) and former Kokuhei Shōsha".
highlights: The present shrine buildings were completed on 7 July 2007 (Heisei 19), after the Construction Support Association was formed in 2002 (Heisei 14) (official "History" and "Compilation History").

In the precinct are the subsidiary shrines (sessha) Susanoo Jinja and Tenazuchi-Ashinazuchi Jinja (shrines of the parent deities of Kushinadahime-no-Mikoto, wife of Susanoo-no-Mikoto), and auxiliary shrines (massha) including Kumano Jinja (the former main sanctuary), Inari Jinja and Atago Jinja (official).

The official site introduces that Tachibana Mitsuyoshi, who toured the Ichinomiya of all provinces in the early Edo period, also visited Tsuno Jinja and drew a map of the precinct in his "Ichinomiya Junkeiki".
tsuno.address: 13,294 Kawakita, Tsuno, Koyu District, Miyazaki 889-1201. Tsuno Jinja shrine office, tel. 0983-25-3256.
tsuno.access: About 25 minutes on foot, or about 5 minutes by taxi, from Tsuno Station on the JR Nippō Main Line (official). About 1 hour from Miyazaki Airport Station to Tsuno Station, and about 45 minutes from Nobeoka Station. By car, about 5 minutes from Tsuno IC on the Higashi-Kyūshū Expressway, and about 1 hour 20 minutes from Miyazaki Airport (official; varies with traffic).
tsuno.hours: Prayer (gokigan) reception is at the shrine office (on the left after crossing the Shinkyō bridge), from 9:00 to 12:00 and from 13:00 to 15:30. The offering fee is ¥5,000 or more (official). The amulet counter at the front of the shrine is open 9:00–15:30, and the amulet counter at the shrine office 9:00–16:30 (official). From 15 July 2026 (Reiwa 8), the shrine office is closed for prayer and goshuin reception from 12:00 to 13:00 (amulets and other items are given as usual at the amulet counter near the main hall). The opening and closing times of the grounds are not confirmed on the official site.
tsuno.parking: Guidance on parking (number of spaces, fees, location) is not confirmed on the official site.
tsuno.goshuin: Given at the shrine office, with reception from 9:00 to 12:00 and from 13:00 to 16:30. Regular goshuin, special goshuin and monthly limited goshuin are all ¥500 (official). The monthly limited goshuin changes every month and is announced on the official Instagram. From 15 July 2026 (Reiwa 8), reception is closed from 12:00 to 13:00. Handling by post is also available (the official site has a dedicated page; the contents are not confirmed).

utsunomiyafutaarayama.name: Utsunomiya Futaarayama Jinja
utsunomiyafutaarayama.summary: Ichinomiya of Shimotsuke Province, standing on Usugamine in central Utsunomiya. The official site explains that Toyokiirihiko-no-Mikoto is the main deity, with Ōmononushi-no-Kami and Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto co-enshrined, and that it is the only Myōjin Taisha in Tochigi Prefecture, listed as "Myōjin Taisha" in the Engishiki register of shrines (a separate shrine from Futarasan Jinja in Nikkō).
utsunomiyafutaarayama.deity_note: The deities enshrined according to the official site are Toyokiirihiko-no-Mikoto (main), with Ōmononushi-no-Kami ("Ōkuni-sama") and Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto ("Ebisu-sama") co-enshrined. In the Nihon Shoki, Toyokiirihiko-no-Mikoto (Toyoki-no-Mikoto) is a prince of Emperor Sujin; in year 48 of Sujin, through a dream divination, he was to govern the eastern lands, and he is recorded as the founding ancestor of the Kamitsukeno no Kimi and the Shimotsukeno no Kimi. In the Kojiki he is listed among the children of Emperor Sujin as Toyokiirihiko-no-Mikoto (豊木入日子命), with a note that he was an ancestor of the Kamitsukeno no Kimi and the Shimotsukeno no Kimi. Ōmononushi appears in both the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki in the reign of Emperor Sujin as a deity of plague and dream revelation, and Kotoshironushi appears in the transfer of the land (existing ID). The names "Ōmononushi = Ōkuni-sama" and "Kotoshironushi = Ebisu-sama" are the shrine's official explanation and are not in the main text of the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki. The official site reveres Toyokiirihiko-no-Mikoto as the founding ancestor of Utsunomiya and says it began when his fourth-generation descendant Narawake no Kimi enshrined him at Araosaki (the present Shimo-no-Miya) (a check of Narawake-no-Ō in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki was not carried out this time; to be confirmed).
history: The official site writes: "This shrine has a very long history, going back to the reign of the 10th Emperor, Emperor Sujin." The shrine records say that in the reign of Emperor Nintoku the land of Keno was divided into upper and lower provinces, and when Prince Narawake, a fourth-generation descendant of Toyokiirihiko-no-Mikoto, was appointed Kuni no Miyatsuko (provincial governor) of Shimotsukeno, he enshrined his ancestral deity at Araosaki (Shimo-no-Miya); it is said that in 838 (Jōwa 5) the shrine was moved to the present Usugamine.

The Engishiki register of shrines, completed in 927 (Enchō 5), lists "Shimotsuke Province, Kawachi District, one deity, a Great shrine: Futaarayama Jinja, Myōjin Taisha", and the official site explains it as the only Myōjin Taisha in Tochigi Prefecture. The official site also calls it Ichinomiya of Shimotsuke Province, and says that one theory holds that the place name Utsunomiya came from a corruption of "Ichinomiya".
According to the official site, the shrine suffered four fires, in 1585 (Tenshō 13), 1773 (An'ei 2), 1832 (Tenpō 3) and the Boshin War, and almost all of its old records were lost.

The official site records that Fujiwara no Hidesato, Minamoto no Yoriyoshi and Yoshiie, Minamoto no Yoritomo, Tokugawa Ieyasu and others received divine favor and donated shrine lands and treasures and rebuilt the shrine buildings (reverence for prayers for victory in battle). It developed as a town at the shrine gate in the Heian and Kamakura periods and as a castle town in the Edo period.
highlights: The subsidiary and auxiliary shrines in the precinct include the subsidiary shrine Shimo-no-Miya, regarded as the origin of the shrine; Nyotai-gū, a deity of safe childbirth; the Jissha ("Ten Shrines"), which enshrines together the Engishiki-listed shrines of the prefecture; and the Tōshōgū, which enshrines Tokugawa Ieyasu (as classified on the precinct guide page).

The official site records that faith in fire prevention (hibuse) has existed since ancient times, and that worshippers from inside and outside the prefecture gather for the winter and spring Tosai (Otariya).
The grounds consist of a flight of 95 stone steps, the Onna-zaka (women's slope), the west approach and others, and have an amulet office and a shrine office.
utsunomiyafutaarayama.address: 1-1-1 Babadōri, Utsunomiya, Tochigi 320-0026. Shrine office tel. 028-622-5271 (official).
utsunomiyafutaarayama.access: 5 minutes by bus or 20 minutes on foot from the west exit of JR Utsunomiya Station; 15 minutes on foot from Tōbu-Utsunomiya Station. By car, 25 minutes from Kanuma IC and 20 minutes from Utsunomiya IC on the Tōhoku Expressway (official).
utsunomiyafutaarayama.hours: Prayers: no reservation needed. Reception is from 8:30 to 15:50; prayers are held every 30 minutes from 9:00 (the last at 16:00). Offering fees for individuals are ¥7,000, ¥10,000, ¥20,000 and so on (revised on 1 April 2026 (Reiwa 8); individual prayer ¥5,000 → ¥7,000). The current hours of the shrine office, the amulet office and the opening and closing of the gate are not confirmed in the main text of the official site. A notice from 2023 gives temporary hours following the prefecture's priority measures against the spread of infection (gate opens at 6:00, closes at 18:00; shrine office and amulet office 9:00–16:00), but these may not be the current regular hours.
utsunomiyafutaarayama.parking: A parking lot behind the precinct (Futaarayama Jinja parking lot). Use is 8:00–21:00; ¥300 for 60 minutes, a maximum of ¥1,500 for 12 hours; free for 2 hours within the opening hours for those receiving a prayer; up to 300 cars. There are wheelchair spaces (official).
utsunomiyafutaarayama.goshuin: Goshuin are given at the reception inside the shrine office for an offering of ¥500. There are also picture goshuin of Ōmononushi-no-Kami and Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto (a set of two) and an original goshuin book. Special goshuin are announced on the official X (formerly Twitter). The reception hours for goshuin are not confirmed in the main text of the official site.

kunozantoshogu.name: Kunōzan Tōshōgū
kunozantoshogu.summary: A Tōshōgū enshrining Tokugawa Ieyasu, standing on Mt. Kunō overlooking Suruga Bay. The official site explains that it began as the Tōshōsha, founded after Ieyasu's death in 1616 (Genna 2), and the shrine buildings were designated a National Treasure in 2010 (Heisei 22).
kunozantoshogu.deity_note: The enshrined deity is Tokugawa Ieyasu (as written on the official site). Ieyasu was a historical figure born in 1542 (Tenbun 11) and does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki. The official chronology says the divine title "Tōshō Daigongen" was bestowed in 1617 (Genna 3). There is therefore no link to a deity of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (criterion 3). The official explanation centers on Ieyasu's deeds and his philosophy of peace ("Onri Edo, Gongu Jōdo").
history: The official site, citing the "Kunōji Engi", records that in the reign of Empress Suiko (around the 7th century) Kunō Tadahito of the Hata clan opened the mountain, built a temple, installed a Kannon Bosatsu and named it Fudarakusan Kunōji; this is the beginning of the history of Mt. Kunō.
In 1568 (Eiroku 11), Takeda Shingen moved Kunōji and built Kunō Castle on the mountaintop. After the fall of the Takeda clan in 1582 (Tenshō 10), the area came under the Tokugawa.

After Ieyasu's death on the 17th day of the 4th month of 1616 (Genna 2), he was buried on Mt. Kunō according to his last wishes, Kunō Castle was abolished, and the Tōshōsha was founded. The shrine buildings were completed and the formal transfer ceremony (shōsengū) was held in the 12th month of 1617 (Genna 3); in 1645 (Shōhō 2) it was called "Tōshōgū" by the proclamation of the title gū (official chronology).

According to the official site, the shrine buildings (main hall, Ishi-no-ma and worship hall) were designated a National Treasure in 2010 (Heisei 22). Many other buildings, such as the Rōmon gate and the Shinbyō (mausoleum), are Important Cultural Properties. In 2015 (Heisei 27), the Grand Festival for the 400th anniversary of the enshrinement was held.
highlights: The National Treasure shrine buildings are in the gongen-zukuri style, fully lacquered and richly colored. Built in 1617 (Genna 3), they are, the official site explains, a representative early Edo building made 19 years before the Nikkō Tōshōgū, and were built by Nakai Yamato-no-kami Masakiyo.
Besides the Shinbyō where Ieyasu is buried, many buildings such as the Rōmon gate, the Karamon gate, the Byōmon gate and the Kagura-den are Important Cultural Properties (official precinct guide).
Worshippers can climb the 1,159-step main approach from the foot of Mt. Kunō, or cross by ropeway from Nihondaira.
kunozantoshogu.address: 390 Nekoya, Suruga Ward, Shizuoka 422-8011. Shrine office tel. 054-237-2438 (official).
kunozantoshogu.access: There is no road up to the precinct for cars. Use the Nihondaira Ropeway (departing Nihondaira Station 9:10–16:45, departing Kunōzan Station 9:30–17:00; adult round trip ¥1,250), or the 1,159 stone steps from the foot of Mt. Kunō (about 20 minutes). From JR Shizuoka Station, take a bus to the Nihondaira Ropeway or to the foot of Mt. Kunō (official). Only stone steps lead to the shrine buildings, and wheelchairs and strollers cannot be used.
kunozantoshogu.hours: Visiting hours are 9:00–17:00, open all year (reception closes 10 minutes before closing). Admission fees: shrine buildings, adult ¥700, child ¥300; museum, adult ¥600, child ¥300; combined ticket, adult ¥1,200, child ¥500. Prayer reception is 9:00–16:00, no reservation needed. Ofuda and omamori are given from 9:00 until the end of visitor reception (at the amulet offices beside the shrine buildings, beside the Rōmon gate, and at the shrine office). However, the official FAQ also says "the reception end time differs by season".
kunozantoshogu.parking: There is no parking in the precinct. Use the free parking lot (about 200 spaces) in front of Nihondaira Station of the Nihondaira Ropeway, or the private parking lots around the foot of Mt. Kunō (official FAQ).
kunozantoshogu.goshuin: Reception is at the shrine office worship reception, 9:00–17:00. The offering is ¥500 (the "Kane no Naru Ki" (money tree) goshuin is ¥1,000, goshuin paper only). You leave your goshuin book before worship and collect it after worship (official).

izawa.name: Izawa-no-Miya
izawa.summary: A betsugū (separate shrine) of Kōtai Jingū (Naikū), standing in Isobe-chō, Shima City. According to the Jingū official site, it enshrines the spirit of Amaterasu-Ōmikami, and as the "Tōnomiya" (the distant shrine) it is deeply revered by fishermen and ama divers. The rice-planting ceremony (Otaue-shiki) on 24 June each year is an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
izawa.deity_note: The Jingū official site writes the enshrined deity as "Amaterasu-Ōmikami no Mitama" (the spirit of Amaterasu-Ōmikami). Amaterasu-Ōmikami is a deity of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (existing ID amaterasu), but here we follow the official position that this is a betsugū enshrining her spirit (mitama). The founding is said to date from the reign of Emperor Suinin, and it is handed down that Isawatomi-no-Mikoto built the shrine building after the tour of Yamatohime-no-Mikoto (official). The Nihon Shoki, year 25 of Emperor Suinin, has an entry in which Yamatohime-no-Mikoto enshrines Amaterasu-Ōmikami at Ise, but the tour of Shima and Isawatomi-no-Mikoto could not be confirmed in the text obtained this time (to be confirmed).
history: The official site says "the founding of Izawa-no-Miya is said to be about 2,000 years ago, in the reign of the 11th Emperor, Emperor Suinin", and tells that after the enshrinement of Kōtai Jingū, Yamatohime-no-Mikoto toured Shima Province to fix the land for the sacred food offerings, and Isawatomi-no-Mikoto built a shrine building at this place and enshrined the spirit of Amaterasu-Ōmikami.
The name of the shrine is recorded in the "Kōtai Jingū Gishikichō" of 804 (Enryaku 23).
The official site records that it is thought to have been positioned as a betsugū from before 804 (Enryaku 23).

The "Azuma Kagami" of the Kamakura period records that when Minamoto no Yoritomo prayed to the Jingū, he sent a sacred horse to Izawa-no-Miya (the official site's explanation). In the Edo period, worshippers visited Izawa-no-Miya after worshipping at the two shrines (Ryōgū).
highlights: The rice-planting ceremony on 24 June each year (the day of the June monthly festival) is designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan under the name "Isobe no Oshinden" (the sacred rice field of Isobe), and is counted as one of the three great rice-planting festivals of Japan.
About 800 m away are Saminaga Jinja (Ōtoshi-no-Kami) and the four shrines of Saminaga-mimae Jinja, which are under its jurisdiction (shokansha).
izawa.address: 374 Kaminogō, Isobe-chō, Shima, Mie (the enshrined location per the Jingū official site).
izawa.access: A 3-minute walk from Kintetsu Kaminogō Station (Jingū official).
izawa.hours: This is the notation common to the Jingū's "betsugū outside the precinct". Visiting hours: 5:00–18:00 from January to April and in September, 5:00–19:00 from May to August, and 5:00–17:00 from October to December (changed during the New Year period). Amulet hours: 6:00–18:00 (until 17:00 from October to December). A separate notation for Izawa-no-Miya itself is not confirmed. The Jingū's prayer reception is at the Kagura-den of the Naikū and the Gekū; reception at Izawa-no-Miya is not confirmed on the official site.
izawa.parking: The Jingū official page for Izawa-no-Miya has no mention of parking, so it is not confirmed.
izawa.goshuin: Amulets (the sword-purification charm 剣祓, the protection-purification charm 守祓, omamori, traffic-safety omamori and the Umisachi-kimori 海幸木守) and goshuin are received at the Shukueiya (宿衛屋) (Jingū official). Amulet hours are 6:00–18:00 (until 17:00 from October to December).

chokaisan.name: Chōkaisan Ōmonoimi Jinja
chokaisan.summary: Ichinomiya of Dewa Province, with Mt. Chōkai as its sacred body (shintai). The name is a common term for three shrines: the main shrine at the summit and the Fukura and Warabioka Kuchi-no-Miya (village shrines) at the foot. The official site has guidance on prayer times and offering fees, but the amulet office hours and goshuin guidance are not confirmed on the official site.
chokaisan.deity_note: The official page on the "enshrined deities" gives only the history and does not name the deity. The Yamagata prefectural tourism site gives the enshrined deities as Ōmonoimi-no-Ōkami and Gassan-no-Kami. Ōmonoimi-no-Kami is a deity who does not appear in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki; the encyclopedia says so too, and the word "monoimi" was not found in the Kojiki (Parts 1, 2 and 3) or in the text of the Nihon Shoki at hand (some books may not be in full text). He is listed as a deity not in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. Gassan-no-Kami is not treated as a separate deity, and no ID has been created for him.
history: The official site records a tradition that the deity was enshrined on the summit in the reign of Emperor Kinmei, in the 25th year, more than 1,400 years ago.

The shrine was ranked as an official shrine in the 11th month of 862 (Jōgan 4), and is recorded in the Engishiki register of shrines as a Myōjin Taisha, together with Gassan Jinja, which stands at Fukura. The official site records that it later became Ichinomiya of Dewa Province.
In the 5th month of 1871 (Meiji 4), the Fukura Kuchi-no-Miya was ranked as a Kokuhei Chūsha. In 1955 (Shōwa 30), the three shrines were combined under the present shrine name.
The main sanctuary at the summit follows the system of shikinen zōei (rebuilding every 20 years), as at Ise Jingū; the present main sanctuary was built in 1997 (Heisei 9).
highlights: It holds the Important Cultural Properties of Japan "Kamakura Bakufu Bugyōnin Rensho Hōsho" and "Kitabatake Akinobu Kishinjō". The official site records that the wani-guchi (a hanging gong), a cultural property designated by the prefecture, is the oldest example in which the name "Chōkaisan" appears in writing (Ryakuō 5, 1342).

In the Agency for Cultural Affairs' database of nationally designated cultural properties, the main sanctuary of the Fukura Kuchi-no-Miya (registered February 2012) and the main sanctuary of the Warabioka Kuchi-no-Miya (registered October 2007) are listed as Registered Tangible Cultural Properties (buildings).

The official festival calendar includes the annual festival of the Warabioka Kuchi-no-Miya on 3 May (Warabioka Enen), the annual festival of the Fukura Kuchi-no-Miya on 4 and 5 May (Fukura Dengaku), the Chōkaisan Hi-awase Shinji on 14 July, and the Gassan Jinja Festival (Tamazake Shinji) on 15 July.
chokaisan.address: 1 Nunokura, Fukura, Yuza, Akumi District, Yamagata (Fukura Kuchi-no-Miya; the location as written on the official site). The Agency for Cultural Affairs database gives the Warabioka Kuchi-no-Miya as 51 Matsugaoka, Kami-Warabioka, Yuza, Akumi District, Yamagata (not on the official site). The location of the main shrine at the summit is not confirmed on the official site.
chokaisan.access: The official site has no access page. For the Fukura Kuchi-no-Miya, the Yamagata prefectural tourism site gives 3 minutes by car from JR Fukura Station and 25 minutes by car from Sakata-minato IC on the Nihonkai Tōhoku Expressway.
chokaisan.hours: The New Year visit guide for 2026 (Reiwa 8) (PDF) posted on the official site says that daytime prayers are held every hour from 9:30 to 15:30 (in the afternoon from 13:30). The offering fee for an individual prayer is from ¥5,000. The official festival page says that prayers for a safe-driving year are accepted at any time at the Fukura Kuchi-no-Miya. The regular opening and closing times of the amulet office are not confirmed on the official site. Because the guide is issued each year, call the Fukura Kuchi-no-Miya (0234-77-2301) before visiting. The hours of the main shrine at the summit and of the Warabioka Kuchi-no-Miya are not on the official site either.
chokaisan.parking: The Yamagata prefectural tourism site gives 30 spaces for the Fukura Kuchi-no-Miya, but the official site does not mention it.
chokaisan.goshuin: The official site has no goshuin guidance page. The top page has an old COVID-19 notice that suspends handing out "ofuda, omamori and goshuin" by hand (the present method and hours of giving are unknown).

izushi.name: Izushi Jinja
izushi.summary: The official site calls itself "Ichinomiya of Tajima Province", and it enshrines Ame-no-Hiboko-no-Mikoto and Izushi-Yamae-no-Ōkami. The shrine rank given officially is Kokuhei Chūsha. The official site has guidance on prayers, amulets and goshuin, but it was last updated in 2009 and gives no reception hours.
izushi.deity_note: The official page on the enshrined deities lists only the names Izushi-Yamae-no-Ōkami and Ame-no-Hiboko-no-Mikoto. Kojiki Part 2, in a small-print note, writes the eight kinds of treasures brought over by Ame-no-Hiboko, son of the ruler of Silla, as "Izushi-no-Yamae-no-Ōkami", and the entry for the 3rd year of Emperor Suinin in the Nihon Shoki records that the things brought by Ame-no-Hiboko, a prince of Silla, were stored in Tajima Province and made objects of the deity. The achievement of opening the rocky hill at the mouth of the Maruyama River, which the official site explains, is not written in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki.
history: The official site tells that Tajima, once a sea of mud, was opened by Ame-no-Hiboko-no-Mikoto, who cut through the rocky hill between Seto and Tsuiyama at the mouth of the Maruyama River, let the muddy water flow out to the Sea of Japan, and revealed the present fertile Tajima plain. The date of the founding is not given on the official site.

The Nihon Shoki records that in the spring, third month, of the 3rd year of Emperor Suinin, Ame-no-Hiboko, a prince of Silla, came to Japan and stored the things he brought in Tajima Province and made them objects of the deity. The Shoki does not describe the founding of a shrine.

The official site records that the present shrine buildings were rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3), and that in front of the main hall, in the sanken-sha nagare-zukuri style, there are a heiden (offering hall) and a norito-den (hall for reading norito).
The official site gives the shrine rank as Kokuhei Chūsha and writes the name of the shrine as "Tajima no Kuni Ichinomiya Izushi Jinja".
highlights: The precinct covers 6,500 tsubo. Past the torii and the Red Gate (Akamon) are the worship hall, in irimoya-zukuri in the maidono style, and, behind it, the main hall in sanken-sha nagare-zukuri. The front porch (kohai) of the worship hall is a flat kara-hafu gable independent of the roof, which the official site records as a building without equal.

The Shinmon gate is a vermilion-lacquered eight-legged gate (hakkyaku-mon) decorated with many kaerumata (frog-leg struts). The official site records that the walls running to the left and right are also vermilion.
In the northeast corner of the precinct is a forbidden area (kinsokuchi) of about 600 tsubo; it is handed down that entering it brings a curse (tatari), the official site records (no entry).

The official festival page lists the Risshun-sai (beginning of spring festival), the Nobori-mawashi (banner procession) on 5 May, the annual festival on 20 October and the Ohanabira Festival on 23 November, among others.
izushi.address: Miyauchi, Izushi-chō, Toyooka, Hyōgo 668-0204 (official site). The street number is not in the official text, but the map link on the official access page is set to search for "99 Miyauchi, Izushi-chō". Tel. 0796-52-2440 (official).
izushi.access: The official access guide says: about 25 minutes by bus bound for Izushi and Tantō from Toyooka Station on the JR San'in Main Line; get off at Torii-bashi and walk 10 minutes east. By car, from Kasuga IC on the Maizuru Expressway go on to the Kita-Kinki Toyooka Expressway, and from Wadayama IC it is about 45 minutes toward Yōka; from the Himeji direction, take the Bantan Expressway to Wadayama IC. Because the official site was updated in 2009, the bus route is to be confirmed.
izushi.hours: The official "Guide to prayers" page says that both individual prayers and company/group prayers accept reservations by telephone and so on, and are received at the shrine office (first shrine visit, yakubarai, Shichi-Go-San, safe childbirth, car purification, passing entrance exams and so on). The "List of amulets" shows ofuda, various omamori and traffic-safety omamori. The reception and amulet hours are not given on the official site, and the site was last updated in 2009.
izushi.parking: The number of spaces and fees are not confirmed on the official site.
izushi.goshuin: The official site has a "Goshuin" page, and the sample of the all-Japan Ichinomiya goshuin book and goshuin shows an "offering fee of ¥300". The place and hours of reception are not confirmed on the official site.

oyamaafuri.name: Ōyama Afuri Jinja
oyamaafuri.summary: A shrine listed in the Engishiki (shikinaisha) enshrined on Mt. Ōyama in Isehara City, Kanagawa; the lower shrine is halfway up the mountain and the main shrine is at the summit. In the Edo period, large numbers of people climbed it in the "Ōyama pilgrimage" (Ōyama-mairi), and it was a center of mountain faith in the Kantō region.
oyamaafuri.deity_note: The official site gives the enshrined deities as three: Ōyamatsumi-no-Ōkami, Takaokami-no-Kami and Ōikazuchi-no-Kami. It explains that Ōyamatsumi-no-Ōkami is the father of "Konohanasakuya-hime", the deity of Mt. Fuji, and that Takaokami and Ōikazuchi are deities recorded in the Nihon Shoki. Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami appears in the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki and is written in the Kojiki as the father of Konohana-no-Sakuyabime (see the existing deity IDs). Takaokami appears in a variant account of the Nihon Shoki, and Ōikazuchi appears in the Yomi scene (one of the eight thunders) of both the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki. The name "Takaokami" cannot be confirmed in the Kojiki, and its relation to Kuraokami-no-Kami is to be confirmed. The name "Sakatoke-no-Kami" given by the official site was not found in the obtained text of the Kojiki, Nihon Shoki or Kogo Shūi (to be confirmed). The deities of the precinct shrines — Tori-no-Iwakusufune Jinja (Tori-no-Iwakusufune-no-Kami), Asama Sha (Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto and Iwanaga-hime), Tenmangū (Sugawara no Michizane) and Katsu Kaishū Jinja — are not the main deities, so they are not included in deity_ids.
history: The official site says that the shrine was founded more than 2,200 years ago, around the reign of Emperor Sujin. Because clouds and mist form easily on the mountain, it was also called "Amefuri-yama" (Rain-Falling Mountain), and is said to have been a place of prayers for rain and a rich harvest.

The official site records that in the Heian period it became a shrine receiving offerings from the state (kokuhei) (a shikinaisha), written as "Afuri Jinja" in the Engishiki compiled in the Heian period.

Around the Edo period it won the veneration of ordinary people under the name Sekison Daigongen, and it is recorded that as many as 200,000 worshippers a year made the "Ōyama pilgrimage" (the official site's description). They went in confraternities (kō), and in 2016 the "Ōyama pilgrimage" was designated Japan Heritage by the Agency for Cultural Affairs.
In 1977 (Shōwa 52) the lower shrine was rebuilt, and the present lower shrine worship hall was completed.
highlights: Following an Edo-period anecdote, the custom of "Nōdachi", dedicating wooden swords, is handed down. The longest one that survives is said to reach 6 meters.

From the lower shrine to the main shrine at the summit is about 90–120 minutes on foot. Ōyamatsumi-no-Ōkami is enshrined at the main shrine, and Ōikazuchi-no-Kami and Tori-no-Iwakusufune Jinja at the Okusha (inner shrine); the "Amefuri-no-ki" (rain-falling tree) is said to have always dripped with dew, which is the origin of "Amefuri-yama".

The Nijūsha (waterfall) near the lower shrine is a place where misogi was performed since ancient times, and there is a tradition that a dragon deity appeared there. The Meoto-sugi (Husband-and-Wife Cedars) are said to be over 500 years old.

There is a Noh stage (Nōgaku-den) for "Ōyama Nō", which has a history of over 300 years; Shinji Nō (sacred Noh) is performed at the autumn grand festival in August, and the Ōyama Himatsuri Takigi Nō (firelight Noh) in October.
oyamaafuri.address: 355 Ōyama, Isehara, Kanagawa 259-1107 (the location of the administration office (shamukyoku), as written officially). The lower shrine is halfway up Mt. Ōyama (about 700 m above sea level), and the main shrine is at the summit of Mt. Ōyama.
oyamaafuri.access: Access guide on the official site: about 15 minutes toward Ōyama from Isehara-Ōyama IC on the Shin-Tōmei Expressway. Visitors by car are advised to use the municipal parking lots. For the administration office, get off at the Kanagawa Chūō Kōtsū bus stop "Shamukyoku Iriguchi". The cable car follows the guide of the operating company (Ōyama Kankō Dentetsu): from the north exit of Isehara Station on the Odakyū Line, about 30 minutes by bus to "Ōyama Cable", then about 15 minutes' walk along the "Koma Sandō" to the cable car station. From Ōyama Cable Station to Afuri-jinja Station takes about 6 minutes (the shrine's official site also says about 6 minutes). From Afuri-jinja Station, go to the lower shrine. The cable car's regular operating hours are 9:00–16:30 on weekdays and 9:00–17:00 on weekends and holidays; adult one-way ¥640, round trip ¥1,270 (after the change of 1 April 2024; the operating company's guide). It may stop in abnormal weather.
oyamaafuri.hours: Telephone reception at the administration office is 9:00–17:00 (official). The hours when the lower shrine and the main shrine can be visited, and the reception hours of the amulet office, are not confirmed on the official site.
oyamaafuri.parking: The shrine-operated Afuri No. 1 parking lot (opened in 2022 (Reiwa 4); ordinary cars only) is ¥900 per day on weekdays and ¥1,000 on weekends, holidays and designated days. The municipal Ōyama No. 1 parking lot is ¥600 for ordinary cars and the No. 2 lot is ¥1,000 (all per day; official). As for spaces, according to the operating company's guide, the municipal lots have 84 in the No. 1 and 44 in the No. 2. The number of spaces in the Afuri No. 1 lot is not confirmed on the official site. Parking at Ōyama cannot be secured sufficiently, and the use of public transport is advised.
oyamaafuri.goshuin: Goshuin are given at the lower shrine, the main shrine at the summit and the administration office at the foot of the mountain (if no priest is at the main shrine, tell the lower shrine after worshipping). There are also goshuin of Asama Sha, Nijūsha, Oiwake Sha and Katsu Kaishū Jinja, and seasonal goshuin. Amulets and other items are given at the amulet office of the lower shrine. The offering fee and the reception hours are not confirmed on the official site.

takase.name: Takase Jinja
takase.summary: The official site calls itself "Etchū Ichinomiya Takase Jinja" and enshrines Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami as the main deity, with Ame-no-Ikutama-no-Mikoto and Isotakeru-no-Mikoto as co-enshrined deities. The official site records that it was raised to Kokuhei Shōsha in 1923 (Taishō 12). Nanto City designates it a city historic site and explains that it appears in the Shoku Nihongi and the Engishiki register of shrines. As for the Ichinomiya of Etchū, Imizu Jinja, Oyama Jinja and Keta Jinja also claim the title or have at times been called by it, so there are differing views. The official site has guidance on prayers, amulets and limited-edition goshuin. The official site itself uses both 高瀬 and 髙瀬 as the spelling.
takase.deity_note: The official guide gives Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami as the main deity and Ame-no-Ikutama-no-Mikoto and Isotakeru-no-Mikoto as co-enshrined deities, and lists among the auxiliary shrines Shinmeigū (Amaterasu-sume-ōkami), Kazenomiya (Shinatobe-no-Mikoto), Inari-sha (Ukanomitama-no-Ōkami) and Tenmangū (Sugawara no Michizane). The official site explains Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami as a child of Susanoo-no-Mikoto, and describes him as the deity who crossed from Izumo to Etchū, subdued the evil deities, opened up the land and taught the ways of farming and medicine. Ōkuninushi-no-Kami appears in the Kojiki, Part 1; in the Nihon Shoki he appears under the name Ōnamuchi-no-Kami in Books 1 and 2 (a variant account in the Nihon Shoki also writes "Ōkuninushi-no-Kami" as "Kuni-tsukuri Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto"). The Kojiki has a story in which Yachihoko-no-Kami (another name of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami) visits Nunakawa-hime of Koshi Province, but it does not mention any relation to Takase Jinja. Isotakeru appears in a variant account in Nihon Shoki Book 1 as a child of Susanoo-no-Mikoto and the deity who sowed the seeds of trees. On the other hand, the name of Ame-no-Ikutama-no-Mikoto, whom the official site describes as the deity of "ikutama" who accompanied the descent of the heavenly grandson, was not found in the main text of the Kojiki, Part 1, or of the Nihon Shoki, Books 1 and 2, that the author checked (to be confirmed). The achievements in opening up Etchū that the official site describes are also not written in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki (within the range the author checked).
history: The official site records that the enshrinement goes back to the Age of the Gods, or is also said to date from the 11th year of Emperor Keikō's reign. As a shrine tradition, it relates that when Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto was developing the Hokuriku region, he enshrined his own guardian deity in this place, and after the land was established he also settled his own spirit as the land-spirit deity (kunitama-no-kami) and returned to Izumo, and it quotes a passage from the Takase Jinja-shi.

The official site also quotes another old record, the 越之下草 (reading unconfirmed), and relates that the deity came across from Koma long ago, that the day of arrival was the 14th day of the seventh month, and that after resting by the Tabi River the deity moved to Takase. This story is also the origin of the name of the village of 雨潜 (reading unconfirmed). It differs in its telling from the shrine tradition that the deity came from Izumo, but the official site does not explain the difference. The official site gives no date.

The official chronology begins with an entry in the Shoku Nihongi for the twelfth month of 780 (Hōki 11), saying that the Takase deity of Tonami District was granted the Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade, together with the Futagami deity. It then goes on to the Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade, in 795 (Enryaku 14), the Junior Third Rank in 854 (Saikō 1) and the Senior Third Rank in 859 (Jōgan 1), and says that the Engishiki lists "Takase Jinja, Tonami District, Etchū Province". The Senior First Rank in 1180 (Jishō 4) carries the note "war; all deities granted rank together".

The Nanto City explanation of cultural properties says that the shrine's appearance as the "Takase deity" in the Shoku Nihongi of the late Nara period, and its listing in the Engishiki register of shrines of the Heian period, show that it was protected by the imperial court. The city has designated the shrine a city-designated historic site (designated 1 July 1966, Shōwa 41). A private database (engishiki.org) also records that it is listed in the Engishiki register of shrines as Takase Jinja of Tonami District, Etchū Province.

The official site records that the shrine front fell into disrepair in the Sengoku period, but its divine standing gradually rose through the veneration of the lords of the Maeda domain, and that it was raised to a prefectural shrine (Kensha) in 1873 (Meiji 6) and to Kokuhei Shōsha in 1923 (Taishō 12).

The Ichinomiya of Etchū Province has not been settled on a single shrine. The official site of Takase Jinja claims the title "Etchū Ichinomiya". The official site of Imizu Jinja claims "Etchū Sōchinju Ichinomiya", and the official site of Oyama Jinja records that the words "Ichinomiya of Etchū Province" appear in the Kamakura-period Shintōshū. An encyclopedia (Wikipedia) and private databases also state that four shrines, adding Keta Jinja, claim the title, but what Keta Jinja itself officially states is not confirmed.
highlights: Nanto City has designated "the Gobutsu-sekki and two other items" held by the shrine (place of excavation unknown) as a city-designated cultural property (designated 26 February 1998, Heisei 10). The city records that the Gobutsu-sekki was made in the middle of the Final Jōmon period, is thought to have been used in ceremonies, and is the largest Gobutsu-sekki in Japan.

According to the official site, the present main sanctuary (nagare-zukuri) was built in 1947 (Shōwa 22), the worship hall (irimoya-zukuri) the following year, and the karahafu-gabled kōhai-den was completed in 1987 (Shōwa 62). The state-funded reconstruction work that began in 1942 (Shōwa 17) was halted by the end of the war. The main sanctuary of the neighbouring Kōreiden is the former main sanctuary, built in 1836 (Tenpō 7), and the official site records that it brings together the very best of Inami carving; it also writes that it has received a cultural property designation. However, the type and body of the designation are not on the official page and are not confirmed on the Nanto City cultural property pages either (the two pages obtained) (to be confirmed).

The official site explains that the "Nade-usagi" (stroking rabbit) in the precinct was placed before the deity in connection with the myth of the "White Rabbit of Inaba", in which Ōkuninushi-no-Ōkami healed the rabbit's wounds (one strokes the same place as the part one wishes to heal while praying). It also introduces "U-no-hi mairi" (Rabbit Day visits), presenting the Rabbit Day (U-no-hi), which comes round once every 12 days, as a day closely tied to the enshrined deity.

In the official list of festivals, the annual festival (reisai) on 13 September is recorded as the most important festival, falling on the shrine's ennichi (special festival day). The Kinengoku-sai on 10 June is described as an important festival that derives from the old custom of an imperial envoy visiting to pray that there be no disease or insect damage.
takase.address: 291 Takase, Nanto, Toyama 932-0252 (official site). Tel. 0763-82-0932, fax 0763-82-3204 (official; checked 16 Oct 2026). The Nanto City cultural property page, however, gives the location of the city-designated historic site "Takase Jinja" as "370 Takase, Nanto City", a different lot number from the shrine's address (291); the city's page gives no reason.
takase.access: The official access guide (checked 16 Oct 2026) says that by car it is about 15 minutes from Tonami IC on the Hokuriku Expressway, about 15 minutes from Fukumitsu IC and about 10 minutes from Nanto Smart IC on the Tōkai-Hokuriku Expressway, and about 30 minutes each from the Kanazawa-Morimoto direction (National Route 304) and the Kanazawa Mori-no-sato direction (Prefectural Route 27). By train, get off at Fukuno Station on the JR Jōhana Line and take a taxi, about 7 minutes (about 30 minutes from Shin-Takaoka Station to Fukuno Station, about 35 minutes from Takaoka Station). Buses from Fukuno Station are not listed in the official guide.
takase.hours: The official "Prayer Guide" says that prayer reception is from 9:00 to 16:00 (open all year, reservations not accepted). The official "FAQ", on the other hand, says 9:00–16:30, so the two official pages give different closing times. On festival and wedding days the reception hours change, and the official news page lists the schedule month by month. The place to return old talismans and amulets is open 9:00–17:00. Items for bestowal (talismans, amulets, ema) are listed with prices on the official "Talismans and Amulets" page. The hours when visitors may enter the grounds (opening and closing of the gates) are not confirmed on the official site.
takase.parking: The location, number of spaces and fees of the parking lot are not confirmed on the official site.
takase.goshuin: In its "U-no-hi mairi" section (dates for Reiwa 8, i.e. 2026: 8 and 20 October; 1, 13 and 25 November; 7, 19 and 31 December), the official news page says that limited-edition goshuin are given between 9:00 and 17:00. It reads as goshuin limited to U-no-hi, but this is not stated definitively. Whether regular goshuin are given on days other than U-no-hi, and where they are received, are not confirmed on the official site. The official site says that a commemorative goshuin book is given to couples who hold a Shinto wedding.

ichinomiyaasama.name: Ichinomiya Asama Jinja
ichinomiyaasama.summary: An Asama Jinja in Ichinomiya-chō, Fuefuki City, Yamanashi. The official site calls itself the "Ichinomiya of Kai Province" and records that it enshrines Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto. The official site records that it is a Myōjin Taisha under the Engi system and was ranked a Kokuhei Chūsha in 1871 (Meiji 4), and the Yamanashi Prefectural Shrine Association (Jinjachō) guide gives the same content. The main sanctuary of the subsidiary shrine Yamamiya Jinja, outside the precinct, is a nationally designated Important Cultural Property. The official news page has guidance on goshuin at the amulet office and on Shichi-Go-San prayers. Because there are Asama Jinja of the same name in many places that enshrine Mt. Fuji, this article writes of it as "Ichinomiya Asama Jinja" to tell it apart.
ichinomiyaasama.deity_note: The official site gives the enshrined deity as Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto, a deity of Fuji and daughter of Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami, also called Ata-kashitsu-hime-no-Mikoto and Sakura-ōtokoji-no-Mikoto, and consort of the heavenly grandson Ninigi-no-Mikoto. The Kojiki, Part 1, records the beautiful woman whom Amatsu-hiko-hiko-ho-no-Ninigi-no-Mikoto met at Kasasa no Misaki as the daughter of Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami, named Kamu-Atatsu-hime and also called Konohanasakuya-bime, and tells the story that she set fire to the hall when she gave birth. A passage in the Nihon Shoki, Book 2 (the second part of the Age of the Gods), also writes that she is a child of Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami, named Kamu-Atakashitsu-hime and also called Konohanasakuya-hime. The official site records that Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami and Ninigi-no-Mikoto are enshrined at the subsidiary shrine outside the precinct, Yamamiya Jinja, and that in 865 (Jōgan 7) only Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto, of the original three deities, was moved to the present site. Note that, as for the official site's description of her as a "deity of Fuji", the words "Fuji" and "Asama" do not appear in the main text of the Kojiki, Part 1, and Nihon Shoki, Book 2, that this article checked, and no direct description in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki was found.
history: The official site records that the origin was the first enshrinement at the foot of 神山 (reading unconfirmed) in the first month of the 8th year of the reign of Emperor Suinin, the 11th emperor (about 2,000 years ago); the place is now called Yamamiya Jinja and is a subsidiary shrine. The Yamanashi Prefectural Shrine Association's account of the history gives the same content.

The official site records that on the 9th day of the twelfth month of 865 (Jōgan 7), the year after the great eruption of Mt. Fuji, Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto was moved to the present site and enshrined. The Yamanashi Prefecture cultural property guide also says that, according to the shrine records, the shrine is said to have been moved from 神山 to the present site in 865 (Jōgan 7).

The Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku, Book 11, records in its entry for the ninth day of the twelfth month that by imperial order a shrine of Asama Myōjin was built in Yatsushiro District, Kai Province, placed among the official shrines (kansha), and that hafuri and negi were appointed to perform the rites. The date is the same as the date of the relocation given by this shrine's official site (the 9th day of the twelfth month), but it cannot be told from the text of that work whether this entry refers to this shrine.

The official site records that this shrine is the Ichinomiya of Kai Province, a Myōjin Taisha under the Engi system, and was ranked a Kokuhei Chūsha on the 14th day of the fifth month of 1871 (Meiji 4). The Yamanashi Prefectural Shrine Association also records it as the Ichinomiya of Kai Province, a Myōjin Taisha under the Engishiki system, and a Kokuhei Chūsha in 1871 (Meiji 4). The Yamanashi Prefecture cultural property guide, on the other hand, writes in the form of a tradition, as an old shrine said to be listed in the Engishiki.

In the Kai Province section of the Engishiki register of shrines (Book 9), "Asama Jinja" is listed under Yatsushiro District as a Myōjin Taisha. As to whether this shrine is that shikinaisha itself (one of the candidate shrines, ronsha), an encyclopedia notes that there is another theory, for example because this shrine stands in the former Yamanashi District, and, saying that other shrines also claim to be the Ichinomiya of Kai Province, records that there is a differing view on the title of Ichinomiya as well. This article decides neither way, and the identification has not been confirmed.

The Yamanashi Prefecture cultural property guide records that in the medieval period the shrine received the veneration of successive generations of the Takeda clan, and that the present main sanctuary of the subsidiary shrine Yamamiya Jinja was restored in 1558 (Eiroku 1) by Takeda Harunobu (Shingen), as known from the ridgepole tablet. The official treasures section also lists a tachi sword by Kunitsugu dedicated by Takeda Shingen (prefecturally designated) and a Heart Sutra in the hand of Emperor Go-Nara (Important Cultural Property), said to have been dedicated by Takeda Harunobu.
highlights: The official treasures page lists as Important Cultural Properties one scroll of the Heart Sutra in the hand of Emperor Go-Nara and the main sanctuary of the subsidiary shrine Yamamiya Jinja. The Yamanashi Prefecture cultural property guide records the main sanctuary of Asama Jinja's subsidiary shrine Yamamiya Jinja (with four ridgepole tablets attached; 1705 Ichinomiya, Ichinomiya-chō, Fuefuki City) as a nationally designated Important Cultural Property (building), designated 28 August 1907 (Meiji 40), and describes it as ikkensha sumigi-iri Kasuga-zukuri with a cypress-bark roof.

The official site records that there is a sacred tree called the Meoto-ume (married-couple plum) in the precinct, in which two flowers, yin and yang, come together and bear a single fruit, and in its treasures section it classes the tree as a prefecturally designated natural monument. It is handed down that a person without an heir who prays and receives this plum is blessed with a child, and the official site records that a ritual of offering a broken twig of the plum before the deity is held on the second Boar Day of the fourth month of the old calendar.

The official site calls the Ōmiyuki-sai on 15 April, nicknamed "Omiyuki-san", the greatest festival of Kai Province, and records that, according to the shrine records, since 825 (Tenchō 2) the deity has made a divine procession on the second Boar Day of the old fourth month to Ryūō Sansha Jinja in Kai City to hold the Kawayoke-sai (flood-prevention rite). After the Meiji period it was changed to 15 April; the route is about 24 km one way, and the official site records that the procession now goes only to Ryūō Sansha Jinja, where the Ninomiya and Sannomiya also make a divine procession.

The official site records the precinct as 3,395 tsubo (a little over 1 hectare), the main sanctuary as irimoya-zukuri with a kōhai porch and a copper-sheet roof, and the worship hall as irimoya-zukuri with a karahafu kōhai porch and a copper-sheet roof.
ichinomiyaasama.address: 1684 Ichinomiya, Ichinomiya-chō, Fuefuki, Yamanashi 405-0056 (as written on the official site). Tel. 0553-47-0900, fax 0553-47-3963 (official). The Yamanashi Prefectural Shrine Association guide also gives the location as 1684 Ichinomiya, Ichinomiya-chō, Fuefuki City. Checked on 16 Oct 2026.
