ichinomiyaasama.access: The official access guide says: by JR, about 10 minutes by taxi from Yamanashishi Station; by express bus, about 100 minutes on the Chūō Expressway bus from the west exit of Shinjuku Station, then a 10-minute walk from the Ichinomiya bus stop; by car, 5 minutes from Katsunuma Interchange (turn right at the "Ishi" traffic light; from the Kōfu direction, turn left at "Ichinomiya Asama Jinja Iriguchi"). Because the official access page was last updated on 30 November 2022, the bus service is to be confirmed.
ichinomiyaasama.hours: The official news page (dated 5 October 2025) gives the opening hours of the amulet office as 8:30 to 17:00 (within its notice about the distribution of special goshuin). The Shichi-Go-San prayers are held, according to the news page dated 15 September 2026, without reservation, between 9:00 (reception from 8:30) and 16:30 (reception closes), with an offering (hatsuho-ryō) from ¥5,000 per person. The reception hours and offerings for prayers throughout the year other than Shichi-Go-San, and the opening and closing times of the grounds, are not confirmed on the official site.
ichinomiyaasama.parking: The official "Parking Guide" page shows, in an image of a map of the surroundings, the precinct lot (26 standard cars), the East lot (52 standard cars; large buses allowed), the No. 1 lot (20 standard cars), the No. 2 lot (20 standard cars; usable only on Sundays and holidays) and the Ōtorii-mae lot (30 standard cars; large buses allowed). The map image was published in November 2022, and a written explanation and the fees are not confirmed on the official site.
ichinomiyaasama.goshuin: The official news page says that goshuin are given at the amulet office, and that the monthly-changing special goshuin has an offering of ¥500 and is given as paper goshuin only (dated 5 October 2025 and 9 May 2026). The opening hours of the amulet office are as in the hours entry above. The offering for the regular goshuin, separate from the monthly special goshuin, and whether they are pre-written sheets or written directly in the book, are not confirmed on the official site.

shitoriyurihama.name: Shitori Jinja
shitoriyurihama.summary: The official site introduces the shrine as the Ichinomiya of Hōki Province and gives its reading as "Shitori". The Tottori Prefectural Shrine Agency lists the enshrined deities as Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto and six others, and gives its former shrine rank as Kokuhei Shōsha (Beppyō shrine). The Hōki Ichinomiya Kyōzuka (sutra mound) in the grounds is a nationally designated Historic Site, and the objects excavated from it are National Treasures. The official site has information on prayers (such as for safe childbirth), the issuing of amulets and goshuin. A shrine of the same name also stands in Kurayoshi City, but it is a different shrine.
shitoriyurihama.deity_note: The official "About the Shrine" page names Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto as the main deity and lists seven deities in all, together with Shitateru-hime-no-Mikoto, Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto, Takeminakata-no-Mikoto, Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto, Ame-no-Wakahiko-no-Mikoto and Ajisukitakahikone-no-Mikoto. The official top page writes Shitateru-hime-no-Mikoto as the chief deity, so the notation differs even within the official site. The Tottori Prefectural Shrine Agency lists the same seven deities. An interlinear note in the main text of the Nihon Shoki, Book 2, Section 9, says that only the star deity Kagaseo would not obey, so the Shitori-no-Kami, Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto, was added to the mission and sent, and Kagaseo then obeyed (the names of the Shitori deity and Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto cannot be found in the Kojiki, Part 1). Shitateru-hime appears in the Kojiki as Shitateru-hime, daughter of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami and wife of Ame-no-Wakahiko, and in the Nihon Shoki as Shitateru-hime, daughter of Utsushikunitama and wife of Ame-no-Wakahiko. The shrine tradition that Shitateru-hime-no-Mikoto came here from Izumo cannot be found in the Kojiki, Part 1, or the Nihon Shoki, Book 2, as obtained.
history: The official site and the Tottori Prefectural Shrine Agency relate, as the shrine tradition, that Shitateru-hime-no-Mikoto, daughter of Ōkuninushi-no-Mikoto, came to this land by sea from Izumo and settled here, where she worked to guide safe childbirth, develop agriculture and spread medicine. The Shrine Agency gives the place where she landed as Kariyazaki, after the transfer of the land, and both the official site and the Shrine Agency record the date of founding as unknown.

The official site records that, because the main industry of this region at the time of founding was the weaving of shizuori cloth, Shitateru-hime-no-Mikoto, who has deep ties with this land, was added to Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto, ancestral deity of the Shitoribe, to make up the enshrined deities. The Shrine Agency writes that this is inferred from the shrine's oral traditions and the like, and says the other five deities are brothers of Shitateru-hime-no-Mikoto or deities closely connected with her.

The Engishiki register of shrines (927) lists a "Shitori Jinja" in Kawamura District, Hōki Province, and the Tottori Prefectural Shrine Agency identifies it as this shrine. The register also lists a shrine of the same name in Kume District of Hōki Province, which the Shrine Agency identifies with the present Shitori Jinja in Kurayoshi City (a former prefectural shrine).

The Shrine Agency cites records of divine rank: Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade, in the Montoku Jitsuroku for 856 (Saikō 3), and Senior Third Rank in the Nihon Kiryaku for 940 (Tengyō 3). In its entry on the Shitori Jinja in Kurayoshi City, however, it writes that, because there are two Shitori shrines in Hōki Province, it is in some respects unclear which shrine these records refer to. Reference works give the reading not only as "Shitori" but also as "Shidori" and "Shizuri", and say that shrines of the same name also exist in Kyoto, Hyōgo, Gunma, Yamanashi and Nara prefectures.

The inscription on the bronze sutra cylinder found in the sutra mound in the grounds records that in 1103 (Kōwa 5) the monk Kyōson buried the Lotus Sutra before Ichinomiya Daimyōjin, enshrined in Kawamura Higashigō, Hōki Province. Yurihama Town writes that this shows the shrine was already called "Ichinomiya" at that time, and the Shrine Agency says the title "Ichinomiya Daimyōjin" is its first appearance in the whole country.

The Shrine Agency says the present main hall (sangensha nagare-zukuri) was rebuilt in 1818 (Bunka 15), and writes that the shrine buildings were selected as one of the prefecture's Hundred Best Buildings in 1998 (Heisei 10). As for shrine rank, it was ranked as a prefectural shrine in 1872 (Meiji 5) and raised to Kokuhei Shōsha in 1939 (Shōwa 14).
highlights: The Hōki Ichinomiya Kyōzuka (sutra mound) in the grounds was designated a National Historic Site in 1935 (Shōwa 10). The bronze sutra cylinder, gilt-bronze standing statue of Kannon Bosatsu and other objects excavated from the mound in 1915 (Taishō 4) are National Treasures (designated in 1953, Shōwa 28), and the official site records that the originals are held at the Tokyo National Museum. Yurihama Town writes that they were designated National Treasures in 1920 (Taishō 9) and designated again in 1953 (Shōwa 28), after the war.

The official site records that this sutra mound has long been said to be the grave of the enshrined deity Shitateru-hime-no-Mikoto. The Tottori Prefecture cultural properties database, on the other hand, says from the inscription on the sutra cylinder that it is a sutra mound built by the monk Kyōson in 1103 (Kōwa 5).

Of the "Anzan Iwa" (Safe Childbirth Rock) beside the approach, the official site relates that a woman suffering from a difficult labour made a vow; on the day her vow was fulfilled Shitateru-hime-no-Mikoto appeared in her dream, and on her way home from visiting the shrine she gave birth safely beside this rock, which is how it got its name.

The annual festival is on 1 May, and the shrine is popularly called "Ichinomiya-san". The official site records that a Yudate Shinji ritual is held on the eve, 30 April, and that on the day local children dedicate the Urayasu no Mai dance and a procession of the portable shrine (mikoshi) and child attendants (chigo) takes place.
shitoriyurihama.address: 754 Ōaza Miyauchi, Yurihama, Tōhaku District, Tottori 689-0707 (official site). The Tottori Prefectural Shrine Agency also gives it as "754 Ōaza Miyauchi, Yurihama". Phone: shrine office 0858-32-1985; head priest's residence 0858-32-0248 (official; checked 16 Oct 2026).
shitoriyurihama.access: The official access guide says it is about 10 minutes by car from Matsuzaki Station on the JR San'in Main Line; by local bus, board at Matsuzaki Station and get off at the "Fujitsu-iriguchi" bus stop, then walk about 20 minutes (checked 16 Oct 2026). The official site does not give driving directions or the bus operator, frequency or times.
shitoriyurihama.hours: The official site gives 9:30–16:00 for accepting prayer requests and for issuing amulets, ofuda and goshuin, and says that visiting the grounds themselves is free at any time, including outside these hours. When the shrine office is unstaffed, contact the head priest's residence. The official top page lists 30 October, 24 November and 26 November in 2026 as days when no priest is present (as of 16 Oct 2026). The offering for a prayer ceremony starts from ¥5,000, and payment is cash only (no cashless payment).
shitoriyurihama.parking: The official site says there is a free parking lot (20 standard cars and 1 large bus) (checked 16 Oct 2026).
shitoriyurihama.goshuin: The official FAQ says goshuin are issued at the amulet office (reception 9:30–16:00). When no priest is present, a pre-written sheet may be given instead, and the site advises checking at the reception on the day for the types and availability of the original goshuin books. The fee and types of goshuin are not confirmed on the official site (the official top page says that information on goshuin and amulets is posted on Instagram, but Instagram is not confirmed).

sumiyoshishimonoseki.name: Sumiyoshi Jinja (Shimonoseki)
sumiyoshishimonoseki.summary: The Yamaguchi Prefectural Shrine Agency records that this shrine is a Myōjin Taisha listed in the Engishiki and later called itself the Ichinomiya of Nagato Province. The main deity is the aramitama of the Sumiyoshi-no-Ōkami (Uwatsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto, Nakatsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto and Sokotsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto), and Emperor Ōjin, Takeuchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto, Empress Jingū and Takeminakata-no-Mikoto are co-enshrined. The main hall is a National Treasure and the worship hall is an Important Cultural Property, both explained by the Agency for Cultural Affairs and Yamaguchi Prefecture. The Shrine Agency page says that prayer requests are accepted without reservation. No independent official site could be confirmed, and the only homepage the Shrine Agency page lists is a Facebook page. It is a different shrine from Sumiyoshi Taisha in Osaka and from Sumiyoshi Jinja in Hakata (Ichinomiya of Chikuzen Province).
sumiyoshishimonoseki.deity_note: The Yamaguchi Prefectural Shrine Agency records the main deity as the aramitama of the Sumiyoshi-no-Ōkami (Uwatsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto, Nakatsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto and Sokotsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto), with Emperor Ōjin, Takeuchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto, Empress Jingū and Takeminakata-no-Mikoto co-enshrined. The Shrine Agency explains the aramitama as an expression of divine power that accomplishes things actively and resolutely, and also writes that the divine virtue of guarding one's course in life is revered ("benefit" here means that people believe it to be so). The Kojiki, Part 1, records that when Izanagi-no-Ōkami performed purification (misogi), the three deities Sokotsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto, Nakatsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto and Uwatsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto came into being, and calls them the "Suminoe-no-Mimae-no-Ōkami". Part 2 records that Empress Jingū stood her staff at the gate of the lord of Silla and worshipped and pacified the aramitama of Suminoe-no-Ōkami as a deity protecting the country. The Nihon Shoki, Book 9, records that the three deities Uwatsutsu-no-O, Nakatsutsu-no-O and Sokotsutsu-no-O told the empress to enshrine the aramitama at Yamada village in Anato, and that a shrine was built at Yamada village with Homutachi, ancestor of the Anato no Atai, as the kannushi who would worship the aramitama. The third deity's name is written differently in the two books: 上筒 in the Kojiki and 表筒 in the Nihon Shoki (both read Uwatsutsu). This passage of the Nihon Shoki says only "Yamada village of Anato"; neither the place name Shimonoseki nor the name of this shrine appears, and it is the tradition of the Shrine Agency and others that links it to this shrine. The co-enshrined Emperor Ōjin, Empress Jingū and Takeuchi-no-Sukune appear in the Kojiki, Part 2, and Empress Jingū and Takeuchi-no-Sukune also appear in the Nihon Shoki, Book 9. Takeminakata-no-Kami appears in the Kojiki account of the transfer of the land. The assignment of deities to each of the five halls is not confirmed in the official materials consulted.
history: The Yamaguchi Prefectural Shrine Agency records the origin of the shrine as follows. Emperor Chūai died because he did not believe the teaching of the deity, and the empress's expedition to Korea was the result of following the deity's teaching. On her triumphant return the empress was taught again by the deity to enshrine the aramitama at Yamada village in Anato; in gratitude for the deity's grace she built a shrine in this place and enshrined the aramitama of the three deities. This is said to be the origin of the shrine. The Shrine Agency adds the year as "AD 200" and cites the Nihon Shoki as its source. The explanation of the Agency for Cultural Affairs also records that the shrine is said to have been founded by Empress Jingū.

The Nihon Shoki, Book 9, records that the three deities Uwatsutsu-no-O, Nakatsutsu-no-O and Sokotsutsu-no-O told the empress to enshrine the aramitama at Yamada village in Anato; that Homutachi, ancestor of the Anato no Atai, and Tamomi-no-Sukune, ancestor of the Tsumori no Muraji, advised that the place where the deity dwells be determined and the deity be worshipped there; and that a shrine was built at Yamada village with Homutachi as the kannushi who would worship the aramitama. The Nihon Shoki writes only "Yamada village" and does not give the name of this shrine. It is the tradition of the Shrine Agency that takes that shrine as the origin of this one.

The Kojiki, Part 1, calls Sokotsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto, Nakatsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto and Uwatsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto, who came into being at the purification, the "Suminoe-no-Mimae-no-Ōkami". Part 2 records that Empress Jingū stood her staff at the gate of the lord of Silla and worshipped and pacified the aramitama of Suminoe-no-Ōkami as a deity protecting the country. The Kojiki does not write this worship as that of a shrine in Anato (Nagato), so a link with this shrine is not stated.

The Engishiki register of shrines lists "Sumiyoshi-ni-masu Aramitama Jinja, three deities" in Toyora District, Nagato Province. The Shrine Agency writes that this shrine is a Myōjin Taisha listed in the Engishiki, and the explanation of Yamaguchi Prefecture's cultural properties also writes that it is an old shrine whose name appears in the Engishiki register. The identification of the register's entry with the present shrine rests on the explanations of the Shrine Agency and Yamaguchi Prefecture.

The Agency for Cultural Affairs' database of nationally designated cultural properties says the present main hall was built by Ōuchi Hiroyo in 1370 (Ōan 3) and was designated a National Treasure on 14 November 1953 (Shōwa 28). The Shrine Agency describes the same main hall as a donation by Ōuchi Hiroyo (the wording differs: construction versus donation).

The tourism portal site "Amahashi" writes that shrine ranks were established in 1871 (Meiji 4) and that this shrine was ranked as a Kanpei Chūsha. This is not confirmed in the official materials of the Shrine Agency or local governments.
highlights: The main hall, a National Treasure, is a long building with a cypress-bark roof in the nine-bay nagare-zukuri style: five single-bay sanctuaries are lined up side by side and connected by linking rooms (ai-no-ma), and the roofs of the sanctuaries carry five chidori-hafu gables. Yamaguchi Prefecture explains it as a rare form with no other example among nagare-zukuri buildings, and the Agency for Cultural Affairs explains that as a whole it forms a distinctive nagare-zukuri.

The worship hall, an Important Cultural Property, is a gabled, cypress-bark-roofed building three bays in length and one bay in depth, with the gable end as its front. Yamaguchi Prefecture explains that old documents record it as built by Mōri Motonari in 1539 (Tenbun 8), and that its details show features of the late Muromachi period. It was designated an Important Cultural Property on 17 September 1954 (Shōwa 29) (Cultural Heritage Online).

The Shrine Agency writes that the woodland covering the grounds was designated a Yamaguchi Prefectural Natural Monument in 1953 (Shōwa 28) as the Sumiyoshi Jinja shrine forest. It also writes that 40 items, including a bronze bell, the Sumiyoshi Jinja Hōraku Hyakushu Waka (a hundred-poem waka sequence) and a gilt-bronze openwork Chinese-style saddle (karagura) with a peony and arabesque pattern (Important Cultural Property), are kept in the treasure hall.

In the Shrine Agency's festival guide, at the 河渡祭 (reading unconfirmed) on 1 December, rice-cake porridge and tazukuri are offered, and a good-luck lottery is held all day. At the Busha-sai on 16 January, the chief priest shoots a sacred arrow. The 御斎祭 (reading unconfirmed), from the afternoon of 8 December to 15 December, is a secret ritual in which the sacred gate is closed and all the priests go into seclusion, so visitors cannot enter the grounds.
sumiyoshishimonoseki.address: 1-11-1 Ichinomiya Sumiyoshi, Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi 751-0805 (as listed by the Yamaguchi Prefectural Shrine Agency). Phone: 083-256-2656 (Shrine Agency). The Yamaguchi Prefecture Tourism Federation gives the same street number. The Agency for Cultural Affairs database gives the location in a different form, "Kusuno, Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi", which refers to the location of the same shrine.
sumiyoshishimonoseki.access: The Yamaguchi Prefecture Tourism Federation's guide says it is about 5 minutes by bus from Shin-Shimonoseki Station (JR), getting off at "Ichinomiya" and walking 5 minutes; by car, about 10 minutes from Shimonoseki IC on the Chūgoku Expressway. Another page of the same federation says 3 minutes by bus, and a wheelchair-travel introduction site says about a 10-minute walk, so the times differ between sources. The Shrine Agency page has no written transport guidance (as of the time of checking).
sumiyoshishimonoseki.hours: The Shrine Agency says prayer requests are accepted from 8:30 to 16:00 without reservation, and writes that on weekdays the gate opens at 6:00 and closes at 18:00 (closing at 17:30 from October to March). Amahashi, on the other hand, gives reception from 8:00 until closing (reservations not accepted), and gives opening and closing times of 6:00–18:00 from April to October and 6:00–17:30 from November to March, so its reception start time differs from the Shrine Agency's. From the afternoon of 8 December to 15 December the grounds cannot be entered because of the 御斎祭 (Shrine Agency).
sumiyoshishimonoseki.parking: Amahashi and the wheelchair-travel introduction site say there is a free parking lot around the grounds. The Yamaguchi Prefecture Tourism Federation's special viewing guide says a large-bus parking lot is available. The number of spaces, fees and hours of use are not confirmed in an official source.
sumiyoshishimonoseki.goshuin: A visit report on Sennen-chō says goshuin can be received at the amulet office to the left of the worship hall. Amahashi lists seasonal limited-edition goshuin (Haru no Zu, Natsu no Zu, Aki no Zu and Fuyu no Zu, the spring, summer, autumn and winter designs) with an offering of ¥1,000 each. The Shrine Agency page has no mention of goshuin, and the fee and reception hours for the regular goshuin are not confirmed in an official source.

yusuhara.name: Yusuhara Hachimangū
yusuhara.summary: The official site calls itself "Ichinomiya of Bungo (former Kokuhei Shōsha)" and records that it enshrines three deities: Emperor Ōjin, Emperor Chūai and Empress Jingū. Ōita City introduces it as having been made the Ichinomiya of Bungo in the early Heian period, as a place where the divided spirit of Usa Hachimangū was enshrined. Ten buildings, including the main sanctuary, are Important Cultural Properties of Japan. Sasamuta Jinja, also in Ōita City, likewise calls itself "Ichinomiya of Bungo" on its official site.
yusuhara.deity_note: The official history page lists three enshrined deities: Emperor Ōjin (Hondawake-no-Mikoto), Emperor Chūai (Tarashinakatsuhiko-no-Mikoto) and Empress Jingū (Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto). In the Kojiki, Part 2, Emperor Tarashinakatsuhiko (Chūai), Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto, the principal empress of Chūai (a name the official site takes to be Empress Jingū), and Homudawake-no-Mikoto (Ōjin; also called Ōtomowake-no-Mikoto) appear. In the Nihon Shoki, Book 8 has Emperor Tarashinakatsuhiko (Chūai), Book 9 has Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto (Empress Jingū), and Book 10 has Emperor Homuda (Ōjin). The prospectus of the official repair support association writes "the enshrined deity Hachiman Ōkami", and the page on prayer rites also writes of the virtues of Hachiman Ōkami, but the official pages we read do not explain which of the three deities above Hachiman Ōkami corresponds to. The divine title "Hachiman" does not appear in the text of the Kojiki, Part 2, and the Nihon Shoki, Books 8 to 10, that we checked. The official annual events page records that "Takeuchi Ōkami" is also enshrined inside the 申殿 (reading unconfirmed), but the same page does not say which deity this is.
history: The official history page records that in 827 (Tenchō 4) Kinki Oshō, an eminent monk of Enryaku-ji, stayed in prayer at Usa Jingū, received a message from the deity, and invited the deity to Mt. Yusuhara; the shrine takes this as the origin of its founding.

The official site records that in 836 (Jōwa 3) Kiyohara no Natsuno, Minister of the Right, received an imperial order and had the provincial governor Ōe no Uku build the shrine buildings. The Ōita City cultural properties page also records that the shrine buildings are said to have been founded in 836 (Jōwa 3). This differs in year from 827 (Tenchō 4), which the official site gives as the origin of the founding.

The official site records that in 1108 (Kashō 3) an imperial envoy came, the four boundaries of the precinct were fixed and taxes were waived; that in 1153 (Ninpei 3) Retired Emperor Toba prayed here and fixed the shrine lands; and that in 1184 (Genryaku 1) Minamoto no Noriyori prayed for the defeat of the Taira clan. It is said that warrior houses such as Minamoto no Yoritomo and the local lords (the Ōtomo, Takenaka and Hineno) continued to revere the shrine deeply.
The Ōita City cultural properties page records that it is said that from 998 (Chōtoku 4) the shrine buildings came to be rebuilt every 33 years, as at Usa Jingū.

The Agency for Cultural Affairs' database of nationally designated cultural properties explains that after a fire in 1749 (Kan'en 2) the shrine buildings were rebuilt one after another, and that the ridgepole of the present main sanctuary was raised in 1850 (Kaei 3).

The official site records that the shrine was raised to Kokuhei Shōsha in 1916 (Taishō 5). The ten buildings — the main sanctuary, East Hōden, West Hōden, 申殿, haiden, rōmon gate, West Gate, Nandaimon, East Corridor and West Corridor (with the treasure storehouse and the Hachiōji shrine attached) — were designated Important Cultural Properties of Japan on 20 June 2011 (Heisei 23) (Agency for Cultural Affairs database; Ōita City).
highlights: The Agency for Cultural Affairs database explains that the main sanctuary is in the Hachiman-zukuri style, joining a rear hall and a front hall, and that the layout of the buildings, with the rōmon gate and the 申殿 set along one axis, is distinctive and modelled on Usa Jingū. The official site instructs visitors to worship by taking off their footwear and stepping up from the corridor of the rōmon gate, and sitting formally in front of the haiden.

Beside the Nandaimon (Higurashi-mon) gate on the approach stands a great camphor tree, a Natural Monument designated by the state. The official site records it as more than 3,000 years old, 30 m tall and 34 m around the roots, and says it was designated by the state in March of Taishō 11.

The official annual events page lists, among others, the annual grand festival on 15 March (formerly called the "Hatsuu-sai"; the page records it as the most important ritual of the shrine), the mid-autumn festival "Hama no Ichi" in mid-September (its origin is the Hōjōe ritual), and the Takeuchi Ōkami Togyo-sai on 1–7 September (Takeuchi Ōkami of the 申殿 is taken in procession to Kaku Jinja).

The official site says the shrine will reach the 1,200th anniversary of its enshrinement in 2036 (Reiwa 18), and announces that a "New Year Special Viewing" will be held every year from Reiwa 8 to Reiwa 18 as a commemorative project. For Reiwa 8, the official site announced that it would be held on 1–3 January, 9:00–16:00. The official repair project page also lists a second-phase project (the 申殿, haiden, rōmon gate and others) following the first phase (the main sanctuary and others).
yusuhara.address: 987 Ōaza Hachiman, Ōita City, Ōita 870-0808 (the official access page writes it as "987 Ōaza Hachiman, Ōita City"). Tel. 097-534-0065, fax 097-536-2475 (official). The foot of other pages on the official site also gives "Kami-Hachiman Sankumi, Ōita City", so the address is written in two ways.
yusuhara.access: The Ōita City cultural properties page gives the following: by bus, take the Ōita Kōtsū bus bound for "Yusuhara" from stop 7 in front of JR Ōita Station, about 35 minutes' ride, get off at the terminus and walk 5 minutes (about 180 steps); by car, about 10 minutes from JR Nishi-Ōita Station. The access page of the official site has only the address, telephone number and map, with no bus or car directions.
yusuhara.hours: The official site records that reception for prayer rites is 8:30–16:00 (no advance booking is possible; go directly to the amulet office), and reception for amulets and goshuin is 8:30–16:30. The hours when visitors may enter the grounds are not given on the official pages.
yusuhara.parking: The Ōita City cultural properties page says "Parking: available, free". The number of spaces and the location are not confirmed on the official site.
yusuhara.goshuin: The official page on amulets and goshuin says "A goshuin is a proof of worship" and records that the offering is ¥500 to ¥1,500 and that reception is 8:30–16:30. For the New Year of Reiwa 8, the official site announced that a commemorative goshuin for the 1,200th anniversary of the enshrinement would also be prepared. The place of reception is not given on the same page.

ohirumemuchi.name: Ōhirumemuchi Jinja
ohirumemuchi.summary: A shrine in Hachimantai, Kazuno City, Akita, commonly called Dainichidō. The official site gives Amaterasu-Ōmikami as the chief deity and records that twelve other deities are also enshrined (the Akita Prefecture Shrine Agency lists 13 deities and writes the name as Amaterasu-Sumeōmikami). The official site gives the founding as the 17th year of Emperor Keitai (523). The Dainichidō Bugaku, offered at the Yōrō Reisai on 2 January every year, is a nationally designated Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property and is also inscribed on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list. The official site has information on prayer by appointment and on pre-made goshuin.
ohirumemuchi.deity_note: The official site gives the enshrined deities as Amaterasu-Ōmikami and twelve others, explaining that this is because the deities of neighbouring shrines were enshrined together after shrine mergers from the Meiji era onward. The official site calls the chief deity, Amaterasu-Ōmikami, "the great deity of the sun". The shrine search of the Akita Prefecture Shrine Agency writes the same deity as "Amaterasu-Sumeōmikami", and also lists Usagi-no-Miko-no-Mikoto, Kichijō-hime-no-Mikoto, Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto, Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto, Toyouke-bime-no-Mikoto, Sarutahiko-no-Mikoto, Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto, Ōtomowake-no-Mikoto, Susanoo-no-Mikoto, Emperor Sutoku, Izanami-no-Mikoto and Ukemochi-no-Kami. The official site records that Kichijō-hime-no-Mikoto has been worshipped as a deity of matchmaking, children, safe childbirth and protection of women; Sarutahiko-no-Mikoto as a deity of traffic safety; and Ōnamuchi-no-Kami and Sukunahikona-no-Kami as deities of recovery from illness. The shrine name "Ōhirumemuchi" is close in reading to "Ōhirumenomuchi", which the Nihon Shoki, Book 1, gives as the name of the sun deity (the reading in its note is "Oho-hirume-no-muchi"); the same note also gives "Amaterasu-Ōmikami" as another name. The Kojiki writes the same deity as Amaterasu-Ōmikami. However, the official site only says that the name was given at the Meiji-era renaming "based on ancient tradition", and does not explain any correspondence with the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (this correspondence comes from checking against the texts of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki). The deity_ids include, besides the existing deities whose names appear in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, the newly added Ukemochi-no-Kami (who appears in the Nihon Shoki) and Kichijō-hime-no-Mikoto (a figure in the shrine's legend). That Ōtomowake-no-Mikoto is written the same as the alternative name of Emperor Ōjin (Homudawake-no-Mikoto) in the Kojiki is an inference from comparison; neither the official site nor the Shrine Agency explains it. Usagi-no-Miko-no-Mikoto and Emperor Sutoku are not included because they cannot be confirmed as deities of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.
history: The official site gives the founding as the 17th year of Emperor Keitai (523) and records that it derives from the legend of the Danburi Chōja (the "Danburi" wealthy man). The daughter of the Chōja became a consort of Emperor Keitai (Kichijō-hime), and the shrine built by imperial order at her wish is taken as the founding. The Akita Prefecture Shrine Agency also records, as the shrine's tradition, a founding in the reign of Emperor Keitai, but gives the year of the imperial order as "Zenki 2" and the original shrine name as "Dainichi-jigen-sha". The correspondence between "Zenki 2" and the official site's 17th year of Keitai (523) is not confirmed.

The official site records that in 718 (Yōrō 2), in the reign of Emperor Genshō, craftsmen who came down by imperial order, accompanied by the eminent monk Gyōki, built halls like the present ones, and that bugaku was performed at the ceremony celebrating this. This is said to be the beginning of the Dainichidō Bugaku. Kazuno City records that it is said to have been passed on to the villagers by court musicians who came down from the capital when the Dainichidō (Ōhirumemuchi Jinja) was rebuilt, and the Agency for Cultural Affairs database also gives the origin "according to tradition" as the Yōrō era (717–24).

The official site records that it is said that a major renovation of the shrine buildings was carried out at the end of the Heian period on the orders of Fujiwara no Hidehira of Hiraizumi, and also records that the course of events is unclear because the shrine suffered disasters many times. The Akita Prefecture Shrine Agency gives this as a major repair of the halls and shrines in 1183 (Juei 2) on the orders of Fujiwara no Hidehira, the Chinjufu-shōgun.

The official site records that at the end of the Muromachi period the shrine came under the protection of the Nanbu clan, which also confirmed its shrine lands, the ritual fields for passing down the bugaku, and its wide mountain forests. The Akita Prefecture Shrine Agency records that the oldest ridgepole tablet on record is one for the repair of the Dainichidō in 1486 (Bunmei 18) on the order of Nanbu Masamori, 15th head of the Nanbu family, and that in 1616 (Genna 2) the shrine was donated more than 80 koku of shrine land by Nanbu Toshinao, the 27th domain lord.

The official site records that at the Meiji Restoration the shrine lost its economic base, such as the shrine lands, returned to being a shrine following the order separating Shinto and Buddhism, and was renamed Ōhirumemuchi Jinja based on ancient tradition, and has continued to the present.

The Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei (Heibonsha; carried on Kotobank) says that it is now called Ōhirumemuchi Jinja and records it as a former Gōsha. Because the Akita Prefecture Shrine Agency and the official site do not record a shrine rank, the dictionary is the only basis, so this is to be confirmed. The same dictionary records that there is also a Dainichidō at Dokko in Hinai Town, which has a deep relationship with the Dainichidō of Azukizawa and Jūnisho-bessho in Kazuno (a separate entry, not researched this time).
highlights: According to the official site, the shrine buildings consist of the haiden, heiden and honden. The present haiden was rebuilt in Shōwa 27 at its original size; it is a hōgyō-zukuri (pyramidal roof) building of nine bays with aisles on four sides (kyūken shimen), and a stage for performing bugaku is set at its centre. The heiden and honden were added in Shōwa 30. The Akita Prefecture Shrine Agency records that the shrine buildings burned down completely in Shōwa 24, that the haiden was built on the original nine-bay, four-sided foundation in Shōwa 26, and that the heiden and honden were added and completed in Shōwa 31, so its years differ from the official site.

The official precinct guide lists the sacred tree Oba-sugi, said to be about 1,500 years old; the Sanzon-seki (Triad stone), which bears the seed syllables of the Amida Triad and appears to have been erected in 1300 (Shōan 2) in the Kamakura period; the sacred horse stable; and the auxiliary shrines Ōnamuchi Jinja, Kumano Jinja and Yakushi Jinja, among others. The list of Kazuno City designated cultural properties includes one itabi (stone slab memorial) of Ōhirumemuchi Jinja at the same address (Hachimantai, Aza Dō-no-Ue 16), designated by the city as an archaeological material on 21 February, Shōwa 54 (whether it is the same as the itabi in the official site is not confirmed).

The Dainichidō Bugaku, offered at the Yōrō Reisai on 2 January every year, is passed down by the performers (nōshū) of four hamlets: Ōsato, Azukizawa, Taninai and Nagamine. The Agency for Cultural Affairs' Cultural Heritage Online records that it was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property on 4 May 1976 (Shōwa 51) and inscribed on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2009. The Kazuno City overview page lists the next performance as 2 January 2027 (Reiwa 9), 8:00–12:00.

In the Danburi Chōja legend recorded by the official site, an honest couple living in Azukizawa received a message from a deity in a dream on New Year's Day and moved upstream. Following a dragonfly (called "danburi" in the dialect of this region), they found a spring among the rocks, and people who wanted its water gathered, and the couple gained wealth. It is said that the daughter they were given served at court, became a consort of Emperor Keitai, and took the new name Kichijō-hime, and that at her wish a shrine enshrining the Dainichi deity was built at Azukizawa in the 17th year of Emperor Keitai.
ohirumemuchi.address: 16 Dō no Ue, Hachimantai, Kazuno City, Akita 018-5141 (the official site writes the number 16 in full-width characters). The Akita Prefecture Shrine Agency writes "Hachimantai Aza Dō-no-Ue 16, Kazuno City" and Kazuno City writes "Hachimantai Aza Dō no Ue 16", so the sources differ in whether "Aza" is included and in whether "no" is written in hiragana (の) or katakana (ノ). For the telephone number, the official site gives 0186-32-2706 (fax 0186-32-2743), the Shrine Agency gives 0186-32-2742, and Kazuno City gives 0186-32-2706 or 0186-32-2742.
ohirumemuchi.access: The Kazuno City tourist guide gives about a 1-minute walk from JR Hachimantai Station and about 5 minutes by car from Kazuno-Hachimantai IC on the Tōhoku Expressway. The official site of the Dainichidō Bugaku Preservation Society also says a 1-minute walk from Hachimantai Station on the JR Hanawa Line and about 5 minutes by car from Kazuno-Hachimantai IC. The shrine's own official site has no transport page that we could find. Train frequency and similar details have not been checked (checked 16 Oct 2026).
ohirumemuchi.hours: [Items confirmed on the official site] Prayer rites are by appointment. Appointments are taken by telephone from 9:30 to 19:00, and an answering machine may pick up. Because the chief priest and the deputy priest conduct them, there are days on which prayer cannot be received because of festivals, events, official duties and so on. The hours for prayer vary somewhat by season; it is normally from 9:30 to 16:00, and other times can be arranged by consultation. The prayer offering is ¥5,000 or more for an individual (¥7,000 or more if there are two or more wishes), and the official site says it is generally ¥5,000 to ¥20,000. [Items not confirmed on the official site] The opening and closing times of the grounds, the hours when visitors may worship, the reception hours of the amulet office and shrine office, and the list of amulets, talismans and similar items (the only mention of amulets is in the goshuin section, which says they are "attached").
ohirumemuchi.parking: No parking information was found on the shrine's own official site. For the bugaku offering on 2 January, the site of the Dainichidō Bugaku Preservation Society says that parking is prepared in front of Hachimantai Station (a 1-minute walk) but that it is very crowded on the day. The location, number of spaces and fees of parking for ordinary visits are not confirmed on the official site.
ohirumemuchi.goshuin: The official site has a section titled "About goshuin", which says that, for reasons on the shrine's side, only pre-made goshuin are available, that the red ink used is ancient vermilion (made by a specialist shop in Nara City), and that, from a religious viewpoint, an amulet is attached. The place, hours and offering for receiving it are not confirmed on the official site (inquiries: the telephone number given on the official site, 0186-32-2706).

chiriku.name: Chiriku Hachimangū
chiriku.summary: The official site calls the shrine "Ichinomiya of Hizen, former Kokuhei Shōsha" and records a tradition that it was founded in 724 (Jinki 1), in the reign of Emperor Shōmu, by Mibu no Harunari, district governor of Yabu District in Hizen Province, who had received an oracle. The enshrined deities are mainly the three: Emperor Ōjin, Emperor Chūai and Empress Jingū, and the Saga Prefecture Jinjachō lists it as a Beppyō shrine of Jinja Honchō. In 2024 (Reiwa 6) it reached the 1,300th anniversary of its founding.
chiriku.deity_note: The official deities page names the main deities as Emperor Ōjin, Emperor Chūai and Empress Jingū, and explains Emperor Ōjin as the deity Hachiman. It also enshrines four deities as subsidiary deities: Naniwa-no-Miko, Uji-no-Miko, Sumiyoshi Myōjin and Takeuchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto. The Saga Prefecture Jinjachō introduction lists only the three main deities, and the Miyaki town tourism page says that deities other than Emperor Ōjin are enshrined together with him. The official site does not explain which deities Naniwa-no-Miko, Uji-no-Miko and Sumiyoshi Myōjin correspond to, and this is not confirmed, so we give them no deity entry here. The Kojiki records that Emperor Chūai (Emperor Tarashinakatsuhiko) took Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto (Empress Jingū) as his empress and that Homudawake-no-Mikoto (Emperor Ōjin) and others were born. The Nihon Shoki, Book 10, likewise records Emperor Homuda (Emperor Ōjin) as the fourth child of Emperor Tarashinakatsuhiko (Emperor Chūai), with his mother being Okinagatarashi-hime-no-Mikoto (Empress Jingū). Takeuchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto appears in the genealogies of the Kojiki under the name 建内宿禰, and in the Nihon Shoki he appears as a serving minister in the Empress Jingū and Emperor Ōjin annals. The texts of the Kojiki, Part 2, and the Nihon Shoki, Books 9 and 10, that we obtained do not contain the word "Hachiman"; that Emperor Ōjin is the deity Hachiman is the shrine's explanation, not a story written in the Kojiki or Nihon Shoki.
history: The official site, Miyaki town and Saga Prefecture record a tradition that in 724 (Jinki 1) Mibu no Harunari, district governor of Yabu District in Hizen Province, received an oracle from Hachiman Ōkami and founded the shrine. The Saga Prefecture Jinjachō introduction gives the founding as the "Jinki era" and writes the governor's name as "壬生春茂". The year of founding and the way the governor's name is written differ by source.

In the local legend introduced by Miyaki town, Mibu no Harunari was out hunting when a white dove perched on the tip of his bow. That night a white-haired old man appeared in his dream and gave him a thousand chestnuts. The next day he went to that place, and a thousand chestnut trees had grown thick in a single night. When he reported this to Emperor Shōmu, the emperor is said to have been pleased and to have built a shrine with his second prince as chief celebrant. The town explains that the place name "Chiriku" also derives from this chestnut legend. The official site's introduction of the subsidiary shrines in the precincts also touches on the old story of the dove perching on the bow.

The official site says the shrine has long been known as a betsugū (separate shrine) of Usa Jingū and that in the Heian period it received the court's reverence as one of the five Hachiman betsugū not listed in the Engishiki (Ōita-gū, Chiriku Hachimangū, Fujisaki Hachimangū, Nitta Jinja and Kagoshima Jingū); as the ichinomiya system took shape in the various regions, it came to be called Ichinomiya of Hizen. The Saga Prefecture Jinjachō also writes "one of the five Hachiman betsugū not listed in the Engishiki".

The official site records that although the shrine buildings burned down several times in the wars of the Sengoku period, Ryūzōji Masaie rebuilt the shrine in 1583 (Tenshō 11), Nabeshima Naoshige donated shrine land of 200 koku in 1598 (Keichō 3), and a stone Hizen torii was dedicated in 1609 (Keichō 14); after that, the Nabeshima family revered the shrine through the generations until the Meiji Restoration. The Saga Prefecture Jinjachō also records Ryūzōji Masaie's rebuilding and Nabeshima Naoshige's donation of shrine land.

The Saga Prefecture Jinjachō records that the shrine was ranked as a Kensha (prefectural shrine) in 1903 (Meiji 36) and as a Kokuhei Shōsha in 1940 (Shōwa 15), and also records that it is a Beppyō shrine of Jinja Honchō. The official site likewise records its promotion to Kensha and Kokuhei Shōsha in the same years.

The encyclopedia (Wikipedia) records that Chiriku Hachimangū has called itself Ichinomiya of Hizen Province since the late Heian period, but that in the early modern period there was a dispute over the title of Ichinomiya with Kawakami Jinja (now Yodohime Jinja), a shrine listed in the Engishiki (shikinaisha). The official site and the Saga Prefecture Jinjachō page do not mention this dispute (within the range obtained). Readers need to know that there are other shrines that also call themselves Ichinomiya of Hizen Province.
highlights: Saga Prefecture announces that it designated the "Chiriku Hachimangū Engi-e" as a Prefectural Important Cultural Property (painting) on 31 March 1993 (Heisei 5). The work consists of two hanging scrolls: one is a Hachiman engi (origin tale) depicting events from Empress Jingū's expedition to the Three Korean Kingdoms (Sankan) to the birth of Emperor Ōjin, and the other depicts a map of the precincts and the founding origin tale of Mibu no Harunari. From the appearance of the buildings in the precinct map, the prefecture estimates that it was made between 1589 and 1595.

The official site records that the stone first torii (Hizen torii) that remains at the foot of the approach slope is a town Important Cultural Property and was dedicated in 1609 (Keichō 14). It is said that this torii was repaired in the project commemorating the 1,300th anniversary of the founding.

The official list of festivals includes the "Okayu-dameshi" (お粥試) on 15 March. The porridge cooked on 26 February and placed in the sanctuary is taken out, and the mold and cracks on its surface are used to divine the weather and harvest of that year in the four provinces of Hizen, Higo, Chikuzen and Chikugo (Miyaki town writes it "お粥だめし"). The regular festival on 15 September is also called the "Hōjōe", and on the Sunday nearest the regular festival, each parishioner district dedicates a gyōretsu furyū (procession furyū) in step with the procession of the portable shrine (mikoshi).

The official site introduces the stone steps of the front approach as the place where Koga Toshihiko, who won a gold medal in judo at the Barcelona Olympics, ran up every day as a child to train his body, and calls them the "Stone Steps to Glory" (the access page writes "Stone Steps of Glory", so the notation varies). It is said that children from local sports clubs can still be seen running up them today.
chiriku.address: 2415 Shirakabe, Miyaki, Miyaki District, Saga 849-0111 (as written at the bottom of the official site pages; the Saga Prefecture Jinjachō also gives the location as Ōaza Shirakabe 2415). Tel. 0942-89-5566. On the other hand, the official site's guide to shipping amulets also gives "Ōaza Shirakabe 2403" as the address of the shrine office. The official site does not explain why the lot numbers are written differently.
chiriku.access: According to the official access guide (the page shows an update date of 10 Sep 2025), take a Nishitetsu bus bound for Saga Bus Center (route 40) from Kurume Station (Kyushu Shinkansen and JR Kagoshima Main Line) or Nishitetsu Kurume Station (Nishitetsu Tenjin Ōmuta Line) and get off at "Chiriku Hachimangū-mae"; the guide says the shrine is right in front. By taxi, it is about 25 minutes from Nishitetsu Kurume Station and about 10 minutes from JR Kurume Station. By car, from Tosu IC on the Nagasaki Expressway, take National Route 34 toward Saga City, turn left at the "Murata-machi" intersection and go straight. The number of buses and their times are not given on the official page and must be checked before boarding (checked 16 Oct 2026).
chiriku.hours: The reception hours of the amulet office and the shrine office, and the hours when visitors may enter the grounds, are not confirmed on the official site. Festival times are given in the official list (for example, the monthly festival is at 10:00 on the 1st and 15th of each month, and the regular festival is at 11:00 on 15 September; the site says the times may change). For prayers in the shrine building, the site says reservations of date and time are accepted in advance (by visiting the shrine office, or by phone at 0942-89-5566).
chiriku.parking: The official access guide says there is a parking lot on the right just past the "Chiriku Hachimangū-mae" intersection. Besides the lot at the foot of the front stone steps, there is also a lot at the back for people who find it hard to climb the steps. The number of spaces and the fees are not given on the official site. From the end of the year to mid-January and around festival days, the roads are narrow and crowded and few cars can park, so the official site urges visitors to use public transport.
chiriku.goshuin: The official site announces several limited-edition goshuin for 2026: special goshuin of "Okame-chan" and "Goshinkō Gyōretsu Furyū" (announced 18 Sep 2026; hatsuho offering ¥800; the date is added to the pre-written sheet), and a limited goshuin for the Tanabata Festival (distribution continues during August; a donation of ¥800 or more; ask at the shrine office or the amulet office). It records that the blue goshuin book is normally distributed at ¥2,500, while the white one commemorating the 1,300th anniversary of the founding (¥3,000) is out of stock. The regular goshuin that can always be received, its reception hours, and whether the limited goshuin are still being distributed are not confirmed on the official pages.
